summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of Lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found that the sample contained nine living worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirchi was adulterated. The Food Inspector took a samples of Lal goveta mirchi, powder from his grocery shops and the sample there was at best worm infested. The Public Analyst found that it was adulterated due to insect pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and 1.5% respectively. On further analysis by P. W. 4, the Public analyst found that there was no evidence in respect of the food article for which no minimum standard or purity had been prescribed or no limits have been prescribed for the validity or its constituents, then sub clause (1) of section 2 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1955, was not attracted and that the Public Food Analyst did not satisfy the requirement of the definition of 'adulterated article ' contained in section 2(1)(f). The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that (i) the evidence by way of the Public Enquiry 's report does not satisfy tho requirements of the 'ad adulterated article of food contained in Section 2(I)(f); and (ii) the prosecution has failed to prove that the Lal mirta powder was adulterated, and therefore he acquitted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was clearly wrong in its pretation of section 3(1) (f). [470C] 2. The words 'or otherwise unfit for human consumption" should be read conjunctively and not disjunctively. If it is read disjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it, sub clause is presumptive and not an absolute test of the quality of the article being unfit for consumption. But the presumption may not be conclusive in all cases irrespective of the character of the Article, and the nature and extent of the vice afflicting it. [470D] 3. The adjectives "filthy" "decomposed", "decemposed" " Decomposed" or "declared" refer to the quality and quantity of article being fit for human use because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or insect infested or is otherwise unfit. [471E F] 4. The expression 'or other unfit for ' consumption ' in sub clause(f) of Section 2 of Prevention of food Adulteration Act means "to overrun or spread in large numbers so as to be unpleasant or unsafe". The phrase "or is otherwise fit for" conjunctively, has been brought out in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal [1980] 1 SCR 472.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order of the Magistrate. He was convicted by the Munsif and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The appellant had successfully proved that he was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law because the presumption in his case could not be drawn against him. [901 B] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , relied on. (2) In the instant case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he also produced receipt of payment for payment of rent. If any money had been recovered by sale of foodgrains, it shall be handed over to the appellant. [ 901 C] Manipur Government vs Mila Chandra, ; , followed. (3) The presumption under para 3(2) could not, therefore, be drawn. If that presumption was not drawn, then the case against him stands unproved because of the exemption which agriculturists enjoy. On the whole, it is clear that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution. [980 E F] Manipur Adminis tration vs Mita Chandra Singh, ; relied on, (4) The conviction was properly reached and the presumption under section 3(1) could be drawn only against the appellant because the prosecution had successfully established that he is an agriculturist. In his case, therefore the presumption was rightly reached. [981 E F]. Manipur Administration V. Mila Chand Singh, , relied upon.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the same land. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit served upon him. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the decision was affirmed, on appeal, by the District Judge. Purporting to this Court under article 139 of the Constitution the plaintiff contended that the defendant was not in fact a monthly tenancy tenant under the plaintiff at the date when the notice to qui vided his tenancy for more than 12 years, but on the expiry of the second yearly lease which happened on 7th December 1926, the defendant ceased to be a tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by holding over as is contemplated by section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. Held, that the suit was not barred by limitation under article139 of the Indian Limitation Act. The Kabuliyat executed by the defendant on 24th December 1924, and the lease deed for 99 years were valid and the plaintiff was entitled to a decree in his favour. The period of tenancy was not based on the terms of the Kabuliant of 1924 but on a monthly rent which was paid by the Receiver or to the proprietor since then. The relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties came to an end on the expiration of the first annual lease, and consequently a tenancy from month to month came into existence in accordance with section 116 Transfer of property Act. Matilal vs Darjeeling Municipality, , distinguished. Held further, that there was no valid agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant for renewal of the period provided for in the Kabulyat. The agreement between them was not an operative document at all and could not fulfil the requirements of section 107 of the transfer of Property.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the respondents, M/s Dagi Ram Pindi Lal Gulati, w/o Shri Pindilal Gulati and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati. The Income Tax officer to whom summons were issued sent the record in a sealed cover through an Inspector along with a letter dated November 1,1972 claiming that the said record was privileged under Section 137 of the 1961 Act. The appellant filed an application for production of the documents relating to assessment of an assessee summoned by the Civil Court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce the Income tax record relating to the income tax records relating to M/S Borizeon Industrial Products (P) Ltd. and Bishamber Nath Kaul Nath. That record was also sent by the IncomeTax Officer in a separate sealed cover alongwith a letter in which it was submitted that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an assessee could be made. The respondents, however, did not produce the income Tax records relating thereto. The High Court held that the question of privilege, as claimed by the appellant, as claiming by the Incometax officer, was important and likely to arise in the course of trial suits in future also, a reference was made by the learned Single Judge on the question whether privilege as claimed could be admitted in evidence ? Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The decision of the High Court is set aside. [562D] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant had acquired no right or privilege under the 1961 Income Tax Act, 1922 and after its repeal Section 137 was substituted by a new section vide Section 138(1)(b) of the Finance Act, 1964. The finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138 (1)(a) has no relevance to the exercise of powers by a court to summon the production of documents in a case pending before it. [563D] 1.2 In the present case, there was no impediment left in the way of a civil court to summoning the production or documents relevant to the case before it and submit the same to the Court in answer to the summons.

A gift by a father to his minor son was not valid unless it was made by a registered deed. The donor died in May, 1946 without leaving an issue. A suit for partition and possession of the property was filed by the plaintiff on April 7, 1944. The defendants contended that when succession opened out on the death of Mammotty, his widow Seinaba was entitled to the enhanced share of 1/4 as there was no issue, and the remaining 3/4 was divisible between 552 Kunhamu and his two sisters, Kunhamun and his four sisters, Kadar Ali. The trial court held that when a gift by the husband to his wife to his daughter in law was valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or by the executor or by his executors of the two and even executors of both the two. The High Court held that the gift by Kadar to his mother was valid and that the decision of the trial court was correct. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the plaintiff had failed to prove that the subsequent holding of the gift was on behalf of her minor son. It is well settled that a gift made to him by a guardian to his father in law is not valid until it is shown that he has been given an opportunity to show his ownership and possession. The strict rule of Muhammadan law about giving possession to one of the guardians of the stated property of the minor is not a condition of its validity in certain cases. One such case is gift by another to his son when the father was alive without delivery of possession to the father, was held to be invalid. Both these cases involve gifts in favour of minors whose fathers were alive and competent. They are distinguishable from those cases in which there is no guardian of the properties in existence. In such cases the gift through the mother is a valid gift. The gift by her husband to her mother in law, in whose charge she was living at her mother 's house and in her care where the husband was also residing, is not void unless it is proved that the father had left behind him even a straw belonging to him to show her ownership and Possession.

The Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration of Hindu Religious & Charitable Institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. The Act provided that the annual income of a religious institution shall be subject to concurrent audit, that is to say, the audit shall take place as and when expenditure is incurred. The Commissioner had to determine the fee for auditing the accounts of each religious endowment. The power of the Commissioner was subject to a three fold restriction : (1) that the total annual income should not exceed 11/5% of the income; and (2) that it should be assessed at 10% of its income. The High Court upheld the contention on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act, and therefore the demand for levy was Premature. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Under the Act a fee though levied for rendering services of a particular type is not to be co related to the services performed for each individual who is intended to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which contribution is to be levied. The concession by the Advocate General at the hearing in Devraja Shenoy 's case, that the amount of contribution payable by the petitioners (respondent) temple should be prescribed by a rule which remained to be made subject thereto, was not correct. [923 G H] (ii) Under section 76(2) of the Madras Hindu religious and Charitable Endowment Act, 1950, the annual value of the religious institution for the relevant year preceding the year is Rs. 1,000/ or more; that the fee does not exceed 10% on its income; the percentage of income levied as audit fee must of necessity be based on an estimate and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amounts demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing. [ 923 A B] (iii) Under sections 76(1) and 77(2), the annual amount of income of each institution for which the contribution is levied should be fixed by rules.

The appellant, a contemner under section 19(1) of the (Act XLIII of 1986), was prosecuted for contempt of Court. The notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed by section 17 of the Act. The High Court held that no appeal lies to this Court against an order issuing notice as nothing yet had been decided by it. In appeal to this court, HELD : An appeal would lie to this 'Court under section19 from such an order although the proceeding has remained pending in the High Court. [509 F] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court ; , referred to. Baradanta Mishra V. Orissa High Courts, AIR 1976 S.C. 1206, followed. Barakanta Misra vs Orissa, A.I.R. 1976 S C. 1205, distinguished. Bargakanta Sahu vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, A I. R. 1976 SC 1206 and Baradbanta Mishra v Orissa High, ; , applied. Barkanta Mishra & Anr. vs Orissa State, AIR 1977 S. C. 1306, disapproved. Barapada Mishra vs JusticeGatikrashna Mishra; , , referred. Baralakanta Pattam Mishra vs The Orissa High court, A R.I., 1976 SC.R 1206; Baradva Mishra vs Jatikrosh Mishra, ; and Barakata Mishra vs justice Gatikushna Misra, AI.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for having committed an offence under section 6(1 A) of the Indian Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 6 A was not on the statute book at the time of the alleged commission of the offence, nor was it applicable to the case as it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. HELD: (i) The words "unless a different intention appears" in section 4 Of the 1952 Act are either covered by the provisions of the , or a surplusage not serving any definite purpose. Even from the history of the legislation it is clear that the main object of the 1952 amendment was to expurgate section 6A of the . [763 B C] (ii) The repeal of an earlier Act which has been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act, for, where an earlier statute is incorporated by reference into a second statute, the repeal of the first statute by a third does not affect the subsequent Act. It is only when the statute amends the text of another, that it amends the subject or theme of it, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. [766 C D] (iii) The word " text" in its dictionary meaning means subject or context. When an enactment amends the language of another it amends a later statute, but can only be amended by it. It cannot be said that the earlier Act applies to incorporated or refers to the amending Act. [781 E F] (iv) In view of the historical background of the amending Acts with a view to establish that the intention of the legislature in passing the said Act was to reprench from the statute Book, the amendment of section 6 B of the Amending Act of 1952 was either covered under the provisions Of the , nor a surplusakshage not served any definite purposes. Even if from the context of the Act it is assumed that the Legislature intended to expound section 6 (1 A), it cannot be held that section 4 of the 1953 Act had no application to a case of repeal of a amending Act, because, in the present case, the insertion of section 7 A was unnecessary and redundant. [783 E F; 784 B C].

The appellant, a son of the former managing Shebait of the debutter estate, purchased certain properties in benami of his wife Oramba Sundari. The properties were sold by a registered deed of sale and they were purchased by the appellant 's father. The respondents filed two suits against the appellant for recovery of moneys due to them from the latter. The trial judge decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed both the suits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution of a decree to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues thus ascertained by instalments. But save and except for these, the old decree as well as the adjudications made thereunder are not wiped out and the parties are not relegated to their rights and liabilities under the original cause of action.[996 D E] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that Oramb Sundari did not bona fide acquire any right which could be protected under clause (b) of section 36(2). [997 A B] (iii) The order for restoration of possession made by both the courts below must be deemed to be the purchasers of these properties within the meaning of clause (c) of Section 36(1); and as the subsequent conveyance of these property in favour of Oram b Sundari, the appellant has been held by both courts below to be a fictitious transaction, it must be held that O Ramba Sundar did not acquire any rights which could he protected under cl. (b).

The respondent company, which was a Hindu undivided family, had executed a deed of assignment in favour of the appellant. The deed provided that the assignee of the decree would not transfer or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed in future if he satisfies the other requirements of Order XXI, rule 16. The appellant company, however, did not apply for execution of the said decree under order XXI, r. 16. A notice under O. XXI, Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure was issued by the Court on October 10, 1951 calling upon Habib & Sons to show cause why the decree passed in favour Of Habib and Sons should not be executed by the transferees against the appellant, and the appellant filed an application for execution under O, r., 21, r, 16. In the meantime, the respondent company had transferred the suit properties to the appellant on October 7, 1951. The respondent company contended that even if the respondent Company did not, by force of the prior agreement in writing read in the light of the equitable principle that the right, title and interest of the transferor in the decree acquired after the transfer was passed, such equitable transfer does not relate back to the prior consent and does not render the transferee a transferee of the judgment debtor 's property. Held: (i) The words "by operation of law" cannot be invoked so as to make an assignment operative to transfer the decree and the right under which it would upon the true construction of its terms, otherwise be inoperative in that regard; and (ii) The respondent Company could not claim to be a transferee by assignment in writing within the meaning of O. 21, rr. 16 and 17 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The respondent, a firm of electrical contractors undertook the job of installing electrical fittings in the houses of its customers which involved the supply and fixing of goods, such as wire, brass clips, wall bracketsand tube light and tube light. The Sales Tax Officer 'B ' Circle Jaipur included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service. The Deputy Commissioner confirmed the order of the Sales Tax officer but the High Court in revision affirmed the order. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The object of the contract is to enter into a works contract merely because they undertake to install or for the articles sold so as to make them fit for immediate service. But whether a particular contract is one for sale of Goods or is an outright or gratuitous. [510 B] (ii) The contract in question was for execution of work not involving sale of property but for work and labour. The test is whether the object of a party sought to be taxed is that the chattel as chattel passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection with the installation are under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution of the Contract of sale. [511 D] (iii) The essential undertaking of the Respondent was not merely to supply windows but to "fix" the windows but also to "Fix" them the windows. The service is not rendered under a different contract nor is the service shown to be customarily or normally as incidental to, the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. [ 511 E] (iv) The contracts in question were set out in the contract and its acceptance was not necessary for the purpose of determining whether the contract in each case was one for work or labour.

The respondent was charged with having committed an offence under section 420 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B of the Indian Penal code and for committing forgery. The Presidency Magistrate acquitted him on the ground that he had not been made a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. On appeal, the High Court quashed the charge framed against Raj Kumar Agarwalla and Shanker Lal but allowed the revision petition filed by Raj Kumar Aggarwalla. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant State that the report which was lodged by Ram Avtar was not a proper report as required under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The report which is lodged by the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar Agarwalala and Shankar Lal was present along with Shanker Lal when the latter broughther plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the said goods was then demanded from Ram Avtar and the accused were discharged. [279E F] 2. The High Court had rightly quashed the charges framed against the respondent. There is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High court. [280F G] 3. The order framing charge against Raj K Agarwalla was quashed by the High, Court on the grounds that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned no case had been made out against him. Charges framed against him were accordingly quashed.

The petitioner, a resident of the State of Kerala, was alleged to have violated fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The petitioner alleged that he had violated fundamental right guaranteed under articles 19 and21 of the Constitu tion. He also alleged that the Railway Board through which apex body is run has controlled and controlled by the Railway Administration and has been constituted a most important commercial activity of the Government of India. As a result thereof, the Railways have become an independent source of transport and were providing the lifeline and link throughout the length and breadth of the country. By 1955 the total length of all Indian Railways was 34705 miles and the capital sunk was more than 900 crore rupees. The rise in the importance of the Railways in the national sphere has been gradual. With the expansion of the railways a high powered body known as the Railway Boards had come to be placed at the apex of control and with the new set up following independence Minister remained incharge to administer the affairs of the Railway through the Board. As early as 1924 by a resolution known as 'Rehabilitation Plan ', the Railway Budget had been separated from the general budget and this historical practice has continued till today. The Indian Railways are a socialised public utility undertaking. There is at present a general agreement among writers that the price policy of such a public corporation should neither make a loss nor a profit after meeting all capital charges and this is expressed by covering all costs or breaking. Keeping the history of the growth of the railway and their functioning in view, the commendable view to accept may be that the rates and fares should cover the total cost of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations if any. The Railway Board has come to the apex and with its new setup following independence Ministers a Minister remained in charge to administer affairs of Railway through Board. The General Conference Resolution of the Legislative Assembly was separated from this general budget. The existing independence Minister continued till now. The Government of Kerala had also been nationalised by a Resolution known as "Rehabilitation plan '. Overruling the Report of 1978, it has been submitted that there were nearly 12 months before the opening of the first Railway track, Lord Dalhousie, the then Governor General of India had said in his minutes: "I trust they (the East India Company and the Government) will ever avoid the error of viewing as private undertakings and will regard them as national works over which the Government may justly exercise and is called upon to exercise stringent and salutary control. This control should not be an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or unnecessarily prolongedly or exacted but which, in my humble judgment, is necessary at once for the interests of the state and for the protection of the public." The Indian Railway Railways are the socialised Public utility undertaking and there is at this present a special agreement among themselves. The Railways have a great impact in holding this great country together and in promoting running its economy. More expansion of railway track was usually for considerations of trade and commerce, troop movement and administrative convenience. More extension of time gradually connecting almost the entire country through a well woven net work of Railways and by the time the country became independent most of the Indian Railways had been nationalised and all these historical practice had been continued till then. The India Railways have considerable impact in the growth and development of the Central sphere. With this expansion, the Government has now developed the railway budget. This historical practice was continued till the year ending March 31, 1983 and from out of such funds, pressing improvements like manning the unmanned level crossings could be undertaken. The major portion of the national domain has been spread to be laid down in 1924 by the resolution known "Re Rehabilitation Plan" which is an integral part of the National lifelines and linkages throughout the country through the Boards.

The appellants had applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer, Baroda under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The application was dismissed in respect of their proprietary jagirs. On appeal by the Jagir holders, the Tribunal held that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41 rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. In reference to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the order of dismissal passed on February 1, 1961 was illegal and ultra vires because the Tribunal dismissed the appeals for non prosecution on account of non appearance of the advocate of the appellant in the appeal. Held: (i) The language of Regulation 20 is correct and must be accepted as correct. Section 13 of Act makes a decision of the Tribunal final and not to be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any Court. In the context of section 20 it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an appeal for non defence but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits even though there is default in appearance of appellants and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal, provided that where the other party had appeared in the appeals or application, the tribunal may restore the appeal or application to be heard ex parte. (ii) The words "decide it on merits" in section 17(1) mean "dispose of the Appeal or to put an end to the appeal". It is also open to a Tribunal in such a case to hear the respondent to hear and decide it on merit. Regulation 20 which provides for restoration of an appeal dismissed for non Prosecution but it was obligatory on the part of the tribunal to decide an appeal on merit even though no default in the appearance of appellant or his agent or lawyer is made out. (iii) The order of the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal dismissing the restoration applications dated July 18, 1961 is defective in law and must therefore be set aside.

The appellant 's father, who was the son of one of the respondents, brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent from the office of trustee of the temple. The trial court held that the dedication had been made by the respondent with the consent of the Advocate General as is permitted by section 6 of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1890, and therefore, he was liable to be removed. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court and ordered the dismissal of the suit. The High Court held that a valid trust had been created in favour of the deity and it was a public religious trust as Shri Ramchandra temple for which the trust was created was a private trust as he was the trustee. On an appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The High court was right in holding that the endowment made by respondent with his consent was not proved. It was not necessary to decide whether the endowment had been properly disposed of or whether it was made for the benefit of the public or for a charitable purpose. The fact that the suit was stated to be dismissed as compromised and the compromise appeared to have been in accordance with section 6 did not amount to setting aside the prior award. (ii) The question as to what should be done with the savings from the income of the village Telibandha to the Gharu Khata which was maintained for the general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication.

The High Court discharged the notices of contempt. The appellants were the President and Secretary of the Bar Avadh Association, which was a party to the proceedings in this Court. They were alleged to have committed contempt of court by not complying with the provisions of section 14(1)(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. The High Court held that the Chairman of the Committee was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar and as such he was guilty of contumacious conduct and the High Court gave them the ground that they were responsible for the passing of the resolution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts had committed contempt because the resolution was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 1, he being guilty of criminal contempt and that the resolution for publication in newspapers was not a proper act. HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the chairman of the committee was acting "in most partisan" under the pressure of Allahabad Bar. [602 B] The High court had rightly discharged the notice. There was no gainsaying that the members of the bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [ 603 B C] The contempt of Court is not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner.

The arbitrators, after giving due notice to the parties and making an award, fixed the hearing of the disputes. The Sub Registrar, Arambagh, on 25th November, 1983, ordered that the arbitrators ' application be heard and disposed of within a period of four months from 28th November 1983. On 26th July, 1978, the Sub Judge directed return of the award to the arbitrators. On 24th July 1984, the arbitrators made an application before the Sub Registrar for registration. The sub Registrar rejected the application on the ground that the limitation for filing the award had already expired and that the award was not registered within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending was between 28th of January, 1978 to 24th November. On 25th of November,1983, the Subordinate Judge ordered return of registration. On 23rd of November 1983, the arbitrator filed an application under section 14 of the . The Sub Judge held that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order, Arabagh passed an order ex parte and directed the parties including the arbitrators to maintain status quo till disposal of Misc. Case No. 74 of 1977 initiated by the appellant No. 1. On 14th August, 1978 the Sub judge ordered return back of the Award to the SubRegistrar for registration on 25rd of February, 1983. The award was made on 28th January,1978 and it was presented for registration before the sub Registrar on 25 th November,83. On 2nd September, 1978 a Sub Judge ordered interim injunction in respect of the parties from maintaining status quo until disposal of the Misc. case No. 73 of 1977. Thereafter, the sub judge passed an ex parte order dated 23rd November, 83 directing return of award to them. The appellant No 1 filed an appeal before the Subordinate judge against the said order and the same was dismissed on 19th June, 1986. On 20th December, 1982, the learned Munsif ordered return on 23rd January, 1983 and directed that the parties should maintain status of quo till the disposal of misc. case no. 74/77 initiated by appellant No l. The respondents filed an applica tion under section 15 of the , before the learned Sub Judge for a direction to the arbitrator to file the award in the court in Misc. Petition No. 28 of 1977 and the interim order was ipso facto discharged. On 19th of September, 1983 the Sub Court passed an interim injunction ex parte against the parties. The High Court set aside the aforesaid order on 6th March, 1981 and directed return back the award. On 22nd of November 83, the trial court ordered that it should be kept pending for registration till the suit was disposed of. On 21st December, 1983 a fresh stamp paper and the valuation application were heard and the SubJudge ordered return to the sub Judge. On 31st January, 1980, the parties filed an appli cation before the Munsif praying for a direc tion on the arbitrator 's Court to file it in the Court in Misc Case No 28 of1977. The trial court passed an ad interim injunction on 6.3.1981 and directed returning back the Award from the court. On 11th of June, 1983 another order was passed by the Subordi trate directing return back to the award for registration and that on 25.2.1983 the Submis sion Court ordered return. On 1st December 1977 the arbitrators filed an ap peal in the High Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the aforesaid ex parte judgment and order dated 19th September,1983 passed by Sub Judge. The learned Sub judge dismissed the application holding that during subsistence of interim injunction the arbitrator could not take back the decree for presenting the same for registration; that the period of eight months was available for registration if the conditions were fulfilled; and that since the conditions are fulfilled, the order made by the court directing the arbitrators should be stayed pending disposal of a Misc. Appeal in the Calcutta High Court. The appeal preferred by the appellants No.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent let out to him a portion of his new building which was not far from " Fida Ali Villa". The appellant had four sub tenants, one of whom was the landlord. The other sub tenants were the sub tenants of the appellant and the other sub tenant. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting. The defence of the appel lant was that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises. As to the claim on the grounds of nonpayment of rent he had also the right of sub letting, which it was alleged, had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. Held, that section 15 Of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act (Bom. VII of 1944) which permitted sub letting on certain conditions, did not violate article 14 Of the Constitution. The provisions of section 15 of the Act were to be read together and not in conjunction with section 15. It was open to a party to waive his right under section 13(1)(e). But this maxim must not be understood as meaning that where a transaction is vitiated by the person left in possession of goods after its completion is always entitled to keep them. Its true meaning, therefore, must be regarded as inserted in the interest of the public also. In the present case the question was not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid him in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 was prohibited and made illegal. The maxim Ex dolo malo malio or nonitur actio, is limited by no such qualification. It signifies nothing more than an intention not to insist upon the right. It may be deduced from acquiescence or may be implied from acquiescence. It might be inferred from acquiescence and may be inferred form acquiescence or consent of the defendant can neutralise its effect. A stipulation in the most solemn form, to waive the objection would be tainted with the vice of the original contract and void for the same reasons. Where the illegality appears, whether the evidence comes from one side or the other, the disclosure is fatal to the case. No consent of a party can neutralize its effect; but where the circumstances are such that the Court will refuse to assist either party, the consequence must be that in fact follow that the party in possession will not be disturbed. The rule of waiver is founded on public policy and it has been held that if public policy demands it even an equal participant in the acquisition of goods before its completion was always entitled and necessity of keeping them.

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject, the random counter check by the random check by and the counter random check, by the agency counter random Check by the examiner, Moderators ' mark sheets sent to Pune for feeding the computer to the computer. The appellant Board examined seven witnesses and after completing the formalities, declared the results of the examination within the specified time. The Board appointed seven enquiry officers to conduct the enquiry. Show cause notices were issued to the students on July 30, 1990 informing them of the nature of tampering, the subjects in which the marks were found tampered with, the marks initially obtained and the amended marks due to tampering, and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardian. They were also informed that they would be at liberty to inspect the documents at the Divisional Board at Bombay. They are entitled to adduce oral and documentary evidence at the hearing. They will also be permitted to cross examine the witnesses of the Board, if any. They would not be entitled to take part in the inquiry. The enquiry officers were to conduct these enquiries. Show Cause notices were served on the students for which they were given opportunity to lead evidence on their behalf and if the witnesses were examined on behalf of the appellant Board, they would he permitted to examine them. The appellants submitted their explanations denying the allegations and denying the tampering. The respondent Board appointed 7 enquiry officers who conducted secondary examination in March 1990 and March 1991, where at the marks granted, after scrutiny by the supervisors of the answers awarded, the declaration of punishment, the declarations of the results were found tampering with the appellant. Thereon, admittedly, it was found that the mark sheets relating to 283 examinees which include respondents 53 in these appeals were tampered, in many cases more than 2 to 8 subjects and in few cases in one subject. As a result, the rules of punishment were relaxedally good. The declaration of their results were withheld pending further enquiry and the rest declared on June 30,1990. Several writ petitions were filed in the High Court against non declaration of the result and the High court directed to take expeditious action to declare the results within the time specified. The High Court directed the Board to take immediate action to declaring the results after notice to the appellants and the respondents. The appeals arise from the common judgment of a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 2646 of 1990 and batch. The main grievance of the appellants is that the High Courts have power under Article 235 to make rules for its administrative convenience, but since the impugned action was not in pursuance of that rule, the action was illegal and cannot be sustained. The question is whether the Standing Committee of the concerned Divisional Board has power under the Act and Regulations to enquire into the use of unfair means committed at the final examination conducted by the Board. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts can hold enquiries, impose punishments other than dismissal or removal subject, however, to the conditions of service and to give acceptance to the contention that the Standing committee is an alien body to the Divisional Boards is to do violence to the scheme of the Act. [798G] 1.2 In the instant case, the High courts have power to make Rules for its convenience, But since the rules are harbinger between the mind of the maker of the order to the controversy in question and the decision or conclusion arrived at, there is no need to examine the concerned officials in the State Board to explain as to how and who dealt with the papers from the time recounting was done in the office till the mark sheet were sent to the Pune feed.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for having committed an offence punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special judge convicted them and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500 each. On appeal by special leave the appellants contended that the prosecution had failed to prove that the money was offered as a bribe and not as compensation in settlement of the amounts legitimately due to the Railway. Held, that the question whether the laying of traps must be prohibited on the ground that by doing so the appellants were guilty of criminal misconduct is one which has to be decided on the facts of each case. The prosecution had not proved that the amount was actually paid to Madan Lal even though he said that he was interested in giving or attempting to give any bribe for hushing up the case. There was no doubt that the appellants and the eaves asked him to do so but as they were also willing to accept it, the case of the prosecution was that Madan Lal was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code. The question whether a trap was laid for catching hold out an invitation for the commission of offences is one of the essential ingredients of the two offences and the application of the presumption referred to in sub clause (3) of section 5 of the Act has to depend on the language employed and given effect to it. In the present case, the intention of the Legislature was to create a distinct offence from simple bribery and that it could not be laid down as an absolute rule that the laying off traps should be prohibited. The fact that the bribe took place in the course of trappings did not make it clear that there was no overlapping of offences.

The appellant Bank, which was the auction purchaser of a property, had executed a promissory note in favour of the respondent. The principal debtor and the surety were to give security for the cash credit facility by borrowing various amounts. By the end of February 1959 the principal debtor owed Rs. 76,368.04 P. In this account the principal debtors enjoyed the cash Credit facility by lending various amounts and by the end February 1959 they had executed the promissory note simultaneously with the two demand promissory notes simultaneously. The surety executed a letter of guarantee in favour Of the Bank. The appellant 's father executed a bond in favour thereof in favour the respondent, which he endorsed in favour on September 16, 1957 offering to give cash credit for the Cash credit facility and also a personal guarantee of the surety. The respondent 's brother who was the surety filed a suit against the principal creditor and the appellant for recovery of Rs.76,368 P.04P. from the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal by the surety, the High Court held that the pledge and personal guarantee were not two independent transactions but they formed part and parcel of one composite transaction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter of Guarantee executed by the principal defendant in favour and endorsed by the sureties to the Bank, the surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "any security" in cl. 5 of the Letters of Guarantee is not aware of any other security offered by the Principal debtor yet once the right of the creditor against the surety is discharged to the extent of the security lost as provided by section 141. [928C] 2. Clause 5 would not help the creditor Bank in any manner. It is not a case of granting time or indulgence to the principal and variation of the credit or taking one set of security in substitution of some other security in the substitution of certain other security. The guarantee of surety is not an association of persons and for continuance of the guarantee in the event of death, retirement etc. of one of such associations of persons or the guarantee remaining intact and effective and legally enforceable irrespective of some defect arising from the internal management of such association of person. [936H 928A] 3. Clause 7 provides for continuing the guarantee where the principal is an association or persons andfor continuance of guarantee, in the case of death retirement etc., of one such association or of such members of such Association of persons. The security is discharged only to the amount of the debt, is entitled to all the securities held by the Bank but such an act on the part of the bank would not have the effect of discharging the surety or in any way affecting his liability thereunder under the letter guarantee. [940C D] 4.

The appellant was the owner of a patel inam land. He worked as patel in the village for several years and after his death he worked as Patel. In 1935, he worked in the patel 's office in rotation of ten years each. The four families went by the surnames of Dongre, Rokade family, one Shivajirao was alive, who worked as a pGujarat. In 1945, he was appointed patel and his brother, the appellant worked as Patel. In 1936, he had worked aspatel in his turn. The village was resumed by Government in or about 1904. He was working as P Patel. On the basis of this enquiry, the Financial Commissioner held that the person actually working as pGujarat was entitled to receive full emoluments of his office and revenue officers had consistently refused to admit any claims to shares in patelki inam lands which were given as emoluments for services to be rendered by the psy institution. The appellant 's suit in 1942 against the Government, inter alia, for a declaration that the lands in possession of the appellant should be resumed and regranted to him was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and that the grant was recognised under a service Inam by the Central Provinces and Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928. The trial court held that (1) the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for emoluments for 91 services to he rendered by patel; and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume and regurant the lands. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant could only succeed if he established that he had a right to a share in the "patelki Inam" lands and Government had no right to resume them. [723 G] (ii) The claim of title by adverse possession can be disposed of in a few words.

The respondents were the father and sons of one B, who died in 1930. The appellant 's father was the eldest son of B. In 1944, B was born to C. A. in Madras. He died in 1943 when its members partly shifted their activities to Bangalore. On March 22, 1955, B died leaving behind his widow G and his daughter G. After his death, B had been living in Madras till about 1930 when its branches were converted into Islam like the members of another sect. The respondents claimed that the family properties were treated as joint family properties by survivorship. The Assistant Controller rejected these contentions and assessed 10 L120 SupCI/72 duty at Rs. 2,05,996.41 P. on the basis that the entire estate valued by him at Rs 12,23,794 was chargeable lo estate duty. On appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the respondents were not entitled to any interest in the property inherited by their father from his ancestors and assessed it under the Act. The High Court also rejected these grounds as also the evidence led by the respondents in support thereof. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High Courts have treated the Khojas as being governed by the rules of Hindu law in matters of property succession and inheritance. [238 D] (2) The right of a son in birth in such properties having been born lone before 1948, had already acquired a right by birth in the ancestral property and consequently having a right to demand partition it did not apply. [239 E F] (3) The rule of Mahomedan law applicable to Cutchi Memons is that the invariable and general presumption was that Mohamedans were governed by Hindu Law as their customary law, Halai Memons had regulated succession according to Hindu law. Thus, from 1847 to 1905 the Bombay High Court consistently treated the Khoias and Cutchi Mazons alike, as if they were on precisely the same footing and urged the necessity of deciding cases of Cutchi memons settled in Madras, Mysore and Bangalore. [240 G H] (4) The finding recorded by the Board was binding on the High Court. It is a rule of Muslim law that the correctness of which is not capable of any doubt, that it applies not only to persons who are by birth but by religion also. Tracing the history and the conversion of Khoj as having retained that part of their personal law to which till their conversion they were accustomed. [241 G H; 239 A] (5) The respondents ' father was born in Madras when its member was converted into a Hindu Law. In the present case, B did not have any such right. He had already been born in India before 1948 and continued to be governed by Mahomedan law. Therefore, he could not claim that the property belonged to the same family as the other persons who had been made insolvents. [242 A C] (6) The fact that B was a descendant of G did not affect his rights under section 3 of the Act because, B 's right expressly saved by section 3 was not affected by section 2 of the . [240 E F].

The appellants are manufacturers of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage and thereafter subjected to an integrated process for the manufacture of different fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not claim that the various kinds of fabric which are produced at an intermediary stage, and thereafter, subjected to a process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to pay excise duty thereon. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the circular. During the pendency of the writ petition in the Delhi High Court, the Central Government by a Notification No. 20/82 C. dated 20 2 1982 amended rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules 1944 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Rules ') and directed the subordinate excise authorities to levy and collect duty of excise on the yarn which was produced at the intermediate stage in the Mill of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of manufacturing different fabrics, and also to direct the subordinate officers to levy duty. The High Court held that the yarn manufactured by the appellants could not be subjected to duty of Excise, and that the same had been specified in this behalf by the Central Board of Excise under Rule 9 of the Rules. Hence this appeal by the Union of India. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The amendment to rules 9 & 49 of Central Excise Act 1944 (which is a proviso thereto) has given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force i.e. February 28, 1944. [707C] 2.2 In view of the fact that the High Courts have taken the view that a continuous or integrated process would not be initially contemplated by Rule 9 or rule 49, there is no removal within the plant itself so long as a commodity is not removed from the premises, there was no removal of sliver from the place of manufacture as envisaged by rules 9and 49. [07D] 2:3 The High Courts had taken the correct view that the removal is the main criterion for the collection of excise duties on the commodity produced or manufactured inside the factory or the place where the excisable goods are produced, cured or manufactured or any premises appurtenant thereto, but also removed within such place, and therefore, such intermediate product although known to the market is produced and is transferred, within the factory for the purpose of payment of duty. [807E] 2 :4 The High court was right in holding that the appellants were not liable to excise duty.

The petitioner, a holder of a permit issued under Chapter IV of the U.P. Gazette dated April 5, 1975, applied for grant of stage carriage permits to ply a stage carriage on the route in question. The petitioner filed his objections to the said scheme and the State Transport Undertaking, i.e., the Uttar Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, the State of Uttar Pradesh published a scheme dated March 7, 1975 under section 68 C of the Act. The State Government published a notification dated April 6, 1975 in the U P Gazette dated May 4, 1975. The hearing authority empowered under section 70 C of Act either with or without modification. The respondent filed an original suit No. 145 of 1979 on the file of Civil Judge, Bulandshahr for a declaration that the scheme published under section 69 C of was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the appellant from finalising and approving the scheme. The Civil Judge declined to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an order restraining the Hearing Authority under section68 L of the act from proceeding with the hearing and approving scheme either with nor without modification; that the contention of the respondents before the trial court was that the suits were not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of Civil Courts in such matters was impliedly barred. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority) under section 6 D of the is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil Court to issue an order of injunction restraining a Hearing Authority from proceeding With the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. Whenever statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction to be excluded insofar as the merits to the case is concerned. If jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil courts have jurisdiction only to examine whether the provisions of the Statute have not been complied with or the tribunal had or had not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure. [544A B] 2. The power of hearing authority under section 63 D of Act is exclusive and in character it is neither open to any civil court to issue any order of restraint restraining the hearing Authority from proceedings with the hear ing and representations made and pass appropriate orders thereon.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(2) read with section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that the appellant, a sister in law, used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. In August 1963 she went to Ambala to her maternal aunt who was employed as a sister. She developed illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. On August 25, 1963 she came to the house of her uncle Russel Nathaniel and his wife 's husband, N. K. Lal, P.W. 2, used the appellant to live at her maternal uncle 's house. The appellant asked him to pay a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . But he refused to do so. On September 4, 1963, the child was handed over to Roshan Lal and when Roshan Lal was called, the appellant asked Nathan Shetty to bring him to the police station and thereafter the appellant brought the money from the pocket of the appellant. The case of prosecution was that Miss Eylene (P.W 2) used to reside in 1962 and that on August 29, 1963 at about 9 p.m. the appellant went to the room of her sister 's father and stayed there with her sister. On the same night the appellant removed a golden ring from his finger. On being questioned the appellant told the police that he never asked for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel, Nathanachi and his mother. The police then took the appellant into custody and recovered the currency notes from the appellant 's pocket. The Special Judge convicted the appellant under section 161, Indian Penal code and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay fine of Rs 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 6(2), Prevention of Corruption Act. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal C. P.C., nor any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel as a police officer he could not be said to have obtained gratification for doing or forbearing to show in the exercise of his official functions favour or disfavour to any per son. HELD: The order of sanction dated December 10, 1963 shows on the face of it what were the facts constituting the offence charged and that a prima facie case was made out against the appellant and in the circumstances of the case the sentence imposed is not excessive.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. The conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sanction accorded by the Chief Presidency Magistrate under section 6(c) of ' the Act without which no court could take cognizance of the offences alleged to have been committed by the appellant, was invalid as he had accepted a bribe from the Railway authorities and had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. Held, that the sanctioning authority accorded sanction in this case was not a valid sanction. The sanction was a valid one. The sanctioning authority had no power under section 7(c). It was not for Mr. Bokil, nor had the High court, while granting the certificate of fitness, to accord his sanction. In the present case the sanction was not valid. The question whether or not there was a proper sanction in the case was a serious enough to justify the granting of a certificate. It was therefore necessary to decide whether the sanctioning accorded in this ease was a genuine sanction. Held further, that it is well settled that the sanctioned authority had jurisdiction under section 4(c), and the sanction obtained by the sanctioning officer was not invalid. The mere fact that he put his signature on a ready made sanction presented by the police did not make him merely signa ready sanction. It could not be said that the Sanction accorded in the present ease was valid.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that the building was bona fide required by him for demolition and for reconstruction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants. On appeal, the appellate authority set aside the order of eviction and restored the order passed by the Rent Controller. In revision, the High Court held that the landlord had no right to ask for eviction on the grounds of demolition and reconstruction. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant landlord has every right to demolish his property in order to build a new structure on the site with view to improve his business or to get better returns on his investment. Such a step per se cannot be characterised as mala fide on the part of the landlord. [275G] 2.1 A landlord has an every right, to demolish the property in the order to construct a new building on the land with view, to improve its business or for getting better return on his investments. Such action would, per se, not be bona fide. [274A B] M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. Ramachandra & Ors., ; , followed. M/S Raval & Co. V.K. Ramachandra and others, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 869, distinguished. 1.2 The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the appellant against his tenants under the provisions of the Act. It is clear that when the objection on the score of the tenant being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14(1)(b) as grounds for eviction are raised in this appeal by the tenants, they are, therefore, irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and tenants when a suit is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to them under the Act.[275C D] M.S. Raval & Company vs K G. Ramchandra & Ors. ; , applied.

The appellant, a grove land holder, was in possession of groves and groves. He filed an execution proceeding under section 6(a) (i) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, for the recovery of certain lands from him. The executing court held that after vesting all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the Act in the State of Uttar Pradesh free from all encumbrances, the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. He also held that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force was provided in section 7(h) of that Act read with section 73 of the , and so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary, could be proceed against by him. He accordingly dismissed the execution application. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court failed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i). after vesting of all the right mentioned in s.6(h), the intermediary can be proceeded with trees in groves; and (ii) even after that decision, according to the respondent decree holder then also that was, after the coming into force of the Land Reforms and Land Reform Act, the only remedy in which he could enforce a right against a mortgage or before the Act comes into force is provided in s 6(h). HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a) The definition of "intermediary" under section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari and Land Abolition Act, 1951, does not mean "interminary grove". It includes grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such. [617 D] (b) The appellant was entitled to the compensation for the lands in question. He could also claim that he had acquired a right of trees from groves in respect of which he was liable to pay compensation.

The appellants were charged with offences punishable under Sections 302, 323, 324 and 326 IPC. The prosecution case was that on 24th December 1986, in which one Suku succumbed to the injuries as a result of the assault during the occurrence, six accused persons were arrayed by the investigating agency for offences punishable u/s 302, 325, 323 and 324 read with Section 149 IPC. They were put on trial and the prosecution sought to establish its case by examining as many as six eye witnesses besides other evidence, documentary and oral. At the trial however four eye witnesses supported their statements recorded under section 161 Cr. P.C., during their testimony in court. The trial court acquitted all the accused except the first appellant with a cycle chain and a knife. On appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against them were set aside. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the prosecution case against the four appellants beyond a reasonable doubt was not established; (2) the participation of the 6 accused persons individually in the commission of the crime was established at the trial; and (3) the evidence of eye witnesses was only against accused Nos. 2, 3 and 5 who alone stood convicted by the High court had inflicted injuries intending to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The intention to cause murder of Suku deceased could not be recorded or sustained. The failure of the prosecution to show that the assembly was unlawful must necessarily result in the failure of charge under Section 149 I.P.C. [90G] 1.2 In a case like this, where there is existence of an unlawful assembly, it is necessary for invoking Section 149, IPC. Where the existence of such an unlawful intention is not proved, the accused with the knowledge that those injuries were likely to cause the death of Su riku may be caused and therefore, he can be cloathed with the liability of causing culpable homicide not amounting to murder. [92A B] 1:3 The intention of causing murder of the deceased as was likely to result in his death is not an unlawful part within the meaning of Section 141 IPC. [93C D] 1(a) There is no evidence that the injuries caused by the first accused with chopper were inflicted with the intention to kill Suku. It is, therefore, necessary in a case that like this to determine as to which of the accused is guilty of a particular offence.

The assessee, a non resident company, had its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into an collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd., (Indian Company) for the supply of certain goods to it. The assessee 's accounting year was the calendar year ending 30th September, 1966 and the renewed agreement too expired in November 1970. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs. 9,25,257 but filed a nil return saving that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile basis. The I.T.O. completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For these assessment years, 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' s plea that it maintained its accounts in cash basis alone and brought to tax the royalty amount disclosed. In these returns, the I. T.O., completed the assessments for the two assessment periods on the ground that it had maintained its account on mercantile system alone and therefore brought totax the royalty amounts disclosed. The Income Tax Officer rejected the assessees plea that the method of accounting was cash receipt basis. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had not been following any particular method of accountancy regularly over the past years. For this reason, it held that it did not actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. It also took the same stand. The Tribunal further held that though the Indian Company made a credit entry in the account of the assessee in its books, it did raise the plea that if the assessee was maintaining their accounts on mercantile method, the Income Tax could not be taxed at all as it would be received in England and not in India. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The fact that there can be cases of non residents to whom section 5(2)(a) will never apply in regard to a particular income cannot be made applicable to such an assessee. [103E] (2) The effect of applying the section would be to take the income outside the purview of taxation though the charge to tax on that income had taken effect on the accrual basis. Further, no occasion for imposing tax on receipt outside India would arise in the case of a nonresident, to whom income accrues in India, Section 5(1)(a). [103G] (3) The Income tax Officer cannot be properly deduced therefrom. But it must be remembered that Sec. 145 is only a machinery provision and cannot qualify the charging section so as to make the latter ednoss. So Section 145(1) should not be permitted to be applied in such circumstances as those arise from the facts of this case. [104E] Raghava Reddi vs T., Andhra Pradesh 44 I.A.T., Andhra pradesh, 44 I .T.R. 720 and Raghawa Reddi vs CLT., A.P.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death but on appeal the High Court confirmed his conviction. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The evidence of the approver is sufficient to connect him with the murder. It is also necessary for there being independent corroboration of the participation of the first accused in the murder; it is also essential that he must be corroborated in material particulars and qua each accused. [834 B] (2) In the present case, the approver 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the appellant. The High Court was unable to agree with the Sessions Judge that it was within their legal province to convict upon such evidence, but the judge should point out to the jury that it is within their jurisdiction to convict on such evidence. [ 834 C] (3) In view of the provisions of section 133 of the Evidence Act which read as follows : "An accomplice shall be a competent witness against an accused person; and 835 and a conviction is not illegal merely because it proceeds upon the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice". It cannot be doubted that under section 114 of the evidence which is as follows: "The court may presume that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in materials particulars. The law may be stated in the words of Martin Btin vs Resin (A.I.R. , referred to. (4) In a case where conviction was based upon the evidence of an approver, it cannot be said that the judge must point out the jury to the Sessions Court that it Is within their competence to convict him on such testimony alone. Therefore though the conviction based solely on the uncoroborated evidence of accomplice is not merely that the accomplice is on his own admission a man of bad character who took part in the offence and afterwards to save himself betrayed his former associates, and who has placed himself in a strong bias in favour of the prosecution, but it must be within their constitutional province to acquit upon such testimony.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution alleged that on July 8, 1961, the appellant committed offences under obtaining a sum of Rs. 180/ for Sri A.D. Singh, Executive Engineer (Electrical), from Ramprit Singh, Superintending Engineer (electrical). On the morning of July 6, 1961 the Electrical Executive Engineer, Sri Ramlakhan Prasad, accompanied by his Head Clerk, the Appellant paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhasan, Patna, and handed over a petition to P.W. 11 Girjanandan Sinha expressing his apprehension that the Executive Engineer or his Head clerk, the appel lant would demand some bribe from him. The appellant denied the charges and pleaded that the entire case had been fabricated against him bydhar, P. W. 16, the Assistant Superintendent of Police, who was a raiding party. After completing the investigation the police submitted a chargesheet against the appellant. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 5 read with s.5(1)(c) of tho Prevention of Criminal Procedure Code. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended that the conviction of the appellant could not be sustained because he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the Act. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal Code and therefore a 'public servant ' within the definition of section 21(9). [688 G H] (ii) The appellant was not a Government servant but he was the servant of the State Electricity Board constituted under the provisions Of the Act 54 of 1948. Under this clause the words "public servant" include every officer in service or paid of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of any other law that he could be said to be a public servants within section 43 of that Act. [688 A B] (iii) The words "Public servant" includes every officer who is so armed. In view of the language of section 81 of the , the officers and servants of the Board are deemed to be public servants only when acting or purported to act, in pursuance thereof, to be performed in pursuance Of any of these provisions of that act. [687 C] (iv) The word "officer" means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances a delegated function of Government. He is either armed with some authority or representative character by the Corporation; or whether his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is armed with such authority or representatives character. [689 E] (v) The fact that an officer is performing duties immediately auxiliary would not be decisive of the question whether he is in the serv ice or pay. of the corporation as defined by section 21 of the Indian Penal code. [695 A B]. (vi) The expression "corporation engaged in a trade or business" includes a banking, insurance or financial corporation for supplying power, light or water to the public. The word 'officer ' means some persons employed to do with another 's affairs against his will and without his leave, that is an office, 'and he who is in it is an officer.

The appellant was tried and convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. He was also convicted for contravening Cl. 4(b) of the said order. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him in respect of contravention of el. 3. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141 (2) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1) of Defence of India Rules, 1962, inasmuch as it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Evidence Act. HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the stock seized from the house of the appellant was illegal and liable to be set aside. [273 G] Rule 141 (1)(2) of Order, 1965, does not empower the court to forfeit the juar. Under r. 1(2), it is essential to the scheme of the Defence ofIndia Rules that the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act. The section contemplates that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid they would have effect unless they are inconsistent with the existing legislation. [272 C D] In the instant case, r. 142(2) was within the power conferred by sub section (1). Rule 141(2)(i) is in the following terms: "141 (2): If in the course of any judicial proceedings a question arises whether a person was duly informed of an order made in pursuance of these Rules, compliance with sub rule (1), or where the order was notified, the notification of the order shall be conclusive proof that he was so informed. But failure to comply with sub r. (1 ) (i) shall not preclude proof by other means that he had information of the Order, (ii) shall, not preclude evidence by proof that the person had information or knowledge that he has been so informed; but a failure to do so may be inferred from the circumstances of the case.

The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge, Farrukhabad for murder of one Kunwar Singh. The trial court convicted them under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced them to death. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts had not properly interfered with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court, in favour of the accused; (ii) the Sessions judge had wrongly convicted the appellants under section 201 read with Section 109 and was therefore entitled to acquit them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court ought not to have interfered with an order of conviction passed by a trial court in favour Of the appellants. [627C] 2.1 In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission thereof, is said to and the doing of that act. Thus, in order to constituting abetment,the abettor must he shown to had "intently" aided, the commission of which is said tO and the do of that acts.
