[625E] 2:2.1 The High Courts ought not have interfered in the order passed by acquittal passed against the appellants because the oral testimony of witnesses even if not tested by holding an identification parade can be made the basis of conviction if the request made by the accused is groundless and the witnesses knew the accused prior to the occurrence. [ 625G] 2(a) The High court ought not, in a way, of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design.

The appellant was charged with having committed the murder of one Deoram Maruti Patil. The prosecution case against him was that he along with other accused had to stand their trial for the murder and there was no basis for his plea of private defence. He was acquitted by the Sessions judge on the ground that one or more of them might have participated in the commission of the offence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the other accused were not identified but more than five. It is true that in the last category of cases the court will have to be very careful in reaching the said conclusion. But there is no legal bar which prevents the court from reaching such a conclusion. [683 G H] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. In the last mentioned case, the Court can come to the same conclusion and convict one of the named accused if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence.[684 A B] Mohan singh vs State, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 848, referred to. The High court was right when acquitted either on the grounds that the evidence was not acceptable or by giving benefit of doubt to them, the result would be in law would be the same as it would mean that they did not take part in the offence and the accused participated in it. [684 C D] Mohan Sing Singh vs The State of Bihar, ; followed. The observations of this Court really apply to a case covered by the third illustration given by us. But the present case falls outside the said three illustrations. In such cases either the trial court or even the High Court in appeal may be able to come to its conclusion that the acquitted accused were guilty either on account of constructive liability.

The petitioner, a clearing agent of the respondent company filed bills of entry on 30th July 1984 for warehousing under section 59 of the . The goods arrived at the Bombay Port on 12th June 1984. The clearing agent filed bill of entry for warehousing and cleared them on various dates between September 1, 1966 and February 20, 1967. The petitioner 's clearing agent challenged the said bill on the ground that since the consignments had been re ceived, stored and assessed to duty much before the promul gation of the Ordinance, they were liable to pay duty at the rate prevailing on the date of warehousing. The claim was rejected by the Income Tax Department on 30.3.1988. On 30th March 1988, the petitioner ' clearing agent moved this Court for relief under Article 32 of the Constitution contending that since there was no prohibition under section 132(1) of the Income tax Act 1961, the goods could not be released. This Court passed an order on 22nd April 1988 and on 22.4.1988, the Customs Department issued no objection certificate to lifting the ban. On 4th April 1988, this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective sheets/coils" which have arrived at Bombay per port as per S.S. "SEA PRIMRosh", will be released forthwith on petitioner ' paying customs and other duties leviable on 21st August 1984. In addition to this payment, petitioner will deposit Rs.5 lakhs and for the balance amount he will deposit a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs and also deposits Rs.50 lakhs and the balance petitioner will furnish surety (which may consist of ITC bond but excluding cash/bank guarantee) and Rs.15 lakhs and furnishing surety (who may consist ous of ITC bonds but excluding bank guarantee/NSC/FDR) to the satisfaction of the Collector of Customs". The petitioner challenged the aforesaid order by filing a writ petition in this Court on 16th April, 1988 and also on 22th April 1989. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that for the payment of duty, the liability of the petitioner to pay the duty is the duty at that time of clearance of the goods. Dismissing the writ petition, this court, HELD: 1.1 The relief under article 32 of tho Constitution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case.

The appellants were the Managing Director of a company which was incorporated in liquidation. The assets and properties of the company were sold to defendants 8 to 10 who were respondents 2 to 4. The sale was fixed for February 2, 1943. On January 16, 1943, M executed an order for Rs. 15,100 being made by the Deputy Registrar of Co operative Societies on April 21, 1942. In execution of this payment order a bungalow belonging to M was attached by the Collector under the Bombay Land Revenue Code on July 27, 1942 and was confirmed on June 23, 1943 and was sold in execution of the decree. The appellants filed an application for postponing the sale which was rejected. On appeal, the High Court held that the debt was not avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the S was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of defendant No. 1 who was the Managing director of the Bank. The High Court also held that there was no evidence to support the finding of the trial court that the debts were not aviyavaharirika and, therefore, in an execution sale under section 155 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, only the right, title and interest of the defaulter i.e. of the father alone which could not include the share of the other members of the joint family. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the debt fell within the term avyabrika by relying upon the payment order made against him; and (2) the sale in execution was under section155 of the Act only "the right, interest and interest" of the appellant No. I which were not accounted for could not be termed an avyaharika. HELD: (1)(a) The liability of the sons to discharge the debts of the deceased father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the son which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the husband and which does not come to an end as a result of partition of the family estate unless a provision has been made for the payment of the just debts of his father. [890 B C] (b) The debt was therefore binding on the sons as they would be deemed to have been represented by the father in the suit. [889 D E] (c) In Hindu law there are two mutually destructive principles, one principle of independent coparceiiary rights in the sons which is an incident of birth giving to the sons vested right in the coparcenary property and the other pious duty of the members to discharge their father 's debts not tainted by immority or illegality. [879 E] In Hindu Law there are three mutually destructive Principles, one the principle of coparcticary rights is that the sons must be made liable for the pre partition debts of their father which were non immoral or illegal and for the payments of which no arrangement was made at the date of the partition. The liability to discharge debts of a father which is not tainted cannot be challenged except on proof by the sons of the immoral or unlawful purpose of the debt and in the absence of any such proof the sale will be screened from the sons ' attack, even after the partition their share remains liable.

The petitioners were the partners of a firm, and they were partners of that firm. The first petitioner was a registered firm. They filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of certain provisions of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, and a notification issued under section 8 of the Act. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of the said sections on the grounds (1) that the tax had not been laid upon "passengers and goods" as authorised by Entry No. 56 but upon "fares and freights", which were different entities, and in support of the contention that there was a difference, reference was made to Entry No 89 of the Union List where power is conferred to tax "fare and freight" and (2) that it was not necessary for the State Legislature to provide for the lump sum rates. Held:(1) The charging section does not offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. It is only in a case where the weight, bulk or nature of the goods may be different, and the rate of tax calculated on actual fares and freight charges is prescribed by the rules. But the imposition of a higher rate of taxation for cemented, tarred, asphalted, negotiated, etc., does not amount to "passenger and goods". The levy of a lump sum payment without guidance is therefore unconstitutional. (2)(a) The levy cannot be said to offend articles 304 and 304. (b) The imposition of the tax on fares and transportations attributable to routes outside the State except in one instance which is contemplated by the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 and to which reference will be made separately, is not a valid restriction. (c) The notification only lays down what lump sum payments have to be in each case, if a lump amount is being paid. The mandatory language is used to fix the amount of the lump sums. Rules 8 and 8A are enabling, and thereby authorise the State Government to accept a lump lump sum sum payment in lieu of the taxes actually chargeable. (3)(a). The notification merely lays down that lump sum amounts may be paid in lieu Of payment of tax on actual freights and freight. If the two rules and the notification are read in this way, the mandatory language was limited to prescribing the lump amount of lump sum rate without payment guidance. (4) The words "may accept" in both the provisos to section 4 are "may be directory", and "must accept". The word "shall" is ordinarily mandatory but it is sometimes not so interpreted if the context or the intention otherwise demands. In re Lord Thurlow Ex Parte Official Receiver, , referred to.

The appellant served a notice of retrenchment on 43 workmen. The Tin Workers ' Union, Ghaziabad, espoused the cause of such retrenched workmen and ultimately the Government of Uttar Pradesh by its notification dated 9th october 1974 issued in exercise of the power conferred by Section 4 K of the U.P. lndustrial Disputes Act 1947 referred the industrial dispute arising out of retrenchment of 43 workmen between the parties for adjudication to the Labour Court. The appellant pleaded its inability in view of the mounting losses and the dispute was referred for adjudication. The Labour Court held that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief of reinstatement must follow, has become final. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (i) that the retrenchment of workmen was invalid for the reasons found by the Labour court and the workman were entitled to the relief effective from the day on which they were sought to be retrenched; (ii) that it would mean that the retrenched workmen had been reinstated in service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The relief of back wages is no more open to challenge. [567G] 2.1 The appellant has already paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the amount so paid plus the retrenchment compensation. It must have paid. Even then it was told that the employer will have to pay Rs.2,80,OOo/ by way of back salary. [568C D] 2(i) The relief for reinstatement has been granted and the award has been implemented and the retrenched workman have been reinstated. The only limited question is whether the Labour Courts in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back wages. [569D E] (ii). The relief that the appellant should be awarded 75% back wages, cannot be said to be arbitrary, vague and fanciful but regular and legal. [570E F] 2.(iii) The appellant is entitled to full back salary for the period of work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the compensation towards the retrenchment Compensation.

The prosecution case was that the deceased was married to Churi deceased near about 1958. In 1964, Churi gave birth to a son named Joginder Nika Ram. The accused and his wife lived alone in their house in Shilaroo. On September 16, 1969, the accused went to the residence of Shri Sudershan Kumar Mahajan (PW 15) Naib Tehsildar who exercised the powers of second class magistrate, in Kotkhai. At about 10 p.m., when Joginder was three months old, Churl came to his house and asked him to sit down and be composed. On enquiry, he told that the accused had murdered his wife by giving her three Khokhri blows. The Head Constable prepared a report and sent it for post mortem examination. The doctor who conducted postmortem examination found the dead body of the deceased lying on the floor. He also examined the blood stained clothes as well as Khokli and other articles which were taken into possession from the spot. The Sessions Judge convicted the accused under section 302 Indian Penal Code, but acquitted him. On appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court had committed an error in maintaining the conviction of the accused relying upon the confession made to him by the accused to the police officer. It was also urged that the evidence of the doctor who performed post mortem exami nation on the dead bodies could not be relied upon as he had caused injuries to Chur l, which were sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of an investigation. Held: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the confession was inadmissible in evidence. It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of investigation. If, however, the confession is recorded at a stage prior to the commencement of the trial, there would be no bar to the admissibility of such a confession. (2) The fact that the person making the confession had gone to see film shows that he was specially empowered by the State Government to record a confession and that the statement was recorded during the investigation of the case. In re Yondra Narasimha Murthy, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 201, relied on. (3) The evidence of P.W. 10 who conducted post mortem examina tion on the body could not therefore be deemed to be devoid of force. It could not, however be said that he had made a report to the Police Officer regarding a murder by the deceased.

The appellant was the defendant 's father. Tarak Lal Lall, a minor, executed a mortgage in favour of one Mst. Gyarsi for Rs. 5,000 and the mortgaged property was sold to the decree holder for a sum of Rs. 1,19,116 11 0. The mortgagee sued in the year 1938 and obtained a preliminary decree for sale on the 17th February 1939, for a certain sum of money. The mortgage was exe cuted on 12th June 1936, in favour Of one Mst Gyarsi. On the 12th of June 1936 the mortgagee instituted a suit against his brothers and mother for recovery of the amount due under the mortgages. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the agreement was proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "the con tract" in section 82 of the Transfer of Property Act, which governs the case, must be read as including sections 82 and 92 of the Indian Contract Act; (ii) the expression "the contract" in the section must be given its ordinary meaning and should not be restricted to a particular transaction between the promisors on one side and the promisee on the other. HELD : (i)(a) The words " the con tract ' in section 83 of the Evidence Act, do not include a mortgage but only refers to the main contract between the parties on the one side. That is why the rule is inequitable and will operate harshly in cases like the present. But the remedy lies in the parties ' own hands. It is open to them to make a contract to the contrary. If they do so, I can see no reason why these provisions should be abrogated in favour o f section in the Contract Act which does not deal with mortgages. [192 E F] (b) The rule is unjust and will apply. But both on authority and the principle of beneficial, as opposed to proportionate or proportionate, interest, equal or distri bution of liability. [195 A B] (c) The provisions of section 82 in the Transfer Of Property Act read with sections 82 & 92 of Indian Contract act are not applicable unless they are prepared to apply. So far as section 43 is concerned, it cannot be said that there was no contract to that contrary. It was therefore clear that section 82 must exclude section 43 because when there is a general law and a special law dealing with a particular matter, the special law deals with a specific matter, and the special laws dealing with such a particular matters, the general. [196 C D] (d) The High Court was right in holding that the words 'the con t tract ' could only refer to the principal contract between them on the 1st of June, 1936, and not to the terms of the agreement. [197 E F G] (e) The scheme of the Act is a provision of the Contract act viewed in the light of the law of mortgage in India including the contribution of law arising out of a transaction of mort gage. It confers rights on the mortgagor who redeems and directs that, in the absence of a contract, to the contra, he must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares. The rule was inequitable and would operate harsh in cases where like the instant case. [194 B C] (f) The Act does not contemplate that the law relating to a special Law dealing with the particular matter is the terms and nature of the transaction viewed in its light.

The appellants, who were holders of Engineering (Civil) and (Mech.) in the Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka, applied for the posts of Assistant Engineers (Civil), and (mech.) for the Public works Department. The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150. The 2nd appellant secured 2483 marks out o 50. The 3rd appellant secured 29.50 marks out Of 150. In the qualifying examina tion, the appellants secured more than the marks secured by them in the interview and 6640 marks outof 150. Both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce was excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R. 657, and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State o f Punjab & Ors.; , , and Mohinder Rai Garg vs The State of Punjab & ors., ; , and that the appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, and the Tribunal dismissed the petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violation to the judgment of this court in Ashok K Yadav & ors. vs The state of Haryana and Ors., ; [1988], Sup. SCR 657 and Mohinder Singh Sain Garg v State of Rajasthan & Ors, [1988]. Sup. SCC 658, and upheld. Ashok Kumar Y. Yadav & Anr. vs Sate of Haryana, [ 1988] Sup C.R, 657, distinguished. Ashok K. Yadav and Ors. etc. vs state of Punjab and Ors.; ; , referred to. 1.2 The Rules were clearly in breach of the dictum laid down by this Court. In Ashok Kumar Gupta & Ors vs State Of Haryana & ors, [1989] Sup (S) SCR 658, the Supreme Court held that the rules are clearly violative of the dicta laid down in Ashok k Yadav & Others vs State , and the appellants have approached the High Court in time. The State Government has already framed new rules, and as such there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. [495E F] Ashok Kumar Singh & Ors . vs State, [883 SCR 657; Mohinder Sain Jain Garg vs state Of Punjab & Anr., ; ; , applied. Ashok Yadav & Ant. vs Govt. of Haryana; , and The State Govt. has already frame new rules. [594F G] Ashok K Gupta & ors vs State & Ors; , ; , relied on.

The deceased was a member of the Indian Administrative Service and was posted as Collec tor and District Magistrate for District Magistrate. The deceased was arrested on 11th April, 1983 and sent to jail custody on 10th July, 1982. He was taken into custody on 11st April,1983. On 14th July 1982, the dead body of the deceased was recovered from a house belonging to the appellant. The prosecution relied upon the allegation of conspiracy, confession and other features to establish the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. The Trial Court rejected the prosecution evidence on this score. The High Court dismissed his appeal and confirmed the conviction as also sentence as awarded by the trial court. In the appeals before this Court it was contended that the prosecution had relied upon a part of the confession, which was not permissible under the law and has been depricated by the Supreme Court and different courts of the country. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As laid down in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , the confes sion of a Co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels necessity of seeking assurance for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [408C D] 2. The statement of a witness who, according to the prosecution, was regularly visiting Sadanand at the jail cannot be accepted as substantive piece of evidence. It is true that the same related to the point of time con temporaneous to the incident. There is evidence that Yadav was very close to Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. The allegation of criminal conspiracy cannot be accept ed. [414D E] 3. The evidence of conspiracy cannot, therefore, be accepted. It would indeed be hazardous to accept a part as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegationof conspiracy cannot he accepted. [413E F] 4.

The appellants companies were controlled by the first company, namely, Greaves Cotton and Co., in one way or the other. The main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were two references with respect to each of the first three companies and three references with regard to the second three companies. The first reference related to wages, dearness allowance and gratuity. The second reference related only to wages. dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concerns. The Tribunal held that the usual pattern of having unskilled, semi skilled and skilled grades should be followed and the various workmen, though they should be known by their designation and not by the class in which they were being placed, should be fitted in these categories. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region principle as well as in leaning on the recommendations of the Tripartite Conference wherein the need based minimum wage was evolved; and (2) that there were different scales of dearness allowance for clerical staff and other staff including factory workmen and referred to a number of firms where the first rate of increment and increased the span of years in which the maximum would be reached. Adjustments made by the Tribu nal were attacked, and so far as clerical and subordinate staff are concerned, it was not necessary that they should have done so, though looking at the financial stability of the appellant, the Tribunal completely overlooked the wages prevalent for these categories in which it had considered comparable concerns so faras clerical and subordi nate staff are involved. HELD: (1)(a) The Tribunal has given larger increments thus reducing the span. But there is nothing in law to prevent the industrial tribunal from granting adjustments to the employees in the revised wage scales even in a case where previously pay scales were in existence; but this has to be done sparingly taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of each case. [372 C D] (b) The Industrial Tribunal had not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and Dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have made comparison for clerical and superior staff, but in doing so the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total pay packet in fixing wages and revision of wages. [373 D E] (c) The award relating to dearness allowance is not always a question depending upon the facts of each particular case. But where the number of comparable concerns is small in a particular region, it would be proper to put greater emphasis on the industry part of the industrycum region principle. Where there are large number of concerns in the same region, they would be justified to put more emphasis on its part of industry cum regions principle as that would put all concerns on a more or less equal footing in the matter of production costs and therefore in the matters of competition. [374 E F] (d) The workmen of the two companies will stand comparison with some of the best concerns in that region. But considering that there is no question of want of financial capacity and that Greaves cotton & Co. which is the main company concerned in these appeals, has a high standing in that area, it is not possible to take into consideration (1)[1963] Supp. 377 for various grades of clerks. It is clear from the examination of these tables and pay scales prevalent in the appellants ' concerns from 1950 that pay scales are not high as compared to pay scales in comparable concern. If anything they were on the low side, there should be no difference in the amount of dearness allowances between employees of different kinds getting same wages.

The appellants were the legal representatives of one of the mortgagors. The respondent 's father died in 1922 after having transferred his interest to the mortgagees. The mortgagee 's widow filed a suit against the appellants for accounts and for accounts to be taken under the Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938. The trial court passed a decree declaring that both the mortgages had been satisfied. On appeal the District Court held that the Rajinama had not the effect of transferring the interest of Annappa 's share by the Raj inama and therefore operated to extinguish the equity of redemption not only of Shiddappa but also of an adverse title on the part of the appellants. The High Court, however, dismissed both the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Rajmama had no express or independent existence and (ii) the suit was barred by limitation under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879. HELD : (i)(a) The appellants were not entitled to redeem the mortgage property in view of the adverse possession exercised by the mortgagees since at least 1905 when the claim of the Annaappa to get the mortgaged property registered in his name failed. [701 B C] (b) The mortgagees came into possession of the property pursuant to the usufructuary mortgage and therefore their possession had a lawful origin. A mere assertion of an ' adverse title by the appellants cannot affect the subsisting equity of redeeming or operate to shorten the period of limitation prescribed for a suit for redemption. [700 B C].

The respondent, a company engaged in the manufacture of carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, mechanically moves accelerated mechanically, climpler machines and stepler machine. The Sales Tax Officer assessed the turnover of carbon papers for the period April 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 2%. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the assessment but reduced the turnover to 6% and also taxed the turnover on paper for the year 1966 67 at 6%. In the writ petition filed before the High Court, the validity of the order was challenged by the appellant company by means of a writ petition before the Allahabad High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. The High Court held that carbon paper did not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part of the typewriter 's turnover, taxed the turn of carbon Paper for the periods commencing from July 1,1966 to June 31, 1966 on the basis that it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6%. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: (1) The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper generally understood. [841 C] (2) The words "food colours" and "syrup essences", which are descriptive of the class of goods, the sales of which are to be taxed under the Act have to be construed in their own context and in the sense, as ordinarily understood and vindicated to these words by people usually conver sant with and dealing in such goods. [864 C D] (3) The word ' paper ' has not been defined either in the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948 or the Rules made thereunder, it has to be understood according to the strict or technical meaning of the language contained in it, but that is to be interpreted in its popular sense, meaning, as normally understood and animated to those words by persons usually conver tant with dealing in and using the article. [884 C] In the instant case, carbon paper was not paper as envisaged by entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification.

The respondents I to 4 were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in the year 1946. In 1951, the appellant issued a notice to the respondents 1 to 4 stating that they had disobeyed their orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. LI(a) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The Labour Union raised an industrial dispute and the Government of U.P. by its notification dated November 7, 1955, referred the question for decision to the State Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that both the concerns were distinct entities situated at different places with accounts maintained separately and governed by different service conditions, though they happened to be under the common management; therefore, they were treated as two separate entities. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the employer in the present case had no such right. The appellant was an employee of the respondent bank and transferred him from one concern to another concern. A substantial question of law involved between the parties and that also raised an important principle governing the right of an employer to transfer his employees from one of his concern to other of his in the circumstances of this case, could not be said to have been raised in the High Court. The employer had the inherent right to transfer him to another place where he chooses to start (4) a business subsequent to the date of his employment. In such a case it was possible to imply the condition of the contract that the employee had the right to do so under the contract of service or under any statutory provisions.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948. The provisions of the , were, inter alia, for the establishment of a Fund called the ' Employees State Insurance Act, 1948. Section 26 of that Act provided for the payment by the principal employer of a special contribution which shall be in lieu of the employer 's contribution payable under Chapter IV in the case of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of both Chapters IV and V were in force. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter V A of the Act on the ground that it was not a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate rendering any service or conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The provisions in Chapter VA of the are ultra vires. They are not to be construed as Acts of Parliament. Nor can read a judgment on a particular aspect of a question as a Holy Book covering all aspects of every question whether such questions and facets of such questions arise for consideration or not in that case. [1093 B C] (2) The High Courts have upheld the levy of special contribution as a tax. Therefore, whether special contribution is to be viewed as a fee, fee or not has no constitutional protection. [1194 D E] (3) A return in proce dure should be treated as a "tax" and not as a 'fee. The Government cannot go on levying employers ' contribution under section 73A of that act without giving a service in return. But from this it does not follow that the service must be given as soon as the contribution is made.

The petitioners demanded regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna. The management denied the claim and alleged that there was no vacancy in the establishment to absorb them and the accumulated loss to the establishment as on 31st March, 1988 was Rs. 10,29,583. A copy of the balance sheet has also been enclosed with the counter affidavit. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him 'of the equal pay for the period during which the same work is taken from him is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal salary for the said period during the which the work is taking from him. [54H; 54A] 2. The principles of regularisation are not arise in this case as there were no vacancies or work available in the Establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for quite some time they have been continued on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work for them. [55B C] 3. The doctrine of regularisation does not arise. The fact that there are no vacancies in the establishments for absorption cannot be a ground to interfere with the High Court 's decision in view of clear findings supported by evidence that there were any vacancies or working available in establishment for absorption. [654D E] 4. The concept of regularisation is not arise here as there are vacancies or works available in an establishment for absorbing the petitioners. The question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arose. The scheme of regularisation has not arise because there are any vacancies in establishment to be absorbed and their retention on the rolls is purely on humanitarian grounds so far as the daily rated workers are doing the same job as the regular workmen and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorption against it nor even paid equal pay.

The appellants were the owners of a part of a land in Touzi No. 911 of Darjeeling Collectors. The property was set out in Schedule A to the plaint and besides a claim was also made to certain other items of the movable and immovable properties, but this appeal was not concerned with these others which were set out as defendants in Sch. B 's plaint. The appellants contended that the suit was liable to be dismissed by reason of the provisions of 0. 9 of the Civil Procedure Code as the earlier Original Suit 58 of 1931 brought by the co heirs to set aside the sale under the mortgage decree had been allowed to be rejected for default and that in any event the plaintiffs ' vendors had no title to convey them any interest in the property. Held, that the appellants were entitled to a declaration that the transaction was void as it purported to convey only 2/2 shares of the land in question to the respondents. The right of the co heir to redeem the mortgage was not an ostensible owner of the entire interest in it and so passed at the court sale. The mere fact that the property was sold in execution of a decree by the National Agency Co., Ltd., did not make out any allegation regarding the transmission of title to the appellants. Held further, that as the appellants had failed to prove their title on the basis of various purchases from the heirs of the respondents, the suit could not be dismissed for default. The rule which spoke of the "plaintiff" being precluded by law from putting forward a fresh suit created merely a personal bar against the plaintiff in the first suit and those claiming under him, the allegations regarding the transfer of title were identical in the two suits.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, and was convicted and sentenced to death. The High Court dismissed all the appeals and confirmed the convictions and sentences passed against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the provisions of sections 173(4), 207A(3) and 207A (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied with, and (ii) as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. HELD: (i)(a) The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions Of section 162 or section 360 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [287 B] (b) The failure to comply with section 360(4) and the irregularity is curable by reference to section 537 of the code, as no case of prejudice has been made out. [286 C D] (c) The defect complained of was curable under section 537, and the High Court was right in holding that non compliance with the provisions thereof had caused any prejudice to the accused. [285 E F] (d) The appellant was not entitled to be allowed to have his case tried by a court of Session, as he had been prejudiced in his defence. He had to meet a straightforward case which they failed to do. After carefully considering the arguments advanced on behalf of the appellant and the evidence adduced before it, this Court would not interfere with the conclusions of the courts below on the merits of the case. [288 E F; 287 A] (e) The High Courts have rightly relied upon the testimony of two eye witnesses, corroborated by the circumstantial evidence referred to above. They had rejected the defence suggestion that the omission was not sufficient to vitiate the trial unless the accused persons were prejudiced in their defence by any omission on the part of police officers concerned or of the magistrate before whom the committal proceedings had fended, had caused prejudice to them in the interest of justice. From what has been said above it is clear that the Magistrate did record the evidence as required by sub section (4) of section 207A.

The appellant 's chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities containing calcium, sodium and other metals through Katcha Channels thereby corrupt drinking water of the wells in surrounding areas. The respondent Municipality accordingly after obtaining the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act 1901, as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955, to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange within a period of nine months from the date of receipt of the notice why it should not he directed to arranged within a specified time. The appellant replied that in these circumstances it objected to the requisition and expressed its inability to carry out the same. The Special Officer held that the discharge of the effluent was one for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and was beyond the scope of the enquiry before him, and therefore, had refused to exercise jurisdiction which was vested in him under the Act. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Special Officer had wrongly decided that lie could not go into the question whether the nuisance in question existed. The objection being in regard to both the matters it was the bounden duty of the Special officer to hold an enquiry with respect to the entire matter in dispute. The procedure laid down in section 153 A is to leave it to the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to the existence of a nuisance which was purely a matter for the objective satisfaction of Municipality and not the existence thereof. The special Officer was bound to enquire into the dispute and make its report both as to whether a nuisance existed, but after issuing the notice different considerations would arise when the provisions of sub section (3) were complied with.

The appellant was charged with the offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case was that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector attached thereto and that the usual formality of preparing a recovery memo and the sealing of goods in bags was also not complied with. On the strength of certain information received on 28th July 1964 that some railway property had been being sent through a Motor transport agency a sub inspector attached to it the Railway Control Force along With another SubInspector attached to a Railway Protection force along with other Sub Inspector, attached to an Railway Protection Officer Force along and Chief Inspector of N.E. Kotwali Chowk Lucknow examined the goods said to be railway stores and kept in 11 bags and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a railway engine. The usual formality was preparing a separate recovery memo, and the sealed goods in the presence of witnesses were sent out through a transport agency. The appellant was convicted under section 4 Of the Act on the ground that he had obtained the property in open market where goods of this kind were usually sold or that he did so for further use. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the prosecution was not called upon to prove that the articles belonged to any particular railway administration and that it had failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession. The fact that the goods were in a serviceable condition did not make out any averment to the contrary that the items mentioned in the report were used or intended to be used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. Mere unlawful possession of the property of any railway administration is not an offence. The mere description of the goods as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 2(b) of the Act. The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about identifying the marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the same goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Again, the mere description as to the goods that new would have to be led to the consequence that the property was actually used by a railway administration could not be accepted for further user.

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The appellants filed a suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised shop in Jaipur. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Anandi paid and accepted the respondent 's rent after determination of the lease. So she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control of Rent and Eviction) Ordinance 26 of 1975 which was replaced by Act 14 of 1976. The respondent landlord filed a second suit for eviction of the appellant from the shop in the Jaipur. In the suit it was pleaded that Smt Anandi was the tenant of the demised premises, and that she had become in possession of the same on the date of her death. The Trial Court dismissed the plaintiff 's suit holding that as the appellants had not carried on the business with the tenant during her life time, they were not entitled to the benefit of the amended definition of the tenant. The High Court held that as Smt. Ri paid the respondent accepted the rent after the determination of lease, she was enti tled to the continuance of tenancy. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment of the High Court, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In case of commercial premises governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard to succession. It may also be borne in mind that in case of residential purposes, the heirs of the deceased tenant cannot only succeed to the tenancy rights in the premises but they succeed to business as a whole. [18D E] 1.2 In the instant case, Smt. Ram vs Govind Kurnar & Ors., ; , relied on. 1.3 The amended definition is applicable to the facts of this case.

The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contribute equally. The workmen claimed that all the workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Tribunal held that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the amount should be taken as dividend to be paid to the Government by the Board. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has treated the whole matter in a very perfunctory manner. The main question for consideration by the Tribunal was the financial capacity of the employer. It had made no effort at all to analyse the balance sheet of the board to show the actual results of its working. It has made no attempt at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the ii under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of Board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities the same considerations applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied. [44E F] (2) The scheme under section 68 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 provides that as far as practicable and after taking credit for any subventions from the State Government the Board shall carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. Under section 64 the State Govt. may advance loans to the Board under section 64 and required to be repaid. [45E F; 46A] (3) The amount of provident Fund and gratuity is expense to be met by an employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial position shows that the burden of payment of gratuity and provident fund can be met without undue strain on the financial condition of the company, that burden must be borne by the employer like the burden to wage structure in the interest of social justice. [46C] (4) The provision for income tax and reserves must take second place as compared to provision for wage structure and gratuity which stands on the same footing as provident fund which is also a retiral benefit. Payment towards, provident fund and gratuity are expense to the employer that burden will have to be borne in by the company like the liability of wage structure. [47E F]. (5) The financial position of the industry as well as the fact that the onus of provident funds and gratuity does not result in loss to the employers is to be taken into account in calculating the profits. Even with regard to the depreciation reserve, the provisions of section 68 may have to he taken into consideration. [48F G] (6) The contribution to the Provident Fund reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciating reserves. Even after the profits could ascertained, the workmen could not be said to have been excluded from considerations of loss that might be incurred as a result of such extension.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for maintenance against her husband. The Magistrate passed an order directing maintenance against the appellant. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed that the appellant should be paid Rs. 150/ per month by way of maintenance to the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the wife failed to prove that her husband was impotent and unable to perform his marital obligations, (ii) the order passed by the Magistrate was not a just ground for refusing to live with her husband because she refused to live in her husband 's house without any physical disability and was therefore unable to persuade herself to live separately from her husband; (iii) the appellant had failed to discharge his marital obligation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the wife was not entitled to live apart from her father and claim maintenance on the ground that she refused living with her son. [707C] 2.1 In view of the finding of fact that the husband had failed tO perform his matrimonial obligations, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a just reason as contemplated by the proviso for the wife 's refusal to live together with her father. [808D] 2:2. The appellant was not an active participant in the sexual life and therefore, the sexual pleasure to the wife is of no consequence and could not amount to cruelty. [700E F] 3.1. In the instant case, the husband having failed to perform their marital obligations the order was passed by a Magistrate without any just ground.

The plaintiff respondent Municipality filed a suit for declaration of its title and for possession of the suit property described in two parts in the schedule to the plaint. The defendants denied that either Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 or Resolution 77 dated 29th February, 1948 vested the said lands except four plots of land mentioned therein in the Bhavnagar Municipality. The trial court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the suit properties till 7th July 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of India. The High Court dismissed the cross objections filed by the Municipal Corporation. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff Municipality has proved its possession to the extent that it is formally handed over the land in question to the State Government on 7th of July, 1947. [222B] 1.2 The suit was filed on 3rd March 1964 and the plaintiff has also admitted that the structures in Rasala Lines were not shown to be that of the Municipality in the Municipal records and even in the plaint they did not claim the structures as belonging to the Municipality. In fact, the Resolution No 37 dated 29 th February 1948 is only a right or an authori ty to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of title itself in the Municipality.[222C D] 1:3 The plaintiff municipality has also denied that the structure in Rasal Lines are not shown as to be the Municipality and even if in the Plaint they did, not claim any structures as belonged to the Municipal Board. [223E F] 2.2 In the suit notice under section 80 Civil Procedure Code, 1908, the plaintiff respondent had admitted that they did neither own the buildings thereon, they were not entitled to recover possession of lands covered by the Survey numbers de scribed in the second part of the schedule. The Government of Saurashtra had treated these orders only as authorisation or transferring power to execute sale deeds and collect rent in respect of Government lands situated within the Municipality, which should normally have been done by the State Govern ment. [228B C] 3.3 In the instant case, the resolution No.37 dated 19.1.1948 was merely a right, an author ities to sell land as represented the Government and not a vested title itself. The suit itself is for possession based on title and the appellant has not proved title.

The appellant was a Class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code for having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of Rs. 150 denomination and obtained a job for one Kallu. The Special judge convicted him but on appeal, the High Court held that no case under section 420 Indian Penal code was made out and he was acquitted of that charge. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant was not an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. He had been rightly convicted by the Special judge under section 5(1)(d) of Act II Of 1947 and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same, both the sentences to run concurrently. [690 C D] (ii) The conviction and sentence imposed upon him were quite in order and this was not a public servant within the definition of section 2(9). [691 E F] Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Lah. 869, followed. (iii)The appellant had been an officer under the Works Manager who was certainly a public servants within the protection of section 20(9), Indian Penal C. P.C., and therefore, he was not in any way performing his duties as such a public duty entrusted to him by the Government. [689 G] Ram Krishna vs Delhi Administration, I.L.R., , referred to.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala Division for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share. The appellants also contested the jurisdiction of the court. The Trial Court upheld both the contentions and dismissed the suit. The Additional District Judge, Patiala, however, allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the building in which the liquor shop was situated was exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The High Court also dismissed the Second Appeal filed by the Respondent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 60 of Code do not apply to an attachment and sales in any proceedings other than in execution of a decree of a civil court. [848C] 2. Section 60 sets out the properties which are exempt from sale and sale mentioned in sub section(1) thereof. The properties, if my, which are exempted from attachment & sale in revenue recovery proceedings under the said Act would only be such properties as are so exempted by the said section. There is no provision in the said act corresponding to cl. (cc cc)of proviso to subsection (1). [849D] 3. The opening words of sub section 1 of Section 58 of the Civil Procedure Code do apply only to execution and sale in any proceeding other than execution of decree of civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorised to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery of revenue due to the State. There was no provision either in the Act corresponding to clause (c) or in the proviso to section 60 set out the property which are not liable to attachment and sell in execution. [884E F] 4. The words "such attachment" in the sub section refer to the attachment and Sale mentioned in subsection (I) of section 58 sets out properties which were exempt from being attached and sold in execution or in revenue Recovery proceedings under this Act. The property, if any, which is exempt from the attachment sale and sales mentioned in Sub section (i) thereof would only such properties are so exempt by the aforesaid Act.

The respondent acquired certain lands in the State of Andhra Pradesh for the manufacture of a chemical plant. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded compensation at Rs. 4,29,360/ and Rs.4,29360/ respectively. The respondent filed an appeal before the Additional Deputy Collector who enhanced the compensation to Rs. 2045,000/ and also the High Court confirmed the order of the Civil Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the accountable person had only a claim lo get an extra compensation which was merely a hope or chance that the compensation might be enhanced; (ii) the respondent had no jurisdiction to issue the notice under section 59(a) of the Act and (iii) the additional compensation received by the legal heirs of Rashid had merely exercised a right to sue for further compensation which is merely a chance that might be increased. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there were no two separate rights one a right of property capable of sale in open market was a highly debatable question and a mistake which had to be discovered after lengthy discussion and debate could not be said to be a mistake apparent on the record. [319C] 2.1 The High court was right, in holding (i). that the respondent has merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collector in his award and (ii). that such valuation was obviously wrong in view of the enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Judge. [330G H] 2(a). In the instant case, the respondent resorted to section 61 because the rectification of any mistake apparent from the record could be done at any time within five years from the date of original assessment. The rectification proceedings had been completed pursuant to the impugned notice which was issued on a wrong assumption that the acquired land still formed part of the estate of the deceased and passed on his death. [333G H; 331A] 2.(b) The High Courts were right in taking the view that seeking references under the Land Acquisition Act and their pendency in Civil Court were primary facts which had not been disclosed by the accountable persons during the original assessment proceedings inasmuch as the lands had vested in the Government long prior thereto they had vested, in the Govern ment. [332C] 3.(c) The rectification proceeding have been completed subsequent to the making of the original assessments, easily led to the conclusion that the values adopted by the respondent for these lands were far below their real and true market value and as such it had escaped assessment to duty. [328D E] 4(a)(i). The rectification is being undertaken on the ground that the initial valuation adopted in respect of the land acquired was based at rates fixed by the 'Land Acquisition Officer, that such valuations were obviously wrong.

The appellant 's election to the District Cooperative Bank, Chandrapur was challenged by the respondent on the ground that he had committed default in payment of the loan instalments due from him. The Assistant Registrar held that the appellant was defaulter under section 73FF(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 and his election was not called in question according to the procedure prescribed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Rules, 1960. The District Deputy Registrar dismissed the appeal against that order. The appellant ' revision petition therefrom under section 154 of the Act was also dismissed on 30.8.89. In the writ petition filed before this Court it was contended for the appellant that the impugned order of removal was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant ' election as a Director of the Bank and that procedure having not been followed, the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 78(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the statute such as in section 78 (1) which deals with disqualification for membership. Under sub section (2) thereof a person shall be disqualified for being elected as, and for being a member of a committee if he (i) is a defaulter of any society; (ii) is not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions of section 78.(1). [682C D] 2. The procedure for an election petition is prescribed by subsequent section of that Chapter. Section 73FF provides that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section(1), shall cease to be a member or committee and his seat shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. Therefore, the moment the appellant became a defaulter and so long that default continues from day to day until it is repaid. Every day thereafter until it was repaid. [683E F] 3. The expression "makes default" or "stands disqualified" being in the present case not after the coming into force of section 73F, but before that date and not after that date. It would be the consequence of such a default. Sub section (1), which says that a person who has been incurred any disqualifications under sub s.(1) shall cease as member of the committee and he his seat shah be deemed vacant. [782G H] 4. The word "make default" in section 73(2) does not derogate from special things take place until repayment. What then would be consequence of default and, therefore, must be taken to have made default on the first day of his directorship and on every subsequent day till the instalment or instalments were paid. [783E F; 784A] 5. The words "m defaults" or 'stands disqualification" being not in the instant case after the Act came into force, it could not be said that default could be on the due date only and thereafter no default but only liability. [784F G] 6. The notice of the Deputy Registrar was in effect to say that the appellants had already ceased to be Director and his post already fell vacant. In this view of the matter there could not he any infirmity either in the notice or in the impugned orders of removal.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government as Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. After his retirement, he was served with a charge sheet dated October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. The respondent was served a charge sheets on October 16.1978 containing allegations that he had committed misconduct and mis conduct during the period of his service. He was given full opportunity to defend himself. On the conclusion of the enquiry, the State Govern ment issued orders reducing the pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The State Government revised the respondent 's pension by 50% and ordered that he should be paid 50 per percent of his pension permanently under rule 188 of Bombay Civil Service Rules. In the writ petition filed before the High Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from the service and the reduction of pension by50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against him. The High Court allowed the writ Petition and quashed the State 's order reducing the amount of pension payable by 50 percent to the Respondent. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was still in service or after the completion of his Service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government servant depend upon the good conduct of the Government servant. [35E] 2.2 The reduction of 50 per centum was too severe and disproportionate, to the proved misconduct proved. The order reducing pension by 100 per cent is too harsh, disproportionate to misconduct proved in the present case. The reduction was too far harsh and proportionate to the charge proved against the Respondent and it amounted to a serious default on his part as a Government Servant. [36F] 2:3 In view of the reduction in pension 50 per% was too high harsh and commensurate to the offence proved against respondent, the reduction was very harsh and not disproportionate to his misconduct proved, and the State Govt. should have taken into consideration the fact that the respondent had retired from serv ice and the reduced pension by fifty per cent would seriously affect his living.

The U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, was in force in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The appellant 's suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they needed the premises in suit to carry on their own business in the shop was not maintainable as no rent note executed by them was not admissible in evidence; and that the notice given by the appellants under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was invalid in law. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that it was valid. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 3(4) read with section 16 of the Act do not intend even prior to the amendment of 1954, to limit the jurisdiction of the Commissioner only to cases where irregularity or illegality was committed by the District Magistrate in granting or refusing to grant permission. It is clear that the power conferred on the State Government under section 7 F of the U. P. ( Temporary) Control Act, 1958, to revise the orders passed by the Commissioner under section 3 (3), is exactly similar to the jurisdiction conferred on a High Court under section 115 C.P., and it will be recalled that the revisional application can be made to the Commissioner merely against orders passed under the relevant provisions of the Land Revenue Act. [560 D E] (ii) The power conferred by section 3 of the , upon the State Govern ment at all material times by section 7F was very wide. It could not be said that the High Courts were in error in coming to the conclu sion that the permission granted by the commissioner in exercise of the powers conferred on him by section 6 F, was invalid. [561 G H] (iii) The jurisdiction of civil courts is excluded in relation to matters covered by the orders included within the provisions of sections 3(3), 16 and 16 of Act. In construing the provision of section 7 E it is not easy to conceive of a limitation as to jurisdiction being relevant in section 3, because, the said provision deals with special subject matters; but the exclusion of the jurisdiction is of the civil courts to deal with applications made by landlords. But quite apart from this aspect of the matter, the words used in section 7(3) are unambiguous. There are 'three ,categories of cases in which the Commissioner can interfere with the order passed by him, or otherwise that the order is unfair or unjust, the State Govt. may in the ends of justice pass an appropriate order revising the order made by the Comissioner or otherwise, that the Order passed by it is unfair and unjust, but a revision in such a case does not appear to be competent under section 2 (3). [561 H; 562 A B] Secretary of State vs Mask & Co. ; , followed.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as Chairman, Punjab Public Services Commission. The Chief Minister of Punjab, who had filed an affidavit denying allegations made against him, stated that he wanted certain students of his to be favoured in those examinations and on failure of Shri Saini to oblige him, his wife, the appellant, the wife, he, the husband, had involved into a false charge. The appellant was suspended from service by order dated September 24, 1982. On October 24, 1983, the Chief Minister issued notice to the appellant under Article 317(1) of the Constitution of India calling upon him to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him. The said notice was served on the appellant on December 24,1983. In pursuance of the notices issued by this Court, the Attorney General of India and the Advocate General appeared in these proceedings. On September 24.11.1982 at about 1300 hours Shri Gopal Krishan Saini, Member, Punjab State Public Service Commis sioned that the Chairman or any other person of a Public Service commission should only be removed from his office by order of the President on the ground of misbehaviour and that on failure to oblige the appellant he was compelled to oblige them. The Advocate General of Punjab appeared in this Court and the advocate General of the State of Punjab appearing in these proceeding. On December 24.1981, the Advocate Genera tial of India filed an application before this Court under Article 318(1), praying for a direction to the President to remove the Chairman/s other member of a public Service Commission from his post. The Attorney General and the appellant were also impleaded as respondents in the proceedings. The petition was heard by a Bench of three Judges who held that the order of removal could not be passed without giving an opportunity to both sides, and that the Chief Secretary had no power under Article 319(1). On appeal, the Supreme Court held that if the incident is proved, the conviction or a decree for damages may follow as a matter of course. But, in a reference under article 317(2), this Court ought not embark upon an examination of facts and that its function is limited to determining whether the person concerned is guilty of misbehaviour, and whether the misbehaviour is of such a nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his appointment. The Supreme Court also held that it would not be conducive to justice to decide on the reference on merits. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court could not have entertained the reference without giving any opportunity to the parties to cross examine witnesses who had already filed their affidavits; (ii) the report of the Chief Justice of Punjab was a kind and enough to justify the President 's opinion that a prima facie case exists for an inquiry and report by this court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of dismissal can be passed after the Supreme court has reported on enquiry to the president that the chairman or other person ought to be removed on any such ground. There is no justification for reading into the Article a provision which is plainly not to be found in it especially a provision in the nature of a condition precedent.

The appellants had instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. 4 of 1939) for setting aside the order dated 4 8 1950 of the respondent declaring the temple as a public temple and for a declaration that the temple was a private one and the endowment being held to be of a public nature. The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellants ' suit holding that the deity installed in the temple is a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The High Court reversed this decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the temples and the deity are not public endowments, but were founded on religious faith and the dedication being of a private nature, the Act had no application and the order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (i) the endowment was of a purely private nature and the intention of the founder was merely to instal a family idol in the temples; (ii) the dedication was of purely private character, the object being to confer benefit on God and the property dedicated to the temple by way of public endowment, clause 15 would have clearly provided that the dedication to the family deity is not changed even if the family becomes extinct; (iii) there was no evidence to prove that the endowment in question was of any private nature. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(i) The High court has not properly construed some of the important features contained in the documents and the evidence and has in fact overlooked certain important aspects which completely negative the fact that the endowments were of a very minor nature and by themselves do not prove that it was a public endowment. [834 A C] (ii). In the instant case, the High Court had rightly held that there was never any intention to treat the temple a public one but the intention was to instal the idol in temples only for purposes of the Pani family, and their descendants. The evidence showed that sufficient care has been taken by the Pani families to see that the dedicated family is not altered even if it were to be extinct. [823 C D] (iii). The High Courts have rightly held in favour of the appellants. The conclusion arrived at by the High court are wrong and are based on mispretation of Ext. A and Ext. 1 and misreading of the oral evidence led in the case, which is the only oral evidence adduced in the trial court. [825 E] (iv) The conclusions arrived at are erroneous and are liable to be set aside under section 100 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The appellant Bank was working as a contractor to the military and other authorities. The respondent, who had an interest in the fund, made out a bill on the military authorities for Rs. 49,633/7 then due to him in respect of his supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement more effectively and to secure the interest of the attorneys, the appellant sent the bill to the Military authorities for payment. Before the appellant received the payment, the amount due under the bill was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained against him. The appellant filed objections in the execution proceedings. The objection was dismissed. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A power of attorney authorising a lender to execute a decree then passed in favour of the borrower or which might be passed in his favour in favour by the borrower may apart from and independently of the section operate as an equitable assignment of the debts or fund to which the order refers. In construing the power of Attorney it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, Malhotra and the Bank was of that borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. The loans were to be advanced by the Bank against the Bank 's bills for supplies under these contracts. [599 G H] (2) A contract authorising a banker to pay money due to the borrower is not revocable mandate. It gives the payee no interest in it. An assignment creates an interest and in the Fund. An actionable claim may be transferred under section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act. Where a document does not amount to a transfer within section 130 it may apart, from and independent of the Section operate as a equitable assignment. A pay order is revocable. It gave the payee any interest in an fund. An assign creates an Interest in the money. An assignee creates an estate in the funds. An act creating an interest does not create an interest or operate as such an equitable assigning of the debt or fund. [600 C D] (3) The power of the Attorney authorised the appellant to receive all monies due or to become due to Malhotra in respect off pending contracts with the Government authorities.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., which had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order in appeal by the Tribunal. But on further appeal to the tribunal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was his salary as defined in section 17(3)(ii) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The High Court answered this question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though salary although undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17 has nothing to do with deductions or with exemptions. It is merely a provision defining the expression "salary". [441C D] (2) In defining the term "profits in lieu of pay", the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the asses see from a provident fund, his own contributions to the fund or any interest on such contributions. From that it follows that the receipts of Rs 27,949/ by assessee in respect of salary have to be considered 'as salary. But then the question is what is meant by "profits" in lieu Of salary. [441E F] (3) The expression "Profits in lieu" has nothing only to do either with deductions nor with exemptions and it is merely an explanation defining the expressions "salary" which is not defined in the Act.

The Bihar Act, 1951, was amended by the U. P. Prevention of Cow Slaughter Act, 1949, which provided that no person shall slaughter any animal unless he has obtained in respect of such other animal a certificate in writing signed by the executive authority and the Veterinary officer for the area in which the animal is to be slaughtered. The petitioners who were both Muslims residing in Uttar Pradesh and carrying on business in that State filed petitions under article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the Act, inter alia, on the ground that the impugned Acts were ultra vires articles 14, 19(1)(g) and 31 of the constitution as they infringed their fundamental rights under article 19 (1) (g). The petitioners contended that the Act was void as it contravened their fundamental right to carry on their occupation, trade or business in spite of the mandatory provisions of article 19(i)(g), and that the Acts were not within the protection of the said Article. Held: (i) that the ban on slaughter of animals specified therein only with a view to implement that principal purpose was to secure the preservation and improvement of stock, which is what is meant by organising agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. The ban on the slaughter of such cows, bulls and bullocks was not valid as it infringed their rights under articles 19( 1) (f), 31 and 31. (ii) that a total ban on cattle of all ages and calves of buffaloes, male and female, was constitutionally valid and was in consonance with the directive principles laid down in article 48 of the Constitu tion. The restrictions imposed by the impugned Act were reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19 of the Consti tution and were not unreasonable.
