(iii) that no restriction could be imposed on the cattle of a citizen, who had already attained majority or usefulness.

The respondent joined the service of the appellant company as a typist on a salary of Rs. 30 per month in July 1936. He was appointed Deputy Manager and Assistant Manager in 1947 in the grade of Rs, 120 10 225. Since 1952 he had been receiving a basic salary of about Rs. 245 per month. On November 28, 1955 an explanation was called for from him with regard to the issue of certain bills to consumers of electricity. The respondent submitted his explanation on December 3, 1955, and in which he said that the charge was vague and that after 1949 he was not in any way concerned with the preparation of summaries and annual statements of accounts of the consumers department. On December 5, 1955 the appellant served a memorandum on the respondent terminating his services with effect from January 31, 1956. The company 's reply to the notice denying the allegations, and the company further stated that it had no desire to enter into a discussion with the respondent as to the propriety of the orders passed against him or for reinstatement etc., and that if the Standing Orders did not apply in the case of the respondent, the proper remedy was by means of a suit. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of suspension and termination of his service. The High Court held that the respondent was not an employee within the meaning of section 2(1) of the local Act and on a breach thereof, the respondent had a right to move the High court for appropriate orders under article 227 of the constitution. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Standing Order No. 2 (a) did not require the issue or pass a token, though the definition of a "employee" in the local law relating to employment was wide enough to include all persons who had been declared to be workmen and under Standing Order NO. 4 the respondent could not be said to have been wrongfully dismissed by his private employer. The proper remedy for the respondent against any alleged misconduct was by way of a writ petition and not by invoking the special jurisdiction of the High Courts.

The appellant company, a private limited company, was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in the years 1961 and 1964 65. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The Industrial Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project could not be treated as a separate establishment because under the Act, a Company is itself an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had not earning profits, so that exemption could not he granted to this company in respect of payment of bonus under section 16 of the Act. The Tribunal held on appeal that alloys Steel Project was a separate Establishment in respect whereof separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so, that no bonus was payable until this Project itself earned profits, or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into produced in 1964 65 and did not earn any profits at all till 1967 68. The appellant company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the workmen that (i) the word establishment ' has been used in section 3 of the , and therefore, an establishment cannot be treated a separate unit because under section 2(15) of the . it is not necessary for the Tribunal to go into the question whether the Company is an establishment or is to be treated separately for purposes of computation of bonus; (ii) the proviso to sub section (2) of section 16 does not stand in the way of this claim, because there was no separate accounts in respect thereof and separate balance sheet prepared for each unit and separate profit and losses statement are maintained. HELD: (i)(a) The Tribunal committed an obvious error, as it ignored the indications which were manifest from the language used in the Act; (b) the Tribunal had gone wrong in ignoring the fact that separate balance Sheets and profit & loss accounts are prepared only for the purpose of complying with the requirements of the Companies Act. [632 B C] (ii)(a). The proviso to section 3 will not apply in such a case. According to him, the proviso would be applicable to establishments consisting of different departments, undertakings or branches which are owned, controlled or managed by a company or a corporation of the nature described in that clause. Obviously therefore an establishment could not, on the basis of consolidated accounts, be treated 'as part of the main establishment owned by Hindustan Steel Ltd., as itself an 'establishment. [643 C D] (b). The Tribunal was wrong in holding that merely because alloy steel Project is owned, managed and controlled by Hindustan steel Ltd., it has to be treat as a new undertaking set up by the existing establishments of Hindustan Steel Limited. [641 G H] (c) The proviso would not apply to establishments comprising of different undertakings or branch set up before existing establishments.

The appellant is a sugar mill manufacturing sugar from sugarcane. The respondent assessing authorities issued notices demanding water cess from the sugar manufacturers on the ground that this industry falls under item 15 "processing of animal or vege table products". The assessing authori ties in all the cases issued notice demanding water Cess from the Sugar manufacturers on account of water consumed by them and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the State Boards respectively for imple ment of water pollution. The appellant challenged the said notices before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition holding that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "process ing of animal" or vecege table product. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing Civil Appeal Nos. 4289 of 1991 and 2346 of 1983, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The sugar manufacturing industry does not fall under Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act. It is a fiscal enactment. In order to bring an industry within any of the entires in Schedule I it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. Sugar cane is not a vegetable though it may be an agricultural product. If the botanical meaning to produce some change in a sub stance, however minor in consequence, the change may be. The act of subjecting goods to a treatment or process need not be such as may lead to the production of any new article. The Act is fiscal in nature. [532C D] 1.2 In order that to bring industrial activity within any one of the entitledres in schedule I it had to be judged by what then was the end products produced by the industry. sugar cane is a transformation of an article which is commercially different from that originally existed in the sense that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity whereas in the case of processing it is not necessary to produce a commer cially different article. Processingu effect essentially different article must have a dis tinctive name, character or use. [525E F] 1:3 The word 'vegetable product means product of or made out of vegetable. In the context in which the word "vegetables" is used in Entry 15 it has been understood as refer ring to edible plants or parts of edible plants. In Order to bring any industry within one of these entires, it has also to be found out from the language according to its natural meaning fairly and squarely read. [500G] 1 :4 The word "vesgetable" has been used in contra distinction to the word 'animal '. Though the learned Judges were not prepared to hold that sugar cane was vegetable, the word `veget able ' has been employed in contrac tively different articles. processing of goods is an action, operation or method of treatment applying it to something. [630E F; 529A] 1.(a) The word vegetable in Entry No.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The Rent Controller passed an order of eviction against the appellant, but the Appellate Authority passed an appellate order of ejectment against the tenant. The High Court in revision held that the practice of profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3)(a) (iii) and therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High court was right in holding that the appellant 's practice of law was 'business within the definition of Section 2(3) (a)(iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. It is not a sound principle of construction that words and expressions used in an Act must take their colour from the content in which they appear. [14D E] Bangalore Water Supply & Sewerage Board etc. vs R. Rajappa & Ors., ; , followed. M.P. Sethurama Menon vs Meenakshi Amma & Ors. A.I.R. 1967 Kerala 88, approved. M P. Sethurma Menon V. Meenakshi Amma and Ors., [1949] 2 K.B. 256, referred to.

The respondent was a debtor to the appellant. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. On appeal by certificate the High Court held that the respondent deposited the sum of Rs., 4,00,000 with the appellant in the deposit account. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) there were six principal reasons to indicate that it was a case of an ordinary loan of Rs 4, 00,000 and not an instance of the sum which was deposited with the respondent; (2) the respondent had no authority to bind the appellant by the letter dated 29 September 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta to the effect that the amount would be payable on demand. HELD: (i) The High Court was correct in decreeing the suit. [575 A] (ii) In a deposit is something more than a mere loan of money. It will depend on the facts of each case whether the transaction is clothed with the character of a deposit of money or not. The surrounding circumstances at the time of the transaction, the pecuniary position of the parties and the surrounding circumstances, the relationship and the manner in which they treated the transaction would throw light on the true form of the transactions. [574 C D] Nawab Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , referred to. (iii) The respondent had not been able to prove that there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943, because he was unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills. All figured in the transaction. A more loan of RS. 4 lakhs only to the account of Messrs Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills and India Supplies from time to time and all that happened in that place of Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills was the creditor of M/s India Supplies on the one hand and Lakshmi Ratan Mills on the other, that moneys were lent and advanced by Lakshmi Ratan Spinning Mills to India Supplies. All speak of the proper maintenance and keeping of books of account and that it is not possible to arrange the presence of the writer of the entry. Suggestion of tampering is a serious one. The original entries were called for from the High court. There was just a substitution of the creditor debitor relationship by substituting the respondent in place of Laxmi Ratan Cotton Mill. All appeared without any doubt to have been written at the same time as the rest of the writing.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under sub section (1) of section 3 of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were served on him on the basis of a warrant issued by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986. In the writ petition filed in this Court it was contended that the period of parole had to be excluded in recok ing the period from 15th May, 1986 to February 28. 1987 and that the petitioner was already in custody at the time the order of detention was served on the detenu. Dismissing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu was already In custody when the order was made does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the Court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining authori ty was aware of the fact that he was already neces sarily satisfied that his order of deten tion became necessary. [844C D] 2. The mere service of the detention order on the petitioner in jail would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention, if that is necessary to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial to the security of the State. May be, in a given case there yet may be the need to preventive detention of a person already in jail. But in such a situation the detaining au thority must disclose awareness of the facts that the person against whom an order is being made is to the knowledge of the authority already in prison and yet for compelling reasons a preventive deten tion order needs to be made. [861B C] 3. The detaining authority must disclose aware of fact that a detenu was actually in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that he had been in detention. In such a case there is suffi cient material to show that the Detaining Authority was aware about the fact of the detenu being already in detention and yet, he was satisfied that the order would be no deterrent to his desperate activity. [862E F] 4. The law laid down by this Court in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Etah, ; , is not applicable to the facts of the present case because there is sufficient material to establish that the authority was aware that the detenue was alreadyin custody and he was yet he been sub jectly satisfied. [863F] 5.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The employment of casual labour was limited on the Telecommunication side. As an alternative to regular absorption, it was proposed that a wage related to the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled casual labour with the benefit of neutralisation for the rise in cost index as applicable to regular employees may be effected as is available to regular employee of the Posts & Telegraphs department at the rates equivalent to the Minimum pay in the pay scales of the regularly employed workers in the Telephone Department. In respect of categories (ii) and (iii), i.e., casual labourers, the wages paid to them were very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to regular workmen of the Post and Telegraph Department at the rate equivalent to minimum pay in pay scale applicable to the regular employees of the Postal and Telegraph department at rates equivalent thereto. The petitioners submitted a statement of demands through the Secretary General, BPTEF, New Delhi, that a wages related to minimum of pay scale for the semi skilled/skilled labour who had not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more with the Department as on 1st April, 1980 and have completed 1200 days of continuous service in a period between 1st May, 1980 to 31st March, 1981. The respondents submitted that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular workmen are enjoying. It was also contended that since they belonged to the categories of casual workers and are being regularly employ ed, they were not entitled for the same privilege which the employees are enjoying, and that the petitioners were not being paid wages far less as applicable under the pay revision scales applicable to them in the Postal Department at rates corresponding to the scale of minimum pay payable to regular labourers. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The classification of employees into three categories namely (i) those who have completed more than 1200 days service and not completed 1200 years of service and (ii), those who had completed 720 day of service or not completed 13 days of work and not completing 1200 days ' service and less than 1200 day of continuous employment for an unreasonably long period is not a wise policy. [608C D] 2. The Government should be a model employer. It implies the existence of certain important obligations which the State has to discharge. The right to free choice of employment, the right to protection against unemployment, the rights to protection from unemployment, and the right of every one who works just to benefit and favourable conditions of work, the Right to protection to unemployment,the right to freedom of choice of work are some of the rights which have to be ensured by appropriate legislative and executive measures. It is true that all these rights cannot be extended simultaneously. But they do indicate the socialist goal.

The assessee, a public limited company, was issued with a notice under section 22(1) of the Income tax Act requiring every person whose total income during the previous year exceeded the maximum amount which was not chargeable to income tax. The assessee did not make a return of his income and added a footnote to the return. The Income tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal rejected the contention of the Department that the amount of Rs 59,026 could not be included in his income as he had suppressed his income or given incorrect particulars thereof, the period during which action under section 34(1)(a) was taken was the extended one of 8 years. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the notice issued under section 33 of the Act by the Income Tax Officer on 27 2 1950 was invalid inasmuch as it was completed four years after the end of the relevant assessment year, and (ii) the Income 'tax Officer had no power to issue a notice tinder section 22 (2). HELD: The notice under s.34(1), read with section 34 (3) of Act must be deemed to have been issued on or before March 2, 1951. [123 B] In the present case the notice was invalid because it was not served within the time fixed by the notice under sub section (1). The Income Tax officer could have avoided the result by issuing a notice to the assessee under section 23(2) and not remaining inactive until the period was about to expire.

The first petitioner is a registered Central Trade Union claiming to represent about 85 per cent of the officers working in various nationalised banks. The petitioners, who are members of the nationalised banks, filed writ petitions before this Court praying for a direction to the Central Government to appoint a nominee of the majority association of each of the banks as a member of its Board of Directors. The circular was challenged by the Reserve Bank of India on the ground that it was contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 (Act 5 of 1970). It was contended on behalf of the Reserve bank that the Circular dated 23.8.1982 was ultra vires section 9 of the Act as it cuts at the root of the representative form of selection for appointment to the Board of directors as contemplated by the statute. Allowing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme in effect postulates all appointments to be by nomi nation. In the case of non workmen, the choice is not restricted to any panel and the only condition postulated is consultation with the ReserveBank of India. [858D] 1.2 The scheme is thus understood by the Government to be limited to the panel of names furnished by the representative union of workmen or non association of employees. The Central Government has a discretion to avoid election even where election is appropriate and feasible in respect of a particular category of persons. The very object of leaving the choice to the central Government as to the mode, which is election or nomination, is to enable it reasonably exercise its discretion in such a way as to give the best form of repre sentation to every category of person mentioned in the Act. It may be possible to appoint one of the deposors by election instead of nomination. It would be perfectly in order for the Central Govern ment to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repres sentatives of the concerned employees, and if necessary, to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. The assessee, who was the respondent in the appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and not to the Income tax Officer, was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income Tax Act. The Tribunal declined to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of the penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay proceedings as well as the collection thereof pending the appeals since that powers were incidental and incidental to its original jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power of stay by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It wilt only be when a strong prima facie case is made out that the tribunal will consider whether to stay recovery proceedings and on what conditions and the stay will be granted in most deserving and appropriate cases where the Tribunal was satisfied that the entire purpose of the appeal will be frustrated or rendered nugatory by allowing the recovery proceed ings to continue during the pendency of the appeals. [69 E F] (2) The power of the stay by a Tribunal is likely not to be exercise in a mechanical way or a matter in course of course, in view, of the Special nature of tax and revenue.[70 G] Polini vs Grey, ; , followed. (3) In the present case, the Appellate Tribunal had no right to move even an application when an appeal is pending before the Tribunal under section 220(6), but the Act was silent in that behalf when an appellate tribunal is pending. It could well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction it impliedly grants the power, of doing all such acts, or employing such means as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory.

The respondent was a constable in U. P. Police Force and was posted as an officer incharge of the Police Station, Intiathok, District Gonda. Complaints were received by him from the Superintendent of Police and the respondent submitted his explanation for his conduct. The Superintendent of police after making enquiries recommended the transfer of the respondent to some other station. On November 3, 1952, the respondent was ordered to be dismissed from service with effect from the said date. The appeal preferred by the respondent against the order of dismissal was dismissed by the Deputy Inspector General of Police but the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court which was allowed on August 5, 1954, and the writ petition filed by the respondents was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Governor exercised his pleasure through the Superintendent Of Police and as the police Regulations were only administrative directions, the non compliance therewith would not in any way affect the validity of the order dismissing the respondent. HELD: The departmental enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the Respondent in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magical inquiry and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 489(2). [677 E F] The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the question, if substantially the subject matter of the Magisterial enquiry and the departmental trial is the same, does not affect its validity.

The appellant was promoted to supertime grade II on February 18, 1971 and was later promoted as Director of Health Services. The promotion of respondents 4 to 24 was challenged by the appellant on diverse grounds: (1) that the promotions were in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules; (2) that there was no justification for creation of posts or for making ad hoc appointments; (3) that in passing a decision on certain facts, the Central Government had set up various institutions for medical relief and medical education. The appellant contended that the promotion of Respondents 4 to24 was invalid because they were not the subject matter of dispute in this appeal; (4) that since the initial constitution of service on September 9, 1966, any future promotion to super time grade II could only be made in promotions from amongst those belonging to Specialists Grade I only, the appellant was entitled to be promoted from that date. The respondents contended that there were some promotions to super Time grade II and that the appellant had not even a remote chance of promotion; (5) that he was not qualified for being promoted to any supertime Grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists Grade II, and that his promotion was in contravention Of rule 8(3); and (6) that as the appellant claimed promotion to Super time grade 11 from February 18. 1971, he should have been promoted from the date on which each of them was promoted. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that all posts must be filled by promotion from amongst persons who belong to Specialist Grade only. [57 D] 2. The post of Director Health Services, Manipur is a promotional post and assigned to a speciality it can only be filled in by promotion and not in any other manner and particularly by transfer. Ordinarily if it is to be filled on promotion yet when some one who is already in that grade is transferred to the newly created post and the newly constituted post vacated by him can be filled, in accordance with the relevant rule, he cannot be said to have been superseded in violation of article 16. [58 E] 3. The word 'category ' has been used in Rule 8(1) (a) of 1966 rules in general and rule 8 (3). The word "category" is not defined in the Rules but it can be read as a whole. It cannot be interpreted to mean that it can have only been filled by promotions yet when one who was already in the same grade is promoted to the later created post, and the post so vacated by the then created post would remain vacant in the newly appointed post. [59 G H] 4. The expression 'categories ' has not been defined in Rule 2(d) of the 1966 Rules. It is difficult to entertain the contention that all 28 posts must he filled by direct recruitment as well as by promotion in the ratio prescribed therein.

The Punjab Security Land Tenures Ordinance, 1953, was enacted whereby ceiling on lands ownership was laid down surplus lands which were taken away for settling tenants and other peasants and peAsant proprietors created proprietorship. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientifically worded. The system of the Punjab Security Act, 1954, which came into force on April 15, 1953 provides that ceiling in land ownership shall be set surplus land. Section 2(5) defines 'small land owner ' to mean a person who has in his possession any land or in the land after the commencement of this Act and includes a person to whom he is an heir. The appellants were tenants of land in excess of the permissible area as set out in section 2(3). They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the Collector 's order on the ground that section 19B read with section 10A did not affect their petitioners ' transfers and that the provisions of section 10 A did not apply to them. The provisions of the impugned Act are designed to achieve the agrarian reform scheme of agrarian reform which is equitable ownership and the reform philosophy is redistributive justice the rural goal being small peaser proprietorship. [632 B C] 2. The object of the agrarian reforms was to preserve the surplus stock in the hands of the State. Section 10A(b) strikes at a gift made by the respondent in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed of some dimensions which Indian jurists will have to tackle. The genre of agrarian reforms is equitable and ownership and reform philosophy was redistribution justice the Rural goal being large peasent proprietorship. What difference does it make as to how you came by a large holding from the standpoint above outlined? The genres of agrarian legislation imputed legislative presumptions and assumed social values valid in a prior era. An Act which has provided for ignoring decrees and orders of courts is to be ignored in dealing with surplus lands. [732 C D] 3. The law takes care to see that such excess is also made available for re settlement of tenants ejected or to be ejected under cl. (i) sub section (1) of section 9 or other purpose notified by Government.

The plaintiffs instituted a suit for possession of certain lands on the basis of a will executed by Amarshah in their favour. The first plaintiff claimed that he was entitled to the Zamindari on the death of Pratapshah and on the date of his father 's death, Pratapshah had become absolute and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof and the plaintiffs were on that account not entitled to claim the compensation payable or payable in respect thereof. The Trial Court held that the genealogy set up by the plaintiffs represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah and on their death, that Amarshash had made a will dated December 8, 1950, setting up by them the first plaintiff as he was found suitable to hold the Zamindari, that the order of the Governor recognising as Dayaram as Zamindar was not binding and conclusive, for it was not shown that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of the power conferred by the Chanda Patent; that the will set up was genuine while the will dated 12th December 1950, set up, by the defendants was a genuine document. The High Court agreed with the Trial Court on appreciation of evidence held that there were no suspicion as to the genuineness of the will and that the scribe who wrote the will did not belong to the village to which Amarsh belonged. It further held that it was impossible for the first defendant Dayaram to produce before the court the will setting up the first appellant 's widow Ratnabai, that he had made the will in favour of the second plaintiff after giving a life interest in favour Of the plaintiffs after giving him a lifeinterest in favour thereof. In appeal by the appellants, the High Court affirmed the decree passed by the Trial court in respect of the Zamindari replying upon the rule of primogeniture and held that according to the custom governing succession Dhanora Zamindari devolved upon Pratapshah on the heirs of Amarshih and that on the demise of Pratapldas the first respondent became entitled to succeed to the zamindari on the strength of Pratapmbershah. The appellants contended that Pratapshah was not genuine, that by the will it created a life estate in their hands and that it rested with Government to confer it; and that under the terms of the Chanda patent the Zamindari devolves on the deceased holder on the succession of Pratapmises and that therefore the order was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari. Held: (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the document was not a genuine one, but that it created an estate in favour only of Pratapstone. It was not intended by the rule that the holder of the zamindari had merely a life interests and on his death the holder was bound to hand over the Zamindari to the next heir in order of succession if the Zamindar had removed him and the heir will get the right; (ii) The grant was for life of the grantee, the Governor was not granting afresh the Zamindari; he merely determines the successor in accordance with the custom of the family.

The appellants filed a suit for recovery of possession of a portion of the ground floor of a building on the ground that the respondent bonafide required the premises in suit. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the provisions contained in section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947 were not applicable to the suit; (ii) the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for a period of one month after the service of notice terminating the tenancy; and (iii) the contractual rent in respect of the premises was not unreasonable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions contained under section 12 (3)(b) of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates Act 1947 are attracted. [635G] 2.1 In the instant case the respondent landlord had made no payment within the period of two months after service of the notice terminating his tenancy. The suit was filed on 11th September, 1963. The respondent landlord filed a Suit on 2nd February 1967. In the appeal to the Supreme Court it is contended that the High court should have held that the case fell under section 13(3) (a) or section 12 of the Act and would take the suit out of the provisions of that sub section. [643B C] 2.(i) The provisions in section 11(3), (4) and (5) of section 12 are attracted, because, the dispute in the present case was one which must have been raised before service of a notice terminating tenancy. [641C D] (ii). Section 12(2)(a), as it then stood, is not limited only to a dispute raised within one month of the service notice of the termination of the tenancy but also to any other mode of raising the dispute at any stage of the suit. [651D E] 2(i) In the present appeal the respondent tenant had made an application on 5th January 1957 for fixation of standard rent under section 11 (3) of Act. The tenant made no application in terms of section 11, (4), and (6) of that Act. [632E F] 3.2 The provisions of sub section (3), and Explanation thereto and confer a right on the tenant where the legislation does not contemplate such a right. The provision in section II(3). of the is attracted. The High Court nullifies the provisions embodied in section 13 and Explanation thereunder and confers a right upon the tenant when the legislation did not contemplate that such a power. [611B] (iii).

The respondent company was incorporated in England. The Aluminium Limited, a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600,000 divided into 360 shares and the Aluminium Company Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on board of directors of the Aluminium Ltd. to act as its representative. The company was reconstituted in 1943 and the respondent company held majority of the shares. In exercise of the power given by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent Company, the Aluminium company appointed three new directors on the board of Directors of the Electric Company. The question for decision was whether in computing the standard profits of excess profits tax for five chargeable accounting periods ending on 31st December 1941 and 31st March 1942, the Income tax Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that the directors of respondent company had a controlling interest therein as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act. Held, that the shares held by the Aluminium Limited were not his votes but were the votes of the aluminium Ltd. In such a situation, in the eye of the law, the controlling interest remained vested in the Aluminium Corporation and was at no time vested in Mr. L. G. Bash, one of the directors, had the authority to exercise the voting power of the company in fact control its affairs at general meetings and as such had "a controlling interest" in the respondent. The shares were always subject to his will and ordering the controlling interests which the holder of the majority of shares had never passed to the agent. The controlling interest vested in M/s. L G Bash was not his vote but was his votes of a third person who held the majority. The directors of a company may well be regarded as having "a control interest" therein, in a company when they hold and are entered into the share register as holders of the minority shares. When a shareholder holding the majority authorises an agent to vote for him in respect of the share held by him, the agent acquires no interest, legal or beneficial, in his shares. The shareholders, therefore, have "a voting interest" within the meaning of section 2(21) and ordering and, therefore. they cannot be said to have "an controlling interest".

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st October 1957, he opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In the year 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promo rions in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948. The respondent was working as an Accounts Officer Grade II, in the State of Karnataka. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to him were promoted on their having passed the S.A.S. examination and on 30th Decem ber 1966, certain persons junior ted to the respondent were promoted. On 21st November 1972, some of the persons junior ly to the respond ent were promoted as Accounts Officer while promotion was denied to him. The writ petition filed by the respondent challenging the validity of the Resolution dated 19th May 1969 and the appointment of some persons senior to him was dismissed by the High Court on 13th February 1973. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the allottees are exempted from passing the Departmental Examination I and Kannada language test for the purpose of earning increments and for promotion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Resolution dated 5th January 1970 cannot be understood as altering the position existing at the time when the Board passed the Resolution by which it had resolved to amend its Regulations. [510C] 2. The resolution dated 5rd January 1970, cannot be interpreted as altering its position existing on that date because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the resolution. The inference that the allotment were exempt ed from passing 'of the examination is not justified. Further before the Resolution there is nothing to indicate that the allotments were not required to pass the examina tion. [511G] 3. The Board itself considered the question in all its aspects and resolved that passing of the S .A.T. Examination was not insisted prior to that Resolution in the case of allot tees for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before. [ 512E F] 4. The Committee considered the ques tion in all their aspects and decided that passing the Sect ion of the Board could have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the Board in exercise o f powers conferred by the statute.

The petitioner, a student of the police custody at about 8 p.m., on 1.12.1987, was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraikela Railway Station and he could not be apprehended thereafter in spite of a search; and the dead body of his son was thrown on the rail track. The petitioner, who was detained and guarded by Police Constable Chhabilakur of Police Outpost Jeraikela, filed a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation made therein consequent upon the death of his daughter 's son. The State of Orissa and its police officers including Sarat Chandra 590 Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur, were treated as a Writ Petition under Article 226 of the Constitu tion for determining their claim of compensa tion made therein. The defence of the respondents was that the petitioner 's mother had managed to escape from police custody on 1 12.121987 at 8 pm. on 1st December 1987 and it was likely that he was run over by a passing train when he sustained fatal injuries inflicted to him while he was in police custody; and thereafter his dead body was thrown at the railway yard near the Police Out Post Jeraipose, where he was detained, and guarded the dead bodies of his wife. The respondents contended that the evidence adduced during the inquiry did not support the defence of respondents and there was no reason to reject the finding of the learned District Judge that the victim died on account of multiple injuries inflicted by him while in police force at the Police outpost Jeriakela, where the petitioner was detained; and that consequently the respondents ' responsibility for the unnatural death of her son was denied. The trial court held that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt and accordingly dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the burden of proof in a proceeding under Article32 or 226 of Constitution is a remedy available in public law based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private law in an action based on tort. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The primary source of the public law proceedings stems from the prerogative writs and the courts have therefore to act firmly but with certain amount of circumspection and self restraint lest proceedings under Article 21 of the constitution seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental right are established to have been flagrantly infringed by calling upon the State to repair the damage done by its officers. [610C D] 1.2 The primary sources of the Public law proceedings stem from the discretionary writs and courts have, therefore, to evolve 'new tools and devise new remedies for the purpose of vindicating these precious fundamental rights. It is an obligation of the state, to ensure that there is no infringement of the indefeasible right of a citizen to life except in accordance with law while the citizen is in its custody. The precious right guaranteed by Article 21 cannot be denied to convicts, under trials or other prisoners in custody, except according to procedure established by law.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The petitioner contended that the two prisoners had been sentenced to imprisonment for life and that the petition filed by them should be allowed. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) Rule 549(4) of the Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails which is applicable to Delhi provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. Journalists or newspapermen are not expressly referred to in clause (4) but that does not mean that they can always without good reasons and without good reason be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. If it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview may have subject himself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. There is a provision in the Rules that if a person wants to interview any prisoner he can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. Taking an overall view of the matter, it cannot be said that there was no reason why newspapermen who could broadly, and we do not see any reason why newspapersmen who can broadly, should be permitted to interview the prisoners. [1187G H; 1189A B] (2) Rule 559A provides that all reasonable indulgence should be allow to a condemned person in the matter of interviews with relatives, legal adviser and approved religious ministers. Surprisingly, but it does not provide that no newspapermen will be allowed to interview them. If the petitioner is found guilty of any weighty reasons for doing so, which he will always expect to be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore we do see no reason how the petitioner should not be allowed again to interview these prisoners. The Superintendent of Jail, Tihar is directed to allow the aforesaid representatives to be present at the time of the execution of the death sentence.

The appellant mortgaged a tea garden to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. The respondent mortgaged the tea garden with an intention to sell it to M. The Receiver took possession of the estate on February 26, 1950 and the appellant was asked to furnish security for the amount due under the mortgage. On March 26, 1951 the appellant filed a suit against the Receiver and the respondent for recovery of the amount in accordance with the mortgage decree. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the respondent 's appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Subordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to enforce the surety bond executed by the appellant as he was neither the successor nor the assign of the District Judge; and (2) under the terms of the bond, the appellant became liable for the loss caused to the tea Garden by fire. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The order for the recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the receiver can be executed against the appellant to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the term of the surety. [360 G] Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where any person has become liable as a surety for the fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of the Court in any suit or in any proceeding consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed by such person against the surety to the amount to which he has rendered himself personally liable. By the bond the appellant rendered itself liable as surety for his fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the orders passed by the court. Therefore, the order for recovery was not liable for loss caused thereunder by fire and it was not possible for him to enforce it.

The appellants were dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat. In accordance with the U.P. Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959, they sold the wheat to the Central Food Controller under the provisions of the U P. Wheat Procurement Control Order, 1960. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants in compliance with the provisions contained in the U .P. Wheat Projections (Levy). The appellants challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court. The High Court held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the Act and that the sales were on that account not liable to be taxed under the UP. Sales Tax Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller; that the price for wheat was paid for sugarcane could not be taxed as there was a "sale", within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2(h) of the Uttar Pradesh Sales Tax, Act, 1947. HELD: The High court was right in holding that there was any contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the term of the u.P., and that sales were not liable for tax under the Act. [682 C D] M/s New India Sugar Mills ' case, ; , followed.

The appellant was detained under the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him on August 7, 1986 and he was informed that his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Act. He was released from prison on June 23, 1986. On August 7. 1986 an order for his detention had been made under section 11 of the Act and his report was more than three weeks after the detention which commenced on the making of the order of detention though it was within three months of the date of the second order of deten tion. The Advisory Board made its report on September 26, 1986, and referred to the High Court for its opinion regarding the sufficiency of cause for such detention. The appellant contended that there had been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) of the Constitution inasmuch as no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months from the date on which its report was made. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was a contravention under the constitutional provisions afforded by Article 22(1) and therefore, the appellant is entitled to be set at liberty. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The substantive requirements are, the only safeguard available to the detenu since he is not obliged to go beyond the subjective satis faction of the authority. [209C] 2.1 In habeas corpus proceedings it is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date when hearing of the case. If the report of the advisory Board is to be obtained within three weeks, it is no answer to saying that the representation though not made within three days was disposed of before the hearing of it. If a reference to an Advisory board is to he made within 3 weeks, the detention though not in accordance with the proviso that if there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of a period of 12 months from such date of detention under the earlier detention order.

The petitioner, who was the father of respondent No. 2, had filed a civil suit for setting aside the award made in terms of the award under section 17 of the . The trial court dismissed the application and the first appellate court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction as the earlier proceedings were not without jurisdiction. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in dismissing the application in terms thereof. [537C] 2.1 A proper arbitration agreement in terms section 2(a) of the is a proper arbitration clause in terms. Section 2(b) of that Act provides that the Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred. In this case, there was no such express or implied prohibition nor any inability of the Judge concerned. [437E F] 2(i) The conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator, is not relevant according to the judicial Committee, whether they had rightly or wrongly decided it. [540F G] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the earlier proceeding was without jurisdiction and that the revision before the High Court suffered from res judicata.

The appellant mortgaged certain properties to the respondent for a sum of Rs. 59,000 and the mortgagee was appointed receiver of that property. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent on January 2, 1941, for enforcing the mortgage of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondent 's claim to recover his debt was protected under section 36 (5) of the Transfer of Property Act and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that if the execution case came to an end on January 30, 1937, the proceedings were within the definition in section 2(22) of , and therefore, the respondent could not be reopened as he had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 28. HELD: The appeal must fail. The order of the executing court dated January 30,, 1937, was made on a petition filed by the appellant under section 53 of the , and the respondent was not an assignee within the meaning of section 2 (22). [589 D] The words "instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of January 1939" in the proviso to sub section(1) are wide enough to include a proceeding in execution for any purpose mentioned in clauses (a), (b) or (c) of Section 2 (21). In the present case, as to whether a sub mortgagee is an assignee of the mortgage debt and of the mortgagee 's right to recover the debt from the original mortgagor. [589 E] The respondent was an assignee under section 3(5) and not an application at all. He had not only received the notices referred to therein but also made request for withdrawal of attachment, which was merely consequential and would follow as a matter of course on full satisfaction of the decree being recorded. The respondent ' claim to recovery his debt is protected under Section 36 (6).

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. He transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family to the appellant, who had been his concubine since 1945. The appellant instituted suits against his widow and sons for recovery of possession of the properties on the ground that they were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court dismissed O.S. No. 62/54 but decreed O. S. No,. 63/54. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: (1) The transfer under exhibit A 1 was not supported by any consideration by way of cash or delivery of jewels. This finding is not challenged before the High Court. [45 B] (2) The transfers were made in consideration of past cohabitation and there was no motive for the gift under exhibit B 1 and A 2. The transfer was without consideration, because, according to section 6(h), of the , the past cohabitations were a valuable consideration and Venkatacharyulu agreed to make the transfers in consideration Of past cohabiting. [46 C] (3) The gifts were not validated by the disruption of the joint Hindu family in 1947. After the disruption, Venkatachariulu was free to make a gift of his divided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concabine. The gifts under exhibit I and A2 were not hit by section 6 (h). [45 D E] (4) The properties gifted under exhibit 1 and B 2 were not saved by section 4 of the . But the properties gifted tinder exhibit A1 and A II were not invalid because, the previous cohabitation was the consideration for his earlier promise to transfer the properties to her.

The appellant Life Insurance Corporation of India, which was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, had its registered office in Bombay. The business of the Life Insurance Corpora tion was taken over by the Life Inspec tive Corporation of india on 9.4.69 and the assignment was made in favour of the wife of the deceased employee. The appellant Corporation issued a notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to the Manager of the LIC at Nagpur directing him to pay interest for the period after date of maturity of the policies. The amount of Rs.341570 payable against the first policy which matured on 14.9.72 was paid by the Corporation to the nominee of the appellant Corporation. The widow of the insured person, before the Income tax Officer, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under Section 226(1)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961 and also the order of the Commissioner withdrawing the notice on the ground that the delay was Occasioned by the I.T.O. in pursuance to the I .T.o. 's notice under s.226(3). The High Court dismissed the writ petition as withdrawn. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant Corporation that the liability for payment of interest had been correctly fastened on the appellant, and no relief had been sought against the IT.U. On behalf of respondent No. 1 it was urged that the I T.O., in pursuance of the I 'T. O. in pursuant to the notice issued under section 225(3), had made the requisite statement on oath under s 226(2)(vi). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The contention that the appellant corporation could not be held liable for payment o f interest for any period prior to revocation of the notices by the l.T.,O. cannot be accepted. [103E] (2) The fact that the Corporation had made a formal statement on behalf o.f. the L.I.C. on 5.12.75, did not involve even remotely the possibility of any risk of personal liability. On the contrary, real risk of the L I.I .C. being treated defaulter under clause (x) thereof, within a reasonable time, without objecting to the demand by denying its liability to the assessee in the manner prescribed in cl.(vi) thereof within a period of one month, without objection, was not made since it involved the likelihood of exposing the LI.I.,C. or any of its officers to personal liability for the income tax dues of the asses see.

The appellant was the Chief Justice of a High Court. He had the advantage of reading the judgment of this Court in Canara Bank Ltd., Bombay vs The Warden Insurance Co. Ltd., and Ors. , and the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law; and the second part of section 29(2) provides that where any special or Local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application by any special local or local laws, a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule is satisfied. The appellant was an advocate in the High Court and was also a party to the Letters Patent Appeal. He was also an advocate on the Original Side of the Calcutta High Court as well as in the Bar Council of India. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended that the special law prescribed by the first schedule was satisfied in the present case; that the appeal was governed by the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore, the appropriate article of the Limitation Act would be applicable to an appeal under section 116 A(2). HELD: (i) The special law is a period prescribed by section 3 of the Indian Limitation Act. It is not necessary for the purpose of computing the period of 30 days prescribed by that Article to apply in order to render the provisions of section 4 of the , applicable to appeals or applications under the Code. [166 D] (ii) The general provisions of the Civil Procedure Code are excluded from those prescribed therefor. In other words, if the special orlocal law prescribes a period within which the appeal should be filed and the special procedure prescribed by it is satisfied, the special Act would apply even to a case where the first Schedule to the Limitation act had not prescribed any period of limit different from that prescribed by tile First Schedule. [167 E F] (iii) The second part, sub section (2) of section 28 of the Act is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or other local law for which a period Of limitation is provided in the first proviso. Therefore what has to be seen whether a suit, Appeal or application under a particular local law is of a similar kind to one for which period of time limit is prescribed in the First schedule. [168 G H] (iv) The expression "appeal" in article 156 of the Constitution means an appeal governed by that Code. Article 156 is not intended to be exhaustive and does not ordinarily deal with substantive rights. It deals only with a question appertaining to the adjective law, such as the law of limitation.

The appellant, a transport service operator in the District of Mathura, was directed to stand for the purpose of allowing passengers to take into and get down from the stage carriages in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court of Allahabad under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the District Magis trate had no power to appoint any area as a bus stand under section 76 of the Act and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses was only a halting place and hence the order made under section76 of the is unassailable. The appellant filed a writ Petition in the High COurt challenging the validity of the order dated 22.5.1986 declaring the old bus stand of T.A. Baldev (Mathura) as authorised Bus stands/Halting place, as authorised bus stand/Halsing place. It was also contended that the route where the bus operators had asked to start their buses at the bus stand and to get down at the same stand, and to pay commission to stand from T. A. Faithfully, Sd 8/10 illegible Executive Officer (Seal) Town Area Committee Town Committee, Baldev (walia). The High CO Court dismissed it on the view that the location of the appellant 's bus stand was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 76 of tho Act confers power on the State Government to make rules for the pur pose of carrying into effect the provisions of Chapter VI. Clause (e) of sub section (2) of section 68 of the Uttar Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 which authorises the District Magistrate to specify places within the limits of any municipality, notified area town or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where public service vehicles may stand either indefinitely or for a specified period of time. The other bye laws provided for a levy of a fee of Re. 1 for every 8 hours or part thereof in respect of the use of the bus stands by such buses and for the issue of a permit on such payment. [713C D] 2.2 Section 76 is also in Chapter VI which is in Chapter IV of the , containing the provisions relating to 'control of traffic ', confers the power on tho State Government not specifically to make any rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and fees, if any, which may be charged for their use. [771C] 2 3.3 The Town Area committee can derive no assistance from this rule. It only authorises the district Magis trict Magistrate to exercise the powers under section 77 of the . The High court was therefore in error in upholding the impugned order passed by the District magistrate.

The appellants were tried for offences under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside their conviction and sentenced them to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. On appeal by special leave the appellants contended that there was an attempt on the part of the appellants to transport paddy to Delhi and so there was no export of paddy within the meaning of para 2(a) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. HELD: The conviction of the appellant under section 3 of the Act is set aside. [665 G] The appellants should not have been convicted under section 8 of the . [665 A B] The sentence of fine only will meet the ends of justice if it is shown that they intended to set fire to a hastack at the time of purchase. Nor can he be convicted of an attempt to commit it. If a man buys a box of matches, he cannot be convicted under the Act if he approaches the stack with the stacks with the matches in his pocket, but if he bends down near the stump with the match in his hands, he does not proceed further in its progress, the acts already done would be completely harmless. [667 C D] The sufficiency of the act of a criminal attempt is a reus of a crime and those which are sufficiently proximate to it amount to an attempt at committing it.

The respondent, a Managing Agent of the appellant company, was appointed as the managing agent of the said company. The remuneration payable to the managing agents was fixed at Rs. 75,77693 and the managing agency commission was paid by the transferees. In the accounting year 1944 45, the Income tax Officer included in the assessable income of the transferees a sum of Rs. 2,37,602 and the respondent, the Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd., received from the appellant and the Managing Agency commission payable by the respective companies to the respective transferees. The Income tax officer assessed the respondent for the assessment year 1944 46 and the chargeable accounting period 1st January 1943, to 31st December 1943, and the original income tax and excese profits tax assessments were made on the basis that they had earned the income by rendering services as Managing Agents to the Companies for the respective periods that they continued to be the Managing Agents and the transferees had rendered the services for the balance of the periods completing the full year of accounting and had earned proportionate commission. The respondent claimed that the managing Agency commission was earned for services rendered and therefore it was taxed in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the Managing Agent and not in the hand of the persons to whom it was assigned, and that therefore the amount of commission which the latter actually received included the Sassoons were liable to tax. The Tribunal held that the respondent was liable to be apportioned between the appellant Company and the assignee (or assignor) as the case might be. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The managing agency remuneration for the year 194445 was not by itself sufficient to vest in the assignee a beneficial right to the entire income payable after the date of assignment. But it was not necessary that at the time when the profits accrued it should have been ascertained and paid in the chargeable account period though it was ascertained and came to be paid in 1944. [351 B C] (2) The remuneration for each year was the income of a managing agent and not the assignee or the sole income of both the transferees, and therefore, the respondent could not be said to have accrued to them during the chargeable assessment period. In determining the place where the profits had accrued it was necessary to find when the profit had accrued.

The other inmate of the House was the appellant 's wife, Kirpa Shyam Shankar (P.W. 17) sleeping in the verandah inside the room. The accused came out of his house and took buck to go down to the courtyard of the deceased 's house. On the morning of August 13, 1963, Sunderpatti, was found in the company of the accused for fast time when she was alive; (4) during the night 3 persons, namely, the appellant and the deceased had some quarrel on the Janmashtami day in the evening and the occurrence had to be persuaded through the influence of their neighbors, Abdullah, Mohammeda neighbour and his wife Abdullah. The appel lant brought her back and thereafter went out to go out of a house where he saw his father going out of that house murmuring something; (5) on the early morning of the next day, P.W 17 was asked by his father to go to the place of nature and when he came back to his verandah, the deceased heard some gurgling sound and he saw the accused going out from the house in the night in the morning and the dead body had been found with severe injuries in her room; (6) on a day about 8 years after the occurrence the appellant came out at 60 p. mur murmanuring something, and thereafter the deceased went back to their house and saw his uncle going out there of the 'house murfuring something and he noticed that the accused had some altercation on the first Janmasami day and in the afternoon he saw him going out and sounding the door of the courtyard and saw the appellant going out. The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. The general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The management of Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd., the management of the Orissa Insurance Company Ltd. vested in the custodian of the New India Assurance Co. Ltd. and vested in it. Under the Act, the Board of Directors was empowered to terminate the service of the officer/employee of the insurer. The appellant challenged the termination order by filing a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge on November 11, 1983. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 5 does not become arbitrary or void offending Article 14. Once the Board reaches a decision to abolish the post, in consequence the service the officer or employee is couched in Rule 5 also capable of that interpretation. [225E F] 2. The rule is not ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution. If so read, the rule is invalid. The Court ought not to interpret the statutory provisions unless compelled by their language, in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [226F] 3. Rule 9 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate services of a permanent employee by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. The employee ordinarily would be superannuated on completion of his 55th year unless the Board continues for an extended period as may be determined from time to time. [227F] 4. Rule 8 was available for taking action for misconduct but was not availed. Therefore, the impugned order terminating the services of the appellant is illegal. What would be the consequence? Normally the appellant was entitled to reinstatement but in our view the ends of justice would be met by directing the respondent to pay him Rs. 1,00,000 as compensation instead of reinstatement and further continuance in service.

The appellants, who were the unsuccessful bidder, challenged the auction of 70 outstill shops for 1970 71 on the ground that they had made arrangements for establishing their shops and incurred an expenditure of about Rs. 1,50,000/ on account of two months ' ' ' fees ' in ad vance, as required by rule 103 of the Board 's Excise Rules 1965. The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice to the appellants under Rule 103 of tho Board 'S Excise Rules, 1965 calling for tenders for establishing 70 outstil shops for 1971 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops in one lot, for Rs. 34,000 per month. His bid was accepted and his name was entered in the prescribed register, and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. Aj Murat Prasad accordingly deposited Rs. 68,000 on account ' of two month 's " fees", in advance, and as required under rule 103. The appellants moved the authorities concerned for the issue of licenses for running the shops from April 1, 1970. They approached the authorities for the issuance of the licenses for starting the shops. Aj benevol Prasad claimed that in the mean time he made arrangements to establish his shops and incur an expenditure for about Rs 1,00,000. He also approached the Authorities concerned for issuing the licenses. Ajreatment Prasad claimed the said amount as expenditure incurred by him. The authorities concerned rejected the request of Ajodhya Narain on the grounds that the Collector had no authority to issue such a notice in view of the provisions of section 22(1) of the Act and the Collec tor had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collector after it had "become final in appeal and revision", and could not direct a reauction. The High Court, however, allowed the writ petition holding that what was purported to be given under the sale notice was not the grant of exclusive privilege but was in excess of the rule making power of the board. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the Collector 's order for accepting Ajodhya P 's bids was not an "exclusive privilege" within the meaning of section 2(a)(b) of tho Orissa Excise Act, 1915; (ii) the collection was in the nature of a tax and section 29 without the expression "or otherwise" in clause (a) of sub section 2 were valid and constitutional. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The State has exclusive right or privilege to manufacture, store and sale any country liquor. [819C] 2.1 The State had exclusive right to privilege of manufacturing or selling any country liquors. The proviso to sub section (2) of section 20 enacts that a grantee of such a privilege shah not exercise it unless he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or the Excise Commissioner. [850E F] 2(i) The State Government had exclusive power to grant exclusive privilege to carry on trade in the manufacture and sale of liquor. It was not therefore, open to the Collector to follow the process of auction for determining the sum payable under sub section 1 of section 29. Once a decision is taken under sub s.(1) to grant the exclusive privilege within any specified area, sub section(2) provides that no grantee of the privilege shall exercise it without "unless or until he has receive a license". [850G H] 2.(ii) The expression "and otherwise" used in clause(a) is not defined in the Act. It is well settled that the State Legislature was competent to enact a regulatory measure and consequently the State legislature had legislative competence to enact such a regulatory measures and consequently, the State Legislatures had legislative power to enact the regulatory measure.

The appellant was charged with having entered into a criminal conspiracy with the deceased for committing the murder of his wife. The prosecution case was that on 25th January 1968, the deceased and accused No. 3 were working in a hotel for the manufacture of medicines. On 26th December 1967, the appellant along with others went to Bombay and demanded money from the deceased when he turned approver. At about 11 p.m., the appellant asked the deceased to vacate the bungalow but he was not allowed to do so. The deceased then left Deolali 's house and went to Deololiali where he was seen by his wife, who was also present there. On 25th December, 1967, at about 10 p.M., the deceased along with his wife went to the bungalow of the appellant and asked him to vacate it. The appellant told him that the deceased had committed two murders prior to that date but nothing happened to him. The police came to the tailor 's shop and gave the key of the godown to accused No 1. The brother of the deceased was also known to him by face. In the month of November 1967, he was taken to Deoliali and on 25.12.1967, he went to Nasik in connection with some court work and they were found near that house locked. On 27th December 1968, he along with other persons came to Bombay where he saw a dead body which had been stolen from the house of one of the accused No 2. The discovery of articles in the godown of Takalkar was as a result of a statement by accused No 3. The evidence of the tailoring witness was that the bones were those of a human being probably a male. The High Court found that there was corroboration in regard to the approver 's story about the conspiracy and the common intention by way of a pre conceived plan to murder Narendra.

The appellant was the owner of an area admeasuring 1,37,961 sq. meters of which he was a Karta of a Hindu undivided family. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to him at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq. ft. on the basis that the total compensation was inadequate and further that the apportionment of compensation between the lessor and the lessee was not proper. He also questioned the propriety of reserving such a large area for the scheme. The Board of Appeal held that the appeal was not maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of the Town Planning officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated November 4, 1971. The appellant then challenged the order of the Board of appeal before the Gujarat High Court by filing a writ petition in which certain provisions of the Act were also challenged as unconstitutional and it was claimed that the Town planning Officer had no jurisdiction to provide an Appeal from a judgment of the town Planning Officer on matters dealing with matters dealt by him. The High Court held that there was no appeal from the decision of Town Planning Officers on matters covered by section 32(1) (iii). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the Act does not provide any appeal from an order of a Town Planning Authority determining the amount of compensation payable to the appellant; and (ii) that in view of the scheme of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, the appeal before tho Board of Appeals was incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating the compensation payable by an owner of land who has not been given a reconstituted plot. [92G] 2.1 The Act does contain the necessary provi sions for estiming the compensation to be paid to or by each of the owners included in the scheme.[93H; 94A] 2(a) The Act is generally accepted meaning of that expression and it is a principle applicable to all cases in which by virtue of the operation of the City Planning Act a person is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part. [94B C] (b) The property or right which is injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme is a property or other right than that acquired for the purposes of the Scheme.

The appellant was the third son of a testator. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughters attained majority, Seetharama should give them to the minor daughters the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the testator.
