The appellant did not accept this right of selection and claimed that he was entitled in law to have the lands taken into account for good and bad quality. He also referred to a decision of the Madras High Court in A. V. Narayanaaswami Gramani vs Periathambi Granmni (1915) 29 M.L.J. 717, which held that the testator intended to give the selection to the legatee and once the selection was made by the legatee he had no right to make a selection. The question for decision in this appeal was whether the legatees have a right to be considered in a case where the testator himself did not make a Selection but still the gift is not so uncertain as to be capable ofcribing a definite intention to the testator, Held, that the test laid down by the English rule of construction is that where the will uses the words " I bequeath money", wheat, oil or the like without saying how much it is possible to say on the construction of a will that the legatee himself indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make the selection but still intended to make it certain. The testator had two closes of land in Ridgway Field and he devised one to one son without indicating which was to go to which son. It is not possible to accept the contention that the legate must be left to make selection for himself.

The appellant filed a suit for joint possession of plots in dispute, being co bhumidars. The trial court decreed the suit for partition on the ground that the defendants were in exclusive occupation of the land or plots in question and that they had absolutely no concern with them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents were in joint possession since after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act. [868C] 2.1 The plea of bar of civil courts ' jurisdiction to investigate and adjudicate upon the title to the land cannot be accepted. Even if no share was given to the plaintiff by the defendants, as the defendants had practised a fraud on her by giving her assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. The Trial Court did not fully appreciate this part 869 of the case made out by the plaintiff and the District Judge in clear terms accepted the same. [864C D] 2:2.1 In the instant case, it is manifest that the possession of the defendants as co sharers would be in law the possession on behalf o the plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during consolidation operation either by the defendant or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiff were sought to be extinguished. [884E F] 2(a) The High court erred in holding, on the basis of the clear evidence, that a fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order nullity. [874F G] (b) In view of the settled position of law, the High Court was not right in interfering with the finding of facts given by the District Court regarding fraud having been committed in the consolidation proceedings. [854G H] Subha Singh vs Mahendra Singh & Ors., ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was nominated as Prime Minister in the Council of Minis ters. He was later elected to the Council on the ground that he had been functioning as Chief Minister when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Deputy Prime Ministers contending that the oath administered to the petitioner as Deputy Chief Minister was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution and that the practice which has been followed eversince the Constitution came into force only for a Minister of the Union and there is no constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The words "in the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution" and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [318C] 2. The word "recording" in the form prescribed in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirement of Article 75(4) of the Constitu tion is only for the Minister of a Union and not for all purposes he is a Minister. Since the Prime Minister is also a member of the Council, he takes the same oath as other ministers are required to take. He maintains that yet in view of the fact that the Constitution describes him as the Prime Mini ters, he took the same rank as the other Ministers and all other ministers signa cates as Ministers. [313D E] 3. The expression "in this form" is descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. In view of this clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister, he does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers along with his other submis sions, the petitioner himself does not press it. [311E F] 4.

The appellant, a Labour Appellate Tribunal, was dismissed by the Labour Appellate Tribu nal on the ground that it had no jurisdiction to interfere with an order of dismissal passed by it under section 49 B(1) of the Factories Act. The appellant contended before this Court that the Tribunal had no power to interfere and revise its discretion in awarding punishment, reduced the punishment by 50 per cent and held that the workers would be deprived of only half their holidays with pay. Held, that the stoppage of work for a period of two to four hours was an illegal strike and the workers thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The workers were acting in combination and their refusal to go back to work on the date of the first November, 1948, amounted to a strike. It was not a case of an individual worker 's failure to turn up for work. The Tribunal had therefore no discretion not to interfere under article 136 of the Constitution. The Mills were granted exemption from the provisions of section 49 A(2) of that Act and the provisions Of sections 49 A and 49 B were not attracted to it. The Mill was granted exemption only from the operation of section IV A of the Act and sections 49A and 49B were not therefore applicable to the case of the Carnatic Mills. Held further, that on a proper construction of section49 A(1), the workers were entitled to privilege leave for the night shift whenever a half a day 's leave was granted to the day shift workers. The closure of work by a body of persons employed in the Mills and the stoppage thereof amounted to an illegal lock and therefore an interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of section 9 B(i) of Factories Act, 1947, fell within the definition of "strike" as given in section 2(q) of 'the Industrial Disputes Act.

The appellant, a producer of cinematograph films, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the (for short, the Act), there is a justification for its display. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 I. P.C., provides remedies. [515D] 2.1 The provisions of section 79 of the Penal Code are general and the certificate issued thereunder. It is an antinomy to say that under section 5A(1 A) of the Act, the Board certifies a film as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292 1.P C., driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay 'C ', driving the producers to satisfy the producer, driving him to satisfy, a ' layman of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 I.p.C.[515G H] 2:2. The certificate issued under section 65A(lA) of tho Act is valid in exhibiting the film. [511E F] 3.1 Section 79 makes an offence non offence. When the offending act is actually justified by law, i.e., by some other provision, then section 79 exonerates them at least in view of their bona fide belief that the certificate is justificatory. Thus the trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the certificate under the Act and, in the light of our observations, it fills the bill under section 79. [ 515E F; 516A] 2 :3. The scheme of the latter is deliberately drawn up to meet the explosively expanding cinema menace if it were not strictly policed. No doubt, the cinema is a great instrument for public good if geared to social ends and can be robbed of the glory and grace expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any department, more so in cinema pictures. [ 516F G] 2(a) The censor is not the moral tailor setting his own fashions but a statutory gendar policmeing films under article 19(2) from the angle of public order, decency or morality. These concepts are themselves dynamic and cannot be whittled down to stifle expression nor licentiously enlarged to promote a riot of sensual display. Anyway, the appeal must succeed and the appellant is accordingly acquitted.

The petitioner was a Government Pleader for the Patna District, 'authorised to represent 'Government in all the civil cases. During the currency of his term plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders were appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant, to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him from consideration. He went to the extent of writing Government to know that Government Pleader had done in hoping for a lakh of rupees. The High Court declined to dispense with the magic remedy. Hence this petition. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The State must evolve a policy in regard to its Law Officers which concedes to freedom to counsel to recommend settlement of cases if they feel it just to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [766C D] 2. The Government Pleader is not obnoxious but nothing savouring of such conduct is made out although we must enter a caveat that Governments under our Constitution shall not play with law 's fees, lawyers and other public sector undertakings should not pamper and thereby inflate the system of costs. [764E F] 3.

The appellants held shares out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50 and the shares were transferred to a private company in proportion of one new share for every three shares held by it in the proportion of the shares held. The face value of the new shares was to be Rs.50 but the shareholders had to pay a premium on Rs. 100 for each new share. The appellants as holders of the old shares were entitled to receive 1,140 shares from the Bank of India at the rate of Rs 100 per share and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the Bank 's funds. The High Court held that the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of a bank by Navjunal Mills Ltd. amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the distributed right to the Bank Of India shares amounted to distribution of dividend within the definition of "Dividend". The shares which had a monetary value were not "dicend" and were taxable as such under section 2 (6A). The shares in question were purchased by the appellants for the purpose of acquiring the new share and the value thereof was to vest in the shareholders. The right transferred to the shareholders was indisputably the value of their right. The Mills could not be compelled to obtain this benefit if it did not desire to do so.

The appellant was declared elected to the Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly. The respondent, who lost his deposits in the election petition, filed an application under section 81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the application. The learned Judge rejected the application holding that except Bahre son of Sher Singh no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the afore mentioned witness was recorded, the Court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidate. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the respondent had not been given an opportunity to examine witnesses who were kept present in the Court and this ground was unsustainable; (ii) the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine such witnesses; (iii) the appellant could not have been allowed to examine more witnesses whose name had not appeared in the list of witnesses submitted in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the rules framed by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the learned Judge is wholly unsustainable. He declined to examine the witness who was present in court on the short ground that the name of the witness was not mentioned in the List filed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 and that he could be produced without the assistance of the Court. [534E F] 2. The scheme clearly emerges from the various provisions of Order XVI, Rules 1 and 22 of the High Courts Rules. This scheme clearly emerge from the several provisions discussed. If the scheme of the various sections is conjointly read and properly analysed, it clearly transpires that the obligation to supply the list as well as the gist of evidence of each witness whose name is entered in the lists has to be carried out in respect of those witnesses who are called to produce documents without applying for summons under Rule 1. If it was implicit in Rule 1A that the party may bring any witness to give evidence or produce documents but this enabling provision is subject to the provisions contained in sub rule(3) to procure the presence of a witness by issuing a summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a person whose name was not shown in the said list. Therefore, sub rule 2 of Order XVII confers a wider jurisdiction on the Court to cater to a situation where the party has failed to name the witness in the order filed under Rule IA.

The appellant, a double M.A., was appointed as Principal of the College by the Management of the college on May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal of Shrinath Intermediate College, Garhmalpur, Uttar Pradesh. The Selection Committee interviewed the appellant and selected him for appointment to the post. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager of the institution at the College on May 1, 1981. On receipt of this letter, the appellant presented himself at the college and took over the charge. The Management did not pay any salary to the appellant though he functioned as Principal. The management did not take any action against the appellant in discharging his duties as Principal and ultimately the appellant approached the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for a writ of mandamus directing the 5th respondent, the Committee of Management of a College, not to interfere with the work of the appellant discharging his duty as Principal or to pay salary. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the appointment of the appel lant as Principal was valid; (ii) the post being a non government aided school, the committee had no power to make the appointment and therefore the appointment could not be invalidated; and (iii) the appellant was entitled to get salary. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of appellant was made by a body not authorised to make it. It cannot be said that the appointment was in contravention of any provision of the Act. Therefore sub sec.(10) is not attracted in this case and the contention must fail. [975F G] 2.1 Sub section (4) specifically confers power on the State Government without making any reference to the Board to make, modify or rescind any regulation. Armed with this power the State Govern ment has authority to sanction or not to sanction the regulations proposed by the Board. Every such recognised institution must have a scheme of Administration as envisaged by sec.

The appellants manufacture "a textile" consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads. The respondents state that "rayon tyre cord fabric" is "manufactured out of raiyon yarn and cord". It goes on to explain that this fabric is "a textiles consisting of fabric" as fabrics. "The appellants state that the manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "pregnate the fabric with rubber" and "fabric" are also mentioned. The appellants state further that "fotton fabrics" manufactured by them are "manufacturing out of " rayonson or artificial silk". The respondents contended that the goods sought to be taxed were not the "end product" as they had been exempted from tax under entry 18 of Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954. The Commercial Tax officer rejected their objections and held that the appellants were exempt from taxation. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the High Court should have interfered with the decision of the taxing authorities at this stage. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The taxing authorities had committed error apparent on the face of the record and that the taxing authority should be left to determine whether the "tyre cord fabric ' is more correctly capable of being described as a fabric or merely pretending to pass off as ar textile fabric. This was really a technical question. [500G] 2. The High Court was right in not interfering with the decisions of the assessing authorities at the stage of appeal. [501A B] 3. The word "f fabrics" used in entry 22AA is "textile fabrics not elsewhere specified". This residuary entry and the description in preceding entries seem to be wide, presumably for purposes of impregnating with rubber, that it may not pass for an ordinary "f fabric", like one of those mentioned in entry 19. [401C] 4. The words "impregnated" in entry 20AA are "textiles fabrics not otherwise specified". There is no provision in the entry to show that this item was meant for "taple fabrics and not for any kind of fabric". Therefore, even if the tyre cord cloth may be the end product for the Delhi Cloth Mills, the crucial question is whether the product for which the Delhi cloth claims exemption Is a textile fabric and not any other kind of fabrics. [ 500E F] 5. The expression "t textiles" in Entry 22AA means a fabric which is also a textile. It must acquire a body and a texture. Presumably it is not just the skeleton of a textile that can be made into a fabric. Mere cord does not become a textile fabrics just because it requires some skill to make it. The wide dictionary meaning of the term "f interpol" does not appear to give the exact meaning of "fregn" as used in the relevant entries entitled to exemption. [525G H] 6. The language of entry 22A(D) of the first schedule to the , shows that it is meant for 'textile fabric and cannot cover everything which could be made to become a fabric just because there requires some skilled skill to do so.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal mines. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was accordingly dismissed from service. The dispute arose out of an industrial dispute arising therefrom. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent appeared to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the labour court Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court Patna. The appellant company filed its respective pleadings. When t he matter was pending consideration the respondent seems to have wrote to the government stating that the Government would be unable to attend to the labour Court Dhanbad since the appellant has been living at Hajur and it will be convenient for the respondent if the Case is transferred to labour court Patna. That application was made without intimation to t he management. The Government transferred the case to Labour court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. The respondent appeared before the Labour Court and issued notices to the particu lar court to the appellant company. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings, but when the matter came up on consideration, it was pending hearing the respondent appears to have made written to tO the Government saying that it will he difficult for them to attend labour court, Dhanbad since they had been residing in Hajipur. When th is stated that it might be difficult to attend t he Labour Court Dhanbad, the appellant Company has been staying at Hajpur and it was convenient for them if the matter is transferred to Labour Courts Patna. On the question whether the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring the case from the labour courts, Dhanbad should have given an opportunity to the management to file a written statement stating that they would be impossible for him at the Labour court Dhanbad, since he had been living in Hajur. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that the respondent was misled by the representation of the appellant workman and transferred it to another Labour Court at Patna. [300G] 2.1 The Government is under legal obligation to record reasons for such transfer. But once a decision is taken to transfer a pending case then the requirement of giving reasons becomes mandatory. The authority is under statutory obligation to records reasons in support of its decision. Reasons would be life of the decision. Failure to give reasons or giving reasons would not germane would be fatal to the decision of the Government. [301A] 2:2. In the instant case, the Government was misled in the representation by the workman. The order of transfer in that case was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee.

The appellant, the manager of a Hotel Imperial, New Delhi, was appointed as its manager in the Hotel Imperial. The respondent No. 3 filed a writ petition challenging the order of reference on a variety of grounds. It was contended that the reference was incompetent because it did not specify how many of the 480 workers of the different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to make a reference under section 10(1) of the Act. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The reference was bad merely because the order referring the words "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Shahanshahi Chandni Chowk Delhi, " as representing the Hotel workers" in the award did not mention any officer of the trade union but only mentions the union itself. The Union could not be made a party to the reference under the Act because it was mentioned therein that the workmen would be represented by such and such union in the matter. The Industrial Tribunal had jurisdiction to entertain the dispute as it had no power to make it incompetent merely because it does not specify what of the workmen concerned. In the present case, the respondent No, 3 was a member of the Hotel and the appellant was responsible for the dispute. It is only where a dispute refers to the dismissal etc., of particular workmen as represented by them that it may be desirable to mention the names of the persons concerned. The Tribunal had therefore no jurisdiction under section I10 of the , to make the reference incompetent, because, in the order referred to the Tribunal under section 1 10(2) of Act, the appellant could not claim to be a party merely because, the reference did not contain the terms of reference.

The appellant was entitled to exemption under Notification No. 281 Cus dated 2 8 1976, granting exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the notification No. 282 Cus, granting part exemption from customs duty on the rod impinge and camboft bushes manufactured in a knocked down condition. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the assessee. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that Heading No. 84.06 did not refer to parts of internal combustion piston engines, but also to 'part thereof 's parts and that Heading 84.04 did not mention 'parts thereof. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The parts of the engine or engines mentioned under Heading No 84.6.06 are excluded from the benefit Of the Notification. [225G] 2. The Tribunal was influenced by the fact that the functions of the bushings and bearings are the same. It may be that two articles have the same function but nonetheless they are distinct and separate. As the functions are not mentioned under heading No.84.06, it cannot be said that parts of such engines were included in the engines mentioned in Heading No., 84.07. [226A B] 3. The intention of the Notification is clear enough to provide that the parts of engines mentioned thereunder will get the benefit exemption as provided by the Notification irrespective of the fact whether they or any of them have already been included under Heading Nos. 8406.06. [227D] 4. The words 'part of such engine, mentioned in Item No. 2 of column (2) do not mean parts of those engines. They are parts of a engine and not a few parts thereof. [228E F] 5.

The appellants filed a suit for declara tion that they were entitled to be in possession and enjoyment of the Dargah. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in appeal, the High Court reversed the decree and held that the plaintiffs were entitled t o manage the Dargah as they were female members. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the courts below proceeded upon an erroneous assumption as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster had been established; (ii) the widows of the deceased defendant from interfering with the plaintiffs ' right and management in the Dargah were excluded from performing the duties of the offices of the Peshimam Khatib and Mujawar; (iii) the widow of the first defendant was not interested in claiming her right to the offerings in the stalls and even if they were enti tled to any right or claim the same was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a serious error in reversing the finding and in taking a wrong approach in holding ouster on the basis of judgment and decree given in suit No. 116 of 1909 and on the ground that Fathima Bee had not made a demand or asked for share of the Hundial collections as such was not entitled to claim any right of Mujawar thus neither Bee Wazir nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in the hundial collections. [526G H] 1.2 The High Courts committed a manifest error in taking an erroneous approach in reversing that finding and taking a correct approach in taking the wrong approach. In taking a proper view in taking such a wrong interpretation, it is not necessary to go into the question of ouster. [525A B] P. Lakshmi vs L. Laksmi Reddy, ; , referred to. 1.3 The High court was right in holding that the rights of Fathma Bee had become barred by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathida Bee had lost their right by ouster. It would be relevant to consider the pleadings of the parties in this regard. [626D E] P Lakshmi vs Laksmitra Reddy, AIR 1972 SC 116; P. Laxmi vs Laskmi Reddy ; , relied on.

The appellant was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. He was allotted certain railway quarters to his employer, who was the authority responsible under section 4 Of the , for payment of house rent allowance. The 1st respondent, who had been employed by the Railway Board as a gangmen, was charged with offences punishable under sections 7 and 11 of the Act for not paying the house rent allowances to him from the 19th August 1948. The appellant 's claim for house rent was rejected by the Authority on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim which should be dismissed in limine. The Authority condoned the delay and allowed the appeal, but the High Court held that the house Rent allowance was not a "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the , and that the appellant was entitled to withhold the house rents allowance. Held, that the definition of "wages ' contained in the Act cannot include the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee; otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages. The definition of 'wages ' in section 2 (vi) is inconsistent with some of the terms of the definition and therefore the appellant could not claim the house rental allowance. That being so, there was no question of the employee relinquishing any such right as was contemplated by section 23. The Act read along with the rules which constitute the terms on the contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one of those places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation, he ceases to be entitled whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him.

The petitioners were detained under the COFEPOSA Act on the ground that they had been in possession of smuggled goods and were not supplied with copies thereof. The grounds of detention were served on them alongwith the order of detention, purporting to have been signed by the Secretary in the Home Department, who was then under President 's rule. They were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs Officers and cooperate in the investigation. This condition was later on related. On February 16, 1980, the detenus made a written request to the detaining authority for supply of copies of the statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of Detention. The detenu also made a representation to the State Government requesting him to furnish the materials relied upon by the detaining authorities in the ground of detention. The State Government refused the supply of the copies on February 18, 1980. Thereafter, the Central Government advised the State Governments to supply the copies. Thereupon, the petitioners moved this Court for relief by petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The delay of more than a month in supplying the copies to the detenus was unexplained and inordinate. [351 D] 2. The detention order was passed on February 15, 1980 and was communicated to the detenu on March 25, 1980 by letter dated March 14, 1980 addressed to the Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra, Home Department. The communication was received by the detenu only on March 26, 1980 after undue delay on the direction of the Central Govt., and that rejection was communicated by letter, dated March 31, 1980 to the petitioners. [352 E] 3. The fact that the grounds furnished to the Petitioners were elaborate, does not absolve the detaining Authority from its constitutional responsibility to supply all the basic facts and materials relied on or referred to in the 'grounds of detention '. There was thus an infraction of the constitutional imperative that in addition to the supply Of the grounds, all the vital material relied upon or referred in the "grounds" must be supplied to the detenue with reasonable expedition to enable him to make a full and effective representation at the earliest. [353 E] 4.

The appellant, who was tried along with others for offences under sections 420 and 423 of the Indian Penal Code, was acquitted by the trial court. The High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons jointly tried. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court was wrong in holding that the decision of the Full Bench holding a joint trial to be maintainable in law was not binding on it, and (ii) the provisions of section 419 were not applicable to the proceedings in Gujarat High Court. HELD: The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Courts by section 554(2)(c) Cr. P.C., and r. 6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provision of the said Code. It is well settled that a joint judgment of two or more accused persons cannot be set aside merely because it proceeds on sound commonsense. Procedure has been described to be a hand maid and not a mistress of law intended to subserve and facilitate the cause of justice and not to govern or obstruct it. Like all rules of procedure, this rule demands a construction which would promote this cause. So construed a jointappeal requiring the appeal to be heard on merits. [879 D E] Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , referred to. (2) In the instant case, it was not possible for the High court to hold that the previous decision was wrong, instead of following the usual procedure in case of difference of opinion with an earlier decision of a single judge. Judicial decorum no less than legal propriety forms the basis of judicial procedure. If one thing is more necessary in law than any other thing it is the quality of certainty. That quality would totally disappear if judges of co ordinate jurisdiction in a High Court start overruling one another 's decision. [ 879 E F] Maharaolalla Ranodia v The Administrator, General of Bengal, , followed.

The assessee was a firm called O.M.V.M., and its two brothers carried on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States. The assessee claimed that it was the assesse 's firm which took over the business of the Hindu undivided family, that the income from the house property owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of assessment for 1939 40 was not liable to be taxed by reason of the provisions of section 25(3) and (4). The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family but rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no discontinuance of the business within the meaning of section 2(6) of the 1922 Act, and that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3). The High Court also referred another question for the opinion of the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when a Hindu undivided Family carrying on business which was taxed under the 1918 Act became disrupted and the members continued the business there could be no discontinuance but only succession by the firm of the assessee 's business, and therefore the assessment of the income must be treated as an assessment of business. HELD: The High court was in error in holding that the foreign business of a assessee was exempt under the 1922 Income tax Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the assessee from foreign business and not the foreign ties itself. [912 D] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs Chugandas & Co., ; , followed. Commissioner of Incometax, Madras vs section V.R.M Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , applied.

The respondent entered into a contract with the appellant company for manufacture and supply of bricks to its Department. The Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for the purpose of manufacturing and supplying bricks to the Department, issued a notification under section 52 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1959, on November 19, 1967, to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, determining the question whether the supplies of bricks by the assessee to the Public Works Department were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of brick was sales and not works contracts. The respondent filed an appeal before the Tribunal against that order. The Tribunal held that there was no contract of sale and that the transaction was a works contract, that the respondent had failed to prove that the supplies were made by it to the public Works Department or that the materials supplied were not of the best quality and in accordance with the specification and specifications contained in the tender documents. On appeal by special leave, the Tribunal held: (1) that the contracts entered into by the applicant with the Public works Department were sale of bricks; (2) that there could be no contract for sale of brick; and (3) that in any case, the respondent was entitled to reject the said articles on such conditions as might be discovered not to conform to the description and quality or these specifications. Allowing the appeal by Special Leave, ^ HELD: 1. The contracts entered with the respondent company were sales of bricks. If it were so, the property in the bricks must have been in the brick was entirely of the assessee. He had not only to manufacture but also to stack for facilitating delivery. The essence of the contract was, therefore, entirely of assessee. [165G H] 2.1 The contracts between the parties clearly show that the contract for supply of materials was ultimately manufactured. The true test in this case is whether in making the contract to brick produced was transferred as a chattel for consideration and it is not possible to hold that the transactions were works contract: [166A B] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs State of Gujarat, ; , referred to. 2.2 In the present case, there could not be any contract for the sale of the bricks after manufacture. The contract provided that the bricks would remain at the appellant 's risk till the date of final delivery. In Chandra Bhan 's case, this was clearly distinguishable on facts.

The petitioner, a member of the Lok Sabha, was elected to the Lok Council on 26.6.1975 and was liable to pay income tax and wealth tax in accordance with the rates prescribed by the Finance Act 1976 which was passed by the Lok Assembly during its extended period which was extended under the provisions of the House of People (Extension of duration) Act, 1976. The petitioner challenged the constitutional validity of the two Acts on various grounds including the extension of time for filing petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution and also on the ground that the duration of the house of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of article 83 of the Constitu tion. The petition was contested by the Union of India on the grounds, inter alia, that the period of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting had ceased to be in operation and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period during which the House was extended. It was also contended that the proclamation of December 3, 1971 had been revoked long before February 16, 1976 and that the Proclamation of emergency dated 25th June 1975 had ceased under the powers conferred by clause (1) of Article 352 of the constitution. The contentions were reiterated in the petition. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Proclamations of Emergency are kept in force by virtue of resolutions passed by both Houses of Parliament approving the two Procamations. The reports of the Rajya Sabha and Rajya Sabha Secretariat which follow the very closely form and manner of presentation of the official Parliamentary Debates in England, are the only record of the proceedings of the respective Houses of the Parliament and the State Legislatures gives ample publicity. The Reports of the meetings of the both Houses are published by them. [457C D] 2. The resolutions passed on February 16 and 1976 approving the resolutions of the Legislative Assembly and Rajya Sabhas respectively were duly revoked by the two proclamions which were issued by the Vice President acting as President of India in the year 1977. Since the two statutes of 1976 had been duly revoked long after February 16. 1976, the validity cannot be questioned. [454E] 3. The resolution of the Assembly and the Rajya Sabhas approving the second resolutions have been duly published in the official Gazette. Hence mere non publication of the resolutions approving the Proclemations of emergency cannot be challenged. [453F G] 4. The orders passed by Parliament and State Legislatures are widely circulated. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament and Legislatures of the States. The report of the Parliamentary Debates though after some short delay is adequate publication of resolutions of both Houses. This ought to meet the contention of the petitioner that any public Act or resolution which affects public life should be given due publicity. [451G] 5. The legislative history of emergency was not in doubt in operation when the House and Rajya Legislatures were in force when the Legislative Council of India was prorated. The Parliament passed the Constitution (Extension) Act of 1976 on 26th June, 1975. The Lok Sabha passed the impugned Acts on 2nd February, 1976, 3rd December, 1971 and 25th July, 1975 respectively. The validity of these Acts had been challenged before this Court in a petition under Article 136 of the Consti tution. It is contended that even though it was not expressly provided that the resolutions passed were duly approved by the resolutions, they should have been published for the very same reason which compelled the Government to publish the Procarnations in the Official Gazette. [452G H] 6.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the decision of the said authorities. The High Court held that the property was a public temple within the meaning of section 84(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, Madras, and set aside the order of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the refusal to grant leave by the High Court under either of the clauses (a) and (b) of article 133(1)(a) could not apply as the judgment and decree passed by it did not involve directly or a claim or question respecting property of the value of Rs. 20,000/ or more; (ii) the appeal did not involved any substantial question of law. HELD: The High court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the property in dispute was private or public temple it was incapable of valuation as it could have either in no case market value. [157 D] (iii) The High Courts were wrong in holding that the properties in question constituted a temple and set up a temple. The subject matter of the dispute has to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property is the private property of that family capable of alienation, the High court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to them the property belonged to the Thoguluva family.

The appellant, a company, was employed by the respondent company as its workmen. The dispute between the appellant and the respondents related to the payment of dearness allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements which were made at present by the appellant. In respect of the former employees, the Tribunal held that the practice of employing men should be stopped. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no justification for the respondent 's contention that only four cases of re employment had been brought to its notice and so the question did not call for any consideration at that stage. The appellant contended that in view of the fact that the re employment of retired persons was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations, the respondent should stop the reemployment of those employees who were entitled to it. Held: (i) The fact that a wage structure in respect of reemployed personnel which is definitely inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appellant by the award , and that cannot be permitted under industrial law was not decisive of the question whether the re employed persons had made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant. (ii) The respondent ' s case was not covered by the decision in Chandi Charan Banerjee vs Chandi Chandra Banerjee, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 869. (iii) The appellant was introducing a wage structures in respect Of the reemployed persons which is certainly inferior to that of the wage scale devised for its employees. The fact of the re employ ment of retired workmen was mainly borne by humanitarian consideration and not by any other factor.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in sterling was to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Financial Adviser and Chief Accounts Officer intimating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of special contribution to provident fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1410(1) of the Railway Establishment Code. The respondent wrote a letter on July 27, 1955, to the Chief Accounts officer stating the sanction for payment. The Chief Accounts Office, East India Railway, requested that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident Funds Account be remitted to the Westminster Bank, Birmingham. On September 26, the Chief Accountant General, Eastern Railway wrote a communication on July 28, 1955 to the respondent pointing out that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The respondent thereupon filed a suit for recovery of the amount in the executing court. The High Court held that the property in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India had ceased to be Provident Fund money long before they were attached and hence they were not immune from the attachment as claimed by the objector. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court was in error in holding that the moneys in the hand of the reserve bank of India ceased to have been provident fund funds and was liable to be attached. [31 B C] (2) The respondent 's contention that the Union of India bad no interest in maintaining an application for removal of attachment was not tenable because the Union had no interest to maintain an application under r.1413(1). [32 D E] (3) The order of attachment passed by the Court on December 8, 1956, was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the .

The appellant was employed as a pump operator in 1963. The management terminated his services by a simple letter which reads: "We are sorry to advise that your services are no longer required by the Company. As such this letter may be treated as a notice for the termination of your services with immediate effect. As per Standing Orders which does not stigze the worker but merely bids him good bye ? Oris it good bye. The appellant was given two extra increments, in addition to normal increments. He was also given extra increments in addition. His pay was fixed at Rs. 10,000/ . In 1968, the appellant was again given two additional increments, and in addition he was given extra increment in addition, in the normal increments, as stated earlier. The workman challenged the termination as illegal, mala fide, illegal and an act of victimisation. The Labour Court held that the action being a simple termination without a sting, the process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the impugned action was not bona fide; (ii) the alleged annoyance with the allegedordination with the appellant betraying sensitive secrets of business; and (iii) the appellant had failed to do so. HELD: The Labour court has misled itself on the law land. [401 B] (a) It is true that this Court, in appeal, as a rule of practice, is loath to interfere with a finding of fact recorded by the trial court. But if such a finding is based on no evidence or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence, or is so unreasonable that no reasonable person would judicially arrive at that conclusion it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set aside such termination. [498 C] (b) The appellant has the power to be exercised by the employer objectively in good faith, which means honestly with due care and prudence. If the exercise of such power is challenged on the ground of being colourable or mala fide or an act or victimisation of unfair labour practice, the employer must disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. [501 D E] (c) The principles of natural justice have been evolved by this Court in several cases and it is not necessary for this Court under article 136 to interfere in such matters. [301 A B] In the instant case, the catalogue of circumstances set out in the earlier part of the judgment strikes a contrary note. The worker was not told when he wrote; the Union was not disclosed when they demanded; the Labour Court was treated to verbal statements like very reliable sources and other credulous phrases without a modicum of evidence to prove bonafides. Some testimony of unseemly attempts by the workman to get at secrets outside his orbit, some indication of the source of suspicion, some proof of the sensitive or strategic role of the employee, should and would have been forthcoming had the case been bona fide. [500 E F] (d) The Labour Courts have misled itself in the law and scrutinising with critical faculties the facts on record, con cluded to the conclusion that the termination was a colourable exercise of power by the management. If it came to the finding that the impugned act was not mala fide it must disclose the grounds for such action so as to be justified.

The petitioners, who were the State of U.P., and its officers, filed a Public Interest Litigation under Article 32 of the Constitution for implementation of the recommendations made by the Advisory Committee appointed by the Government in pursuance thereof. The Court directed the Indian Medical Council to take up action against those responsible for the tragedy. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said recommendations on various grounds including that they were not fully implemented and that appropriate legal action be instituted against them, that the victims had suffered irre versible damage of their eyes which had rendered themselves wholly incapacitated; that the State Government did conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure for the patients; that it was only after the institution of these proceedings that the Court directed that the Indian medical Council should take up steps against those who have suffered, and that the appropriate legal remedy be instituted by the victims. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the unfortunate victims had suffer irre vantsible damage to their eyes as they were acting pursuant to and under the authority of the Government; that there was no violation of any principles of natural justice in the matter of awarding relief, and directed the Union of India to initiate appropriate action against such responsible for its tragedy; that in view of the salutary objective of this kind litigation, it would not in any manner be prejudicial to the re spondents. The State of Uttar Pradesh filed an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitu tion challenging the validity and legality of the aforesaid recommendations on several grounds including the fact that the injured victims had been suffered irrepa versable damage of the eyes which has rendered them wholly incapacitated. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The National Medical Council and the State are directed to take into account the recommendations in regard to the norms for the conduct and management of eye camps. [255B] 1.2 The Revised guidelines dated 9.2.1988 by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare vide their No. T. 1/ 2019/86Pt II dated 9th February, 1988 are filed before this Court. The National medical Council and State are requested to take a decision on the question of the liabili ty of the victims for such other bene fits under any of the existing schemes now in force in the State, their cases shall be considered for such benefit. [254C D] 1:3 The Revised norms issued by the Union Government on 9.1.1988 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, it is not necessary that the alleged victims had sustained irrepav erable damage to the eyes as their lives have yet to be established conclusively. These matters would have to be gone into in the criminal and other proceedings that may be pending or in the contemplation of the Govern ment.

The petitioners, who were members of a political party in 1929, challenged the action taken by the State Government under Section 10 of the Bidhanti Prahachar Samiti (Taking over management and Control) Act, 1984, on the ground that they had no locus standi to file this writ petition. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the petitioners were not entitled to file a writ petition in view of Article 226 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The State Government has taken the power under Section 3 of the Act as ultra vires of the Constitu tion. It is clear from Entry 25 of List Ill (concurrent list) Schedule 7 of the constitution to enact this law that the Samiti shall be reconstituted in accordance with the Constitution to elect by a Board and all the functions, properties and affairs of the Samiti were taken over by the Committee. [171E F] 1.2 The State has no intention even now to end this temporary arrangement of the Samitis. It was also directed that the authorities appointed by the Board or the State Govern ment shall restore back all assets and properties of the Society to the Karyapalika and byabasthapika Sabha which were functioning in 1984 and which we are restoring will within six months from the date of this Order will hold proper elections in accordance With the Constitution, to elect Byabastha pika and Karyapalka. This is necessary because the period of the Karyapapalika has come to an end although from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. It would have been different situation if the State felt that it wanted to do so what this Samiti was doing and further acts of education and for that purpose if it had taken steps to start similar functions at the 173 state level probably the things would have be different. But here is simply concerned with the taking over of the management temporarily it could have provided for the restoration of the elected body in due course. It appears from Entry 26 that a temporary arrangement was made because the management of the Samahhas Praha Prachar Samiti was not in proper hands and the temporary arrangement is only to improve the functioning of the society and ultimate it has to be handed back to the elected bodies under the constitution of the Committee itself. [172F G] 1:3 The State had no intention to restore the Samiti and therefore, the State had a right to appoint the whole of the Board which will take place of not only the Managing Committee i.e.

A Hindu widow, who died in September 1927, instituted a suit for a declaration that the deed of gift executed by her daughter in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on the reversion. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) A final settlement of the terms of marriage was made at Deoghar and the terms which were settled between the parties were that (a) that Sumitra Devi would arrange for the gift of ornaments worth about Rs. 51,000 only; (b) that she would arrange the gift to her daughter as dowry; (c) that a gift of four houses at Asansol was made by her in September 1938 and possession of the houses was also given to her; (d) that the story of delivery of possession of these houses to Kamala Devi did not make it absolutely clear or specific that the promise related to the four particular houses which were the subject matter of the subsequent gift. [457 C D] (2) The High Court was in error in holding that the gift was not in excess of the powers of the brother and could not operate beyond the life time of Sumitra 's daughter. [465 E F] (3) In view of the fact that the concurrent finding of the courts below that there was no " sankalpa" or promise of a gift to the daughter as her marriage was not lawful, it was open to any other serious criticism.

The appellant was the election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The polling took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. Tej Singh, respondent secured 25571 votes whereas Avtar Singh secured 25 571 votes. There were three other candidates also in the field, viz., (1) Sathi Ruplal, (2) Jagdish Chander, and (3) Jagdish Chandra, who secured 25572 votes. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh and Avtar Singh was about the votes polled by Tej Sing Singh. As the margin of votes between the defeated candidates and the returned candidate was very small, viz. 123 votes, if such a misrepresentation was not made, in all probability the votes would have gone to the appellant (Asok Singh) and therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered. The first respondent filed an Election Petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court challenging the election on the ground that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency wherein he had mentioned that Ruplals had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him (Tej Singh) would be deemed to be a vote for Ruplala. The High Court dismissed the Election Petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by Tej singh were proved beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant was entitled to succeed on the grounds of corrupt practice as contemplated by section 123(2) of the Act having been adopted by the first respondent (Teja Singh). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The election petition must succeed on a short point. The main corrupt practice alleged by Tej Kaur and Ruplnal was in fact printed at the instance of Tej Singh. Therefore, it is clear that Ex P 1 and P 2 which contained the appeal purporting to be of Ruplatal were in fact printing at the behest of Tej Sing. [419C D] 2. The allegations of the corrupt practices are clearly proved beyond doubt and the appellant has proved beyond any reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practice particularly when the printing of posters by Tej Pal Singh was in reality printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing. Therefore the conclusion reached by the High Court is unassailable.

The respondent, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The appellant filed an application for contempt against the respondent, alleging that he had committed serious breach of trust and threatened the writ petitioners to withdraw the said writ petition and pursuant to that, eleven officers withdrew from the petition. The High Court dismissed the application holding that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that as no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High Court in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt, section 19(1) was inapplicable and the appeal was incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the High court is to punish. When no punishment is imposed by the trial court, the High COurt cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or power to punish in a particular manner, the exercise of jurisdiction or the power will involve the acting in that particular manner and in no other. Article 215 confers jurisdiction or powers on the High Courts to punish contempt for contempt. When the High Curt does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the Supreme Court does not exercise its jurisdic tion or power under article 215 of the Constitution. It does not, however mean that when the High Commis sioner erroneously acquits a contemnor guilty of criminal contempt, the petitioner who is interested in maintaining the dignity of the court will not be without any remedy. Even though no appeal is maintainable under section 19 (1) of the Act, the aggrieved party under section19(1), can only be the contemnor who has been punished for contempt of Court. [892F H; 893A B] 2. The right of appeal under section 20(1)(a) of 'the Act arises only when the Supreme court erroneously acquis sfully guilty of a criminal contempt. The aggrieved party, under section 14(1). can only he contemnor who had been punished by the Court for contempt and not on the ground of porpriety or any other consideration. [884C D] 3. In the instant case, there was no right of Appeal under section 13(1); the petitioner in such a case could move this Court under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. It is true that in considering a question whether the alleged contemner is guilty of contempt or not, the court does not exercises its jurisdiction nor power to punishing for contempt under article 214 of the constitution. [864D E] 4. The remedy against the erroneous decision of the trial Court is not barred by section 19 of the . [893F G] 5. In a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the Court and the contemnor.

The appellant was a minor at that time and became a major in or about 1925. He owned two inam lands at Mundhava which were then numbered Pratibhandi No. 71. On 1st July, 1863,ricity sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7,999. The sale deed provided that in default of payment of rent tooccupier or her heirs the purchaser would have no right whatsoever left over the property. On 18th August, 1870, Ladha Ibrahim sold his lease rights to S Girdhari Balram Lodhi for a sum equal to the assessment of the two lands to the heirs of Bird. The appellant was then in financial difficulties and passed a permanent lease of both these numbers to one Ladhadas Sheth. He was in financial difficulty, passed a temporary lease of two old Both the same numbers to One Ladhaldas Sheth. She owned two Inam lands at Mhava. She died in or around 1925. In 1938 she owned two inams at Mundharva which are then numbered Part B and C. The land sold by R was in arrears. During the year 1928 rent again fell into arrears. On 21st August, 1903, Latradas sold his rights to One Girdhari Baluram Lodhi for about three years. The rent note provided that "in default of payments of rent" tooccupier shall not be discharged of rent. " In 1948, the appellant was in direc tions to pay rent to the respondents on the forfeiture of a lease. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant and the trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the decree of the lower courts granting possession of land to the respondent on the ground that the lease had determined by forfeiture for non payment of rents. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that notice as contemplated by section III(g) of the Transfer of Proce dure Act, 1908, is necessary for the determination of a 'lease for nonpayment of rent even where such lease was executed before coming into force of the . (2) that the statutory provisions of section 111(g), as such cannot be made to govern the present lease which was executed in the year 1870. HELD : (1)(a) The High Court was right in holding that the matter was one of discretion and both the lower Courts had exercised their discretion against the appel lant and that being so, unless they were satisfied that the discretion was not judicially exercised or was exercised without proper materials they would not ordinarily interfere with it in second appeal. [1023 B] (b) The provisions of the Act which are statutory recognition of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience cannot be accepted either as correct or precise. Of course, to the extent that those sections of the , give statutory recognition to principles of justice and good faith, they are applicable also to cases not governed by the Act. [1123 C] (c) The requirement as to written notice in writing as a preliminary to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of lease is not based on any principle of equity or good conscience. It has to be seen in every case whether the particular provisions of Act relied upon restates a known rule of equity and if it is merely a new rule laid down by the legislature without reference to any rule of law, equity cannot be said to have been made applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into operation of the. [1109 G] (d) The provision as to notice in written notice under section III of the does not require them and it cannot be held that what has been enacted in sub section (g) is the rule applicable in this case. [1016 C D] (e) In exercising the discretion, each case must be judged by itself, the delay, the conduct of the parties and the difficulties to which the landlord has been put should be weighed against the tenant.

The Associated Cement Companies Limited, a company, was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The workmen employed in the said quarries had a union called Kymore Quarry Karamchari Sangh and the four workers concerned were at the material time the office bearers in the union. In connection with the implementation of the recommendations of Second Central Wage Board for the cement industry, the management served charge sheets on three of the respondents, one of whom was an employee of the appellant company. The second charge was that the employees of the Company had stopped at the gate and he was unlawfully obstructed from visiting the querry premises. Since the second charge against the respondents was partly proved, the fourth charge was partly established and the fourth was partly found proved. The third charge was partially proved against the employees while the additional charges were partly proved against them. A departmental enquiry was held against the management for having restrained the Quarry Agent from entering the quarry premises. The respondents were called upon to submit their explanation in respect of the charges to the General Manager who after considering the same and after taking into account the previous service record of the Respondents, by his order dated 31st December, 1968 dismissed the respondents from service. The appellant challenged the Award before the High Court by means of a Writ Petition (Misc.) No. 128 of 1970 contending that the Arbitrator had misconstrued Standing Order 17 and that no second opportunity was required to be given to the Respondents and in the alternative interference with the punishment of dismissal in respect thereof was vitiated because no second chance was given to show cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of the order as required by the Standing Order No. 17. The High Court dismissed both the Writ Petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Appellant that the learned Arbitrator had mis construed the certified Standing Order dated 17 and had jurisdiction to consider both the aspects and that the arbitrator in the facts and circumstances of the case had justifiably interfered with the dismissal of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan, especially on the ground on which he did so. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award of the Arbitrator was otherwise fair and valid. The solitary ground on Which the inquiry was held to be invalid by the Arbitrator and the High court would disappear and the Arbitrator could not have entered into merits of the matter or interfered with it in short time as possible. [368C D] 2.

The appellant was the owner of a land in Malabar to which the provisions of the Madras Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 were applicable on 11th day of April, 1955 or which was unsurveyed on that date. The appellant filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the vires of section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969. The High Court held that the benefit of the above section would apply only to persons whose occupa tion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believe to be competent to grant such leases or had come into posses sion with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. It was not within the contemplation of the legisla ture to confer the benefit on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The intention of the Legisla tor is to grant protection only to person whose posses tions had a valid origin in that sense they had neither bona fide believing the lands or to be lawfully believed the land to be Govern ment 's land of which he could later seeking assignment or has taken the land on lease, from persons who bona fide belief believed the Lands to be government 's ' lands of whose occupation is unlawful in their origin. The expression "in occupation" occurring in Section 7D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". [114E F] 2.1 In computing the period of occupation of a person for the purpose of clause (c) of the proviso to section 7 D, it is necessary to examine the setting and context in which the said section occurs. This will require a conjoint study of the provisions con tained in Section7D. [114F] 2(a) The intention behind the legi ture was to grant relief only to those whose occupan tion had been unlawful in the origin. In such circumstances, the High Court was fully justified in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of Section 7 D. [115E F].

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. He was prosecuted under section 135(b) (ii) of the . The Collector of Customs, Bombay, ordered confiscation of the seized articles and imposed a fine of Rs. 2,000/ , and in default to three months further rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption contained in section 123(1) of 'the Act corresponding to section 128(A) of , could not be applied as the goods were not seized under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant had been convicted only under section 13(1)(ii). The burden of proving that he knew that the goods must have been smuggled or imported in contravention of the law was on him to prove that they were not smuggled goods. [541G] 2. Section 123(i) of Act clearly lays down a procedural rule, and it could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Indeed, the complaint itself was filed on 30 10 1968. The prosecution evidence to show that the appellant knew that goods must had been smuggled into India without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory; and, therefore, the burden of proof under section 123 (1) was on the accused to prove his innocence. [542A B] 3. Section 106 read with section 114 of the Evidence Act clearly lay down a substantive rule and it would apply only to goods seized under that section. The admissibility and sufficiency of evidence in certain cases could not enable the Courts to come to the conclusion that the imported goods must be known to the appellant to be smuggled even if he was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty. [543C] 4. Section 114, read with s 114 of Evidence Act, is sufficient to enable the prosecution to come into the conclusion, that the Customs must have be known, to the appel lant, to be imported even if the appellant was not, a party, to a fraud evasion of customs.

The appellants were the President of a Municipal Council constituted under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The Association was formed in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa States Companies Act and the appellants filed an application to be joined as plaintiffs. The Registrar of the Society was appointed by the President. The appellants contended that the Association was not registered as a company under the Vindhya Pradesh State Companies (Extension of Laws) Act, 1950, and that the object of the Association being to acquire gain by the individual members thereof, it was not necessary for the Association to have its objects rendition of accounts in enforcement of an illegal contract of partnership. Held, that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for accounts of the association which was dissolved in February 1948 and they were entitled to have their subscriptions returned; on the contrary they had asked for a return or refund of their subscriptions; on failure to do so, they had a remedy against each other for contribution or apportionment in respect of the partnership dealings and transactions. The Society was not one for accounts for a dissolved firm but for accounts which were asked. The suit was not maintainable as there was no direct compulsion that a partnership firm must be registered, though the disabilities consequent on non registration may be extremely inconvenient. Held further, that section 4 (2) Of the Rewa state Companies Act was not applicable to the case and the application of section 72 of the Indian Contract Act was barred by section 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The provisions of section 71(3)(a) of that Act were inapplicable in the present case as they had no application to a suit under the repealed State Companies Acts, 1935, being prohibitory in nature.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 51 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognizance of the offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C., 1973 and that as an investigation by the police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the learned magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of offences against the respondents when there was no scope or occasion for taking cognisance of the same offenses. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the accused, holding that the Magistrate acted contrary to the provisions of section 210 Cr.P.C. 1973 and issuing summons. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the complaint did not spell out therediants of the alleged offence; that the investigation was still continuing and pending in so far as the petitioner is concerned and the investigation shall continue; that as the investigation by police was commenced in relation only to thesame offence, he would be require to stay proceedings on a complaint and called for a Report in the matters from the Police; and, that the Special Judge acted without jurisdic tion in taking cognisable of the offences. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The allegations made in the complaint taken on their face value would not amount in law to any offence against the "Act". [470C] 2. The complaint does not spellout thered iants of an offence alleged. A complaint only means any allegation made orally or in writing to a Magistrate with a view to his taking action that some person, whether known or unknown has committed an offence. It is trite jurisdiction under section482 Cr. Procedure which saves the inherent power of the High court, to make such orders as may be necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, has to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. In exercising that jurisdiction the High Courts would not embark upon enquiry and whether the allegations in the complaints are likely to be established by evidence or not. That is the function of the trial Magistrate when the evidence comes before his. [470D E] 3.

The petitioner was convicted for the offence of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court, in revision, set aside the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Sessions Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no jurisdiction under section 389 Cr. P.C., enlarge on his own bond without sureties, a person undergoing incarceration for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or as convict who has appealed or sought special leave ? HELD: (1) The petitioner 's conviction is not sustainable in law because he is poor and the courts have powers to enlarge him on his bond without surety. [346 D] (2) The Court of Sessions may release a convict on his bail, or on his bonds. But the court of appeal may release him on bail, on his self bond.
