[347 E] (3) In the instant case, the petitioner was released on bail by the High Courts and he had obtained an order for bail in his favour. The Court could not grant bail to him without sureties. He would be released on his executing a personal bond without any sureties. [348 G] (4) The object of bail is to insure that an accused person will return for trial if he is released on the own bond, without sureties and with sureties. When suretyship is insisted on or heavy sums are demanded by way of bail or local bailors alone, it uses the words 'bail ' and 'security bond ' loosely as one or the other both. [349 C] (5) The court of Sessions can release a person on his personal bond only without sureties but in cases where there is reasonable assurance that the individual will reappear before the Magistrate to give bail, the Court or the authority granting bail may have to use the discretion judiciously. When the accused is too poor to find sureties, there will be no point in insisting on his furnishing bail with sureties, as it will only compel him to be in custody with the consequent handicaps in making his defence.

The assessee, a manufacturer of textile Mills, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52 on the ground that it had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 in its capital employed in the undertaking 'Eldee 's business and that the capital employed by it was a newly established undertaking. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle, Amritsar, rejected the claim of the assessee to include the amount of Rs. 1,460 as an allowable expenditure under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's claim on the view that it was not a separate entity and that it could not be regarded as a separate unit. The Tribunal also held that the decision of the Appellate Tribunal in coming to the conclusion that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact was based on no evidence, and that there was no question of law involved in the case. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the High Court had the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the tribunal. The refusal of the Income tax Tribunal to state a case for the opinion of the High court did not amount to an error apparent on the face of the record and was therefore a fit one for appeal by certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. Held, further, that in deciding whether a question of fact arose out of an order of Tribunal, the High Courts must have regard to the relevant matters before arriving at its conclusion. If the conclusion of the Tribu nal was based upon some evidence ignoring other essential matters, it cannot be regarded a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. Non inclusion of the income of 'Castle ' in the assessment of the asses see may have been a relevant circumstance but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Tribu lal had relied.

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was impleaded as a party to the writ petition filed by V.P. Duggal, respondent No. 1. The Minister concerned heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The High Court directed that the Minister concerned might give personal hearing to the parties. In the meantime, the Minister was also directed to file his affidavit. In compliance with this direction, the Secretary of the Department filed an affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the petition. On November 18, 1974, the High Court passed an order directing that the Secretary in charge be impleaded as party. The State Government thereafter heard the matter and made its speaking order. The respondent No,. 1 challenged the validity of the later order of February 18 1975 on the ground that it was not a proper party to this writ petition. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The direction for impleading of the Minister as a necessary party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations in the writ peti tion and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not persuaded to interfere with the order made by the State Government adding the Minister to the Writ Petition as a respondent No party. [97A B] (2) The directions for impleading the Minister in the charge of irrigation Department as a Respondent No. 2 were given by this Court with a hope to apprise him of the allegation made in his petition and thus, to afford an opportunity to controverting these allegations, it was directed that he be impleaded in the Writ petition.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The appellant filed an application under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 260 of the Act on the ground that the amount due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent was under section 258 of the . The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction to realise the amount and issued warrants for attachment of the movable property of the Respondent. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The words "rent on land and buildings" in section 259(1) of the , are governed by the words "recoverable by a Board etc." They are meant to govern "a Board or a Military Estates Officer". It was not necessary that the application should be made to a Magistrate. Further, if the word rent is given a restricted meaning as has been done by the High Court, that word would become purposeless. On the other hand it must be held that where the liability to pay rent arises purely on the foundation of a contract between the Board and the tenant, nothing in the Act or the Rules has been brought to our notice particularly after r. 42 was repealed long before 1954 when the words 'rent on lands and buildings ' came in section 258. (ii) The word "recovered" in the context obviously means "claimable". for section 259 itself provides for the manner of recovery. Therefore, where rent of land or building under the management of a Cantonment Authority falls to be recovered by a board or a military Estates Officer under the Act that liability can be enforced by the authority concerned either by instituting the suit or by making an application to a magistrate. (iii) The expression "recovers from the person cannot obviously be regarded as rent in so far as the Board is concerned. For, the Board was not the landlord of the occupier and what it recovers from his person could obviously be described as rent.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman in the District of Bikaner, Ganganagar, Merta and Barmer in Rajasthan. The appellant was later on transferred to Jaipur. On the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January 1973, he was deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. At the instance of the appellant, the Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court/or the Labour Commis sioner for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the appellant cannot be held to be a workman employed for manual, unskilled and clerical nature and that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act were not aplicable and the reference was incompetent. It was contended on behalf of the management that the dispute referred to the labour Court/Industrial Dis trict was maintainable and if not to what relief he was entitled to. The Labour Court held that it could not be said that the termination itself was illegal. On appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to come within the definition of workman under the Industrial Dispute Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's services were terminated, the employee has to be 'under the employment to do the work of one of the types of work referred to in the Section i.e. manual, skilled and/ clerical nature. The finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. It is seen from the documents produced before it that some relate to the existing position of the stock of goods of the company in the area and the action taken to ameliorate stocks. It would not be the duty of the Company to procure orders for the company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell the product of the respondent company directly through their wholesalers who in their turn sell the products to the various dealers appointed by the company, in order to promote the sale of the product. From 475 perusal of the records produced before this Court it is clear that the appel lant was employed to do canvassing and promo ting sales for the Company.

The appellant company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government (Sanitary Engineering Department) for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Sampat 1999. In Samvat 2000, proceedings were initiated against the Company and the Company was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of Gair Maurusi tenant. The Company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the land in question was not covered by section 181 of the Code as it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act 66 of 1950, and that he could not, by virtue of the provisions of that Act become a pakka tenant. In second appeal, the High Court held that the lease in question did not come within the purview of section 181, because, the Company had been successful in showing that the plaintiff (the company) never acquired the status as Gair Muurusi tenants in respect of the land. The High Court also held that since the Company failed to pay the rents agreed upon between the parties, fresh terms were agreed upon by the parties. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that subsequent to the withdrawal of the appeal from this Court, fresh agreement was agreed upon and between the Company as well as the State Government, that the rent and rents had remained unpaid for a long period in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The finding of the Additional Collector is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable to be questioned in these proceedings. [179G] 1.2 In terms of section 182(2)(i) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code 1959, as amended by M.P. Land Revenue (Amendment) Act 66, 1950, which was the law in force until repealed by the Madhya Bharat Act No. 66 of 1951, the company was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the code as it has not become vested in the State long prior to the coming into force of the Act No 67 of 1950.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 was passed by the State Legislature to provide for the regulation and publication of draft compensation assessment roll and final compensation assessment rolls. By section 1(3) of the principal Act, the lands were deemed to be in the possession of the holder and compensation was payable on the basis of the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent was in consistent with article 3 A of the Constitution. The Orissa Land Reform Act 16 Of 1960 was repealed by the Amending Act 15 of 1965. By a notification dated December 9, 1965, the State Government brought into force the provisions of Ch. IV of the Act other than those contained in Ch. III and IV of Chs. III. The appellants challenged the validity of section 45 of the amending Act on the ground that (1) the Orissa Land Regulation 14 of 1965 was not applicable to them as they were not a law in force at the date of acquisition, (2) the notification issued under section 1 (3) was in operation when the principal was enacted and therefore the ceiling limit prescribed thereby became effective even though Ch. 4 was not extended by a notification under section I(3), and since the subsequent legislation sought to restrict the ceiling limits and to vest the surplus land in the Government under section 45 as amended, there was no ceiling limit applicable to the landholders under any law for the time being in force which attracted the application of the second proviso to article 31 A. Held: (1)(a) The right to compensation which is not less than the market price when the land is within the ceiling area applicable to him under any Law providing for the acquisition by the state of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within that limit applicable. (b) The proviso to Article 31 A of tho Constitution guarantees a person, for compulsory acquisition of his land, the right to comPensation which is less than market value, when the lands are within the limit applicable under any Act for the purpose of any law providing for acquisition by State of any property in an estate in an Estate owned or controlled by the Government. By virtue of section 44 of the Principal Act the interests of persons to whom the surplus lands were being held as a landholder or raiyat shall be fifteen times, fair and reasonable rent may not prima facie be regarded as determination of compensation according to the principles specified by the Act. But article 31A which applies to the statute in question provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the marketvalue of that part of the surplus which is within tho ceiling limit under the principal act. The right of compensation which was not less then the market values of the lands falling within the Ceiling limit fixed as originally fixed under the 1960 Act and the guarantee of the Second proviso to Art 31 A was never made operative by a Notification under section l(3).

The appellants were the widow of one of the reversioners, who had a son named N. section Krishnaswamy Aiyangar (Plaintiffs) and the second appellant in the suit. The first appellant was the sole owner of the entire joint estate by virtue of an oral partition effected between N and his two sons. N died without issue any actual division of properties by metes and bounds. N filed a suit for a declaration that the joint status of the family was disrupted by the notional partition effected amongst Mathurbhai and Kashibhai in 1913 and she, as the next heir of Shankarbhai, was entitled to succeed to Shankarbhai 's share of the properties on the death of Bai Kashi. The trial judge held that there was no concluded joint status by an informal partition between Mathurbhai, and Kasibhai in 1933 and she had lost whatever interest she had in her husband 's property. On appeal the High Court allowed the appeal and gave a declaration in favour of the appellants to the effect that there were disruption of the joint family in the year 1913. The High Court held that the adoption by the widow, by the second wife, was invalid in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (1) that the deed of surrender executed by her did not become infructuous or inoperative and thereby the widow having lost whatever she had interest she could make a surrender of her husbands property for more than the statutory period; (2) that as the widow 's estate was in this case completely extinguished by adverse possession exercised by the defendants, she had, in fact, no interest left in her deceased husband 'S 's properties and therefore could not be surrendered to the reversioners. HELD: (1)(a) The surrender of the estate by a Hindu widow is not to spilt up the husband ' 's title by adverse posses sion against her prior to the date of surrender and these rights would, in law, endure during the entire period of the widow"s natural life. [353 E] (b) A surrender is a voluntary act on the part of the wife and she is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. Instances do arise where an alienee has paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on the expectation of enjoying it so long as the widows would remain alive and his expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the portion of the deceased widow, which no doubt protects him necessarily. [354 G] (c) The mere fact that the widow had lost her husband property by adverse pos session is not enough to disentitle her from claiming possession of the property during the widow life time or at any rate during the period of her widowhood. Such surrender is not an alienation and as the reversioner does not derive his title from her, there is no principle of law under which the acts of the reversioner could bind him. [355 A B] (d) The reversionary right to challenge it is no part of a widow 'Sreeramulu vs Kristamma, I.L.R. , Lachini Chand vs Lachho, I L.R., and Lachinichand vs Lachi Chand, IL. R. ; referred to.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1946. The Cotton Mills Company was established by the Central Government under section 169 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958. In 1970, the Central Board of Directors of the Cotton Mills and its Managing Director became the Chairman and Managing Director of the said company. In 1969, the appellant company decided to promote another company and accordingly the Polytex Company was incorporated. In 1971, the said two companies decided to encourage another company to promote a further company and thereafter to promote an earlier company. The appellant company also decided to sell some of its members. The sale proceeds of the Polymer Company were held by the Cotton Mill Company in 1970. In 1972, the Board of directors of the appellant Company took over the management of the newly established polytex Company in which the Cotton mills had acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each. From 1975 76 on account of a very serious set back in its financial position the Cotton mill company could not meet the wage bill, the dues payable to the employees of the cotton Mills and they made a further order under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertaking (Durs Recovery) Control Act,1958 appointing a Receiver in respect of the shares of the polytex company held by it. The said sale proceeds were distributed amongst the members of the respondent company. On October 27, 1977, the Collector passed an order under Section 128 A of the Act requiring the Board to keep an extraordinary general meeting of the Company for considering and if thought fit, to pass with or without modification as required by law. The Board of Director of Swadeshi Polytex Ltd., was appointed as the chairman of the meeting on March 23, 1984. On November 27,1977, the Registrar of the High Court passed an Order under Section 129 A of Act requiring that the Board shall keep an extra general meeting called for the extraordinary general meetings of the company since it was likely that one or the other member might raise it as an issue at the next meeting. The resolution also asked the Polycotex Company to treat the said notice as a special notice under section 284(2) and (5) read with Section 5 of U. P. Government Electricity Undertakings (Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order, the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares in question and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton Company had lost its right to exercise its voting rights in respect thereof. [867C] 2.

The petitioners filed a suit in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for declaration that they were owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others. The Panchayat filed a written statement inter alia pleaded that the court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The trial Court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. The petitioners ' case was that the Panchayat had no sort of right in the suit property and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly claim a declaration that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat deh. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the Civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamlat or not and whether it belonged to the Panchayat or not. [836C D] 2. The High Court held that the jurisdiction of the civil courts had not been taken away by virtue section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act which had been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act. [ 837E F] 3. The contention of the Panchayat before the trial court was that it was shamat deh and that it had no right or title in it. This question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the act and not by the Civil court. [864F G] 4. The suit had not, therefore, been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat. It is no doubt true that the plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with others of the land had avoided to seek a declaration from the civil Court that the disputed land belonged to them as shamil deh.

The Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board is constituted under Section 5 of the Electricity Supply Act 1948. The Andhra Pradesh Electricity Board was engaged in generation, distribution and supply of electricity in the State of Andhra Pradesh. Electric energy is supplied for industrial, commercial and agricultural purposes. To such of these industries, using energy about a particular level, it is supplied at a higher voltage. These industries are classified as high tension consumers (H.T. consumers). All the appellants herein belong to that category. Section 49 of the Act empowers the Board to notify the terms and conditions upon which it will supply electricity to a person. It is also empowered to frame uniform tariffs in that behalf. The appellants have been classified as low tension consumers. They are classified under high tension consumer (HS.T.). All the appellant herein belong, to that Category. Section 9 of the Andhra Pradesh Act empowers Board to declare the terms on which it would supply electricity. The condition requiring the consumer to pay surcharge at 18% per month for non payment of bills within 15 days after the expiration of each calendar month is that the consumer failing to pay to the Board any sum that may become due for payment to the Electricity Board and not paid within the prescribed period. The deposit is liable to be reviewed by the Board from time to time having regard to the factors mentioned in the said clause. The proviso thereto prescribes that no interest would be payable on security deposit if there was a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in consumption security deposit since it has direct bearing on the level of supply in consumption of electricity. In view of the judgment of this Court rendered in M/s. Jagdamba Paper Industries (P) Ltd. vs H.S. Board, ; , the appellants are entitled to deduct the interest already accrued on the deposit made by them in terms of clause 20(a) and (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. The respondent Board is directed to examine the question of enhancement of rate of interest payable by the Electricity Boards.

The petitioners were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967 and 1970. The Class I posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and Technical Officers Grade I were filled by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission. The Recruitment Rules provided for the recruitment to the different cadres in the Telecommuni cation Centre. The Special Pay was not being paid to the petitioners. In response to the said advertisement, the petitioners were selected for appointment to the posts of Assistant Directors or Deputy Director and were working throughout the Telecommunication Research Centre. On the question whether they were entitled to the special pay which was granted to the trans ferred officers who were working in the telecommuni anation Centre, this Court, HELD: The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong are not given any Special Pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telecommi cation Research Centre to prevent persons of inferior caliber amongst them getting into the said centre. It does not mean that persons who are directly recruited and working in that centre are inferior to those who enter the centre by transfer. It is clear from the above answer that the Government had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions and responsibilities were the same as between direct recruits and the transferred officials had to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same. [1011C D] Randhir Singh vs Union of India & Ors., ; , relied on. In the instant case, the direct recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout their Telecommunication Centre for more than six years. Still the Government did not show any eagerness to grant special pay to the direct recruit working in Tele communication Research Centre, which is not in their general line.

The appellant was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara. He had framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry was held and he was dismissed from service with effect from August 1, 1965 by an order dated August 1. 1965. The appellant then filed a petition under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court which was allowed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Labour Court had no authority to deal with his case under the Standing Orders and consequently the Labour court had jurisdiction to try him. HELD: (i) The scheme of section 7(1) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946 as amended by Maharashtra Act 22 of 1965 shows that the power to try offenses punishable under the Act is to come into operation as laid down in section 45. [737 A B] (ii) The object of which was to make numerous changes in the Act shows that it contains all the powers of the Labour Courts in the matter of all disputes mentioned and gives jurisdiction to punish certain offenses under the Bombay Act. It does not lay down the procedure for the attraction of such jurisdiction. [700 D] (iii) The Legislature nowhere intended to make a complete departure from the procedure to be adopted when powers under section 78(1D) were to be exercised. Rule 5 of the Madras Industrial Relations Rules, 1947 shows how an application is to be made and the period within which it is to he made. It must be held that a person who is dismissed would be an employee within the meaning of section 3(13) of Act and therefore the Labour Appellate Court was a creature of the statute and it could only exercise such jurisdiction as the statute confers on it.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were tenants from month to month. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif, Ranchi praying for their eviction. The Munsif accepted the appellants ' case and passed a decree for eviction against them. The respondents then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction. The learned Single Judge allowed the application and set aside the order of the Munsif. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lants that the suit was not maintainable before the Munsiff, and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The proceeding has to be treated as a suit and his decision as a decree therein. It has to he kept in mind that it is the same court before which both a suit under section 11 and an application thereunder are to be filed. [975C] 2. In a case dealing with compulsory retirement this Court in M.R. Singh vs The Chief Commissioner (Admn.) Manipur & others, AIR 1929 Patna 141, a suit was dismissed as against one of the defendants who in the proceeding of execution of the decree filed an objection to an attachment order under Order XXI, Rule 58 C.P.C., which was recorded under that rule only. The court proceeded under that Rule only. [951E] 3. In the instant case it is not wholly immaterial as to whether the original application filed by the appellants before the Subordinate Judge was not in the form of a plaint specially when the necessary verification was also there at the foot of the petition. The only differ ence may be as to the amounts of court fees payable by the appe lants in the first court and by the respondents before the Judicial Commissioner and the High Court but that should not come in the way in construing the correct nature of the proceeding. [949G H] 4.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent, who was elected as Secretary of the Society. The trial court allowed the suit and dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the trial court had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting the withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power and the High Court had rightly held that only remedy of the appellant was to file a fresh suit. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held in so far as the finding of the trial Court that Hari Narain Swami had been duly elected as the Secretary of Society is not the Secretary. [236B] 2.1 In passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The principle has been followed in this country for more than a century. In Vilakathala Raman vs Vayalil PETITIONal Raman, Madras 27 Law Jour 238 nal Reports 172, the trial courts had vacated its previous order regarding satisfaction of decree on the ground that the same was obtained by the judgment debtor 's fraud on the court. The appellate Court has also held that the only remedy for the appellant is to file fresh suit and not to entertain a fresh application. [237D E] 2:2. In the instant case, the High Courts were wrong in dismissing the appellant 's application as not maintainable. If the appellant had actually consented to it, the court had the power and duty to investigate the matter in exercise of its inherent powers, and the only right to the party is to institute a suit. [238E] 3.1 The principle that has been laid down in Sadho Saran Rai & Ors. vs Anant Rai & Others, AIR 1923 Patna 483, pointing out the distinction in cases between fraud practised upon the court and fraud practised on a party. Let us consider the cases in which consent decrees are challenged. If a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree on that ground he did not give his consent, the Court has the power to duty and duty lo investigate the case and to set aside the order if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. [239F G] 2(a) The High Courts had inherent power to correct its own proceedings when it is satis fied that in passing a specific order it is misled by the one of them. The Court has inherent power, and only remedy to the Party is to Institute a suit.[238G H; 239A B] (b) In the present case, though the consent decree was obtained on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually agreed to it. However, if the case of the party challenging the decree is that he was in fact a party to the compromise petition filed in the case but his consent has been procured by fraud, the courts cannot investigate the matters in exercise thereof in the exercise of their inherent power. [240D E; 239B] (c) The principle laid down by this Court in Sadiq Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Ram Rai & others, AIR 1924 Patna 483 is that in the absence of a prayer for withdrawing the suit, the prayer for withdrawal was not made on behalf of the plaintiff.

The appellant was tried along with the co accused for the offence of murder and the trial ended in his conviction. The High Court confirmed the conviction but convicted him under section 7 read with section 109 Indian Penal Code. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Ordinance promulgated by the Governor General on January 12, 1946, was a temporary Act and its duration was limited to an effective life of six months only from the date of promulgation. Sub section (3) of section 1 of the said Act provided that in respect of Ordinances made under section 72 during the period specified in section 3 of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" were omitted; but the period mentioned in section 2 of the Ordinance was enlarged to a period of six years only from that date. [655 C D] (ii) The emergency on the happening of which an Ordinance can be promulgated is separate and distinct from and must not be confused with the emergency, which occasioned the pawing of the Act and the clear effect of the words of the ordinance on section 72 as they stood with the omission of the word " for" in section 72 with the addition of the expression "for the space not more then six months therefrom ". [656 D E] (iii) The Emergency under which the Governor was invested with the power to promulgate an Ordinance under section 73 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, was in operation on July 11, 1953, the date on which the offence was committed by the appellant and the appellant was rightly convicted by both the courts below. [643 B C] (iv) The ordinance having continued in operation even after April 1, 1946 when it was promulgated during the periods between June 27, 1940 and April 1 1946, the Ordinance ceased to be in operation before July 11 of 1953, when the Ordinance lapsed or ceased to operate.

The appellants were convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the death sentence on the ground that it was not within the province of the court while dealing with an appeal confined to sentence under section 302, I.P.C., 1898, nor was it constitutionally permissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence of death should be curtailed or not is for the Parliament to decide. The onerous option to spare the lives of the appellants to be spent in prison or to hand over them to the hangman to be jettisoned out of terrestrial life into "the undiscovered country from whose bourn no traveller returns" is the crucial function. This Court has in Rajendra Prasad 's case, set aside the judgment and sentenced the appellants on the grounds that (1) the High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a), I. P.C.; (2) the law of punishment under section 300, IP. C., 1898 had been largely settled by this Court and the High Courts were bound thereby; (3) the onerous option could not be exercised because it was a functional failure because of the casual way the punishment factors are dealt with, as if the nature of crime was the sole determinant of the punishment; (4) the crime may be shocking and yet the criminal may not deserve death penalty. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants have not received reasonable consideration for the question of the appropriate sentence. [1071C] 2. The Sessions Judge was justified, in confirming their death sentences under section 354(3) Cr. Pc., 1898. [1171D] 3. The conviction and sentence passed by the High court were neither 'reroneous nor 'arbitrary or excessive ', or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '. Nor was it legally permissible for the Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression "special reasons" occurring in section 354 (3), Cr.Pc., 1973. [1107G] 4. The sentence of imprisonment for life, irrespective of the gravity of the clime as the surrounding circumstances i.e., virtually abolish the extreme penalty, would amount to unwarranted abridgement of the discretion legally vested in the trial court and constitutionally upheld by this court. [1008C D] 5. The Court 's attention was drawn to Ediga Annamma 's Case, [1069F] 6. The law of sentence is the law 'of punishment under Section 302 I.p.C. but it is neither feasible nor legally permissible to define or circumscribcribe the ambit of the term "special reason" occurring therein. [1017G H; 1018A] 7. The appellant has not received any reasonable consideration in the question. The only thing in a Judge decision binding his decision is the principle upon which the case is decided and for this reason it is important to analyse a decision and isolate from it the ratio decidendi. In the leading case of Qualcast (Wolverhampton) Ltd. vs Haynes, [1974] 4 S.C R. 713, referred to.

The appellant was a Income tax Inspector. He was suspended by an order dated 30th September, 1953, by the Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the ground that he had entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in 1939, and wrongly joined together. The appellant 's case was that he was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. He challenged the order by a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it on 17th November 1969. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order refusing the certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to the Supreme Court must have been before this Court. [584 D] (2) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity is denied that some points which the litigant considers importan may have escaped notice. But what is more important is the litigants must have complete confidence in the results of litigation. This confidence tends to be shaken if there is excessive delay between hearing of arguments and delivery of judgments. Justice, as we have often observed, must not only be done but must manifestly appear to be done. [585 C D] Smt. Ujjam Bai vs State of & Anr., ; , followed. (3) The High Court refused the certificate on the grounds that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave.

The appellants are the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The sales tax authorities treated the contracts between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. as one for export and the other for the purpose of levy of sales tax. The Sales Tax Authorities held that the contract was a single sale which could be said to cause the export, but the M/s Binani Bros. (P) Ltd. vs Union of India & Ors., [1975] Supp. S.C R 169, relied on. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales were completed within the state of Andhra pradesh and therefore the M,M.M.,T. C. was not the last purchaser of goods within the meaning of the State. The High Court held that there existed a bond between the parties and the appellants were complete within the territory of India. Dismissing the appeals to this Court, HELD: (1) The contracts between two merchants and the Corporation are different contracts and it is the S.T.,C. which entered into independent contracts with their foreign buyers on F.O.B. basis. Under the contracts the seller 's duty is to place the goods "free board on board" a ship to be named by the buyer. When the seller delivers the goods for loading on board he normally obtains a mate 's receipt which he transmits to the buyer and the buyer takes actual delivery but eo instanti it is delivered in implement ing each separate contract in the chain. In string contracts or chain contracts delivery is made by the original seller and eoin instanti, it is deliver in implement ment under each separate Contract in the line. [444 B C] (2) The tests are that there must be a single Sale which itself causes the export or is in the progress or process of export. There is no room for two or more sales in the course of export and there is no need for two, or more sale in the nature of export.[444 D E] (3) The test is that there should be a Single sale which itself results in the movement of the goods from the export to the importer. [447 A B] (4) The contract between the merchants and Corporation are often the same contracts as they are in the present case, the last purchase in the State is the M .M.C., for this sort of F.F.O.,B. contracts but because in this type of contract the seller "s duty was to deliver the goods F. O.B." Once they are on board the seller has delivered them to the buyers and it was natural that they should thereafter be at the buyer 's risk.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October 1974. The services of the appellant were terminated with effectfrom 19th November, 1974 and on the expiry of this extended period of probation, his service was terminated by letters dated 12 th October,1974, with effect From 19th Oct., 1974 when the extended period for probation expired on September 8, 1974 when he extended the period of his probation. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination order and seeking permission to participate in the proceedings which motion was granted. The High Court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the Appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per day from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking approval to participate, in the proceeding which motion is granted. Respondent filed a petition before the Labour Court challenging his dismissal order and sought permission to participated in the Proceedings which motion being granted. On evaluation of both oral and documentary evidence held that the termination of the service was in accordance with the standing orders justifying the removal of the employee on unsuccessful probation during the initial or extended period, and therefore, the termination in this case according to the Labour court would not constitute retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act. The Labour Court held that since the appellant was not shown to have been placed on probation in the initial appointment letter but in view of subsequent orders there was a period of Probation prescribed for the appellant and that his service had been terminated during the extended or extended periods of probation and therefore the termination was neither illegal nor unjustified nor unjustified. The appellant filed an appeal by special leave against the High 's order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to invoke the fiction enacted in sub section 2 (a) it is necessary to determine the first relevant date i.e., the date on which a workman has actually worked under that employer for not less than 240 days. Sub section (2) specifically comprehends a situation where a workman is not in continuous service within the contemplation of sub section (1) for a period Of one year and he will satisfy the eligibility qualification enacted in section 25 F. On a pure grammatical construction, it cannot be said that the workman concerned continues to be in service with all consequential benefits.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by the Settlement Commissioner, Patiala and East Punjab States Union. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in view of the settlement Officer 's report with some other officer he was not satisfied that the appellant had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Ude Singh. The appellant challenged the authority of the Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submitted that the procedure followed by him was irregular. Held, that the order terminating his employment under the terms of employment was in the nature of an order of punishment and the provisions of article 311(2) had not been complied with. The termination of service was by way of punishment, because it put a stigma on his competence and thus affects his future career. In such a case he is entitled to the protection or article 311 (2). Ram Narayan Das vs Ram Narayan DAS, A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 689, referred to. The enquiry made by the settlement officer was not in exercise of this authority reserved under the provisions Of article 311 and an order consequent upon such enquiry and order consequent on the report made in the enquiry will not fall within the principle of Ram Narayan Dass 's case. Ram Narayan Singh Das vs State of Orissa, A I. R. 1960 section C. 689 and Ram Narayan D Das vs The Chief Justice of India, ; , followed. Ram Narain Das vs Shri Narayan Das, A,I. R., 1960 S C.R., 689, distinguished.

The appellant State Government was aggrieved by the promotion of respondents Nos. 3 to 46 and others as Professors in supersession of their claims for promotion. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's order dated July 25, 1969, in regard to the appointments of respondents No. 3, 46 and other persons as Professors. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Commission had not consulted either in regardto the principles to be followed in making promotions or transfers; (ii) the selection made by the State Public Service Commission for promotion was invalid because it was not consulted in the manner required by section 133 of the Constitution and as such the selection was bad. HELD: (1) The High court erred in taking a contrary view. [873 D] (2) The question whether the requirement of consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed that the Commission was consulted in regard thereto. It is not provided by section 134 of the constitution that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the candidates, or that it was also not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting only of one of its members so long as the Commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [864 F G] (3) The fact that the State had consulted the Commission under section 133(2)(b) of the was not a ground for the High Court to interfere with the selection in question, nor did it affect the validity of the selection.

The petitioner was a citizen of India. He was convicted by the Patna High Court under section 120B, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The petitioner contended that he had the right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed by article 19(1)(a) and that as an editor of a newspaper he is entitled to all the benefits of freedom of the Press. Held, that the fundamental right under article 19 (1) (a) of the Constitution includes freedom of press and expression and that the provisions of articles 194(3) and 194(4) are not constitutional laws and not ordinary laws made by Parliament or the State Legislatures and therefore they are as supreme as the provisions in Part III. The Legislative Assembly claims that under article 194(1) the Legislature has all the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons at the commencement of the constitution. The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the provisions Of the Constitution and the rules and standing orders regulating procedure of the Legislature. That clause provides for powers, immunities and immunities of the House and Houses of the State Legislature and of a member and committees thereof. It does not in express terms make that clause subject to article 194 (3) of that Article. The power, privileges, immunities or immunities of a House of the legislature are only those of the Legislative Assembly of the United Kingdom and its members and committees and they cannot be said to have been so exercised unless it is saved by any law prescribing reasonable restrictions within the ambit of article 19. The right conferred on a citizen under article19(1), therefore, includes freedom from speech and expressions which include freedom of propagation of ideas and their publication and circulation. Article 194(2) does not make that provision subject to any of the provisions contained in Part 111. The Legislature has no power to take action in respect of the said publication or by the authority of a house of such legislature, but it is open to Parliament or State Legislatures to enact laws which are inconsistent with article 19 and article 194. The legislative Assembly claims to have the privilege of preventing the publication of its proceedings and the right conferred by article 194 is not affected by any other law prescribing such reasonable restrictions.

The respondents, who were working as Readers in different faculties in the private college, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the circular dated March 23, 1971 issued by the Director of Public Instruction (Higher Education) Orissa, which was challenged by the appellants on the ground that they were drawing salary more than Rs.600/ and that the Government scale for Readers was Rs.660/ respectively as on the date of taking over of the management of the College. The High Court accepted the writ petition and held that the respondents were entitled to consideration by the Public Service Commission for appointment as Readers under the Government in the manner laid down in the circular. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High Courts erred in directing the Gov ernment to take into account, experience, the service of the respondents while they were in the college since according to him, the necessary qualification is eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.) and Chineswar Rao (No. 10); (ii) the respondents being lower than that of the Readers in the Private College much later than the four of them were promoted even earlier than No. 9 and no. 10; and (iii) the appellants were not entitled to be considered by the Commission for appoint ment as Reader because they had put in more than eight years of service as a Reader. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question is entirely different when as in the present case, the respondents answering the test of educational qualifications, as well as experience of teach ing in a recognised private college are discriminated amongst the very category of Readers on an irrational and illusory consideration. Denial of an opportunity to the Respondents in the matter of employment under the Govern ment under Article 16 of the Constitution is clearly violative of Article 16. [778G H] 2.1 The High Courts were right in directing that the Govnment should take into consid eration as experience, and later for consideration of their suitability by the public Service Commission. Their names shall be referred to the Commission accordingly. Whether they will be suitable for appointment or not is an entirely different matter.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) C.P.C., but the State Transport Authority rejected their applications on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A), the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others, is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled. The appellants filed writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the scheme on the grounds that once it had been published, the Corporation was not competent to grant temporary permits and that the Corporation had applied only 3 permits. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts held against them. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 68 F (1 A) and section 68 G(1 C) are not relevant for the present purpose. They are not applicable in the present case because the scheme has already been published by the State Government under section68C in respect of the route under section 69C. The Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. [986 D F] (2) Section 69 F(I) C provides that if no application for temporary or permanent permit is made under section 88F(l A), no temporary permit can be granted to any one else if the Corporation has applied for all the permits. But section 68 H(1 B) does not admit of such a construction. The authority under the Act must not lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be the service available to the travelling public. While interpreting the provisions of the undoubtedly competing claims between the Corporation, and other private operators may be examined with reference to the provisions Of the Act. But the overall consideration namely the service is for the benefit of the travellingpublic should never be overlooked for a moment.

The appellant was the son of a Hindu female who died in 1927. On March 22, 1927 he executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the said properties in favour of the respondent 's maternal grandfather. The appellant claimed that his family was governed by the custom prevailing in the Punjab and under this custom the property in suit was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father. The trial judge held that the property inherited by the respondent was not ancestral property but that the impugned transactions were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. He, however, held that as the appellant was not born at the time when the mortgage deed was executed and so he was not entitled to challenged it. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench were not correctly decided. [1102 B] (ii) The doctrine of stare decisis is applicable because the rule of stare overruling is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that grievous wrong may result. [1103 C] (iii) The principle of stare Litigation is not applicable because it has come through a female who succeeded her father in default of male heirs. [1001 D E] (iv) The rule of obiter dictum applies because the doctrine of decisis really applies because it does not apply because the case of stare decisions is wholly unsustainable as a decision on the point of law relevant to the controversy.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum for offences under section 449 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November, 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came and while one of them was armed with dagger, he inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. The other two were acting jointly in furtherance of the common intention of all of them to kill Ebott Ali. The Sessions Judge accepted that verdict but convicted the appellants under section 302 read with 34 of Indian Penal code. On appeal by the appellants, the High Court held that there could be no conviction under section 149 of the Code unless murder had actually been committed and that therefore no charge under section 307 read With section 34 was sustainable in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that : (i) there can be no convicting under section 448 of the Penal Code unless the murder has actually been done by several persons in furtherance Of the common object of all, and (ii) the act did not result in death. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the offence "in order to commit" of an offence punishable with imprisonment for life must be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine. [882 B] (i)(a) It is not correct to say that any house trespass was committed "in the order to committing it of an offense punishable with death" but has failed to accomplish the purpose, it will be proper to say, that he had committed the house trespass in order to the committing of theft. [ 882 C] (b) The words "in orders to commit ' in section 34 are used to mean "with the purpose of". If the purpose in committing the house is the commission of an act punishable with life imprisonment for the offence of house trespass, it becomes punishable under section 450 of the Act. Similarly sections 451 and 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code are not sustainable in Law.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration of his title to the lands in question. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collaterals from succession to self acquired property of her father has been varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter which is binding on the parties. Indeed, it has been held in Qamar ud Din vs Mt. Fateh Bano, I.L.R. , that if the Riwaj i am produced is a reliable and trustworthy document, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up, which if left unrebutted by the daughters would lead to a result favourable to the collateral 's. If on the other hand, it is not a document of the kind indicated above then such a Riwi am which is a valid and reliable document must displace the initial presumption of the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's book. [1195 F G] (2) The High Court was right in holding that there was no force or substance in the contention that even if the presumption as to the correctness of Riwa i am was weak, the respondent had not cited a single instance of a daughter having excluded the collateral from succession into the selfacquired property of his father. [1205 G] In the present case, the High court took the view that the evidence as to succession to the property of Harnam Singh was of no assistance to the appellant for the reason that the statement in Riwab i am which was a reliable document had been carefully prepared and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer, the appellant has failed to discharge the onus that was thrown on her as a result of the production by the appellant of the Rwaj i.e. 1913.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a company which was acting as managing agents and also as executor or administrator of estates of deceased persons. On April 7, 1949 he applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in the proceedings before which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrseep Chishm Fairirbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also in his capacity as managing director, director, managing agent, administrator, trustee, administrator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the decision of the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority who ultimately referred it under section 57 to the High Court of Calcutta stating his own opinion that the stamp duty was payable on the power "for as many as respective capacities as the principal executes the power". On appeal by certificate, the appellant contended (i) that the instrument in question consisted distinct matters and must be stamped in accordance with section 5; (ii) that it was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty leviable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities; (iii) that section 6 of the Bengal Act was not applicable to the case as it was not a single power of Attorney liable for a single duty under article 48(d) (1); and (iv) that in any event the instrument could be viewed both as a deed of dissolution and a deed Of partition effects also a partition of the family properties as Secretary Board, in Secretary, Board of Revenue vs Alagappa Chettiar. Held: (i)(a) that when two persons join in executing a powerof attorney in respect o all the matters in which he could act, it should be held to be distinct matters for purposes of section 5 and that the instruments were chargeable with a single stamp duty; (b) that though the instrument was executed by one individual, if he fills several capacities and the authority was general, there would be distinct delegations in respect thereof though with the limitations imposed upon them by reason of the capacities which he enjoys.

The assessee company was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance 1949, which came into force on March 16, 1949, and the Raj Reorganisation Act (XXIII of 1941) was extended to it. The assessee claimed that the said Ordinance had not been used by him as he had not made any claim for depreciation allowance under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but only in 1947. The Income tax Officer rejected this contention on the ground that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words "if a claim had been made" and there was no justification for reading these words into the Ordinance. On appeal to the Supreme Court, Held: (i) The Bhavnagar War Profits Act was within the words 'any law relating to tax on profits of business ' in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, 1950, and that the words used therein were not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. (ii) The High Court was right in answering the question referred to it under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, as amended by the Income tax (Amendment) Act (XXXIII of 1942). The words "any law" in the first portion of paragraph 2 were used to qualify the phrase "any laws relating to income tax on business". The Removal of difficulties Order added the words any law relating tO tax on profit of business" in paragraph 3 of the removal of Difficulties order. The High Courts had rightly decided that the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar war Profits Act, was a deductible amount in computing the written down value of the assets.

The appellant was a contractor with the respondent State of Karnataka. The contract pertained to construction of a Main Station Building of a Power House at the Raichur Thermal Power Plant at an estimated cost of about Rs. 1.8 crores. The appellant had two types of equipment and their deployed ment i.e., (1) should have executed atleast 300 cubic metres per month of brick work at one site; (2) should be had an annual turnover of atleast 1 crore for each of the preceding three years; (3) should had an yearly turnover of at least 1 crore during each of these three years. The last date for receipt of application form for issue of blank tender books was to be between 23rd January, 1989 and the other items were altered to read as follows: "1. Last date for Receipt of 10.2.89 to books 16.2 89 to books 15.21989 to books 17.3.89 complete tender books: upto 3.00 P.M. on 6.2 .89. The N.I.T. specified three 'minimum requirements ' viz., that the intending tenderer should have execute atleast 300 square metres per day of brickwork at one place; and (4) should not have executed at least 300 cubic metre per month for each completed three years." The appellant was informed by the respondent that the last date of receipt of the application form was to commence from 6.1.89. In response, the appellant submitted a complete tender book containing details of work done etc. as furnished by each of them. Four of the firms were found to be pre qualified by the Chief Engineer and tender books were issued to them. Only three of them submitted completed tender books. The first was examined by the Managing Director as well as an independent firm of Engineering Consultants, namely Tata Consulting Engineers (T.C.) who had to be fulried even before the forms of tender could be supplied to any intending contractor. The second was that as against the requirement that the applicant should have execution executed at atleast 300 sq. metres per year of brick works at one sites, the certificate from Vasa vad Cements produced by the M.C.C., had also been furnished only on 21.6.89 and that the details called for in para V could be furnished at any time before the final award of the contract. The Managing Director rejected the appellant 's contention that the extension of time given to it was only to the effect that it would be too extreme to hold that the omission to supply every small detail referred in para I and not para V was satisfied, on an overall view, that there was nothing unfair or arbitrary about the award of contract.

The appellant was the owner of a house. He had taken possession of it on October 10, 1947 and cultivated their respective lands and settled down in the village. After the confirmation order confirming the exchange, the Additional Custodian passed an order confirming that exchange. The appellant filed an application before the Custodian General for confirmation of the transaction but the application was not disposed of by the Additional Collector. Thereafter, he passed an Order confirming the Exchange and the further orders dated October 20, 1952, confirming the sale and the consequential orders made in connection therewith. The Custodian General confirmed the exchange and directed that possession may be given to the appellant and that the Patwari may be informed accordingly to take necessary action in the matter. On November 25, 1953, the appellant filed a petition under section 27 of the (Central Act XXXI of 1950) for confirmation on the ground that the Custodian had no revisional power which he purported to exercise, and that as soon as the application for confirmation was made long prior to the time when the office of the Custodian was set up and he was clothed with powers of revision, the Custodian could exercise revisional powers under section 28 of the Act XXXI Of 1950. The High Court held that the order of confirmation was perfectly bona fide and set aside the order confirming it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power of revision vested in the CustodianGeneral under section 26 of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act XXXIof 1950 is not applicable to an order passed by the Custodian or Additional Custodian on his application for a confirmation pending on the date when Central Act XXXI was repealed. [1139 C] (2) The second portion of section 58(3) refers to the whole range of things that may be done, or action that may he taken under the previous Ordinance and the rules framed thereunder while the first portion of s.58(3), relates to the legal consequences resulting under the Ordinance or the rules from certain facts or acts completed prior thereto. Without attempting to be accurate, it may be stated in general terms that the scheme underlying section 58 (3) appears to be that every matter to which the new Act applies has to be treated as arising and to be dealt with, under the new law except in so far as certain consequences have already ensued or acts have been completed prior to thereto. [11039 C D] State of Punjab vs Mohar Singh, ; , followed. (3)(a) The scheme underlying s. 58(1) of the Central Act LXVII of 1950 is that every matters to which a new Act applied has to he treated as pending and to deal with it. The application can be dealt only by the custodian General only functioning under the earlier law. [1039 C E] (b) The Custodian, in the present case, had no power under section 25(2)(a), to revise the original orders of the Additional Commissioner or Additional Collector on his applications for confirmation pending before the date of Central Act XXXIII of 1950 came into force and superseded the earlier legislation in this behalf. [10939 G] (4) The order of the High Court is one passed by virtue of the wide powers vested in Custodian General under section 23 of the , and that clause (c) thereof must be construed as referring to matters ejusdem generis with clauses (a) and (b). But once the attribute of finality in respect of such an order is affected by subsequent legislation, it does not appear to be of consequence that it was affected by a provision for appeal and later by provisions for appeal. [10839 C G] State Of Punjab vs Jagjiwan Singh, , followed; State of U.P.

The appellant company, a small scale establishment, was granted with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings and nuts, fittings and bolts, nuts and bolt, nut and bolting, nut, fittings, nut & bolts etc. were made and/or sold. These establishments consisted of bulk of workers employed in the tiny, but numerous establishments. The charter demands included inter alia claim for 4 months ' wages as bonus for the year 1965. The arbitral board rejected the demand for bonus on the ground that what was pleaded profit based only bonus was only a profit based bonus and therefore fell within the Bonus Act. The award of the Tribunal was challenged by the appellant before the High Court, which dismissed it in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Bonus Act is all comprehensive and no kind of bonus can legitimately be claimed by the workmen. The demands referred by the State Government under section 10(1)(d) specifically speak of payment of bonus by the employers which have become customary and traditional in the particular concern. It does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act, but only a claim for bonus based on custom. [602 D E] (2) The bonus Act is a complete Code and what is not covered by its provisions cannot be awarded by the Tribunal. It is true that if the Bonus Acts are a complete code and what was not covered in its provisions can be awarded, but it is quite conceivable that the codification may be of everything relating to profit bonus in which other types of bonus are left untouched. The objects and reasons of the Bonus (Amendment) Act are the soul of the law '. If the Bonus Ordinance is a completed code and whatever is not governed by its provision cannot be award by the tribunal. It was true that the Bonus Amendment Act is not a complete scheme and what it seeks to provide for bonus to persons employed in certain establishments ' not in all establishments. Moreover, customary bonus does not require calculation of profits available, because it is a payment founded on long usage and justified often by spending on festivals and the Act gives no guidance to fix the quantum of festival bonus; nor does it expressly wish such a usage. [613 A C] (3) The Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it under section 33 of the Act. [643 D E]. (4) The question whether the payment has been over an unbroken series of years, is not relevant at this stage since the Tribunal has not yet enquired into the merits. The effect of the arbitral board 's negation of the profit based on the custom or conditions of service in these establishments is a different matter with which we are not concerned at this late stage since it was raised before the Tribunal and the counter statement by the employer before the tribunal and the Counter Statement by the employees before the Tribu nal. [641 C D] (5) The Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide on the merits of the subject matter of the dispute.

The petitioners in the Haryana Writ Petitions were selected for recruitment to the Punjab Civil Service (Judicial Branch) after qualifying in a competitive examination. They were appointed as Subordinate Judges in 1950. By an order dated December 31, 1976 they were promoted as District Attorneys from the Haryana Superior Judicial Service with effect from July 7, 1970. The petitioners who were officiating continuously in the Superior Judicial service of the State as Additional District and Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to the appointment of respondent 3 directly to that service lost their seniority over them over by reason of their confirmation being allotted a date of confirmation which was one day later than the date on which they completed his probationary period. The High Court set aside the reversion order on certain other grounds but held that the power to confirm a District and Session Judge resides in the High Court and not in the Governor, that the powers to confirm the District and sessions judge resided in the State of Haryana and that the said power to confirmed a District & Sessions Judge resides outside the High Courts. The State of Punjab appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High court. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the High COurt acted upon the amendment made by the Governor of Punjab in consultation with the Punjab High Court, and not the Governor; (ii) the power of confirmation vested in the Government under article 309 of the Constitution and all other powers enabling him in this behalf, made the Punjab Superior Judicial Services (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976, with retrospective effect from April 1, 1970; and (iii) that the rule of rotation as between promotees and direct recruits at the time of their appointment was violative of Article 235 of the Constitu tion. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts were not justified in applying the rule to a District Judge residing in the Punjab State. [1044C] (2) The seniority of the members of the judicial service is so integral and vital to the control of the high Court over them, that any erosion thereof would both be violative of article 235 of Constitution and equally run counter to the settled concept of independence of judiciary which is now coming to be recognised as the basic feature of the constitution. It follows therefore that if seniority of members of Superior Judicial services is once deemed to be not within the control or the High Curt under Article 235, then in fact it could be determined by the State Governments by making rules even without reference or consultation with High Court. [1144D E] (3) The rule of rota cannot be read into the rule prescribed by rule 8 of the Punjab Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1963 1072 as in force on April 1 1970. Rule 12 of the Haryana High Court Rules, 1962 provides that seniority of direct recruits and promotees shall be determined with reference to the respective dates of their confirmed confirmation. The rule is not in any manner violated thereby. There is no direct decision on the question whether the Governor has the power or authority to regulate seniority of subordinate courts. [11044E F] (4) The rules must now be understood to mean that the High and Court cannot deny to a member of the subordinate judicial service of State the right of appeal given to him by the law regulating him conditions of service.

The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 1975 was promulgated by the President of India on October 18, 1975. Clause (5) of article 371 D of the Constitution provides that notwithstanding the expiration of the said period, the President may by order require the State Government whenever he considers it expedient so to do so to organise any classes of posts in the civil services of or class of civil service of any class or classes of civil posts under the State into different local cadres for different parts of the State and allot ance with such principles and procedure as may be specified in the order. The appellant, a Junior Assistant in the Commercial Taxes Department, was promoted to Senior Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal District comprising of Warangabad and Warangal division consisting of Adilabad and Karimnagar Districts. He was also promoted to the post of Senior Assistant Sub Inspectors, Zonal Seniority of Warabad District comprising the Warangal local area comprising of Hyderabad, Warangal and Warana. The Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal allowed the Representation Petition filed by the appellant and remitted the matter to the Tribunal for considering the effect of the Government order in G.O.Ms. No. 1648 dated November 20, 1982. The Tribunal after considering the effects of the G.Os. issued in GOMs. No.(1648) dated November 21, 1982 held that in the im pugned order that G.S.Ms No. 162 E dated October 18 1975 issued under Para 5(2)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh public Employment ( Organisa ment of Local Cadre and Regulation) Direct Recruitment Order 1975 for that "the order ' no allotment of cadre in terms of para 4 of the order was issued constituting a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts. The writ petition filed by him challenging the said order was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Senior Assistant for Adilabad division consisting oth er the Revenue districts is illegal, contrary to order issued in the GOMS. No(1648). [574G H] 2.2 The phrase 'or constituted otherwise" occurring in the definition of local cadre in paragraph 2(e) of G. O.Ms., No. 581 dated October 20, 1975 issued by the State Govern ment under Article 371 D is only relatable to the power given by the Presi dent to the State Gov ernment to organise local cadres, but the exercise thereof is hedged with a limitation of twelve months from the date of commencement of the Order. Therefore, the phrase 'constituted otherwise ' in paragraph 3(7) of order is only to organise a separate Cadre in respect o the category of any posts exist in a zone under para 3(1) of Order. [574E F] 2:3 The word 'or otherwise ' was given by this Court in Kochuni States vs State of Madras and Kerala, ; Subba Rao, J., as he then was speaking for the Constitution Bench interpreting Expla nation (a) to section 6 of Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 as amended in 1950 and repelling the application of ejusdem generis doctrine laid down therein. [575F G] 2 :4 The word "otherwise" is of wide amplitude.

The appellant mortgaged certain lands to the respondent No. 1 for a simple mortgage of Gadi Sirampur in favour of the Manager of the Court of Wards. The respondents filed a suit against the appellant and the manager of the court of Wards for recovery of the amount due under the decree. The trial court held that the appellant was not bound by the mortgage decree and decreed the suit.
