On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree on the ground that it was not binding on the appellant as he was not a party to the suit and that the Patta could not be put an end to by the auction sale of the mortgaged property. The High Court also held that though the mortgagor had in good faith granted the lease for a limited term, the lease was for a fixed term and stipulated a fair and reasonable rent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the patta could not he put an effective end to the sale by the sale of mortgaged property and that as the mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of temporary leases to middlemen or cultivators, the appellant had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption. HELD: (i) The High court was in error in holding that the lease in favour was valid and binding against the mortgagee. [1104 B] (ii) The mortgagor could not therefore be said to have exercised his right of redeeming the mortgage, that the execution sale of Gad Sirampuram including the four villages in question was binding on him and that he had ample opportunities to redeem it if they desired but failed to choose to do so. [1110 C] (iii) The appellant could not succeed because he had no power to grant the permanent lease in question to the respondents. The fact that there was no allegation in the plaint that the respondent 's lease had the effect of rendering the security of the Bank insufficient, did not affect the validity of the mortgage. [111 D] (iv) The mere fact that the mortgage was granted in good belief was not decisive of the question whether the appellant could grant leases which were not wasteful in its effect the mortgagee 's security. The mortgagor had ample time to redeem and if he wanted to resist the claim of the mortgagee, he would furnish a complete answer to the claim. If the lessee failed to establish this position he would have certainly no defence to an action at the instance of the mortgagor. [112 E] (v) The fact of the case that there were no allegations in the mortgage suit that the defendant had ample power to issue permanent lease was not conclusive of the existence of the loan and so long as nothing took place, to impair the value or impede the operation of the mortgages the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for such a term. [114 G] (vi) The case of Banee Pershad vs Beet Bhunjan Singh, ; , referred to.

The petitioner had to execute the work within 9 months. It was his claim that while executing the work he sent the bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on November 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent invoked the jurisdiction of the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 of the Act. The Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68, the cause of arbitration shall cease to have effect in respect of the dispute or difference. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Court has the power and jurisdiction under sections5 and 12 to grant leave to the applicant in exceptional circumstances to revoke the contract of arbitration. [368E] 1.2 In commercial reference of the kind in question it is an implied term of the contract that the arbitrator must decide the dispute according to the existing law of contract, and that every defence which would have been open in a court of law can be equally proponed for the arbitrator 's decision unless the parties have agreed which is not suggested here to exclude that defence. Were it otherwise a claim for breach of contract containing a reference could cause of action. [369B] 1:3 The Court had the power under sections 3 and 12(2)(b) to grant permission in exceptional cases to revoke an arbitration agreement. In all cases it was not a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or he should enter upon reference for adjudication. [370C] 1 :4 The Court, therefore, has the powers and jurisdiction to grant such leave to a contracting party to the contract. It is open to the parties to plead in the proceedings before him of limitation as a defence. [367E F] In the instant case, the petitioner had put forward his claim in July 1979 and the respondent had not acted thereon till November 28. 1989. The respondent invoked clause 69 and issued notice to the petitioner to refer the case for arbitration. Clause 68 provides reference to the arbitration agreement of all or any of the disputes or differences enumerated therein that have arisen between the parties, at the instance of either party to contract. [371F G] 1.(a) In a modern arbitration the principles of equity must be applied just as they would now be applied in a Court of law. The jurisdiction under section 5 and section 12(1)(b), is discretionary. It should exercise the power sparingly, cautiously and with caution to permit a party to terminate the contract or to reduce it by giving an option to the other party to rescind the arbitration. If the party defending may not rely on the statute of Limitations, he can rely on such statute of Frauds, or the Act partially replacing it. [372F G; 371A] (b) The cause of Arbitration is, therefore. hopelessably barred claim as the petitioner by his conduct slept over his right for more than 10 years. Statutory arbitrations stand apart. [373B C] 2.2 The Court in Pegler vs Railway Executive, 1948 Appeal Cases 332 at 339, approved.

The mortgaged property was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The mortgagor 's estate vested in the State of Bihar on January 1, 1956 as a result of a notification issued under section 3(1) of the Act. A final decree was passed in the mortgage suit on October 1,1956. Thereafter the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the for passing a final decree on September 19, 1955. The mortgagors applied under that section to execute the mortgage decree against Bakasht lands. The judgment debtors objected to the same on the ground that the execution petition was barred by the principles of res judicata and further on July 23, 1960 for default of the judgment debtors. A third application raising the same ground was rejected by the executing court but the High Court in second appeal reversed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (1) that what had vested in them was the non bakasht land as well as other lands and therefore the Bakash t lands did not have the protection of section 4(d); (2) that the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the Land Reforms and Land Reforms Acts, 1950; and (3) that it was not necessary for them to proceed exclusively with the execution. HELD : (1)(a) The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to scaling down of debts due by proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates had been taken away from them by the notifications issued under s 3. Therefore, in construing section 4 (d), it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection afforded by the Act and cannot avail any remedy outside the Act by instituting or any other proceeding in the court of ordinary civil jurisdiction. [912 D E] (b) The procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed, in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision of the claims officers and the decisions of the claim officer or the Board have been made final by the Collector.

The appellants, who were members of the All India Services (I.P.S.) Service, challenged the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Services Examination Rules, 1954 by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the second Proviso to Rule 3 of the C.S.E.C. was illegal since it makes a discrimination between the successful candidates of Central Service Group 'A ' and Group 'B ' service as in the case of Group 'C ' service, as in that case, Group 'D ' service is not restricted by the second schedule to Rule 17 of the Rules. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the High Courts. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso thereto makes a further discrimination vis a vis candidates appointed to Group ' B ' and group 'A service. [972D] 1.2 In order to have a proper understanding and appreciation of the scope, object and intent of the impugned proviso, the first proviso imposes an onerous restriction that they should first resign from the service to which he has already been allocated on the basis of the previous C.E., and that if they fail to join either of the services as mentioned in the second Schedule then their allocation based on one or both the examinations, as the case may be, will stand cancelled. In other words, a candidate failing within the ambit of this proviso can appear in the next Civil Services examination unless he has first resigned from the Service and in other words it declares a candidate who is otherwise eligible in terms of Regulation 4 as ineligible unless he first resigns from the serv ice to which the he has been allocated, nor would he lose his original seniority in the service. The second schedule further provides that a candidate, who accepts allocation to a service and is appointed to a Service shall not be eligible to appear again in the Civil Service Examination unless he had first resigned form the service, provided he is within the permis sible age limit, without having to resign from service to whom he has flied. [962E F] 1:3 The second Proviso thereto makes it a further discriminatory restriction that it should first relinquish the services to which they have been allocated and appointed to one of those services in either of those Services, Group A ' or Group B '. In the instant case, the second part of the proviso to rule 4 of C.P., 1954 is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India and is contrary to law.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the . The grounds of detention were served on him on 25th November, 1986. He challenged his order of detention on various grounds including that he had not been given any opportunity to be heard before the Advisory Board and that he was not a friend of the detenu. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to the assistance of Sundararajan as a friend; and that the Advisory Boards had given their findings and reasons for rejecting the request of the appellant on the ground that he did not represent the case of the detenue. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have been better placed before the Board and assist it with a view to justifying the detention orders; and in any event, the Advisory board had given its findings and reason for rejecting his request. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The refusal by the Advisory Committee to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan was not justified. It is quite clear upon the terms of sub section (4) of section 11 of the Act that the detenu had no right to legal assistance in the proceedings before the advisory Board but it did not preclude the Board to allow such assistance to the detenu when it allowed the facility of appearing before the board through a legal practitioner. [793G H; 795A] 2. The order of the High Court is quashed and the appellant is directed to be set at liberty forthwith.

The Government of India issued a notice under r. 75 A (5) of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, to the appellants requisitioning the same managing agents from the respondents for information as to stocks of hessian and the name of the registered stock holders. The appellants were served with notices of requisition and acquisition on the respondents. The Government filed a suit against the appellants in the High Court under 0. XXI, r.75 A (1) of Defence of india Rules, which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the orders of requisition were invalid as they did not comply with the provisions of 0. XXIX of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such the suit was barred under section 16(3) of Act. HELD: (i) The order of requisition was properly served on the managing agents of the mills, and therefore the proper persons to be served with the orders were duly served. [833 G] (ii) The notice of acquisition was given to the various managing agents in their capacity as managing agents for such mills and such mills as the managing agent of the Mills would also be estopped from denying that cash had been paid for the goods to which they relate. Therefore, the orders passed by requisition were valid and binding on the respective defendants. [861 B] (iii) The appellants could not be allowed to contend that the order of requisitioning was invalid because it did not provide for the manner of service and as in its opinion r. 119 (1), 0. XIX of Code of Criminal Procedure, applied, the service of a notice on the owner, and (iv) the order was not valid and enforceable.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned was 1963 64. For the assessment years 1964 65 and 1965 66, the assessee claimed that the said sum set apart by way of contingent liability under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, should be included in its capital for the purpose of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Tribunal held that no action could be taken against the assessee under Section23A. In appeal by the Revenue, the High Court answered the reference in favour of the Revenue and against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the provision made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision and not a reserve. [113D] Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , distinguished. V Goel Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. vs Commis sioner of Income tax, Andhra pradesh and Ors. vs C.I.T., Andhra Pradesh, etc. , applied. Metal Box of India Ltd. Vokar Sultan Tobacco Cooperative Ltd. & Anr. vs The Commissioner of Incometax, Andhrapradesh, ; followed. Metal box of India vs Their workmen, [1964] 65 I.T.R. 869; Metal Box Co. of India (P) Ltd.v. Commissioner of lncome Tax, A.P., etc. ; , referred to.

The petitioners, who were working as temporary Assistant Engineers in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class I) were subjected to written and personality tests and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. On the other hand temporary Assistant Officers, who had been recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Service Commission and by direct recruits to the Indian Railways Service of Engineering (Class 1), were subjected on competitive examination and those who were recruited by promotion, but neither to a personality test nor were subjected either to written or to a personal test. The petitioners contended that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of the results of the competitive examinations and those appointed on the strength of selection by the Union Public Services Commission. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The classification of temporary Assistant officers and members of the Indian railway Service of Class I was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [1025F] 2.1 The distinction between the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case wherein this Court held that relief of equality was being denied to the petitioners because of the history, origin, structure and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed as to the validity of the given weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, but it would otherwise be imprudent now at this point of time to dig up old issues. [1125G H] 3.2 The classification made by Direct Recruit 's cases is not permissible by means of successive writ petitions. However, some people did get impleaded as parties in that case to project their ratio. Similarly when absorption had been made possible and its paceened with weightage, it is difficult to find fault with the scheme at this stage of time. [1225A B] 3:3 The decision dealing with important questions concerning a particular service given after careful consideration should be respected rather than scrutinised for finding out any possible error. It is not in the interest of service to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interests of justice nor in the inter est of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be computed from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of full length of services subject to maximum of 5 years, it would be otherwise imprinted that principles of constructive res judicata should not bar the re agitation erected by Directrecruit ' 's Case. [11025F G] 3(a) The decision deals with important question concerning a specific service given before direct Recruit Class II Engineering Service of Engineer Class I. [1012B C] (b) The decisions dealing with relevant questions concerning the particular service gave after careful considerations should be equally respected rather as scrutinised for found out any error. [1005C D] (c) The principle of constructive Res judicata is not applicable to cases where the same has been earlier decided by a competent court by a judgment which became final.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to death by the Special judge under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed his conviction but on appeal, it was held that the offence alleged to have been committed by him within the specified areas were required to be tried by a special judge under the provisions of the . Held, that the appellant could not complain of any violation of article 14 of the Constitution as he had no jurisdiction to transfer any case from any Special Judge or to make an order under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The power conferred by sections 9 and 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance was wide enough to include within its scope certain offences which were punishable with imprisonment for life and not in respect of offences committed by a person other than the ordinary procedure prescribed by the Act. It could be exercised only when there was some illegality or irregularity in the procedure adopted or there was a failure to observe any reasonable procedure. The restrictions imposed on the exercise of legislative power under sections 9, 10 and 11 were not unreasonable. The fact that the deviation from normal procedure prescribed in the Ordinance were not so many vital or as in the Bengal case did not affect the result of the defect of the absence of a reasonable or rational classification was no ground for holding that section 11 of Act violated article 14. The appellant could be convicted under the Ordinance only if there was an illegality or impropriety in the method adopted or the procedure prescribed. Held, further, that section II of the Bombay Ordinance which authorised the State Government to direct "offences" and "classes of offences" to be triable by a Special judge was void as offending article 14 Of the Constitution inasmuch as it gave no power to the State Govern ment to direct any class of cases or classes of offences. The notification issued under section 5(1) of the Act was not invalid on the ground that it violated article 19 Of the Constitu tion and the notification which had been issued thereunder offended against the equal protection clause in article 14,of the Constitution.

The appellants were tried for the offence of murder by shooting at a house of Mauji Lal. The prosecution case was that the deceased Mauji Lai had complained before the Sub Divisional Magistrate that Mool Chand (A 1) and Sheo Gopal (A 2), had committed theft of timber belonging to the village, managed by him. A few days later on 26.1.1968, the deceased made a report to the Sub divisional Magistrate that the appellants were guilty of theft of forest belonging to Mauji but he was acquitted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court convicted all the accused persons and sentenced them to life imprisonment for life. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the first information report was not inspired by any inordinate delay and that there was nothing on record to show that there had been any oblique motive for concocting a false story of the occurrence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The first information Report was recorded to the police station at 6.05 A.M. on 17.2.1968. There was sufficient light in the eastern kotha and the lantern in the western kothas of the house of the deceased. It is not improbable that P.W.7 who had come near the scene of occurrence would have either fallen down or returned to his house. There is no substance in the criticism that independent witnesses have not been called to depose about the occurrence as eye witnesses. They were of the opinion that the incident could have been witnessed only by P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8. The evidence of P. Ws. 1 and 7 does not inspire confidence. It was not improbable if they had seen some of the offenders and that their evidence could not be relied upon because he has intentionally made improvements in his version about the incident. [581 D E] 2. The appellants were rightly convicted by the High Court for the offences under section 396 I.P.C. and the sentence awarded to them by the trial court was confirmed by the learned Judges of the High Courts. [580 A B] 3. There are several cases between the parties. About a month before this occurrence, Mauji lal had complained that the assailants were moving in and out of the houses of the appellant at the time of the incident and also that the fact that they received injuries at the hands of the dacoits was not disputed before the Sessions Court. Merely because P. W. 7 did not have sustained any injury during the occurrence, it cannot be said that he had intentionally made improvement in his versions about the alleged occurrence. [583 C D] 4. The motive given by the appellants lends assurance to the evidence of the other prosecution witnesses to the extent that their testimony is corroborated by the evidence on record. Merely as P. PWs.

The appellant employer terminated the employment of 785 some of its employees during the initial period of probation and some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. The employer terminated their services on the grounds of unsuitability. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised questioning the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance of section 25F. The appellant Corporation challenged the decision of the Labour court before a Division Bench which upheld the decision. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that (i) the discharge of the employees amounted to termination as defined under section 2 (oo) and those order were bad; (ii) the termination of service was based upon unsatisfactory service during the period of ' probation '; and (iii) the employer terminated his services on ground of unsu suitability. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly come to the conclusion that in these cases the order Of retrenchment was bad for non compliance of section25F of the Act. [793G] 2. The necessary consequence of non compliance with section 25 F of the is that every case of termination of services by act of employer even if such termination was involved a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking was to be treated as 'retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice, compensation etc.

The assessee, East Eastern Railway, disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. The Commercial Tax Officer assessed the assessee to sales tax under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and therefore a sale of goods took place. The High Court also dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It was an activitywhich may be described as necessarily ancillary or ancillary for its business, as carrier. of thegoods. It may be an activity that may be considered as necessarily allied or ancillary. Its business as a carrier of goods. It can be regarded by no means necessarily incidental to its main business as the carrier of such goods. [781F G] 1.2 The activity is so disposing off the goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of disposal so disposings of the smuggled goods was connunctive, to the main activity of carriage of the property by the railway. It being an activity, which may he regarded as integral or ancillary, to its 'business as carrier, of the same goods. The Railway was a "dealer" for the purposes of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1942. [780A B] 2.1 In the case of the assessee South Eastern Railway what were sold were unclaimed goods. the railway was a carrier and it is engaged in selling scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The railway was not a carrier. On 6 June 1959, he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assesse 's activities. The Sales Tax Officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not "dealer". On 6th June 1959 he made the order rejecting his applica tion on the ground that the disposed of unclaimed or unconcected goods came into possession of the assesses but not as a result of any activity of purchase or manufacture for sale. It also held that the systematic and organised charac terical business carried on by the asses see was a 'dealer ' within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Act.

The appellant was charged with the offences of conspiracy and forgery. The prosecution case was that the appellant had a current account in the Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China Ltd., which was used to be used by the Directors for meeting losses suffered by them in forward transactions in shares carried on in the name of the Bharat Insurance Company. During this relevant period, the appellant was also a Director of the company during the relevant period. The appellant had its current account with the Punjab National Bank, Bombay and China Limited. In 1946, Dalmia was co opted a Director on March 1, 1949 and was again elected Chairman of the Company on March 19, 1949. Dalmia was a subsidiary of the appellant company. During that relevant period the appellant bad its current accounts in the banks of India. The Income tax authorities found that Dalmia had no control over them as the Banks had not been informed that Dalmia was empowered to operate on the company 's account in 1953, to purchase and sell securities and that thereafter Chokbani on his own purchased and sold securities. According to the appellant, he was under the impression that what he did amounted to giving of a loan by the Insurance Company to the Union Agencies and that there was nothing wrong in it. Dalmia had not informed Dalmia that Dalmia would be authorised to operate in the company accounts in 1953. The question for determination was whether Dalmia could have acted on the appellant 's own account in view of the resolution dated May 8, 1951 passed by the directors of the companies. Held: (i) The fact that the funds of the Insurance Companies were diverted to Union Agencies by the appellant and payments made to the Bank by the latter were not in accordance with the resolution of May 8. 1951, was a mere ruse to show that Dalmia did not want to know about the dealings with Bhagwati Trading Company. (ii) The appellant was under an impression that the money was being received from the Insurance company for nothing which was due to Bhagwati Trading Co., Bombay, and therefore the falsification of the journal vouchers related back to the original diversion of the insurance company 'S moneys to the Corporation Agencies. (iii) The resolution dated June 8, 195o, did not mention the name " Bhagwati Trading company" in the letters to the head office of the Bank at Delhi as communicated to the Head Office of the Trust Company at Delhi and on the basis of which journal vouchers were to be prepared by Dhawan and entries were to he made in the accounts of the Union Agency at Delhi.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Gujarat. They were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the new State of Bombay. The appellants were allotted the service in connection therewith and were posted in the Secretariat atversedi times between the years 1961, 1962 and 1963. These rules governed the servants who were allotted under the Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules, 1957. Those rules governed their servants who had been allotted to the State. The officers of the secretaries of the said Secretariat were transferred to the Secretariat in 1962 and they were posted from the districts of Bombay to Ahmedabad. In exercise of the powers under article 309 of the Constitution the Government of Bombay sanctioned certain rules called "The Alloced Government Servants (Ansorption) Seniority, pay & Allowances Rules, 1958". Those rules were superseded by r. 138 of the Bombay Civil Services Classification and Recruitment Rules, 1939. The respondents who were appointed to serve as Superintendents in connection With the affairs and administration of the old State of Saurashtra and Kutch challenged the validity of the order of the Government on three grounds : (1) that the order violated r.138 of the Recruitment Rules framed by the Government in 1957; (2) that it contravened the proviso to cl. (6) of section 81 in that it altered the conditions of service of those officers; and (3) that there was no violation of the proviso. Held, that the State Government had the authority to transfer the appellants from the Districts and to assign them duties in the secretariat and to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the Secretariats performing ministerial duties. The appeal must accordingly be allowed.

The petitioners were dealers in cotton or oil seeds. Their business was to purchase ginned and unginned cotton for manufacturing yarn and selling the said cotton also to registered and unregistered dealers both inside and outside the State of Punjab. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 on the ground that they were in conflict with section 15 of the Central Act. The High Court struck down certain portions of the Act on the grounds that they contravened section 15 Of the Central Sales Tax Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the Amending Acts were not retrospective but no machinery was provided for enabling the dealer to discover that the goods had been taxed before and the single stage at which the tax is to be levied and because under section 15(1) of the State Act there could be only one levy and collection of tax at one stage, either on sale or on purchase. HELD: (i) The Central Act itself gives power to the legislature to choose a rate of tax not more than 3 per cent of the taxable turnover. The tax is well within that limit and therefore the Legislature has chosen the maximum and has left it free to the authorities to impose the tax within that maximum regard being had to the requirements of revenue and the expenditure necessary for the State. [553 B C] (ii) The scheme of the States Reorganization Acts makes the laws applicable to new areas until superseded, amended or altered by the appropriate legislature in the new States. This is what the legislature has done and there is nothing that can be said against such amendment. [554 D E] (iii) The Act itself gave power to it to choose the rate of taxation at not more then 3 per centum of the turnover. It was not within the competence of the Legislature to pass such an Act retrospectively. The scheme was therefore quite clear and were quite sufficient to make the amended Act accord with the Central law. [555 E F] State of Madras vs N.K. Nataraja Mudaliar, ; , followed.

The Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938 came into force in the State of East Tanjore and the Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act was passed by which a sum of Rs. 1,08809 was directed to be paid by defendant No. 1 and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties. The appellants who were the successors of three original plaintiffs filed a suit against the respondent claiming relief under the Agriculturists ' Protection Act, 1940, on the ground that as the decree had already been passed by the High Court definitely negativing his claim to any relief under ' the Agriculturists Relief ' Relief ' Act, such application was not entertainable by the lower court. The trial judge held that defendants 2 to 7 were entitled to have the debts scaled down and directed that the amount so deposited together with the payments already made completely wiped off the amount due under the decree as scaled up by the District Judge in favour of defendants 2, 3 and 7. On appeal by defendants 1 to 7, the High COurt held that they were entitled tO have the debt scaled over and directed the court below to enter up full satisfaction of the mortgage decree. The High Court also directed that on payment of the amount directed to the be paid in accordance with the judgment, the appellants would pay into the court the sum of RS. 49,255 with interest thereon at 6% per annum from 1st October, 1937, and that the amended decree directs that the said defendants do pay into court the amount of Rs, 49, 255 with interest thereupon at 6 per cent per annum. The respondent appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The appeal must be allowed. (ii) The High Courts ' approach to the case has not been a proper one and the conclusion it has reached cannot be supported in law. The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant No 2 and 3 was not binding on them or their shares in the joint family property. (iii) The subsequent con tention between the two parties arrived before the High court clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debt and the security had been split up, and in our opinion it is not possible for the respondent to contend that the mortgaged debt remained indivisible.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of possession of certain premises on the ground that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the City Civil court had no jurisdiction to try the suit; (2) that in any event the City civil court had jurisdiction under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, to entertain and try such a suit; and (3) that there was a lawful subletting of the premises to them. The appellants appealed to the High Court which dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1 ) that the city Civil Court had no jurisdic tion to entertain a suit as the first plaintiff was not entitled in law to sublet the premises in question to the second and third plaintiffs, and (2 ) that there had been a lawful sub letting of the said premises within the meaning of section 28 Of the Bombay Rent Act. Held:(1) The City civil Court had jurisdiction in the matter of eviction of the first appellant from the premises under section 13 of the Act. The suit was essentially a suit between a landlord and tenant within the protection of the Indian , and the question whether the appellants were tenants would be a claim or question arising out of the provisions of the , arose out of such a claim which arose out Of the Act or any of its provisions which had to be dealt with by the Court trying the suit. The jurisdiction to decide all claims or questions arising out Of a Act or of its provision was not only a suit, between a tenant and a tenant in which relationship is admitted but also a suit in which it is claimed that the relationship of landlord and a person within the definition of "tenant" in section 28 and no other. (2). The City Court had to determine whether the plaintiffs had established their claim to be in possession of the suit premises in accordance with the provisions Of the , and whether they had lawfully sublet the same to the first defendant or not.

The appellant was appointed the managing director of a private company in his place from the date of his death. On July 7, 1955, an agreement was made between him and the Company by which he was appointed managing the managing Director of the company. The appellant was authorised to appoint the managing directors on August 7, 1956. On September 22, 1957, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that he had ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the meetings. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was void in view of section 312 of the new Act and set aside the decree of the City Civil Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The first proviso to section 86B of the old Act does not empower a director to appoint his successor. It only prohibits him from appointing his successor but does not prohibit the appointment by a director of his successor in office instead of transferring the office to him. [337 C] (ii) Section 312 of new Act does no apply to a private limited company. It forbids an appointment of a managing director for more than five years "at a time". It permits the managing Directors to be appointed otherwise than by the company, and it is legitimate to infer that by using the word "his" the section talks of "assignment" in it can mean "appointment". The section says that a director shall not be able to assign his office. It does not prevent a director from assigning his office but only means "the section talks" of "his". The first part of section 86 B is therefore inapplicable to a public limited company and the directors have to be so appointed except to the extent the articles otherwise provide.

The respondent landlady filed an eviction petition against the appellant tenant under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the appellant was unlawful sub tenants. The High Court in revision held that the eviction petition was maintainable as there was no evidence to come to the conclusion that the appellants had sublet the shop to M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction Petition was not maintainable at all. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. It is certainly open to the appellant to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. [420B] 2.1 In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it was surely not open to them to raise this objection at the very late time and thereby matters for more than a number. [421C D] Chhotelal Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, ; , referred to. 2.2 In the case before this Court no such objections had been raised even till the course of Special leave and it is surely not permissible to the appellants to raise an objection in a very belated stage and thus, there was absolutely no evidence on record to come at all to the finding that the partners had sublet their shop to the said firm. [ 420D] Chhotalal Pyare Lal 's case relied upon by Mr Nayar, however, is distinguishable from the facts of the instant appeal.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1973 was enacted with a view to imposing ceiling on vacant land in the whole of the State including land situate within the urban agglomerations. The Andhra Pradesh Act was passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature on 1st January, 1973. The validity of the Andhra Act was challenged before the Andhra pradesh Legislature on the ground that it had become void and inoperative. The High Court upheld the challenge and held that the enactment of the Central Act did not have the effect of invalidating the whole or of the A.P. Act merely remained on the statute book and for some inexplicable reason, it was not brought into force until 1st Jan, 1975. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the landholders that (i) the Andhra Nadu Act had become invalid as being outside the legislative competence of the Parliament; (ii) the A Pradesh Act merely remains on the Statute book and not for some immutable reason, and (iii) the provisions of the Act were repugnant to the provisions in the Central Acts so far as land situate in the other areas of the state of Andhra Pradesh are concerned. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The A. P. Act is a agrarian reform legislation and it is protected against challenge on the grounds of infraction of Articles 14, 19 and 31 by the protective umbrella of Article 31A. [1158G] 2.1 The Andhra Act is admittedly an agrarian reform Legislation and it was protected against attack on the basis of violation of Articles14, 19(1) (2), 19 and 21 by the A P. Legislature.

The appellants, who were the Managing Agents of a company, were dismissed from service by an order dated September 18, 1953. The Industrial Tribunal held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953, must be taken back into employment without condition and of the two men who came later, one was ill. On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that the notices were invalid as they had not been given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in respect of them and that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to give them permission to dismiss Chattoraj. HELD : (i) The Tribunal had considered the case of each workman under the four categories mentioned above and ordered reinstatement of 25 out of 74 workmen and granted to 24 of the workmen directed to be reinstated equal to half basic pay for the period of forced unemployment consequent upon suspension. He must be reinstated as soon as the award became operative. [688 G] (ii) The Industrial Tribu nal had not considered the justification for dismissal of Chattorj. In either view, the order of his reinstatement was unjustified. [687 A B] (iii) The fact that the appellants were in custody was not taken into consideration by the Tribunal and it was held that the charge sheet on which Chattorraj was suspended had not be proved. If the order was passed only subject to a formal charge being delivered to him and what conceivable answer he could give thereto, there would be no question of principle involved.

The appellant University invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for appointment) Act, 1974 recommended the names of Dr. Urea Kant as also one of the respondents in the writ petition. The respondent No. 1 was selected and appointed Dr. Uma Kant as Professor in Bot any. On the basis of the recommendation of the Selection Committee, Dr.Urea Kant was appointed as Professor by the University. Dr. Laxmi Kant retired on 30th September, 1989 and Dr. Love Kant retired from service on 30 th September, 1990. Dr, Urea was selected for appointment as Professor of Botsany in the Department of Bastany. Dr., Shiv Sharma, Dr, Smt. Umakant, Dr., Urea and Dr, Nathawat were appointed as Professors in the Departments of the University of Rajasthan from time to time after joining of the persons from the main list from 1978 to 1990. The appellant Dr. G.S.Nathawat retired on 31st September, 1991 and Dr.,Urea was appointed Professor in that department of the Botan and Dr Nathawwat on 30.9.1989. Dr Uma Kant was selected by the Selection Commit tee on 20th June, 1989. Dr Urea, Dr Shiv Sharma and Dr Lovekant were appointed Professor of the Department in the same college on 20.6.1989 and Dr Umakant was selected on 23.7.1989 as Professor. DrUrea, who was already selected and kept in the reserve list was appointed by the Committee. Dr Nathi Kant retired after 30th Septem ber, 1989 on the said post. Dr G.N. Bhardwaj, Dr . Shiv Sharma etc. filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challenging the appointment of Dr Natawat on the ground that the Selection committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a person selected by selection Committee had been appointed the reserve List stood exhausted and the person named in the reserved list stood exhausted, and the candidate named in that reserve list stood exhaust. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The purpose of preparation of a reserve list is to find out whether the incumbent recommended in the Reserve List by the selection committee was exhausted and if the reserved List is exhausted and/or the reserve lists is of no avail, and becomes extinct. There was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve listed alive for a long period of one year.

The petitioners were owners of plots of land in Bombay. They had applied for permission to change the existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay, asking him to alter the development plan prepared under the Act. The petitioners ' complaint was that the list of sites reserved for public purposes was not for the first time submitted by the second respondent to the Development Committee on February 8, 1964 showing for the purpose of a park in the area and merely marked by green colour without any specification and designation, by resolution. No such modification could have been made under section 9 of the Act as it was not covered by any of the entries in List 11 or III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The second respondent filed an application for permission under section 17 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, contending that the Development Plan submitted by him was for the First time submitted on January 2, 1962 and that the same had been approved by the Government. The first respondent contended that the development Plan was not prepared and published in terms of sub section (1) of section 4 even before carrying out a survey of the area referred to in sub sections (1), (2) and (3) of the said Act, and that no modification could be made under Section 9 of that Act. Held:(i) The time fixed under section 4 read with section 11(3) forms an unreasonable restriction on the rights of a person to hold his property. The procedure adopted by the local authority for purposes of sections 12 and 13 is not arbitrary, uncontrolled and capricious but has to be judged in the light of the facts disclosed in the affidavits. (ii) The authority had to proceed on the basis of the tentative plan and the report of the development work committee prepared under section 22(1). The procedure prescribed by sub section 2 read with sections 4 to 16 was not arbitrary or capricious but had to be based on some rational and reasonable relationship to the object to be attained by the Act and, in fact, it had to go by the larger interest of the population at large and the generations to come. (iii) The provisions of the Land Acquisition Act were not violative of article 14 of the Constitution as they were not within the competence of the local authorities to pass the Act, but were only directory and not mandatory.

The Indian States entered into an agreement with the Government of India, and the Government agreed to a cease fire and to restore the status quo as at 1.1.1965 in the area of the Gujarat West Pakistan border. The Government of Pakistan, after considering the matter in the light of their respective claims and evidence produced before it and the decision of the Tribunal, passed an award on 30th June 1965, which was challenged by the appellants in a writ petition filed by them under article 32 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition summarily. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Award merely fixes or demarcates the boundary between the State of Gujarat in India and West Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and by the Award no cession of Indian territory was contemplated. [151 D E] (2) The award did not purport to refer to an obligation to cede Indian territory without the authority of a constitutional amendment. It was not shown that it had the characteristics of the Rann terrain. There was no reliable evidence about the enjoyment of the benefits of the land in the Sector by the inhabitants of Kutch. [149 E] In the instant case, the Award merely fixed or demar cates the boundaries between the Sind and the R Annas. The highly discrepant claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch State authorities before the Kutch District Court were not accepted. [150 F G] (3) The fact that the dispute related to the boundary of India and Pakistan was determined in 1948, did not support the claim made by the Government. It is true that the territory of the entire State merged with the Dominion of India but that was de facto under the administration by India but being de jure under the Administration by India, it had been validly and legally become a part of the territory which formed part of India. But unless there is evidence to show that in thelets over which the Maharao of Kutch had sovereign rights, acceptance of the award is not required to be implemented by a constitutional amendments, the mere fact that this area was administered by the Maharashtra State did not lead to an inference that the disputed sectors were part of Pakistan. [152 A B] (4) The Tribunal rightly held that the Award was not invalid on the ground that it was made in pursuance of an amendment modifying the boundary. [153 D E].

The mortgagor executed a mortgage in favour of the mortgagee for an annual royalty of Rs. 2,000 payable in two equal instalments, the first in the month of May and the second in the year of the Vikram and the other in the months of May. The mortgagor assigned his interest in Mauza Chaitan to one Mahendra Nath Rai and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his interests in Mauza Bansjora and Simitanr for repayment of the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs 1/8 per mensem and further agreed that in default of payment, the mortgagee do recover the amount due by sale of his interest. The mortgagors also undertook to issue notices to the tenants calling upon them to pay the amounts according to the assignment. By paragraph 14 it was agreed that the mortgagees were to receive the instalment of royalty payable in Chaitra in respect of Mauza Bahaldih and Bahalder. By the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922, the mortgagor created a mortgage on the mortgaged property in favour Of the mortgagee with an annual rent of Rs 2,500 advanced to him and interest thereon. The terms of the mortgage were substantially the same as the covenants of the earlier mortgage deed. On August 27, 1922 the mortgagor executed another document whereby he agreed personally to repay the amount, and encumber his share in Mauzas Bansjorora and Chaitanr with any one and that the alienations made by him would be null and void. The mortgagee also undertook not to transfer or assign Mauzs Bahaldaphora and chaitanr to anyone else but to secure payment of Rs 5,500 borrowed by him. In paragraph 14 the mortgagor agreed that he would receive the amount as royalty from the tenants under mining leases in Mauza Bahastih in satisfaction on his mortgage claim, unless it was mortgaged to him. The mortgagees also undertook that the mortgagee would pay interest at a rate of 1/2 per cent per mensem on the amount of Rs, 5, 500 borrowed by them. In para 14 the mortgagors agreed that they would receive only the instalment due to them from the mortgagor according to terms of their contracts. It was further stipulated by paragraph 7 that the mortgagor had assigned his right in Mauza Bahldih or part payments of principal interest after April 14, 1925 and on the date of payment by him by instalments specified therein by way of interest for peaceful realisation of the annual interest of Rs I,000 every year. The mortgage deed recited that the mortgagors were to pay a sum of Rs 100 which was agreed to be paid by the mortgagees to the mortgagee and the interest thereon; and that in case of default the mortgagor would compensate the mortgagee in respect thereof. The suit was filed more than twelve years after the date on which the mortgage amount payable, and prima facie it was barred by limitation. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit in respect Of the first mortgage was not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage was partly simple and partly usufructuary and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment of principal or interest within the meaning of section 20 of the Limitation Act. The High Court also held that there was no force in the contention that the mortgage being partly simple, and partly simple usufructuary, the suit must be dismissed. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (1) that the mortgages were not hit by article 132 of the Indian Limitation Act because the mortgagee had lost his interest therein in Mauza Bansjuna and Similr which could not operate to extend the period of limitation for the suit, (2) that there is no force either in the mortgage or in the evidence of the mortgagor 's case. HELD: (1)(a) The intention appearing from this covenant is clearly to encumber Mauz Bansas Bansora and Bahadih.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. The respondent employed as many a small time workmen in the said factories. In order to provide transport facilities to its employees, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi places enroute to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and crossing, and also to TLCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month for the transportation of employees from Chinchvad and back was levied for the purpose of transport of employees. The appellants contended that even if a nominal charges were realised from the employee that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passengers, so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is charging section of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. A combined reading of rule 2(i) and section 2(7) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 framed under the Bombay Act, 1940 makes it clear that vehicles which could not be termed as public service vehicles fell within the ambit of the charging section. [362E F] 2. The word 'public service vehicle ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. Thus qua the public employees form a separate class and cannot be said to be public service as contemplated by rule 2 (i). [362F G] 3. The transport provided to employees of the company was reserved for them only and no other member of it even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. In these circumstances, it cannot be held that the transport vehicle provided to its employee by the appellant could be a public motor vehicle in any sense of the term. [361F G; 362A] 4. The words 'public services vehicle ' have got a uniform connotation and mean a carriage or other omnibus when used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the section. Thus, qua the private employees form the employees form separate class, cannot be treated to be Public service vehicles in any manner of the terms. [363F G]. 5. The definition of 'public motor vehicle ' in section 2 (7) clearly indicates that the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public road. It is true that the term 'public Service vehicle ' had not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules, but that does not create any difficulty because having regard to the Preamble of the statute it is clear that the dominant object of the legislation was to impose tax on certain classes of public service Vehicles. [365B C] 6.

The appellants, who were the residents of a locality, applied for a licence to be granted by the State Government under section 8(3) of the M.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1952, for a period of six months. The application was turned down by the District Magistrate on 29th June 1977 and the appellants filed a petition under Article 226 challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the District magistrate had no jurisdiction to issue the licence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the District Magis trate had no power to refuse the grant of a "no objection certificate" as he was influenced by an extraneous consideration, namely, re opening of Paras Cinema with a permanent cinema having a permanent license having been opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a 'temporary licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Govt. the State Govern ment could not refuse the granting of such a licence; (ii) the appellants were not acting bona fide in vindication of their own rights but they were a fence or a cloak for the owners of Paras cinema, and the grant/ renewal of the same had passed muster long before 10th February 1976, and therefore the order granting no objection certificate was violative of the principles of natural justice; (iii) the State government had not given any opportunity to the successful objectors and decided the appeal at their back and thus the decision was rendered in violation of the principle of natural Justice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants were neither acting bona fides nor a cloak of the owners or a plot for the owner of Paras Cinemas. They had no locus standi to file the objections. [802C] 2. The District Magistrate was influenced in an extraneous considerations and he was not influenced by any extraneous consideration. There is nothing in the Act or Rules which requires the licensing authority to invite objections before grant of such licence when there was a permanent or quasi permanent cinema, but the licensing Authority may in its discretion permit a touring cinema to operate at a place where there is already a permanent and quasi permanent Cinema, but it cannot be said that the "no Objection" certificate was granted. [702G] 3. The Rules contemplate filing of objections by local residents. That is the stage when no objection Certificate is applied for by the intending applicant for such a certificate. But there is no provision in the Rules or the rules which requires such an application to invite objection before grant is passed. If the duty to give notice and hear the party is not mandatory, the actual order passed on a matter must be shown to have injuriously affected the interest of the party which was given no notice of the matter. [ 802E F] 4.

The appellant sued for specific performance of a contract on the ground that by a letter dated September 2, 1957, the respondent agreed to assign the mining lease to the respondents. The appellant contended that the communication was not supported by any consideration and that the service of a copy of the plaint along with the writ of summons was a communication of acceptance. Held, that the suit was not barred by section 3 Of the Contract Act as it was not an acceptance of the offer but was intended to be an acceptance. It was not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint; nor was it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy through the medium of the Court. The communication of an acceptance is not necessary unless there is an acceptance on the application for shares and the acceptance is communicated to the applicant before the filing of the suit, see Boys vs Ayerst ; Fryon Specific Performance, 8th ed., article 306, Pomeroy on Specific performance, 8 8thed. Article 306, pleder on Specific Performance is not an accepted offer unless there was an acceptance or the application made for shares. The acceptance of an offer by serving copy of a plaint through the means of the court cannot be treated as having been done without the sanction of the State Government and the approval of the Central Government and that as the governments concerned could not be compelled to accord the necessary sanction and approval, the contract to assign mining lease could not he specifically performed. The High Court was in error in holding that the assignment of the mining leases could not legally be made without the requisite sanction of tho State Government.

The appellants were office bearers of a company which was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar. The company filed a complaint against them under section 3(3) read with section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 alleging that they had failed to pay the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The Magistrate held that the prosecution was not maintainable and quashed the investigation. On appeal the High Court held that there was no substance in the contention that the complaint made before the police did not disclose a cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture and therefore the power conferred on the Government under section 2(a) of the Act could not be challenged. HELD : The contention must fail. (i) The impugned order contravenes the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19 (1). No fundamental fight is conferred on a buyer not to pay price of the goods purchased by him or to pay it whenever he pleases. [677 E] Ch. Tika Ramji and Ors. vs The State of U.P. & Ors., ; , followed. (ii) The power conferred under section 4(1)(f) of Bihar Act is a pre Constitution Act and it could have continued to be in force only till it was altered, repealed or amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [676 G] Ch Tika Ram and Ors vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors. ; , applied.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage industrialisation. The Government of Mysore by an order dated 11th August, 1975, issued directions that the incentives would be given to starting new industries in the Mysore State. In pursuance thereof, the Government had on 30th November, 1966, directed the incentives to start new industries. On 12th January, 1977, the State Government issued another order stating that the incentive would be extended to starting fresh industries in Mysore State with effect from 1st May, 1974. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June 1969 when the order dated 12th June, 1969 came into effect and before 949 the order was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment of considerable funds. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of the Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30th 6 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be regarded as good law since the benefit given to the new industries is by way of refund of sales tax paid to the extent provided in the Order. [410C] 2.1 The State Government had failed to establish the requisite ground or basis of such concession granted under order dated 31st June,1969. [951F G] Union of India vs M/s Indo Afghan Agencies Limited, ; Century Spinning and Manufacturing Company Limited & Anr., [1970] 3 S.C.R. 854; M/S. Indo Afegan Agencies Ltd. vs State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors., ; and M/ s. Indo Fghan Agency Limited & Another vs The Ulhasnagar Municipal Council & Anr, [1970], 3 S C R. 853, referred to. 2.2 The doctrine that a concession granted by the State itself was beyond the powers of the State or how the State can say so either is not correct.

The appellants were tried for offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 to 6 of all the charges. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appel lants under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but set aside their conviction and sentences. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (i) the prosecution case was not established beyond reasonable doubt; (ii) the appellants had been acquitted in respect of all charges; (iii) the non applicability of Section 149 IPC was not justified as there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime, and (iv) the High court fell into error in confirming the conviction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellants acted in the furrance of their common intention of murdering the de ceased. They are accordingly convicted under Section 302 readwith section 34 I.p.C.[857E] 2.1 The non applicability or applicability of section 149 IPC is therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants under Sections 302 read and 34 I P. C. [857F G] 2:2. The prosecution case that apart from the seven accused there were other un unknown persons who are involved in t he crime, was long standing enmity between the parties. During the last 30 years there had been murders and rioting between the two factions, there had be long standing dispute between the particu lar intention of killing the de cease. [864C] 2 :3. The non application of section 34 IPC is, therefore, not bar in conviction under Section 7 read with section 34 l.P C. Both Sections 149 and 34 IPC deal with a combina tion of persons who become liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences. [884D] 2(a) The non applica tion of appellants under sections 148 and 149 I P C. is, however, not justified because (i). the common object of the unlawful assembly was to kill the deceased; (2) the injuries caused by the appellants were deep penetrating wounds and remaining abrasions; and (ii). the injuries on the person of the deceased could only lead to one inference namely that the common intention was to murder the deceased.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 was completed on 25th Decem ber 1965. On 4th April 1968 the Income Tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment of his income for the year 196667 and requiring him to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice. The assessee raised objections against the reassessment proposed to be made by the Income tax Officer but the objection was over ruled and an order of reassessment was passed by the Incometax officer including the sum of Rs 48,500 as capital gains and bringing it to tax. The Income Tax Officer issued a second notice under Section 148 of Act seeking reopen the assessments of the asses see for the relevant assessment year. The notice did not state what was the income alleged to have escaped assessment but by his subsequent letter dated 4th March 1969 the Incometax officer intimated to the assessee that he proposed to fix the fair market value of the house sold by him on 25 December 1965 at Rs. 65,000 as against the consideration of Rs 16,5,500 for which the house was sold and assess the difference of Rs 50,500 in the hands of the assesses. The appellant raised objections to the reassessment proposing to be effected by the income tax officer but the objections were over ruled. An order of re assessment was passed on 4th May 1968 by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner including the amount of Rs, 48,521 as capital gain and bringing to tax the difference between Rs. 48,000 and Rs. 50,000. The appeals filed against the said reassessment were dismissed by the Tribunal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of assessment having been made without giving any opportunity to the assesse to submit his return of Income within 30th days of service of notice, the notice did no state what he had to do so and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to assess the sum as capital income. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Tribunal is set aside and the matter remanded to the High Court for deciding the question whether the assessee has not been given an opportunity to submit its return of the Income 's income within thirty days of notice. [657C] 2.1 In the instant case, it was not the contention of the Revenue that the property was sold by the assessee to his sister in law or five of her children who were directly connected with him and the assessee had actually received more than what was declared by him. It is for the Revenue to show that each of these two conditions is satisfied and the Revenue cannot claim to have discharged this burden which lies upon it, by merely establishing that the fair value of capital asset as on the date of transfer exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assessee in respect of the transfer. [643E F] 2:2. The object and purpose of enacting sub section (2) of Section 52 is extremely restricted because it applies only where the transferee is a person directly or indirectly connected with the assessee and the object of the statement is to avoid or reduce the income Tax liability of the transferor to tax on capital gains. [641G] 2(a) The object of imposing the condition of difference of 15% or more between the market value declared by assessee and his children is to prevent or reduce, the income of the business from being carried on in any manner whatsoever, the consideration actually received by the assesses as a result of the capital asset.

The appellant was charged with the offence of Food Adulteration Act, and was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court in appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human consumption. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food. Even if this be true it is not so widely known a fact that black quality Til seeds were not used in the course of pooja. It cannot be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the Food Inspector that they can be used as "feed" only as a substance used for pooja and not as human food. [318 F G] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. 2. The appellant must get the benefit of doubt. But in this case it is a question of common experience that black co Til seeds contain which are ordinarily used for human habitation as food and the appellant was rightly convicted by that Court. [332 B C] 3. It would be unsafe to base the conviction on such shaky foundation. There had to be credible evidence to show that black til seeds were ordinarily used as a food. If that were so, the burden would have shifted on to theers of the shoulders of accused to prove what he had stored was not really food meant for consumption but an article kept for a special use. [333 C D] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Admn., ; , applied.

The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17.6.1969 to the defendant, asking for a declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. The plaintiff gave a notice under s.80 of the C.P.C., on 17th June 1969, asking the defendant to give a declaration as to whether the order dismissing the suit was inoperative or not. The defendant gave notice on 19.9.1960. The suit was dismissed on 31st August 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed in October 1966. Thereafter he filed his suit on 30th September 1969 asking for declaration that he order of dismiss ment was inoperative, and he continues to be In service. This suit has been dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose as required under article 58 of the . The plaintiff 's appeal was rejected on 31.8.1966. He then preferred an ap peal to the higher authority and the High Court dismissed his second appeal on 31 8 1966. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended that the suit is barred by limitation because (1) the suit had not filed within 3 years from that date; (2) the defendant 's suit was within time; (3) the plaintiff gave notices under s 80 of C. P.C. on 17 6 1969 and filed his written statement, asking that for a decree of dismissal be inoperative and (4) the period spent in complying with the requirement of notice under sec tion 80 of Civil Proce dure Code was available to the plaintiff in addition to the period of three years. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The cause of actions shall be taken not from the dates of original adverse order but on the date of preferring of the appeal or making of the representation shall be take into consideration in the matter of fixing limitation. [46C] 2.1 In every case only when the appeal is made, the appellate authority has disposed of the ap peals, the right to sue first accrues for purposes of Article 58 of tho , great hardship is bound to result. On one side, the claim would not be maintainable if laid before exhaustion of remedies; on the other, if the departmental remedy though availed is not finalised within the period limitation, the cause of such action would no more be justiciable having become barred by time. [47E F] 2(a) The suit had been dismissed on 30.8 1966 when the order was made by the Collector when the appellant 's second appeal was dis missed on 31th August 1966 and the matter was remitted to the trial Court for disposal in ac cordance with law.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of Subordinate Judge Chittoor, for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienations effected by his father as well as the sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so a preliminary decree for partition was passed in his favour in respect of the said items. The appellant then applied to the High Court for a certificate under article 133(1) (a) of the Constitution, but the High court rejected it on the ground that the decree sought to be appealed from was one of affirmance and there was no substantial question of law raised by the proposed appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appeal must be allowed. (i) A preliminary decree has to be split up into different parts and the words "appealed from" have to be treated as words of limitation. It is suggested that in cases where different causes of action and different claims and reliefs have been combined decrees are in fact passed though in form there may be one paper on which one decree is drawn; and so it would be inconsistent with the scheme of the Code to divide the decree into several parts by reference to its relation to different claims or subject matters. [465 D E] (ii) The principle of affirmness on which the provision rests postulates either affirmance or variation by the appeal. The principle is an independent additional test and its effect has to he judged by interpreting the words used in the relevant clause. Reading the clause as a whole and giving the material words their plain grammatical meaning it seems prima facie to show that the two courts have not entirely agreed and so they are not bound to file an appeal against the whole of the decree.
