[467 E F] (iii) The principles of affirmity on which a provision rests clearly indicate either affirmness or variation with the appeal, and in that sense if a variation is made in regard to it is an integral part of the decision or the grounds given for it, the order passed by the High Courts cannot affect the character of the appellate decree. Unlike the order of costs which is entirely in the discretion of the Court under section 35 of the Civil Procedure Code an order as to interest which the court can make under section 34 of the C.P.C. is an order not as to the whole; and if that be so, the clause could be harmoniously construed to mean that in determining the character or the appellate decrees the court should be considered as a full in relation to the decision of the trial court. [463 A B] (iv) The word "decision" in article 133 (1)(a) has merely partially recognised the fall in the price of the rupee and so, it cannot be read as showing the intention to restrict the appellant 's right in any manner. In regard to the provisions of article 133, there is no material change made by the Constitution since the position under section III of the code forms part of a dispute between the parties. [464 C D] (v) The question whether an appellate decree is one of affirmedance or not depends upon the context and the context is plainly inconsistent with that contention. In construing the clause, it is obviously necessary to bear in mind that the clause deals with the constitutional right of the litigant to make an appeal to the Supreme Court; and it would he inappropriate to adopt a technical or pedantic approach in interpreting the word 'decree ' in the operative clause. [455 E F].

The High Court alone had jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of an order of the District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes. The High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under Section 115, C.P.C., to have exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or (b) to have acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally with material irregularity, the High Court may make such order in the case as it deems fit. " In the result, the appeal and the associated special leave petitions must be dismissed. The question whether a revisional order of a District Judge under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act can be revised by the High court under section 116, CP. C., is not justiciable before this Court. [40E F] M/s Jupiter Fund (Pvt.) Ltd. vs Dwarka Diesh Dayal & Ors. ; , followed. The District Court alone has jurisdiction under s. 115, Civil Procedure Code. In the instant case, the District Court had no jurisdiction to exercise its revisional power under section 23, C P.C. in respect Of an order arising out of a suit of value less than Rs 20,000/ and above or below Rs. 20,00/ , if a case arising out o. an original suit instituted before 20th September 1972, is pending. [41F G] In the present case, since then the suit has been disposed of, all proceedings for grant of interim relief must be regarded as having lapsed. The Special Leave Petition has become infructuous and must be rejected accordingly.

The respondents were the owners of certain land belonging to them. The appellant 's land was acquired under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme at public expense viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The Special Officer issued a notice under section 53 (2) of that Act on February 8, 1984 to the respondents for personal hearing under section 54 (3). The respondents filed their reply dated September 8, 1975 stating that they needed the said land to start new businesses in the State of Rajasthan and for that purpose to utilize the notified land for establishment of a branch office and for construction of two 'Ministers ' bungalows in Civil lines and therefore the proceedings for acquisition of the notified lands would not be withdrawn. The respondents challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it was issued without jurisdiction as the Government had no power or authority to proceed with the enquiry under section 51 (2). The High Court held that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the petition filed by the respondents purporting to be under article 226 of the Constitution in the Calcutta High Court and the rule nisi thereon had been issued without any jurisdiction as required by section 52 (2), and that the ad interim ex parte prohibitory order passed against them was not a rule ni cisi. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The notification dated February 8 1984 issued by the State Government under section52(1 ) of the Act could not be issued till February 8 , 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction to the State. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 22 (2); nor did the respondents place any material before the Special officer to show that they really needed the notified Land for the purpose of expansion of their business activities to the state. [605G H] 2. The mere service of a notice on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B Brabourne Road Calcutta i.e. within the territorial limits of the State is not an integral part of the cause of action. The entire cause of actions culminating in the acquisition of land under section 48(1), therefore, arose within the State 's territorial jurisdiction before making such interlocutory orders.

The appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises in suit on a monthly rent of Rs. 250 and the building was assessed to house tax and water tax on 1st October 1971. The respondent filed a suit for eviction and for arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the building in question had been constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and therefore the view taken by the trial court that the construction was substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the new Rent Act was manifestly erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the premises which were not ten years old on the date of the suit and was exempted from the operation of the New Rent Act had no application to the building. [337C] 2.1 In order to appreciate the contention of the parties it will be relevant at this stage to refer to section 20 of the 1956 Act providing a bar to a suit in respect of eviction on the grounds mentioned in cl. (a) to sub section (2), viz., arrears of rents, if at the first hearing of the Suit the tenant in default pays all arrears of Rent to the landlord or deposit in court the entire amount of rent & damages for occupation and occupation of the building due from him, such damages for using and occupation for the purpose of supervising the construction or guarding the building under the building, due from the appellant, such compensation for use, occupation and use of the buildings due from them, such charges for use of and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the landlords ' cost of the suits in respect thereof after deducting therefrom any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section(1) of section 30. [336E G] 2:2. The appellant sought protection of the old Rent Act which became applicable to the premises during the pendency of the litigation. But during the pendancy of the proceedings it completed ten years. Then the question arose whether the new rent Act will be attracted if the building completed ten year during the course of litigation. [333G] 2(a) The appellant in the present case sought protection under the new Act which was manifestly wrong. The landlord had not become ten years of old on that date and the new tenancy would become applicable. Admittedly the building had become more than ten years earlier on the dates of suit. But, during the pending litigation it completed 10 years. [332C] (b) The new Rent Acts will be applicable if the conditions comtemplated in those sections are satisfied. Section 39 also indicates that the parties are entitled to make necessary amendment in their pleadings and to adduce additional evidence where necessary. [340D E] 3(a).

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents filed objections thereto, and the appellant filed an application under sections 17 and 20 of the , for a decree in terms of the award except as to a part which he held to be in excess of the claim. The appellant contended that the agreement for reference did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, and that the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that therefore it fell within item 12. Held, that the arbitrator had been authorised by the Governor acting through his Secretary to execute the agreement in question. The agreement did not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents. The award was not a copy of the arbitration agreement, but a copy which was sent to the respondents was not available. When the third copy was received in court, the respondents paid the requisite stamp duty under section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act and had validated it. Held further, that as the copy of an instrument could be validated and "acted upon" and in consequence there was no valid reference to arbitration, the document in question was not the original and not a certified copy thereof. The words "certified copy" appearing thereon were a mis description and cannot have the effect of altering the true character of the instrument. There is nothing in section 175 (3) which does not prescribe any particular mode in which authority must be conferred. Normally no doubt, such conferment will be by notification in the Official Gazette but there is nothing to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person, and when that is established the requirements Of the section must be held to have been satisfied.

The respondent retired as Superintendent, Directorate of Industries on September 30, 1983. On various dates in that year he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the orders passed by the department. In the year 1980 some complaints were received in the Department against the respondent pertaining to the purchase, of sign Boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1985 against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In this case, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The prosecution alleged that the sign boards purchased in 1979 were in contravention of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea raised by the Respondent was accepted by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is always open to a prosecution on the ground of unexplained unconscionable delay in investigation and prosecution on facts of a given case. [918C] 1.2 The object of Rule 3.2 is not to place an embargo on prosecution of a government servant after his retirement for grave misconduct or negligence during the period of his service, after the lapse of a particular time which has been fixed in the instant case as four years would fall within the purview of "conditions of service" as contemplated by Article 309. [951E] 1:3 The embargo on the prosecution spelt out by the rule is not only against public policy but also the purpose of Rule.2.2, there is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said rule. By applying the well settled rule of reading down a provision so as to bring their cases within the ambit of reasonable classification, if the purpose for granting immunity from prosecution is ensuring peace of mind in old age can be a good ground for immunity from prosecutions committed by a person, there seems to be no reason why such immunity may not be available to all old persons and should be confined only to government servants.

The respondent company was a public limited company. The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 5,000 preference shares. In September 1936 the respondent company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent of the share capital which was considerably less than sixty per cent. On the question whether the provisions of section 23 A were correctly applied for the three years ending March 31, 1948 and March 31 1949, HELD: (i) The Explanation raises a presumption and does not purport to define a company in which the public are substantially interested. It is now settled law that the distinction between the controlling group and the public is not coextensive with that of a shareholder or a group of shareholders as would render the company one in which it is a company, in which there is no controlling member or group and therefore the public were substantially interested is not a question which can be decided by this Court. [17 C D] (ii) The test to determine whether shares of the Company carrying less than twenty five per cent voting power are not shown to have been allotted unconditionally or acquired unconditionally to, or acquired by unconditionally or beneficially held by the public must be satisfied when less than seventy five per centum of the voting power is allotted unconditionally. [18 E] (iii) The word "company" in section 23A means what a company which, in the public interest are substantially substantially interested, is.

The appellants were charged with the contravention of sections 7 and 9 Of the Essential Supplies Act (No. XXIV of 1946) on two counts, namely, that they had been authorised to take delivery of the goods specified in the " ready sale note" and that the goods had actually left the Mills ' premises and delivered them to the appellants. The trial court convicted the appellants under sections 7 & 9 Of these Essential Supplies (Notion XXIV of 1945) on the ground that the godown belonged to the first appellant but the original name was Dharsi Moolji, that he had been appointed by the firm to take possession of the stock in the godown and not for payment thereof. The High Court held that the prosecution had established their case and convicted them under sections 9 Of those Essential Supplies ' Act (Act XXIV of 1947). Held, that the appellants were rightly convicted under section 7 and were entitled to the benefit of doubt. The fact that the first respondent was appointed by a firm to carry on business in Bombay did not mean that he was either a principal or an agent of the buyer. The appellants had no direct connection with the transaction of the kind described as "Important" towards the head of the marked portion "Im portant". The words " whom physical delivery of goods has been made" in column 2 of the "ready sold" meant physical delivery and actual delivery of cloth in bales or in pieces but not cloth which, though paid for, is still in the physical possession of a seller. The words 'when a person is in such a relation to a thing that so far as regards the thing, he can assume, exercise or resume manual control of it at pleasure, and so faras regards other persons, the thing is under the protection of his personal presence, or in some receptacle belonging to him and under his control.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 165A, Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Special Judge convicted them but on appeal the High Court held that there was no evidence to show that the misconduct had been committed in the discharge of their official functions as a public servant. In appeal to this Court it was contended that: (i) the offence under section 5 was not an offence and therefore the conviction could not be sustained; (ii) the charge under section 161, Indian I.P.C., was not proved against both Dwivedi and Thakkar; (iii) the second part of cl. (d) relating to the obtaining of the valuable thing etc. related to the object of the public servant namely obtaining of a bribe; and (iv) the use of the word "officer" in cl. 5(1)(a) was not necessary that the accused should abuse his position as a Public servant or that he should have obtained the money while acting as apublic servant. HELD: (1) The High Court had rightly held that the second portion of cl.(d) did not apply to cases of a Government servant who commits an act punishable under the said provision even though when the act is committed by him he was holding a different position which is not that of a public officer and in which capacity alone he could fall within the definition of "public servant". [337 C D] (2) The use of word "Officer" in clause (d)(a), namely, obtaining of bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion, was not decisive of whether the second clause was intended to combat other evils. It could be said that there had been abuse by a Government Servant of his position and as such he could not, therefore, become a public servants within the meaning of cl: (d). [338 G H] (3) The word "otherwise" in el. (a) of section 5 means any other than corrupt or illegal means or otherwise than those mentioned in that clause. That abuse may be by corrupt or unauthorised means or illegal but the legislature does not want to limit itself to these kinds only and so goes on to use the word 'otherwise".

The petitioners, who were employees of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway, challenged the claim of their wages for equal work and had asked for a direction to treat them at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal Work. The Railway Board 's order was not given effect to by this Court. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioners were employees and do not belong to the open line. They have asked for direction to treating them at part with maintenance work and to declaring that they were entitled to pay equal wages for Equal work and have asked For their regularisation. [144E] 2. The Railways Manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not effective P. several instructions issued by the Railway Board and Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before this Court to show that the Administration was anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. [143G] 3. The Administration is anxious to consider appropriate steps for removing the difficulties facing by casual labourers but there are perhaps soughness in enforce them. The railway Establishment Manual has not made provisions of their protection, but implementation was not effective. [145A B] 4. The scheme formulated under orders of this Court, though such status were acquid ed, casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway Administration and cannot be avoided.

The appellants were members of the Association carrying on business in partnership. The Forward Markets Regulation, 1952, was amended by the Central Government under section 6 of the Act and a new bye law was framed which provided that "the Forward Markets Commission shall call upon contracts to be closed out, to be settled at such rate, appropriate to such contract and with effect from such date as shall be fixed by the Forward Markets Commis sioner and provisions of clauses (3), (4) and (0) of Bye laws 52A in so far as they apply to hedge and call contracts shall apply as if they formed part of this bye law. The appellants were the members of a Association carrying out business in India. They had, prior to December 1955 entered into "hedges contracts" in respect of cotton including "hedge contracts". The terms and conditions of forward contracts in cotton including 'hedge contract ' were governed by the provisions contained in certain bye laws of the association as they stood at the date when the contracts were entered into. The terms, conditions and conditions for forward contracts were governed under the provisions of certain bye law of the associations which provided inter alia that "The Forward Markets Act, 1952 (LXXIV Of 1952) shall take effect". The appellants challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Association on the ground that it was beyond the powers of the Government to frame bye laws and that the Association was in law incapable of conferring that power on the Forward Market Commission or on any other body. Held, that the power conferred upon the Forward Marketing Commission by section 12 of the Forward Contracts Regulation Act, 1951, was not a power which could be assigned to the Commission under cl. (f) of section 4(f). The power of the Central Govern ment to make bye laws in respect Of all or any of the matters specified in section II or in the absence of such specific provision as is expressly made out by any specific provision of the enactment, was subject to the condition that previous publication was not necessary. The word "under the Act" in cl. 2 of the Schedule means "by or under this Act". The power conferred on the Commission by cl. 14 of the Order was a power exercisable by the Commission and not by the Government.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estate Zamindaries Ltd. The following table sets out the amounts received by it from the Company and the years in respect of which they were received : Year of declaration of dividend (1) Year of assessment of dividend 1951 52 (2) Year ending on 31st March 1948, (3) Year 1359 B.S., Rs. 37,125/ . The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ were taxable as dividend and the remaining amount was not taxable as dividends. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term leases after 31st day of March 1948 was not in the hands of the assessee but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax, 1922 and that on the facts and circumstances of the case the distribution to the assessee of the said amount attributable to Salami received for the year 1359 B, 1358 C.S. Rs. 29,250/ was not capital gain. The Appellate Tribunal held that the entire amounts were income in the hand of the asses see and taxable as the income of the assesses from other sources. On reference under section 66(1) of Indian Income tax , 1922 the High Court answered all the questions in favour of the Revenue. In appeals to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court had to decide on the fact of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain and whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains.

The Kerala Forest Act, 1961 was enacted to prevent depleting forests, conservation of forest and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The State Acts regulate preservation of forest produce and regulates possession of the forest produce, failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil was either found in transit or in possession of manufacturers it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1) (f) of the Kerala Forest (Development Act, 1962 for short). The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to prevent replenishment of forest Produce. The Forest Act provides procedure for preservation of forests and regulates Possession of the produce. The Act prescribes procedure for preserve of forest. The forest was a 'forest produce ' within the meaning of section 2(f) (i) of that Act. The appellants challenged the jurisdiction of the Court in C.C. Nos. 145 and 148 of 1988 on the grounds, inter alia, that the Forest Conservation Rules, 1980 were not applicable to the 's case as they were not forest produce. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'forest ' is generally used as a word wood oil. It cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the object and purpose of the Act. Extraction ofwood wood even by mechanised process would nonetheless be a wood oil within the definition of forest produced. From this it could be concluded, if it be concluded that the 'forest Produce ' is ' wood oil ' within section 2 (f). The restricted meaning sought to put up by the accused would frustrate the object, and the literal interpretation would defeat the purpose of Act. [501C D] 1.2 The word forest ' in section 2 of the Forest (Constitu tion) Act has to be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be limited in such manner so that to defeat or frustrate the purpose and object of the act.[502D E] 1:3 The word wood is generally defined as a 'stones '. It is settled law that the word 'include ' is normally used as 'a word does not take away its ordinary meaning. [403B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the Forest Act and the Parent Act (Forest Conservation) Act seek to subserve. The restricted interpretation given therein if given acceptance would lead to manifest frustration of the purpose for which the oil is extracted is not decisive. Therefore, the word wood ' in the definition has to he construed in a sense in which it is being understood in trade, business or transaction known to the trade is also inapplicable to the factual context. [500F G] 2:2 The meaning of the word forest oil ' in Section 2(k) of Kerala Forest Conservation (Forest) Act, 1981 is inclusive of definition.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Ganganagar for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code but was acquitted. The High Court convicted him on the ground that there was no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal and that he had been falsely implicated in the case. Held, that the evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could be drawn therefrom. The appellant was rightly convicted by the High Court. The evidence in this case was not free from suspicion and not sufficient to convict him. The conviction of the appellant was bad as it had not been proved that it belonged to Bhagwandas. Although this court will not interfere with the findings of the High Courts because its conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from that of the trial Court, yet where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused was guilty, this Court would set aside the conviction. The Supreme Court has held in Sunderlal vs State of Madhya Pradesh (A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 289) that the High court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are substantial and compelling reasons justifying interference with the finding of the courts below because its conclusion on the evi dence as to guilt or the innocence of a accused differ in that of those High Court, but where the prosecution is such which no Tribunal can legitimately infer, from it, that it was not proved that the appellant belonged to the Bhagwandas and that his statement was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon.

The appellant company was an all India complex having its establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar there were disputes between the management of the appellant 's factory and its workmen represented by their union, which were referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the constitution of the said Indusco Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the said amendment purported to amend its constitution so as to extend its membership to the company 's other establishments, the reference extended to them and also gave it clear that the disputes referred were between the workmen of that factory and the management and the workmen employed in that factory. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Tribunal 's award. The High Court held that there was no error in making its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at their other establishments and that it acted beyond jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal erred in holding that the dispute raised by the union was in respect of the employees of the company wherever they may be stationed. [559 D] (2) The award is operative in respect only of the workmen in the appellant company ' factory at Jamshedpur and not the workmen at Their other establishments. [560 E F] (3) The Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , referred to. (4) The Industrial adjudication made by the Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant Company to grant special leave demanded by the Union. The result is that except for the overtime rate allowed by the tribunal which we confirm, the rest of the appeal has to be allowed and the Tribunal should be allowed.

The assessee firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939. In 1934 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership with M/s. Hakam Malani T. Malani, who had entered into a partnership with the assessee firm. The assessee claimed that the firm was a dissolved on April 1, 1939, and that firm alone was entitled to relief under section 25(4) or in the alternative under section 26 (4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3), or (4). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to the family firm was governed by the Indian Incometax Act, 1918, and on that account the assessee was entitled on the dissolution of that firm in March 1943 when the assessee wag dissolved. On appeal the Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner. Thereafter as directed by the High Court of Punjab under section 66(2) of Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, the assessee company was dissolved and on August 31, 1942, the business in timber which was carried on by that firm was taken over by the assessee. The High Court agreed with this view and held that the assessee could not be said to have been carrying on business at the commencement of the Income tax Amendment Act 7 Of 1939, after Act 7, 1939 came into force. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the partnership in the present case was dissolved by March 31 of 1939 and therefore the firm alone could be entitled to the benefit provided in section 25 (4), or 25(5) of Indian Income Tax Act, as the assessee had ceased to carry on business immediately after the dissolution. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the appellant was entitled under the dissolution on August 1, 1943, to the benefits of section 25 of the Incometax Act.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , subject to certain conditions. The permit was renewed for a period of five years and thereafter it expired on April 26, 1967. On May 3/4, 1963, the State Transport Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In second appeal by the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal, the High Court held that the Secretary to the Regional Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 and that the Tribunal had no jurisdic tion to entertain the appeals and to interfere with the order of the Regional transport Authority granting the permit which had already been affirmed in appeal by it. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the issue of the permit was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 120, and that no appeal lay under section 64 of the Act against the order granting the renewal of the stage carriage permits. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appeals before the State transport Appellate Tribunal were not competent under section64 of the . [189G] 2. Section 64 has to be read with rule 178 of the Rules which prescribes the procedure for appeal to the various authorities Appeal is a creature of the statute. There is no dispute that section 64 creates rights of appeal against the grant of permit and other matters with which we are not concerned here. There was no appeal provided for under section 65 against an order issuing a permit in pursuance of an earlier resolution of the State Government granting the same permit. [189A B] 3. The appeal before the Mysore Appellate Tribunal is, therefore, not competent to be under section 63 of the and both the Tribunals had no Jurisdiction to entertain appeals and interfere with its order granting a permit which has already been confirmed in appeal.

The appellant challenged the election of respondent No. 1 on grounds of corrupt practices under sub sections (3) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no contravention of the provisions contained in sub sections 3, 4 and 5 of section 124 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that under the provisions of Order VIII Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure a meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 wherein the appellant 's supporters were present and the respondent No 1 was declared elected. The appellant also relied on certain letters written by several voters who stated that they remained within the house and could not vote because the village called Nagola. It was further contended that the speeches were made by the appellant with reference to two letters that the letter would indicate some of the terms of the transaction. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The statement in question has to be first a false statement bearing on the personal character and conduct of the candidate which is to be protected from malicious or false attacks. The statement complained of must be one which is reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election. Under the provisions relating to corrupt practices, the appellant was entitled to have the publication with the consent of the respondent or his election agent. [901 D E] (2) The statements in question had to be made by a candidate at Hapur Town Hall Maidan. The allegations about the speeches on the office of the Republican Party were not mentioned either in the Vir Arjun or in the Hindustan dated 7 February, 1967. It is obvious that if the appellant had been chased he would have made report to the Election Commission or to the police. [948 G] (3)(a) The provisions contained under sub section (4), (5) and sub section(4) require the publication by the consent or of the candidates or his Election agent. In the present case, the offending speeches did not offend the provisions either sub section 3A or sub section 4 of Section 123 of Act. [949 B C] (b) The appellant failed to prove that respondent No1 was guilty of corrupt practice under sub Sections (3), (4A) and(4). [948 E F] (c) The High Courts rightly commented on the absence of any report either to the Commission or the police authorities about the alleged occurrence.

The appellants filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. The learned District Judge held that in view of the provision of Explanation I to Section 47 of the C.P.C., the judgment debtor was not competent to maintain the appeal as one under Article 136 of the Constitution. The certificate was granted by the High Court on the basis of which the appeal is filed. The appellants contended before this Court that the certificate was not maintainable in view Of clause (3) of Article 133 of the Con stitution, and Article 134 of the Consti tution, and that as held by the learned Judge of the High Curt, the application was not incompetent in view thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The period of limitation for delivery of possession of property purchased at the court sale has been reduced to a considerable extent, but that also cannot be taken into consideration for the purpose of interpretation of the provisions of the Limitation Act. [362E F] 2. Article 134 is not applicable to an application for setting it aside sale. In other words, an application seeking deliv ery of possession can also be made within a period of 12 years from the date on which the decree or order becomes enforceable or where the decree is passed and the latter for an applicationfor delivery of posses sion has been fixed as provided in clause (a) of Explanation II to Section47. [363F G] 3. The provisions of Article 134 are for two different purposes, the former being for the execution of a decree for possession so as to invoke the provision Of Article 136.

The first respondent, a member of the Kerala Legislative Assembly from the constituency in all the constituencies was declared elected by a margin of 1873 votes over his nearest rival. The appellant was declared duly elected by the margin of franchise votes over the nearest rival, and the first respondent filed an election petition claiming that he was entitled to be declared duly constituted from the said constituency. In support of the petition, the first respond ent alleged various corrupt practices on the part of the appellant. The High Court dismissed all the aforesaid corrupt practices except two, viz., (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987 a day prior to the election, pamphlet containing a news item in daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983, and (ii) publication of a wall poster, both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first Respondent. The first respondent alleged various allegations against the appellant with respect to printing and publishing on March 23, 1987, a day before the election of the Appellant to the Kerala Assembly from Mattan Constituency No. 73 was declared void on the ground that the appellant had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The petition was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant: (i). printing and publish on March 21, 1987 the day prior thereto a day anterior to the Election, pamphlet contained a news article in daily 'Malayal Manoraama ' dated May 2, 1983 and (iii) publication on 3rd March, 1987. The election to the State Assembly from all the constituency was held on March 25, 1987 and the appellant was elected by margin of votes over respondent No. 1. On May 8, 1987 respondent No 1 filed an Election Petition claiming a declaration that the election was void and that he be declared elected from the aforesaid constituency. The Election Tribunal accepted all the said corrupt practices but dismissed the petition holding that both these acts amounted to corrupt practice within the mischief of Section 100(4). In appeal by special leave it was urged on behalf o f the appellant that (i ) the words "any person with the consent of a candidate or his election agent" in section 123(1) thereof, and "the publication by a candidate" or his agent or by any other person with his consent and connivance of the candidate or respondent No 2 were used to denote the corrupt practice; (ii). publication on the wall at the instance and with the knowledge and connivance and of the election agent and was distributed by them among the electors knowing the imputation to be false and calculated to affect the prospectus of respondent No l. The Tribunal also found that the pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily " Malayala" published in daily MalayalManorama was marked as exhibit P 1 and two photographs of the wall poster were marked as exhibits P 2 and P 3. On appeal by the first res pondent, the High court held that both the acts amounted tain to corrupt practices under Section 123 (4) and were sufficient to void the election. Hence this appeal by Special Leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant 's election agent was not guilty of any corrupt practice as defined in section 100(5). [728E] 1.2 In the light of past expres sion of the people and in view of the mandatory provisions of Section 83(1), it is clear that the publication by the candidate, his agents and workers could have made complaints both to the Returning Officer as well as to the police in that connection with the election and that the first appellant was guilty of corrupt practice. [729F] 1:3 The appellant had proved that Ganganagar cinema theatre belonged to Chowdhary or his sons.

The petitioners who were paying the rate of land revenue under section 20 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 challenged the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 granting sanction to the plan submitted by the respondent No. 5 for construction of a hotel on the said land. The Municipal Corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a green belt or recreation ground in the interest of general public. The petitioners filed writ petitions challenging the legality of the order of the Government of Maharashtra dated 25.7.1978 exempting the disputed land under section 21 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions holding that after the Municipal Corporation had decided to revise the development plan, no appeal would be competent to the State Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966. In the appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the Municipal Commissioner was not justified in rejecting the application for approval of the plan; (ii) the respondent authority had misunderstood the provisions of section 46 of the Land Ceiling Act inasmuch as the draft revised development plan had been published and the plan was submitted by respondent No 5 and conditioned by the Respondent No. 2; and (iii) the sanction of the development Plan was not in accordance with the directions of the respondent Corporation. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly rejected the application of the Municipal corporation for review. [928E] 1.2 The contention that the draft development plan has since been published is without any substance and is rejected. [936G] Life Insurance Corporation of India & Anr. vs Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.3 In granting exemption on the ground of availability of 75,000 sq. of vacant land is available for the development of gardens, it was open to the Municipal Corpora tion to accept the verdict of the appellate authority and it has done so by not challenging it in the High Court or before this Court. [940A B] 1.(i) The respondent Corporation had passed a resolution on 3.12.1973 extending the reservation for park to 7,000 square yards out of the disputed property. As a matter of fact, Counsel submitted that granting exemption was very much time barred and the appellate author ity was justified in allowing the appeal.

The appellants were the employees of a company which had closed its industrial undertaking. The Industrial Court framed an issue whether the employers had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing a continuing lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 (`the 'Act for short). In the complaints filed before it, the appellants contended that they had finally closed the industrial undertaking and were not guilty of any unfair labour practices. The employers contended that the Industrial undertakings of the employers never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen are not being re employcdent and new hands are being recruited. On behalf of the employer it was urged that the industrial undertakings of employers had never been closure or at no rate have resume working in complete and that they were not being retrenched in full. The appellants also contended that there was a closure of the industrial Undertaking and that it was not a case of lock out. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The closure must always be permanent and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary or for a period. The employer may close down industrial activity bonafide on genuine eventualities as a result of which workmen are rendered jobless. [68E] 2. In the instant case, the Industrial Court has not imposed a lock out or has closed down the business. Even if the suspension of work is ordered it would constitute lockout but is necessarily permanent and temporary or a lockout was necessarily temporary for a fixed period. [69F G] 3. The management may close up industrial activity bona fide and wants to re open, bonafide wants to reopen, bonafide and wants the closure to start the industrial activity. Even when the suspension is ordered, it would be constitute lock out and permanent that lock out is necessarily temporarily or for such a period.[70E F] 4. In order to be assured that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit, the employer may closing down the industrial activities bonafide on fide eventualities such as temporary or permanent lockout are necessarily temporary. The fact that the closure has to be irrevocable, final and permanent would not make a device or pretence. Therefore, the correct approach ought to be that when it is claimed that the employer is not guilty Of imposing a lock Out but has closed the Industrial establishment, it is not necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closing down of the industry may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employee at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [70F G; 71A B] 5. The real test for determining whether the employer has resorted to closure of industrial activity is, (i) whether the closure is brought about malafide or whether it could have been avoided; and (ii) whether it was bona fide. If the closure was brought about mala fide and whether it can have been stopped, bonafide or for reasons beyond the control of the management, the Court would be entitled to come to the conclusion one way or the other. [71G H] 6. The question as to whether the workmen had committed unfair labour Practice must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. In deciding whether the discharge was a bona fide one or was a device to terminate services of workmen or whether the refusal by an employer to continue employment to employ any number of persons employed by him, depends upon the facts of each particular case. [72A B; 70G] 7.

The assessee company purchased shares of certain value of Rs. 1,86,47,733 representing investments in the shape of shares and securities. The Income Tax authorities accepted the plea of the assessee company that it was a dealer in shares and immovable properties during the assessment year 1939 40 and assessed it on that basis. For these years and for the assessment years 1943 44 and 1942 43 the assessee Company claimed to be a dealer or an investor according to its own memorandum dated October 2, 1942, which stated that it had purchased the shares of Rs,. 1,33,930 in the year ended 30th June, 1931, shares of the Associated Building Co. Ltd., were redeemed and the proceeds were taken for the purpose of relinquishing the managing agencies of the various mills under their agency and the shares held by the assessee in the Sassoon Group of Mills were handed over to the respective purchasers of the value of the shares and shares. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the assessee 's claim that it could not be said that there was material on the record to support the finding of the Income Tax Officer that the assessee had been a dealer and not an investor, and held that the investments were held by it as the stock intrade of its business which it carried on during the previous year and also in the preceding years. The High Court dismissed the assessee appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The proper construction of statutory language is always a matter of law and therefore the claim of the assesses that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities etc., cannot be taxed as business profits. [52 C] G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. vsC.I.T., ; , referred to. (2) The High court must accept the findings of the Tribunal on the primary questions of fact; but it is open to the High Court to examine whether the Tribunal had applied the relevant legal principles correctly or not in reaching its final conclusion. [53 D E] G Venkataswami Mudaliar & Co., vs C.I,T., , followed.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge. In 1949, he filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, placing him on suspension until further orders, and also for an order suspending him pending enquiry into certain charges. The High Court dismissed the petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 4 of the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which came into force from October 1, 1953 was only a Tribunal as provided in r. 4(1)(a). There had been some argument before the High Court that having regard to its setting, the proviso should be read as qualifying sub rule (2), it was not necessary for the Government to refer the cases of all Government servants drawing a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above to a Tribunal. [422 C D] (ii) Rule 3 of the Rules does not show an intention to depart from the procedure laid down in the Madras Civil Services Rules, but only sub rule 2. The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of academic interest, as the Rule did not show any intention to departure from the prescribed procedure laid in the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Act. [420 C] (iii) Rule 13 of the Madras civil Service (Dis Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal Rules) which came to be in force when the enquiry against the appellant was started, does not give an intention either to depart form the procedure as laid down by the Madras High Court or to hold a fresh enquiry into grave charges under r. 17(e).

The appellant was a registered holder of 2674 shares of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The net dividends so deemed to be distributed in respect of those shares were Rs. 61,051 and Rs. 3,73,099. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 34(1)(b) of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 18 of 1933, for some reason which was not clear from the record, failing which the appellant had escaped assessment. The appellant contended that the principle of those cases applied only when the registered share holder is alive and the beneficial ownership in the shares is vested as a result of some transaction inter vivos in a person in whose name the shares do not stand in the company 's register but not where by the grant of representation to the estate of a registered shareholder who has died, the representative is invested without his name being entered in the register with the rights of the shareholder. Held, that the income received by a legal representative which would, but for the death of the deceased, have been received by such deceased person, is to be regarded for the purpose of assessment as personal income of the legal representative to assess tax on such receipts on the footing that it is the personal income. Commissioner of Income tax Bombay City II vs Shakumtala and others (I.L.R. , applied. The principle of these cases applies only when a registered shareholder is alive, but the beneficial owner in the share holder dies, a different interpretation of the same expression in the context of notional income would be impermissible. Commissioner Of Income tax, Bombay City vs Shakuratala and Others (I I.L R. , followed.

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government may from time to time be recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler. The appellant was a Ruler of Basdposhdar or Jagirdar within the meaning of article 366(22) of the Constitution. He entered into a contract with the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered upon an agreement in December, 1947 with the State Government of Madhya Pradesh to be merged with the Union of India and the State was to be formed with the said Central Provinces. The Ruler of this State became the Ruler. On December 15, 1947 he entered a contract whereby he was recognised by him as the Ruler and his rights in relation to the governance of his State were recognised. He was also a maufidar. In January 1948, he executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion Government of india with effect from January 1, 1948. The Rulers of this country entered into agreements with the Indian Dominion of indi cation for the purpose of the privy purse guaranteed by article 291 of the Consti tution that the Ruler would be transferred to the Government and full India and exclusive authority, jurisdiction and powers over the Baster State with effect form January 1 1948. On August 14. 1947, the appellant executed an instrument of Accession in favour of the Dominion Of India on the same day. The Governor of Baser issued a Instrument of accession to the Indian Government whereby he undertook the administration of that State. He also ceded to the Govern ment 's of India the full and exclusive jurisdiction and power over the other States with effectfrom January 1. 1948. In February 1951, he was allotted certain villages in Schedule A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitu tion. The High Court certified under article 132(1) that the appellant was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and C of his Petition under articles 227 and 227. Held, that the High Court rightly held that the petition was not maintainable as these villages had not yet been recognised by Government of the India as the private property of the appellant by virtue of article 363(1). The expression "mahal" in section 2(m) of 'the Act means "a person who, or that which exercises rule especially of a supreme or sovereign kind". The effect of the Merger Agreement was clearly one by which factually a Ruler became an Indian State merged with Madhya Pradesh. It was common ground in the High COurt that the villages in question were exempt from payment of rent or tax.

The respondent was working in Shillong since the year 1979. He was transferred to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred from Shillong to Pouri (Uttarachal Pradesh). The respondent approached the Tribunal for a declaration that his transfer was illegal and violative of Rule 15(1)(a) of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1987. The Tribunal quashed the order of transfer on administrative grounds and held that the transfer was ordered on administrative ground and was unexceptionable. The High Court quashed the said order of the Tribunal. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 15 says that "the President may transfer a government servant from one post to another". That the respondent is liable to transfer anywhere in India is not in dispute. It is not the case of the respondent that order of his transfer is vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does say so merely because certain guidelines issued by the Central Government are not followed, much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. [433E F] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; , referred to. 1.2 The transfer is not an arbitrary or illegal order. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the competent authority competent to transfer. In this case the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order transferring. It could not substitute its judgment for the said authority for that. [ 432E F; 432A] Bank vs Jagjit singh Mehta, [1992] 1 S.C.C 306, referred to 2. The guidelines say that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted at the same place. While choosing the career and a particular service, the couple have to bear in mind this factor and be prepared to face such hardship if the administrative needs and transfer policy do not permit the posting of both at one station without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employees. In such a case the couple had to make their choice at the threshold between career prospects and family life. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service with the incident of transfer to any service with that incident of Transfer to any place in India, subordinating the need of other employee. In these a case, the two spouses would be posted as far back as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authority should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two wives to live together at one Station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative need and the claim of other persons. [ 431E F, 432A B] Bank Of India vs Jaswant Singh Mehta ; , followed.

The appellants were tried for the murder of Jawahar. The second charge related to rioting a rioting which resulted in his death. The third charge was that the first accused, Alto, armed with sticks, A3 armed with spears and A4 armed with deadly weapons, attacked at Jawahar with stick (spear stick) and A6 armed with lathis, A5 armed with aruval (bill hook) and a knife (spunti stick) on the deceased. The fourth charge related t o the assault on the first appellant. The appellants were convicted under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34, I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal by the State, the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1 to A3. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted into the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [325E] 2. The intention of the appel lants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325, IP. C. read with 34, 1.P.,C. [327F G] 3. The High Court while dealing with the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case came within the mischief of Section 326 read with section 34, IPC read with Sec tion 34, Cr. P.C., read with Sections 34,I.P C. [324A] 4. The appellant shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial Court within four months from today. In the event of non payment of fine, they shall undergo rigorous imprison ment for five year.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents for recovery of certain amounts claimed by it on account of the loan together with interest due thereon. The suit was decreed and the Bank was directed to pay the same to the firm and its partners. Being dissatisfied with the decree, the Bank preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour of the Bank and dismissed the suit against them. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that (i) the words `special Indian law ' in section 4(e) of the Act refer only to a special law enacted by an Indian Legislature, and not to a law made by the British Parliament as different from any Act enacted by the Indian Parliament; (ii) the Banking Companies Act is a special statute enacted by Parliament specially for India. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Banking Companies Acts are quite legal and valid. [968G] 2.1 The Banking companies Act is not a special legislation enacted by British Parliament. It has been held by the Andhra Pradesh High Court that section 4 (e) while speaking of any special Indian law, is only speaking of special Indian Law made by an English Legislature. In view of the said definition, the expression `special ' in Section 4(f) of Act means a special Indian statute enacted under the Indian legislature. [986G] Krishna Murthy vs Krishna Murthy, AIR 1983 Andhra Pradesh 347; approved. 2.2 The Banking Company Act is an ordinary law enacted for India specially for the country. It is not disputed that the Banking companies Acts are a special Law enacted by a British Parliament and the Banking Company is a Special Law enacted in the United Kingdom. [987C] Krishna Rao Murthy vsKrishna Murthy, ; , referred to.

The petitioners who were sugar factories in the State of Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the notification issued by the Government fixing the ex factory price of sugar produced by them in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, North Bihar and North Bengal. The contention was that the impugned notification merely fixes ex factory prices and that it did not fix any price at which the persons purchasing sugar from the mills would sell it so that it was open to the middleman who bought sugar from those factories to sell it at any price. Held, that the notification merely fixed ex factory rates and that there was no reasonable safeguard against the abuse of power by the Central Government if it was ever minded to abuse its power. The impugned notification did not contravene article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as it was not based on any rational or intelligible differentia which would justify the fixation of price. The notification merely laid down the factors which should be taken into consideration in fixing the price and thus these factors were a check on the power of the Central Govern ment to fix prices arbitrarily. The Government had ample power to fix the exfactory price, i.e., the price for the consumer, but it did so only in respect of factories in Uttar Pradesh. The State of Bihar vs Bihar, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 869, followed. Held further, that there is no discrimination between different regions or between producers and middlemen in view of the economic factors which control the price of Sugar in India depends upon the price at a fair level and make sugar available at fair prices. The price fixed by the impugned Notification was not arbitrary but was based on an intelligible differentia and could not be challenged on the ground that it gave rise to unreasonable restrictions on the right to carry on trade under article 19 (1)(f) of ' the Constitution.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 referred the dispute between Messrs. Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works Limited, Calcutta to a Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , for adjudication of industrial disputes in accordance with the provisions of the . The Tribunal held that there was a rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 instead of taking the fluctuating rate in the index between 1954 and 1955. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Government made the order of transfer on April 9, 1957, i.e., after section 2 of the Amending Act 18 of 1957 was deemed to have come into force on August 28, 1956, and it must be held that the Government acted within its powers in transferring the dispute pending before the Second Industrial Tribu nal to another Tribunal constituted under section 7A of the Act. (ii) The order of the transfer made on April 10, 1957 was not terminated in accordance by law. The agreement was self contained and started a new chapter regulating the relationship of the parties to the dispute in respect of matters covered by it. The award must be deemed to be superseded by the new agreement. In regard to matters covered under it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement or to the date on which it was so amended did not appear to have been pressed before the Tribunal. (iii) The Tribunal wrongly relied upon exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal, that the said figures relate only to working class menials and the corresponding entries in regard to the working class cost of the living index do not indicate so much increase as in the case of the menial class.

The appellant was served with a memorandum asking him to hand over the charge of all the properties of the Mutt and its endowments. The Executive Officer did not take any effective steps to implement the scheme, nor did he take any action to implement it. The appellant moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the notice served on him by the Executive Officer threatening to take over the administration of the Math and its properties under the scheme. The High Court held that some provisions of the Act contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the scheme was not completely implemented till 1952, and (ii) the appellant had a definite alternative remedy under the latter Act, but this plea was rejected by the High court on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the guarantee guaranteed by article 19(1)(f). HELD: (i). The contention must be accepted. It is no doubt true that section 103(d) provides that any scheme settled or modified by a Court under the earlier Act shall be deemed to have been settled or modify under the provisions of that Act without examining whether all the provisions Of the said schemes are necessarily justified by, or consistent with the relevant provisions of this latter Act. But it is not necessary for the Court to examine whether all those provisions of an earlier scheme are necessarily valid or consistent. [257 C D] (ii). The scheme was framed and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity in the light of the fundamental right guaranteed to him under article 19 of the Constitu tion. It was not open to the appellant, therefore, to challenge the validity of the scheme on the grounds that it deprived him of his fundamental rights under article 14. [260 D] The contention that since in the present case the scheme had not been completely implemented until 1952, the order was not implemented does not make any difference to this legal position. If the broad and unqualified proposition for which Mr. Sastri relied was accepted as true, then it would virtually make the material provisions of article 19 in respect of fundamental rights retrospective operation.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in a school run by the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 days and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. He was not paid salary for the period of summer vacation during all these years. Although the appellant continues to serve as Hindi teacher he was appointed on December 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing Committee of the School. He worked with repeated spell of 89 day appointments and one days break in both the spells. Since the period for summer vacation had not been approved by the educational authorities, he filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12,1982. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of Section 3 of the Validation Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the appellant is entitled to been regularised as Hindi teachers with effectfrom July 12 1982. Though the appellant continued to served the school to date under orders of the Managing Committee even after 1986 has not been approve by the Educational authorities for almost 4 years with short breaks. The number of teachers in the State of Haryana who are thus appointed on such ad hoc basis must be on or after 1st December, 1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services". The appellant filed a Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitu tion challenging the validity of Section 4 of the validation Act. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that since the appellant had been appointed on ad hoc capacity for 89 days, he was entitled for regularisation as a Hindi Teacher with effect form from July 13, 1982 and continued till 18th July, 1986 and continued until 18th7.1986. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. The validation Act covers field upto 31st December 1984. [994C] 2.1 The Validation Acts cover the field up to December 31. 1984. In order to make the existing educational set up effective and efficient it is necessary to do away with ad hocism in teaching appointments. An appointment on 89 day basis with one day breaks which deprives a teacher of his salary for period of 15 summer vacation and other service benefits, is wholly arbitrary and suffers from the vice of discrimination. The validating Act covers this field upto the December 31 1984. It is needless to say that the State Government is expected to function as a model employer.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti. He was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on the ground that he was disqualified for being chosen to the post of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti and that his ground was not disqualified from contesting the election. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 3 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules 1965 does not convert the office of Chairman into an office or profit. [427 D] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, ; , followed. (ii) The appellant has failed to establish that the allowances payable under rules 3 to 7 were result in any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of Panchayat Samiti, and consequently there is no question of any disqualification arising. [448 C] Ravana Subanna v G. S. K.aggearappa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 653 at p. 656, referred to. (iii) The payment under rules 4 to 7 was in addition to the payment under r. 3. The fact that the right to receive it accrues only when the journey is outside the district would not make any difference because this payment would result in profit to the payee. [ 427 E] Ravappa Subanna & G.Kaggeappa, , distinguished.

The appellant was tenant of a Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from erstwhile owners in 1963, a year later they filed a suit for eviction against the appellant. The Trial Court held that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin sheds marked with letters CDGH had been made out with permission of the respondent, the tenant was liable for eviction. The Additional Civil Judge set aside the order of the first appellate court on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act, 1952. On a second appeal made by the respond ents, the Additional Civil judge set aside tho order of eviction and dismissed the respondents ' suit on the finding that none o f the constru cions constituted materials justifying appellant s eviction under sec tion 14(C). The High Court also held that construction which converted the tenanted premises into double storey structure, materially altered the accommodation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the disputed constructions included a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two rooms and tin shed shown by letters BCDH had constructed by him without the consent or permission of respondent landlords; that the suit premises was sub ject to the provisions of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts committed error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the Trial Court and the relevant evidence placed before it by the parties clearly show that the partition wall did not actual ly alter the accommodation or was likely to substantially diminish its value; [975C] 2.1 The construction put by letters C DGH had not materially altered either in the form or structure of the building, as it could easily be removed without causing any damage to the building. One portion of the tin roof was already in existence on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion. Construction of a Chabutra, Almirah, opening a window or closing a door by temporary structure or replacing of a damaged roof which may be leaking or placing partition in a room or making similar minor alterations for the convenient use of the tenanted accommodation, having regard to the purpose for which the accommodation may have been let out, it could be removed at any time without causing damage to such building. [976E F] 2:2. The material alteration contemplate change of substantial nature affecting the form and character of the buildings.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Thereafter, the respondent filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C., for setting it aside ex parte order. The High Court allowed the revision petition, set aside the ex parte judgment of the trial court and upheld the passing of the ex p parte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The judgment of Trial Court setting aside the exparte decree was correct. In any event no error of jurisdiction was committed by it. [1031C] 2.1 The High court went wrong in interfering with the exp parte decree and restored that of the Trial Court. There was no error in the judgment of High Court. [1132D] 2:2. The appellant company had no knowledge of the exparte order, even otherwise before 29 71975 when its attorney constituted Shri Nawlakha was concerned merely with sales and had nothing to do with legal matters generally or with receiving summons in particular. It is denied that service on Shri Nawrakha cannot be regarded as due service on the Company. The first part of clause (b) has got to be understood with reference to the other provisions of the Code in order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons.

The respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 145 of the Cr. P.C., for the breach of the peace and for passing an order on the 29th July, 1976 declaring him to be in possession of the land in dispute. The Magistrate passed an order directing the appellant to be put in possession. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr.P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court held that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there was an apprehension of breach of peace, it was not necessary to record a finding about the existence of a dispute likely to cause a breach of law and once he records his satisfaction in the preliminary order, that there existed an imminent apprehension of the breach. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the High court is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [96H] Ramarao vs Shivram & Ors., ; , referred to. 2. In Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors, ; , this Court held in Ramarao V. Shivram and Ors., that once a Magistrate finds that there is a breach, he can continue the proceedings. It was not correct on the part of the High Courts to have interfered with the order passed under sub section (5) of section 145 nor was such a case set up by any party before the Magistrate or before the High COurt. [952D E] Ramrao vs Shivrasram & ors., ; and Hari Ram and Ors.

The appellant was a public limited company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and its Managing Agents were the firm of Messrs. K. R. Thyagaraja Chettiar and Co., whose partners were Mr. Thingaraja Chetty and Co. The company was resident and ordinarily resident in British India, its head office being at Madurai in Madras State. It carried on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, and for the purpose of that business purchases it from X for Rs. 5,000, and paid that amount to X. Neither this purchase nor the payment of Rs.5,000 to him would appear in the books of the company. Instead, the books were of A 's own constituents and the appellant was selling yarn only to X for a price of Rs 5,500. The books showed these goods as purchased by X for the value of Rs 50,000.
