The appellant contended that the sales standing in their names were genuine and that in fact, no profits were made by it in those transactions, that it purchased only cotton only from the intermediaries and did pay them the amounts as shown in the accounts. Held, that the appellant had a right to refer the question to the court under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because there was no accrual of income or profits under the statute. The fact that the transactions were sham and fictitious did not make it clear that the profits were earned by the intermediaries as distinct entities chargeable to tax under section 3 Of the Act. Commissioner of Taxes vs Melbourne Trust (A.I.R. , referred to.

The assessee, a company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth, claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 paid to its General Manager for the assessment year 1948 49 under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The claim was disallowed by the Income tax Officer on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish. He also found that no general practice of giving commission at the rate of 25% existed in the assessee 's line of business. On appeal the Appellate Tribunal held that the post of General Manager carried the equal responsibility to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of the business after the death of Shri Vaish and that the commission paid to him was nothing but wholly for the purpose of carrying on business. The High Court, however, held that in view of the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of Rs 75,467 paid to the General Manager was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the assessee within the meaning of section 10 (2)(XV) of Income Tax. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the circumstances of the case the amount of RS. 37,733 paid to one Vaish by the General manager was not really paid wholly for carrying on its business and that therefore the commission was not deductible under section 1(2) (xv). HELD: The principle of this decision applies to the present case. [530 B] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; , followed.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited. He was dismissed by an order dated January 15, 1954, on the ground that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and prayed for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order terminating his services with effect from January 18, 1954. An application under article 226 and 227 of the Constitution was dismissed summarily by the High Court. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court on a certificate granted by the Supreme Court. Held: (i) that section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act recognises this position, by providing that the workman who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represented by an officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member. The Secretary of the Union had no authority to enter in any compromise on behalf of the union and the appellant was not bound by it. (ii)that section 36 Of the Industrial Dispute Act recognises the great importance in modern industrial life of collective bargaining between the workman and employers. It is well known how before the days of collective bargain labour was at a great disadvantage in obtaining reasonable terms for contracts of service from his employer. As trade unions developed in the country and collective bargaining became the rule of law, it is necessary and proper to take note also of the fact that when an individual workman becomes a party under the Industrial disputes Act he is not independently of the Unions which has espoused his cause. It was well known before the ordinary rule should be that such representation by an Officer of the trade union should continue throughout the proceedings in the absence of excep tional circumstances which may justify the Tribunal to permit other representation of the workman concerned.

The appellants were the tenants of one of the respondents. The suit for ejectment was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent against defendant No. 1. On appeal by defendant No, 2 the District judge set aside the decree on the ground that the entire appeal had abated as no application for bringing his legal representatives on record was made within time. The High Court allowed the appellants ' appeal holding that the surviving appellants could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in view of the provisions of O. XLI, r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the appeal by the surviving appellant was not competent in the circumstances of the case and therefore the provisions Of 0. XLI r. 3 of OXLI should be applied to the facts of this case as the nine appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and the surviving plaintiffs could have filed the appeal as representing all the other non appeals. The right of the surviving plaintiff was not coextensive with that of the defendants to continue as tenant of one or the other of the landlords and not as a tenant of the other landlords when they had a joint right to eject him or to have him as their tenant. It is not possible for the defendant to continue in view, the appeal filed by the appellants was not incompetent. The discretionary power cannot be exercised to nullify the effect of abatement of the appeal so far as it affects the rights of the legal representatives under the decree. Held further, that r. 2 of OXXII of the C.P.C., which is applicable to the case, does not apply to the present case as there was no inconsistency between the previsions of r. 9 of OXXXII and those of r, 4 of O .XLI. The discretion conferred on the appellate court by 0. XLIII of O 'XLI could be exercised only in exceptional cases when its non exercise will lead to difficulties in the adjustment of rights of various parties.

The appellant tenant was a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954. The Rent Act came into force on December 1, 1962. The appellant tenant had been receiving rent from the tenant until the time he filed a petition for eviction (1967) the statute which regulated the right to eviction being the Delhi Rent Control Act 1958 which regulated his right to evict, where under the general law, they do not have such a right in praesenti. It follows that before a landlord can institute proceedings for recovery of possession, he has to make out his right (a) under the Berar Act, which regulatedthe right to eject, where, under the General Law, they did not have so, but only by 15 days ' notice expiring with the end of the month of the tenancy. The respondent landlord had been received rent from a tenant until he filed an eviction petition for his eviction ( 1967) the Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord had obtained rent from him till the time the appellant filed a suit for eviction. The trial court upheld the contention and dismissed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant tenant fell back on certain defences grounded on ss.106 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that no notice to quit had been given, nor notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the lease caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(g) because the Tenancy Act did not apply to the lease. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the lease had expired by efflux of time limited under section 111 (a), and no notice terminating tenancy under s.111(g); (ii) the forfeiture was needed; and (iii) the termination of the period of 11 years the landlord had not assented to the holding over of the tenant 's tenancy under S.111 (g). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court rightly held that there was no valid notice in law for valid determination. [920C] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant landlord has all along staked his case on the application of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that the appellants were fit to be retained in public service and that he ought to be dismissed from service. The Governor accordingly dismissed the appellants ' writ petitions challenging the orders of dismissal. The appellants contended before this Court that (i) the order of dismissal passed against them was not justified on the ground that it was made by the Governor when expressing his satisfaction under sub clause (c) of the proviso to cl.(2) of article 311 of the Constitution, and (ii) the Governor 's satisfaction did not extend to the inexpediency of which the Governor was satisfied. HELD: (i). The order of the Governor did not satisfy the requirements of sub clause(c) as contained in article 311(2) itself. This provision is confined to guaranteeing to the Government servant an opportunity to be given to him only at the later stage of showing cause against the proposed punishment to be imposed on him. [491 D E] (ii). The Governor 'is also satisfied that in the interest of the security of the State it was not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity of showing causes against his conviction on a criminal charge; or (iii) the Government servants had been given an opportunity for showing cause before imposing the proposed penalty. No satisfaction is recorded that it is inexpedient to hold such inquiry. [490 E F] Khem Chand vs The Union of India, ; , followed. (iv) The Governor was not satisfied that it had no reason why the Chief Secretary should not have stated on oath in the earlier paragraph instead of merely making a submission of his in a subsequent paragraph. The order passed by the Government in this case did not comply with the requirements Of sub clause.(c) and the unamended article 311 (2). [490 G H] Khemchand vs Union of india, ; and K. K . Tatia vs State of Assam, ; referred to.

The petitioners and respondents 5 and 6 are the Sunni Community of Mohalla Doshipura. They are alleged to have committed certain offences under sections 25 and 26 of the Constitution in the matter of enjoying their religious faith and performance of religious rites, practices and observances on certain plots and properties situated in the said Mohalla and buildings and structures thereon belonging to the Shia community by holding Majlises (wailing) and taking out processions with Tabut Tazia, Alama, Zuljinha etc. for performing their religious ceremonies and functions on the said nine plots and structures therein. The petitioners and other respondents are alleged as representing the Sunni community of MohallaDoshiparaura. The allegations against the various officials of the Shias of Mohalla Posura and the structures thereon belong to the Sunni communities known as Shia Community by holding a religious denomination having a common faith and they observe MOHARRAM but in a different manner. The case of the petitioners and respondent 5 and six as representing Sunni community is that the members of their sect numbering about 4000 constitute a religious belief having a Common faith and They observe MOwar Temple (w failing and taking away processions) with Tabus Tazira, Alma etc. For performing these religious rites practices, practices, observances and functions, on the aforesaid nine plots, and structures on some of them, particulars whereof are as under: Plot No. 246, 247/231134 and 247/1130 in the aforesaid Mohalla and building and structures thereof belong to Shia communities and buildings thereon belonging thereto. The said religious belief is practised by the men folk and the women folks of the Shaas of Village Doshipsura and that the membership of Shia Wakfs concerning the plots and structure thereon belongs to the Haria community over the concerned plots and constructions in question is the registration of these plots and buildings. The Petitioners and other Respondents 5 and6 as representing Shia sects of Mohalla doship, Varanasi City (formerly Adampur) in the city of Varanasi and in particular are seeking a declaration that the plots of land bearing plot Nos. 245, 246, 248/23, 247, 248, 248 and 247 (1130) in their respective Mohalla and structures upon some of the same, as representing Mohamed community of VillageDoships, Varanasi are based their customary rights to perform the aforesaid religious rites ceremonies, practices on the plots, the said properties and structures.

The assessee, a limited company, had disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10,200 and claimed set off of the loss of Rs,.3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1965 66 corresponding to the previous year ending on 31st December, 1965. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and 1961 60 the loss was claimed it was excluded in computing the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the assessee 's claim. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the loss had not been determined as required under section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. The High Court also took the view that in the order for assessment year 1957 58 it was claimed that it was a notional capital loss. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the Revenue, it was contended that the benefit conferred under section 23(3), regarding intimation of losses deter mined by the Income tax officer did not apply to the loss falling under the head 'capital gains ' in the computation of income and as such the claim was not admissible. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The assessee is entitled to have set off under the provisions of section 74(1)(b) and section 80 together. [1164D] 2. The benefit conferred by section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim of set off was admissible in our view ' on a bare analysis of these provisions, and without reference to anything more. [1106E] 3. The expression "capital gains" in section 74A(1) (b) is not defined in the 1922 Income Tax Act, 1961.

The respondent was recruited as Defence Quality Assurance Service (D & P) in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production ( Air) (D&P) (C & D) Department of Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). The recruitment to the Defence Engineering Service was made by the Defence Research & Development Organisation, Ministry of Defence, Government of India, Ministry o f Defence, on 24.12.1985. The respondent was promoted as Defence Production Quality Assurance Services (DQAS) in 1962. He challenged the said promotion before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad Bench, holding that he was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years and was not entitled to continue in service upto 60 years. The Tribunal held that the re spondent was not a liable to retire at the time of his retirement till the date of his arbitrary retirement till he attained the age o 60 years and that he would continue in serv ice till he attains the age Of 60 years, unless he had been retired. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of the Defence Academy was increased, it could not be held that they were entitled to the benefit of the power so exercised in the facts and circum stances of the case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The denial of the benefit to the enhanced age of superannuation to the members is violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [24D] 1.2 The denial was not justified by the appellant nor could it be said that the respondent belonged to another unit, viz., DAQAS. The classification made between them has no rational basis and no nexus of such classification to the object sought to be achieved has been shown to have been achieved. [25E F] 1:3 The denial to the benefits of enhanced superannuation age to the member of one of the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of article 16 of Constitution. The denial is not justified. [26F G] 2.1 In spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the ages of 58. years. It has been unable to understand this indefensible action on the part of the appellant or could it not be said, that the respond ent was not enti tled to the said benefit. [27F G].

The appellant was the election of councillors to the Sangli City Municipality. The counting took place on June 3, 1967 and the petition was filed on June 24, 1967. According to the election petition the result of which had been published in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967, that the first respondent had used malpractices at the election by arousing his religious sentiments and securing votes by false personation were also levelled therein. The appellant 's case was closed on the same day and arguments started on August 22, 1968. On August 21, 1968 the appellant made an application before the Judge for issuing summons to the two persons as his witnesses but the learned Judge rejected that application. The High Court dismissed the petition in limine on October 4, 1968 holding that the trial court had not transgressed the limits imposed by the Act and as such it was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the procedure adopted by the trial Court was wrong in that the two witnesses who were examined as court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the learned judge had in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21. 1968; (2) the trial Judge had in his exercise of the jurisdiction vested under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution could not have been exercised on the facts of the case by the issue of a writ of certiorari, as there was no fair trial of the petition to the prejudice of the appellant; and (3) the High Court was not right in refusing to quash the order. HELD : (1)(a) The High court had jurisdiction under articles 227 and 227 to interfere with the order of the trial judge based on the evidence of these witnesses. [975 B] (b) In the instant case, the allegations of corrupt practice were of a serious nature and if the appellant was found guilty of the commission thereof, the period of five years ' disqualification would certainly not be inappropriate. The charge in that pamphlet that he had turned the Kabarasthan into a brothel and was trading in illicit liquor for which was alleged to have been convicted is not established. [986 C] (c) In view of the unsatisfactory nature of the issues framed, the whole trial is vitiated. [98 D E] (d) The first issue was rather confusing and misleading. Instead of framing a separate issue with regard to each charge of corrupt practices committed in respect of each of the pamphlets, the second issue should have specified the different heads of corrupt Practice committed in relation to each of these pamphlets. [99 G H] (2)(a). The first publication dated 8th June 1967 and subsequent bearing the date 8th and the second bears the date 975 of the second.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The tax payable on the sales effected between April 1, 1956 and July 31, 1957 was six pies in the rupees. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification as being ultra vires the powers of the State Legislature under article 213(1) of the Constitution. Held: (i) that the Validation Act is intra vires and the impugned notification dated December 3, 1956 is intra vided. (ii) that it operates retrospectively. It cannot be said that the validation Act was not ultra vires on the ground that it was passed before section 3 A was issued. The Validation Act was intra vires. The validating Act is not ultra rites the powers conferred by article 286(2) of Constitution and any other provisions of the constitution bearing on the question. Even assuming that the provisions of a. P. Sales Tax Act XV of 1948 contemplate a levy of tax in future, that does not affect the power of the legislature under entry 54 to enact a law with retrospective operation. The validation Act is therefore ultra vires. (iii)that it operates prospectively and the Validation was intra vices. That has to be determined solely on the construction of Entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, because the validating Act does not validate the impugned Notification. M. Biri Works vs Sales Tax Officer, ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the broad facts bearing on the instant case were the nature of aspersions cast upon the appellant and his family members which resulted in the death of a girl aged about twenty four years. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, brutalisation, criminal companionship, versatile, criminal associateship etc. [592D] 2.1 The offence of rape is violation of human rights by all canons. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychicaling, healing, releasering the stresses, release of stresses and release of reformation in his home, what wit libidinous 'brahmacharisacharis 'bharramachari 'sbrahmsacharis. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, handcuff orders or remissions, the young appellant has inflicted on his cousin 's wife snatching a tricky opportunity. Even so, the incriminating company of lifers and others for long may be counter productive, and in this perspective, it blend deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The assessee, a limited company dealing in land, maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946, the Land Acquisition Officer awarded compensation at Rs.30,10,873 on account of permanent acquisition of the land, and a sum of Rs.12,276 out of that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assessee on the date of the award. On appeal by the assessee before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax, the Tribunal held that the compensation received by the assesse related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was therefore a trading receipt of the business carried on by it and therefore a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax, and that the High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue. In second appeal before this Court, on behalf of the appellant, it was contended that the amount of compensation received was not a receipt as contemplated by section 4(1)(b)(i) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, but only an offer made by the Land acquisition Officer, and not when the land was taken over by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year 1956 57. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that when land was acquired by the State Government under section 5(1) (b)(ii), it could be said that the right to enhanced compensation accrued only when it became payable, i.e., when the Collector awarded the compensation, and recompute the entire income on the 'basis of the final compensation. [395C D] 2. The expression "accrue" or "arise" in section 4 (1)(a) of Income tax Act, 1961, means something tangible, something in the nature of a debt, 395 something in an obligation to pay an ascertained amount. Till such time no income can be said to have accrued, whether in fact paid or not.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the respondent landlords on the ground that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961. The appellants ' case was that the respondent landlord had withdrawn all his defence to the application filed by him and submitted to a decree for eviction unconditionally. The trial court accepted the appellant 's objection and dismissed the execution case. On appeal, the High Court held that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. Undoubtedly, a compromise of such suit is permissible under the said provision of law. [882C] 2.1 A compromise of a suit is impermissible under the provisions Of law. Ordinarily, a compromised of such a suit was permissible under section 12(1) of the Act. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 3, Rule 23 when it says "where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". The protection given is inherentin the language, of Order23, Rule3 when it said "Where it is established to the satis faction of the court that a decree has been adjustment by any valid agreement or compromised. the Court shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit." [883G H; 884A B] 2(a) The protection under Order 23 Rule 3, when it states "where a suit had been adjusted" by any unlawful agreement or .the court shall pass such decree in terms thereof so faras it relates, inter alia, as to the eviction of a tenant from any accommodation let for non residential purposes mentioned in clause (f) of section 12.

The assessee company, carrying on business as selling agents of a Textile Mill, claimed that the loss incurred by it was a capital loss. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the amount of Rs. 11,88,000/ was a loss relating to shares held by the company in its investment account. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In further appeal, before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the losses incurred by the Company were a capital one and not a loss which could be taken into consideration in the application of section 23A(1). The Tribunal accepted the contention and held that under the circumstances the Directors were justified in not declaring any dividend in respect of those years. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Income Tax Officer was wrong in holding that the assessee had incurred a capital gain. [864 F] Commissioner of Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., ; , followed. (ii) The Tribunal was right in holding on the facts found by the Tribunal that there could hardly be any doubt that the assesses had suffered a capital profit. But, all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend. [874 F G] Commissioner Of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadli Bannerjee and Co., , followed (iii) The statute does not say 'having regard only to losses previously incurred by a company and to the smallness of profits made. No answer which can be said to be in any measure adequate can be given to the question "unreasonableness" considering these two matters only. Their Lordships are of the opinion that the Statute does not show 'having regards only to loss previously incurred but also 'to the small extent of the profits made '. [884 C] Commissioner, Income tax V Williamson vs Diamond Ltd., , referred to.

The respondent, a displaced person, filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh, under section 12(4) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, alleging that an order made under section 13(4), as amended by the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holding (U.P.) Act, 1954, was appealable under section 39 of the Act. The Civil Judge held that an appeal lay under section 37 of the said Act to the District Judge against the order of the Civil Court and that no appeal lay to the High Court. On appeal, the District judge reversed the decision of the trial court and modified the award by substituting it as a result of which the respondent was allowed to get an order modifying the award. The High Court held that the Civil judge was not justified under section 15 of the , in modifying the decree merely because he disagreed with the finding of the arbitrator, but on appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Section 37 of Act does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 40 of the . In the present case, the effect of section 46 and section 47 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12(6), 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the Consolidation of holdings Act. Section 37 applies to arbitrations in the consolidation of Holdings. The effect of the section is that the decision or the arbitrator under sub section(4)(a) shall be final. (ii) Section 12(5) must be read with section 37 Of the Act, and if it is so read it is quite clear that what is made final is the decision on the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings, if any, have been taken under the provisions Of the . The effect is to apply sections 15, 16 and 30 of the to the proceedings before the arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. (iii) Section 13(6) must therefore be read and section 37 applies not to arbitrations referred to in section 37 but also to section 39.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. He was promoted to the said post on that date. The promotion was challenged by him by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The classification made on the basis of educational qualification was permissible. The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to the cadre of Executive Engineers, be classified on the foundation of educational qualifications. The Rule provides that graduates should be eligible to such promotion. It is for the authorities if they so desire, taking into consideration the nature of work, the requisite qualification for the work and the necessity for making such a classification that quotas could be prescribed on the strength of educational qualifica tion. [372B C] 1.2 The rule provides that graduate shall be entitled to such promotions to the exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [373C D] 2.1 In the absence of the rules and regulations, the authority can act by executive instruction find direct instruction in support of the Government in Mysore state Road Transport Corporation vs Gopinath Gundachar & Ors., ; , followed. The State Road Transport Corpora tion vs Gopinath gundachar Gundaracharla & Ors. ; ; H.C. Sharma & others vs Municipal Corporation of Delhi & Others; [1966] 3 SCR 767 and S.M. Pandit & Ors, etc. vs state of Gujarat & Ors.; , ; ; State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao, ; ; Union of India and others vs Dr. Mrs. S.B.

The petitioners in the first petition are members of the Judicial Association. They have filed applications under Article 32 of the Constitution for a direction to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and various High Courts of the country and ancili al order directing that the Union should fill up all the vacancies in the Bombay High Court. The petitioners contended that the petitions were not maintainable as they had been clubbed together and heard from time to time. In response to the rule, the Union Government took the stand through the Attorney General that the petition was not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies was in the superior courts. The Union of india took the stands through the Advocate General that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union to provide the sanctioned strength in the subordinate Courts and these cases were allowed to proceed. The Attorney General, however, withdrew the objection regarding this Court 's jurisdiction and made a statement that he was of the view that it is of the opinion that it would be the constitutional duty of the union to provide sanctioned strength. In reply to the Rule, the Attorney Genera tional Judges as well as the proposed appointees were also asked to name three High Courts for each State. The petitions were heard from times to time and were disposed of by a common judgment. The Court held that while the matter was pending before the Supreme 'Court, the States had been divided into the Union Territories and the High Courts in the States were covered by Chapter V and Part VI of the Con stitution. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the petitions under Article 226 of the Consti tution were not tenable; (ii) the petition under Article 136 was not a justiciable matter; (iii) the petitioners had been singled out of vacancies in different High Courts and the number of Judges was also increased. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The appointments to the superior judiciary are not justiciable. It is for this Court to suggest that the matter requires to be looked into again a reference should be made to the Chief Justice of India and there can be a fresh look at the matter only if the Chief justice of India permits such review of the case. [555C D] 2. The power to appoint solely vests with the executive and that the executive after bestowing such consideration on the result of consultations with the judicial organ of the State, would be at liberty to take such decision as it may think fit in the matter of appointments. [556E F] 3. It cannot be said that the Chief Justices of the States and the Chief Ministers of India before the Presi dent of India were not invited to make any appointments to them without any delay. The President has to take into consideration the opinions of all of them and he should not accept the opinion of any other authority. [560F] 4. It would be open to the Central Government over ride the opinion given by the constitutional authorities in the country, on due application of his mind, has given finality to the process at his level, there cannot ordinari ly be any justification for reopening the matter merely because there has been a change in the personnel of the Chief Minister or the Chief Minis trate. [559G] 5. The recommendations of the appropriate dignitYe have to be examined in the view of the fact that by the Amendment the Chief Secretary of India would become the Chairman of the Commission. In case the Commission is not constituted, the two questions indicated above are of vital importance to the efficient functioning of the judicial system in the Country require consideration and there is an element of immediacy in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. [561F G] 6. The Judges of the High Court and the Supreme Courts have been set up by a constitutional Amend ment, and the choice of Judges to the President has been considerably reduced.

The respondent was a Relieving Head Cashier in the appellant 's Bank. He was served with a charge sheet on him under Rule 19 of the Bipartite Settlement dated January 19, 1966. The Enquiry Officer conducted the departmental enquiry against the respondent and concluded the enquiry against him by the end of 1979. He then gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and then passed the impugned order of discharge on January 14, 1980. The respondent challenged the said order of dismissal before the High Court which dismissed it. In appeal to this Court it was contended that since the initial appointment of Shri U.B. Menon was nobody in the hierarchy of authorities to impose punishment on him, the initial defect, if any stood removed, stood removed and, therefore, the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent and without jurisdiction. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment. [201G] 2.1 In the facts and circumstances of this case, the High court was right to quash the impugned ordi cation of punishment on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the learned Single Judge for the first time and therefore, it should not have ordered payment of 'all consequential bene fits flowing from the declaration that the impugned Order was bad in law. [202E] 2:2. The doctrine of incompetence, prejudice or mala fides is of no consequence so far as the question whether an ex employee can validly be appointed as Enquiry Officer to enquire into the conduct of an employee. [204G] 3.1 It is aimed at the prevention of public and private mischief and the protection of public interest. It avoid endless confusion and needless chaos. It, therefore. endless uncertainty and needless confusion and it fails the entire edifice on which the foundation is built collapses and with it fails. The whole edifice on Which the edifice is built disappears and with its result the edifice stands built collapsed and withit it fails in the entire substratum on which this edifice is build collapses. [205G H] 2(a) There is no merit in the contention that the High COurt ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. To put it differently, according to the learned counsel for the appellant, the high Court should have remitted back the matter with a direction that the competent authority will proceed to dispose of the departmen tal enquiry from the stage of the report submitted by the Enquiry Offi cer. [203G H; 204A] (b) The High COun tive Court was in error in directing payment of all consequential benefits.

The appellant, a owner of a building bearing municipal door No. 3776 situated in the main switchri Bazar, Delhi, was constructing and urgent repairs on October 16, 1965. The respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, addition as well as alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was old and required repairs". The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order refusing sanction. The High Court held that the Commissioner could decline the sanction only if there was a contravention of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act, and that the reasons given for rejection were wholly irrelevant and not germane to the sanction asked for. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents: (1) that the Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi had statutory force, and (2 ) that the plan submitted by them did not contravene any provisions of sub s.(2) or section 336 of the Act. HELD : (i) The High court was perfectly justified in holding that the order of rejection passed by the Commissioner was legal and valid. [171 E] (ii) The Master Plan was prepared under section 7 by the authority on September 1, 1962 and it had come into force as contemplated by section 11. Though section 8 contemplates the preparation of a Zonal Development Plan simultaneously with the preparation, the Master plan will stand modified or modified. At present it is the Master Plans that holds the field. If a Zonal development Plan comes into operation and if it contains a proposal regarding the width that a road should have, all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period, the reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 will be that if any particular and definite use of the site for the building, by the respondents would contravene the provisions of any other law '. [172 G H; 173 A] (iii) The appellant will have to establish that any land or part of a land or building in that zone, it cannot be put to a different use. If neither of the plans provide for the particular use of any land nor building in the area or Zone section 14 would have to be followed and parties will have been given an opportunity of placing any objections or making any representations offering any representation.

The appellant was the Minister of Industries and Commerce Department, and was working under the appellant No. 1 as Rajpramukh and the President of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of India in the Commerce and Industries Department. The Chief Minister of Vindhya pradesh made several applications for procuring the cancellation of the said order and on the 13th January 1949, the Chief Minister made an endorsement at the foot of the application that the appellant had been detained on the way for some other business of his. The Judicial Commissioner held that the appeal to the Judicial Commissioner from the acquittal by the Special Judge was competent and that there was no infringement of the fundamental rights of the appellants under articles 14 and 20 of the Constitution. Held, that the order of conviction and sentence passed against the appellant were not justified on the evidence given by the two independent witnesses Gadkari and Perulakar. The statements made by the appellant Nos. 1 to 3 were inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by them. The statement made by appellant No 1 was inadmissible in law as it appeared from the evidence that the appellants had made the statements before them. It was not necessary for the prosecution to prove the correctness of the statements made to the two witnesses, but the statements were admissible under section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and were therefore inadmissible in any case. The evidence of these witnesses was not such as to inspire confidence in the mind of the Court. The basic merit of the administration of criminal justice in the State lies in the fact that the person arrested by the police is entitled to come before an independent and impartial Magistrate who is expected to deal with the case without the Magistrate himself being in any way a partisan or a witness to police activities. There was another danger and that is the Magistrates are put in the unenviable and embarrassing position of having to give evidence as a witness and then being disbelieved.

The plaintiff respondent was serving as a constable in the State Police. He was prosecuted for having assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh, who was also charged with offences under section 325 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and several other sections. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the order of dismissal was illegal on the grounds that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. The High Court, however, allowed the plaintiff 's appeal against the decision of the first appellate court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules 1934 directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the reason that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. [825E F] 2.2 The High Courts should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The first appellate Court should permit the plaintiff to file additional evidence in regard to the further orders passed against Kahan Singh subsequent to the civil court 's decree in his favour, and to argue before the High Court that the case involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Courts in the manner it has been done. [826B C] 2:3 The High court should have considered the plaint filed for finding off the cause o f action for a suit and thereafter in that perspective deter mining the correct Article of the limitation Act applicable. Serious objection has been taken against the observations of the First Appellate Court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned counsel for the parties, this court, HELD : 1.2 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High court shall permit the defendant to file an application for admitting additional evidence. [827B] 2(a) The High COurt should have examine the plaint in respect of finding out t he cause of a suit. Serverse objection has not been taken by the respondent that the aforesaid Kahan Sing had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order dismissing his dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and should have remanded the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. [824E F;825A] 2.(b) The finding of the Additional District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation was applicable to suit where an orde r is impugned, as being in void. [823B C].

The respondent assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The sales were effected by the assessee 's mills at a certain rate for the purpose of manufacturing tea. In the assessment year 1959 60, the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of cotton from its income. The sale was effected on April 17, 1958, and the delivery orders addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to the Mills changed hands, but the amount realised was not paid on September 18, 1955. In a reference under section 66(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922, the High Court held that the transactions were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the assesses in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the respondent 's non speculative business. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) In considering the effect of the position that the property in the goods passed to the ultimate endorsee of delivery orders, it is necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual delivery of the goods to the transferee. Even if the goods are delivered to the transferor 's transferee, the first transfer also will be a valid transfer. What has to be seen in such cases is whether the ultimate purchaser of the p.D.Os has taken actual delivery. It is erroneous to think that if any transfer of the P.D.,O. is not followed up for actual delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set Off only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. The object of the explanation is not to invalidate the transaction which are not completed by actual deliver ment or transfer of commodity. [184 D E] (ii) In construing Explanation 2 to section 24(1), the legislature did not intend to affect any transaction of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was no actual or physical delivery, loss, the losses, ifany, would he a loss. in a speculation transaction in the explanation.

The first respondent was a candidate for the general seat and the other reserved for a Scheduled Caste. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent on the ground that he had been improperly rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The Election Tribunal decided in favour of the second respondent but declared the whole election void. An appeal to this Court was filed with special leave. Held, that the nomination paper must be signed "by the proposers and seconders in the usual way prescribed by the Act but in the ordinary way" it is not defined as "sign". The word "subscribe" in its ordinary meaning means "a particular assent, the element of signing " has to be incorporated into any provision of the Act. It must be construed in the sense set out above. The word 'subscrib" is not used in the special way prescribed under the Act and it cannot be ignored merely because a special meaning has been given to the word " Subscribe". In the case of illiterate persons unable to write their names it is necessary to guard against misrepresentation and fraud by requiring that signatures should be formally authenticated in a particular way. A special statutory cloak of protection is thrown around them just as the ordinary law clothes pardanish in women and ignorant persons and likely to be imposed on with special protective cover. The words " subscribe " in the context of making a signature and the making of a mark are to be treated differently. The Returning Officer was therefore bound to reject them under section 36(2)(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

The appellants, workmen of the Company, went on an indefinite strike with effect from August 30, 1972. On September 7, 1972, the company put up a notice stating that the strike embarked upon by the workmen was illegal and those participating in the said strike were liable to disciplinary action for misconduct as per Company 's certified standing orders Nos. 22(b) and 24(a). The appellants filed complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with regard to the alleged unfair termination of their services, alleging that they had abandoned their service and had not voluntarily abandoned their services. On October 2, 1972 the company issued notices to the workmen asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the company. The appellants contended that the action of the respondent in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal, arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Tribunal rejected the contentions and held that the appellants had voluntarily abandoned the service of the respondents and had no intention to abandon their services and that at any rate the termination of the services could only be in terms of the Standing Orders and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service, it was not open to the company 's employer to indicate that the company could terminate the services of the workmen on the ground of abandonment of their service because of their going on strike in enforcement of their demands. The High Court dismissed the appellants ' writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Standing Orders did not give for treating workmen as had abandoned service and that the Labour Court could not by imposing a new term of employment unilaterally convert the absence of work into abandonment of employment. [621C] (2) The impugned action on the part of the appellant clearly amounted to a change in the condition of service of its employees during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced. [625E F] (3) The appellants were entitled to relief.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees had mortgaged certain house belonging to the trust to one Sahebaba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. An action instituted by the mortgagee against the trustees for the recovery of the mortgage amount due under the decree and in an application for execution by the mortgagor the mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs.5,000 by the executing court. The Trustees thereafter applied under 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 out of the amount in deposit with the Court. The Subordinate Judge passed an order disposing of the application and directed that Rs.250 out of which the amount was paid over to the appellant be paid over. In appeal against this order by the trustees the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees bad failed to comply with the requirements of r.89 of Civil procedure, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set it aside the auction. The High Court in revision held that the provisions of 0.21 r. 90 of the Civil Procedure Code were not complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set the aside the said sale. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the District court had no jurisdic tion to set at naught the order of the District judge and that the High Court had jurisdiction to interfere with the order passed by the District Judge. Held, that the powers under 0s. 115 of the C.P.C., were not properly exercised and the District 'Court had no Jurisdiction to set them aside. The District Court was competent to set up a larger Bench for hearing the matter. Such a Bench is constituted by the Chief Justice. A Single Judge of a High Court is ordinarily bound to accept as correct judgments of Courts of coordinate jurisdiction and Division Benches of his Court and of this Court. He has no power under 0, 21 r., 89 of Civil Proce dure Code to set an order for recovery of money due from the trust by sale of the property of the trust.

The appellant was a clerk in the Post and Telegraph Department. He joined the post and Telegraph Depart ment as a clerk on June 4, 1935. The Director Postal Services by an order dated April 21, 1970 retired from service under Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules. The said order was challenged before the High Court which dismissed it holding that there was no firm inity in Rule 2 (2) and that the retirement under Rule 1(2)(a) of Pension Rules could only be done at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service, and that Rule 2.(2) was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retire ment under Rule2(2), of Pension rules should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest, is not a statutory rule. [808C] 2.1 The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitu tion of India and as such cannot be statutory. [800G] Union of India & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to. 1.2 Rule 2046 of the Rules is a statutory Rule and is identical to Fundamental Rule 56(j). Para 620 is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) of Constitution of India. This rule has no parity with Rule 2.

The assessee firm was carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1944 to 31st March, 1943 failing in the financial year ending 31st December, 1942 failing in which sales took place. In the assessment year 1942 41 to March 31, 1943, the assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/s Biharilal Balkishan in the accounts styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose. In April, 1945 to 29th September, 1941, sales took places from May 30, 1941 to September 29, 1941 failing in its financial year ended 31st October, 1942 and March 31st, 1943. Sales took place from May 28, 1941. The sales were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 4th April, 1943 and March 1, 1943 falling in the Financial Year ending 31 st March, 1944. Sales taken place from June 30, 1940 to September 30, 1942. Sales taking place from July 26, 1943 was completely differ ent from the business carried on during the chargeable accounting periods. The assessee had taken the jungle on August 28, 1943 for sale and had extracted Katechu from 23rd November, 1942 to March31, 1943 which included the period 1st of April, 1941 and March 30, 1943 in failing in that financial year. The Sales Tax Officer held that the assessee was entitled to set off in respect of the deficiency of profits accruing in the year 1940 41. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. In further appeal, by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that during the relevant two chargeable accounting years ending 31th March, 1942, and 31st May, 1943 the sales took from May, 30, 1944, failing in t he financial year beginning March 31. 1943 and no part of it was sold. The Appellate Tribunal accepted this contention and confirmed the order of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner. On further appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that since the chargeable account ing periods ending 31rd March, 1941 were occupied with manufacturing activity alone and there were no sales either during or until 30th May, 1941 subsequent to 29st September, 1942 the assessment was completely different from the carried on for the chargeable period ending 31.3.1942 to 31. 3.1943. The High Court also held that though chargeable levy was an annual charge and generally for the purpose of levy of the annual charge the profits of the chargeable chargeable accounting Period must be computed on yearly basis in terms of the definition of "accounting period" under section 2(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it is contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that during these two chargeable account periods, though there were sales effected in the next year, the profits accrued to the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The concept of " Accounting period", in the context of the 'chargeable accounting period ' can be harmo nised.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up vacancies expected in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the KPSC. The applications were invited for filling vacancies expected on the basis of the vacancies available in these two branches. The Kerala Public Services Commission invited application for filling the vacancies expected under the quota at the time of selection and also the procedure of the examination. The candidates had to appear in the written test conducted by the K PSC as per Notification published in Kerala Gazette. The marks specified for these posts were: B. Sc. in Engineering or mechanical Engineering of Kerala University, or its analogous equivalent as required by the Special rules of Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to sit in the common list prepared by the Public Service Com mission. The number of options was not fixed either by the Single Judge or by the Division Bench of the High Court. On the contrary the direction given by the learned Single Judge and the Division bench of the Karnataka High Court were set aside. In these appeals, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the KSC had advised 239 candidates according to separate lists for Civil Engineer and Mechanical Engineers prepared on the strength of examination already conducted. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The KP SC has made the order as it appears from the judgment of the Madras High Court in effect upheld by the division Bench of Kerala High Court and the Public Services Com missioner of Kerala proceeded to prepare separate lists. But facing difficulties, in view of the difficulties faced by the Kerala Public service Commission and the Government of Kerala, it is necessary to clarify the position and give necessary directions. [775B C] 2. The expression "the common list" in clause 4 of the Government order No. G.O.MS 101/79/PWDE&D dated 27th September 1979 issued by the State of Kerala is also referred to a common list although no common list was directed to be prepared or was prepared by KP.SC. This was obviously an inadvertent mistake. Since there was no common List and since no option was given to the Special Leave Petitioners before this Court by the judgment dated 28th April, 1980, it could not be said that there were any valid ground to reverse the judgments of the Division Court.

The respondent filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts. The trial court passed an order on 26th December, 1981 holding that the partnership deed of 1979 was void and void and for passing a decree for dissolution. The High Court dismissed the revision application filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit is governed by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act and not by section7(iv) (f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The valuation put by the respondent before the High Court on the plaint is arbitrary and unacceptable. The court fee paid by the plaintiff was in excess of its pecuniary jurisdiction. It is true that in a suit filed for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore, put a tentative valuation upon the suit but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenaksundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849, it was held that when the valuation put on the plaintiff appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable the court may reject it leave and it can leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. [510C D] 1.2 In a suit under section 7 (iv)(c) of Court Fees Rules, the plaintiff has the absolute right to put on plaint any value he wishes and the court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter. While examining the issue it will be open to the trial court to take into consideration the statement in the plaint that the plaintiff had been ousted from the partnership business. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary Jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII C.P.C. [511D E] 1:3 The High Courts have consistently confirmed this right of the plaintiff and he has not discovered any decision to the contrary. In such a case it is not only open to it but its duty to reject such a valuation. [ 512E F] 2.1 In a Suit for accounts, the court shall not examine the correctness of the valuation given by the defendant and to revise the same if it is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. It will be competent to give his own tentative valuation. Ordinarily the Court shall not examining the correctness or the valuation chosen but the plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. [ 511E F; 512A] 2:2 The principle underlying both the clauses (c) and (f) is substantially the same and the Full Bench governed the case. In the instant case, the valuation of Rs.150 as has been done in the case before the Court was arbitrary and untenable. It was not open to a court but its duties to reject it such a value.

The assesses claimed exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question. The assessing authority rejected the claim of exemption on the ground that the industries run by them were "traditional industries" which were not eligible for exemption. The assessee 's writ petitions challenging the decision of the Assessing Authority and the High Court were dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assesses that (i) the G.S.D./ Flour Mills case was in favour of the assessees; (ii) the assessee had not opted for the scheme of deferring the payment of tax under the rules framed for the purpose; and (iii) the notification issued by the Government on 12.1.1983 was beyond the scope of the rule making power conferred on it by section 12(1)(i). Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The G.D/ Flour Mills ' case was clearly distinguishable from the facts of the present case. [626G] 2. The notification dated 3.7.1983 issued by Government on 13.12.83 was beyond its scope and could not be treated as one merely clarifying an ambiguity in the earlier one and hence capable of being retrospective. It cannot take away the exemption conferred by the earlier notification. [625A B] 3. The Notification dated 3/7. 1983 amending the 1981 notification with retrospective effect so as to exclude what may be described in brief as "trained industries" but also certain other industries which may not be "trainted" one or not. Secondly, the attempt of the State to read a further condition into the notification excluding "tra conditional industries" from the exemption was never denied only to "tra permissive industries". Thirdly, the attempts of the state to read as a matter of record, that subsequent to the decision in G. S.D. / Flour Mills, apart from pleading that the earlier scheme and procedure should be read into the Notification, were equally plausible. [ 625B C] 4. The State Government had not intended the exemption to be availed of by certain categories of industries. It was not open to the State Government, particularly in view of section 22D, to frame such scheme for the pur pose as it may deem fit. The provision for exemption, however, needs to be spelt out, under section 12 (1)(ii). [627C D] 5. The power to defer payment of sales tax by a period of 10 years is discretionary and not subject to any restrictions or conditions set out in the notification.

The Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1970 were framed by the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in consultation with the High Court. Rule 2(b) provides that a Member of the service ' means a person appointed in substantive capacity to the service under the provisions of the Rules. The proviso thereto requires that the first available vacancy will be filled by direct recruitment and the next two vacancies by promotees and so on. Sub rule (2) of Rule 12 provides that all other candidates who are appointed to the Service shall be on probation for a period of two years. Rule 17 provided that the initial recruitment shall be made from amongst the members of the Delhi Judicial Service promoted to the Services. The petitioners were members of that service and they had won their point. They were working at the relevant time in temporary posts which were created by the Delhi Administration in the cadre of Additional District and Sessions Judges. In that capacity, some of them are working on deputation as members of one or the other Tribunals in Delhi, like the Industrial Tribunal or the Sales Tax Tribunal. The Union of India, the Delhi Adminis tration, Delhi, filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the validity of Rule 8(2) and (3) of Delhi Higher judicial Service Rules 1970. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District & Sessions Judges and that the direct recruits who are recruited to the Delhi Higher Administrative Service should rank for seniority along with direct recruits only if they are appointed in a substantive capacity. The respondents contended that seniority of promotees must be fixed in accordance With the respective date of their regular officiation as Addl. District and Session Judges and not from the dates when appointments were made to the services under Rule 16 and 17. It would be incongruous to say that the petitioners have no application and are distinguishable. Allowing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in three years of assessment in respect of the income of the family of Parshad. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, "annulled" the orders of assessment of the assessee in the status of association of persons and in appeal by the Tribunal, confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. On a reference made at the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax, the High Court held that the income belonged to Parshad and he was liable to be assessed personally in respect thereof. The High Court also held that on the facts and circumstances of the case the appeals filed by the assessee were maintainable in law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression "any person" used in section 34(3)(a) proviso 2 at p. 346 means a person intimately connected in the aforesaid sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. [391 D] Commissioner of Incometax, U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate ; , followed. (2) The Income tax officer was not competent to make the direction. He could only direct the Income tax Offi cer to do what he has failed to do. It is not necessary to pursue the matter further. [392 E] Commissioner off income, U P. vs Delhi Coal Systi cates ; , applied. (3) The power of the Income Tax Officer under section 31(3) of the Act was not unguided and uncanalised. The powers of the Assistant Com missioner were not unguided. He had no jurisdiction to make a direction against the Income 'tax Officer.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by him. The appellant claimed to have a share in the joint Hindu family properties, and an accounts in respect thereof. The trial court decreed the respondent 's claim on the basis that the compromise did not bind the appellant and so he was bound by them. On appeal the High Court held that the appellant was not bound to set aside the prior compromise decree between his father and the respondent and that the plaint was governed by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act, and that it was open to him to value his claim on a memorandum of appeal under section 7(iv)(b) without an amendment of the valuation made in the plaint. Held, that the High court was in error in holding that the valuation for the purpose of court fee should be taken as the valuation even for the purposes of jurisdiction and it was not open to the appellant to value the relief on the memorandum of appeals. The suit was therefore competent under section 5 of the , and the proper court fees payable were Rs. 100,000. In the present case the trial court had rightly held that a suit was competent under article 17B of Schedule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The question whether the appellant could claim relief under section7(iv) (b) or section 7 (v) of the Madras High Court Fees Act, 1933, did not arise for decision in this case. The authority and jurisdiction of the High Courts in enacting r. 11 was not in dispute. The provisions of sections 13, 14 and 15 had to be applied to suits filed on the Original Side of the Calcutta High Court, and the appellant had to pay court fees both on the plaint and on the Memorandum of appeal.

The appellant, a publisher of Newspapers, holds a lease in perpetuity from Government of the plot No. 148 Barakhamba Road New Delhi. In the year 1980 respondent No. 1 sought for and obtained permission from the NDMC to erect a high rise building on plot No 148 Barkhamba road, New Delhi, which was granted by the Central Govern ment on 30th April 1966 in accordance with the mandatory requirements of the statutory Building Bye laws promulgated under the Punjab Municipal Act 1911. The appellant also applied for and on 29th August 1980, it obtained sanction from the Government of India for construction of "Statesman House" a high raised building on plots No. 149 Barakhan Road NewDelhi. In June 1985, however, there was no impediment to the sanction. On 29th December 1986, respondent No 1 sought permission for and obtain ed, and obtained sanction of the building plans on or before 5th May 1989. The NDMC by its communication dated 9th March 1988 gave clearance to the building plan in relation to the Union territory of Delhi and that the proposed build ing did not also provide for a "podium/pedestrian walk way" made mandatory by the Zonal Development Plan for 2 years. In July 1985, there were no impediment on high rise structures. But this prohibition was lifted on 18th July, 1984. On 30th December, 1986 respondent No I sought permission from NDMC to build up a high lying building of an area of 1,62,000 square feet and paid Rs.63,40,918 as betterment levy. On 4th May, 1982 it applied for, and on 6th May 1981, the sanction was revalidated for a further period of two years. The sanction was again revalidulated for a second period of 2 years, and in June 1985 another plan incorporating substantial changes in the plans necessitated, as it was claimed, by the changing require ments of printing technology and the plans as earlier sanc tion did not meet these altered requirements. On 6th December 1988, respondent 1 filed a Writ Petition in the High Court for an appropriate order directing the Corporation to convey its formal sanction of building plans or release the same to the petitioner Company on or after 5th day of May 1989, and also to convey the formal sanction to the NDMC. The High Court considered the objection raised by the Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic) as unrelated to the bye laws as applicable to the situation and held that the objection from that source should not interdict the sanction of plans by the NDMC and in the course of the order dated 28th April 1989 finally dis posed of the writ petition, the High court considered the objections raised by respondent No l and 2 on 27.10.1987, and directed the Corporation accordingly to convey their formal sanction for the construction of 'Statesman ' at a high level building on Plot No. 147 Barakinda Road, NewDelhi, which had been constructed in 1987. The Corporation thereupon filed a writ petition in the Delhi High Court seeking appropriate order restraining the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws promulgated by it under the Delhi Municipal Act, 1911 in relation ties to the union territory of the Delhi and for a direction to the Corporation and the Corporation not to deal with the application for sanction.

The joint family carried on the motor bus service and also money lending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". The family also Possessed immovable and movable property. The family was running a grocery shop, liquor shops, etc., in which the family business was being run by the plaintiff. The plaintiff who was running the liquor shops had no desire to conduct the liquor business jointly or in partnership with his brothers after the expiry of the licence. He gave notice to his brothers through pleader on December 12, 1945, stating inter alia that the parties had agreed to appoint an arbitrator to ascertain the profits earned by the use of the capital belonging to them alone and that the suit was not barred by res judicata or by Order II, rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court held that although the motor business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family business yet as it was carried on by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 Of the Partnership Act, he held that the two brothers carrying on the business after the death of the deceased were jointly liable to account. The High Court in appeal affirmed this decision. Held, that the cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit is barred under Order II rule 2 (3) C.P.C., and the suit being barred by both res judicata and Order II Rule 2(1)(3), C. P.C. no further question as to the applicability of section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act can possibly arise under the circumstances.

The appellant was employed as a cleaning and dyeing Works in Bombay. The appellant was working on the Wadia Mahal Salt Works situate at Wadala, Bombay without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the , read with r. 4 of the Rules framed under the Act. The main question for determination in this appeal is whether these Salt Works come within the definition of the word " factory " under cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act and if so, were they 'manufacturing process " within the meaning of that expression. Held:(i) The Salt Works would come within an 'factory ' as defined in the , and the appellant was rightly convicted by the trial Court. (ii) The word "premises" is not restricted in scope to buildings alone but includes premises, buildings or lands appurtenant thereto. The word 'premises ' has been used in a wide sense and it is not confined to open land and buildings. The Salt works are parts of a building and they may be used for the purpose of a factory. (iii) The words "manufacturing" in section 2(m) refer to an entire area which may have within it several separate buildings. Further, the Act has sufficient provisions empowering the State Government to exempt the occupiers from complying with certain provisions of the . The Salt and Works Act is for the welfare of the workers and deals with matters connected with the health, safety, safety and working hours of the employees, employment of young persons and employment of children. The Act does not contemplate that every factory must have a building, and necessary permission for its construction or extension is to be obtained. Of course, every factory has a site and previous permission of the State Govt. or the Chief Inspector may be necessary before the site is to he used for purposes of a Factory. (iv) The appellant 's Salt Works do come within section 2 (m). The word factory " in cl. 3(m), includes premises and buildings on land, and buildings thereon; the subject matter of the controversy in the case was not the same as that of the Salt Works.

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State of Mysore in 1935 as Instructor of Tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions.
