In 1949, three occupational Institutes (Polytechnics) at Hassan Devangere and Chintamani were started in the State. The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangre. He joined duty there on December 1, 1949. On December 1. 1949, he was again posted on deputation as Instructor in Tailoring. In 1955, for no fault of the respondent, the Government passed orders reverting him to his parent department. The period between his reversion and reposting to the Polytechnics was treated as leave. On the re organisation of States with effect from November 28, 1949, the respondent was again transferred on deputation in that Department. In 1953, he joined duty on December I, 1949 and was absorbed in that department by Government in consultation with the Public Service Commission. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Services Commission who examined it and by a communication, dated February 2, 1960, made these recommendations in favour of the Respondent. The Government did not accept the representation. On April 21, 1965, the State Government issued a notification whereby the promotions of the respondents therein were given effect from that date irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions. But by a subsequent notification dated May 17, 1950, the government directed that the promotions should be related back to 1949 and he be given the benefit of the revisions of pay scale including weightage benefit. The appellant challenged this order before the High Court contending that (i) the absorption of K. N. Chetty and five others, with effect on November 28 was not justified; (ii) the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in the service or the Department; and (iii) the promotion of K as Assistant Engineers from a particular date was not made in pursuance of any principle of policy or statutory rule but was done as a matter of concession. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption should be confined back to the 1949 and that he would be entitled to all consequential benefits from such absorption including the benefit already granted to him. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that (1) K. V. Rajalakshmiah Setty vs State of M.P., ; , followed. (2) The respondent 'was not similarly situated as K.N. Chetty; and, therefore, K. S. Nathan and five other officers who were similarly situated should be absorbed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The absorption of the employees which came on deputation from another department to the polytechnics and all of them, except the respondent were absorbed permanently in the department of Technical Education with effectfrom November 28 1949. [259 B C] (b) The High court was right in holding that K. K. Chetty & five others were not similarly situate because there was a break in the respondent service with the Department for a short period in 1955 56, could not by any reckoning be treated as a break of his service.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court, complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents, filed a writ petition in this court complaining of practices indulged in through social organisations for procuring the work offered to foreign parent. The letter referred to a press report based on "empirical investigation carried out by staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "The Mail" and alleged that not only Indian children tender age are under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. The petitioner also sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies engaged by social organisation and voluntary agency engaged in offering Indian Children to adoption to Indian parents. This Court issued notice to the Union of India, the Indian Council of Child Welfare and the Indian Councils of Social Welfare, to appear in answer to the writ petition and assist the Court in laying down principles and norms which should be followed in determining whether a child should be allowed to be adopted by foreign parents and if so, the procedure to be followed for that purpose, with the object of ensuring the welfare of the child. The Indian Council has in most cases where an application is made by a foreign parent for being appointed guardian of a child in adoption, and such application should be processed only through a social welfare agency or recognised by the Government of India or the State in which it is operating, or to put it differently in the language used by the Indian council of Social welfare or the Indian Miss Welfare or the American Council for Child Welfare or any other recognised social welfare agencies to which notice is issued, prepares what may conveniently be described as a child study report and submits it to the Court for its consideration. Ordinarily an adoption proposal from foreign parent is sponsored by a social or child welfare agency recognised or recognised or approved by the government of India.

The appellant company was a Company. The workmen received the bonus at 108 rate of 13.51% and demanded payment of bonus at the maximum rate of 20% as provided in the Act. In respect of the year 1965 66, the company claimed that this amount represented 13 51% of the available surplus and claimed payment of Bonus at the rate of 12.51%. The workmen also claimed a return at 6% on the gross profits shown in its profit and loss account. The Company contended before the Tribunal that the allocable surplus had not been properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit and Loss account as expenditure had to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. The Tribunal accepted the evidence of the Unions and held that such payment was not an item which could be deducted from the gross profit under the Act as claimed by the management. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the amount of bonus payable to the workmen of the Indian Cable Company Limited for the accounting year 196566 should be added to arrive on the actual profits and deducting therefrom the prior charges under section 6 and 7 of the Act, but not the bonus payable for the year 1964 65. The company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended that the Tribunal had committed an error in law corrupting direct tax after deducting bonus. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was justified in adding back the amount to gross profits as per the profit & loss account and the provision made for payment of compensation to workmen was prematurely retired, namely, ex gratia payment equal to retrenchment compensation under section 25 of the Industrial Disputes Act. [114B] (ii) The claim for re allowance on set off was not justified because the company had already declared and paid Rs. 14,22,922 representing 13.50% of its total salary or wages. Therefore, the balance amount that the Company will have to pay by way of bonus to make up the 14.02%, as stated above, is Rs. 53,714.19%. [114C] (iii) The company had not furnished the requisite particulars. The Unions had also furnished interrogatories requiring the Company to furnish certain particulars. Therefore the recomputation of available surplus will have been made after making a calculation of direct tax without deducting bonus payable.

The appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on July 7, 1975. He was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28,1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d). His Service Book shows that he had an excellent record of service. But there was one dark spot. In 1969 when he was working as Commercial Tax officer in 1957, the next higher post of Member of Sales Tax Tribunal was abolished and his services were terminated by the Board of Revenue. The appellant challenged the order of termination before the High Court which allowed the petition holding that the said charges could be dropped. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored once he is promoted. Sometimes past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, it is indeed odd to retire a Government Servant after promoting him to a Selection post. In the instant case, the appellant was not at all entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, one might hark back to similar or similar entries in the past, read them together in all the past. [771C D] 2. The Government was entitled to consider the entire background of the appel lant including that of part of the same which was earlier before his promotion. But, with nothing of the sort, it was indeed odd that retire a government servant after promoting he to a selection post. If there was some entry not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion one might help to assessment present conduct.[771E] 3. When there is no doubt about the wisdom on the promotion of the ap pellant, the Government cannot be allowed to digging into the past and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit government service. [81B C] 4. The fact that the appellant has been promoted as a Deputy Commissioner in 1968 does not mean that the previous history should have been completely ignored. When the appellant is promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1962, he was promoted to a post. After his promotion as Deputy Commis sioner there was no entry in the service Book to show something adverse to the appe lant apart from the 1969 entry. All that we could find was some stray mildly deprecating entries such as the one in 1964 which said: "He is sincere and hard working". He exercises adequate control over subordinates. He exercises sufficient control over subordinate subordinates. [80C E] 5. The earlier history of Government servant must be completely overlooked once he was promotion. Sometimes, past events might help assess present day to assess conduct. but when there was nothing in this present conduct cast any doubt about his wisdom of promotion, the decision of the Government retiring him from service is not at least favourable to him after his promo tion. [79F] 6. The order of the High court retiring the appellant from service was quashed. The effect of the order was that the charges should be dropped and that all the charges framed against the appellant except for a minor penalty were nowhere noted in the personal file of the de ceased Government servant.

The appellants who were the owners of motor transport vehicles in certain areas in the Kumool District of Andhra Pradesh filed petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of three schemes framed under Chapter IV A of the national , nationalising motor transport in certain area in the Kurnool District. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the provisions of the schemes were not ultra vires and void as they contravened article 19(1) (g) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The scheme was not violative of section 68 C of the , because it was not in fact framed by the Corporation but was made with a view to cause prejudice or in the hope that whether they have basis in fact or not some of them at least stick might be with the same particularity with which they had been made. [319 F G] (ii) The schemes were framed under section 68C of the Act and the rules made thereunder were duly approved by the Government. The scheme did not contravene article 19 (1)(g). It was not therefore open to the Corporation to make a grievance that it was in fact prepared and published by the Chief Minister. [353 C] Dosa Satyanarayanamurty etc. vs State of Andhra pradesh, ; , followed. (iii) The provisions of sections 46 and 48 of the were not violative Of article 19 of the constitution. They had to be quashed as not warranted by law. When the judgment in the above appeals was pronounced on January 27, 1964 the learned Advocate General represented that the scheme was taken as a result of the opinion formed by them after an examination of the entire question. It was also contended that the schemes which were published by it were not in conformity with section 68 D(3) of Act and that the approval by the Transport Minister must be held to be vitiated by mala fides of the Chief Secretary. [354 C] (iv) The High Courts have rightly held that there was no proof that the Transport Department acted merely as the tool of the chief Minister in order to carry out his behest, and it was asserted that the decision to frame the schemes was taken by the authority concerned after an examining the entire matter. It is not correct to say that the Government had no power under section 69 C to issue a permit by reason of section 63F(1). [354 D] (v) The policy to give directions as to policy to the corporation is one which would be comprehended by section 68 F(1), but there is some other authority which functions as the Regional Transport Authority for the purposes of the article, such an authority might be that which would he comprehended by s.68F(l). [355 G] Dososa Satyanarayanaamurtry etc.v. State of Madras, ; and Dosa Venkataraya namy etc., vs The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, ; referred to.

The appellant was a public limited company registered under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The appellant was assessed to sales tax for the assessment year ending 31st December 1954 in respect of its return. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii), the appellant had to furnish declaration forms duly filled and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry, the Commercial Tax Officer made an order disallowing the claim for exemption in respect Of the said sales made to the purchasing registered dealers amounting to Rs. 22,46,006 6 and levied on them additional tax of Rs. 1,49,778 4 6. The assessee thereafter filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Calcutta for issuing an order directing the respondents to issue duplicate declaration forms but that application was rejected. The High Court held that the clear terms of the clause read with the proviso imposed a condition on a dealer for claiming exemption thereunder and that the conditions imposed by the said sub cl.(ii) alone were complied with, and that in any case, the department had failed to produce the relevant documents to establish that the declaration forms alleged to have been lost were in fact issued by them. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The proviso cannot be construed as laying down a condition for giving exemption but only as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way. If so construed, a dealer is not precluded in a case where the authority concerned is empowered to take evidence in respect thereof any particular matter; but that does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemption. [631 B C] (2) The object of section 5 (2)(b)(ii) of the Act and the rules made thereunder is self evident. While they are obviously intended to give exemption to a dealer in respect o sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks to prevent fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax. In the nature of things, in view of innumerable transactions that may be entered into between dealers it will wellnigh be impossible for the taxing authorities to ascertain in each case whether a dealer has sold the specified goods to another for the purposes mentioned in the section. Therefore presumably to achieve the twofold object namely prevention of fraud and facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the prescribed manner. [ 630 E F] (3) The provision prescribing the exemption must be strictly construed. The substantive clause gives the exemption and the proviso qualifies the substantive clause. In effect the proviso says that part of the turnover of the selling dealer covered by the terms of sub cl. (ii) will be exempted provided a declaration in the form prescribed is furnished. To put it in other words, a person cannot get the exemption unless he furnishes the declaration in prescribed form.

The petitioner, a prisoner in the State of Bihar, was convicted for offences under sections 395 and major offences by the Sessions Judge, Patna. He was sentenced to death on the ground that he had been in jail for over six years and was not in jail since then. The petitioner contended that his detention was illegal and in violation of his constitutional obligation under article 21 of the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or liberty except in accordance with the procedure established by law, it is not enough that there should be some semblance of procedure provided by law but the procedure unnder which a person may be deprived from his life and liberty should be reasonable, fair and just. (ii) Article 22(1) provides that any person shall not be deprived 'of his life nor liberty except according to the procedure prescribed by law. The right of free legal services is, therefore, clearly an essential ingredient of "reasonable, fair, just and just procedure" guaranteed by article 21. This is a constitutional right of every accused person who is unable to engage a lawyer and secure legal services on account of reasons such as poverty, indigence or incommunicado situation and the State is under a mandate to provide a lawyer to an accused person if the circumstances of the case and the circumstances require of justice so required. (iii) Article 31A provides that "no person shall he deprived of any life or personal liberty except, in accordance, with the provisions established by Law, it was not enough, that there must be some imblance or procedure provided for law but that the procedure which does not make available legal services to an assessee person who was too poor to afford a lawyer would apprise them of their right to apply for bail and help them to secure release on bail. (iv) Article 39A is the constitutional obligation of every person accused who is able to engage lawyer and obtain legal services from the institutions run by the welfare department. The State cannot avoid its constitutional obligation to provide speedy trial to the accused by pleading financial or administrative inabiltiy. The power of this Court under article 32 of the constitution is of the widest amplitude and it does not mean that there can be some limitations on procedure provided in law but those which are unmoved by such enormous misery and suffering resulting from totally unjustified deprivation of personal liberty. (v) Article 19(1)(g) provides for free legal aid to the poor and the needy is an essential element of fair procedure. The Court should consider the individual factors peculiar to each case. These factors are peculiar to the each case and it would be most difficult to anticipate. One relevant factor would be the competency of the individual defendent to present his own case. (vi) Article 14 provides that when article 21 provides for a person shall have the right to be heard by counsel, he is not guilty, though he has a perfect one. He requires the guiding hand of counsel at every step in the proceedings against him. Without it, although he has good reason and reffection with the rules of evidence. (vii) Article 38A provides for an absolute legal service programme to provide free legal service to the person accused if the circumstance of the ease and the facts of the cases are pending investigation by the police in each sub division of the State as on 31st December, 1978 and where such cases have been pending for more than six months, the State may provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application to the Magistrate in that behalf. Sometimes the Magistrates also refuse to release the undertrial prisoners produced before them on their personal bond but insist on monetary bail with sureties, by which reason of their poverty they are unable to furnish bail.

The appellant was the landlord and the respondent a protected tenant. The respondent filed an application under section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application on the ground that the provisions of section 34(1 A) were not applicable to the present proceedings. On appeal by special leave the appellant contended that the provision of section 33(2 A) should have been taken into consideration by the Revenue Courts in deciding the application of the landlord under section 30(2). Held, that the date on which the tenancy terminates must be the date of the notice or the date thereof and not the date when the right to terminate the tenancy accrued. The Amending Act did not affect any vested right of the landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the period of notice. Consequently, the provisions Of section 34 (1 A), which were in accordance with the previous law ineffective, could not be applied to the proceedings under that section. The date on the right was to terminate a tenancy and no further proceedings may be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof. It is only when the period has expired and the tenancy has terminated that the landlord acquires a vested right to obtain possession of land. Therefore, the Amending Act does not affect the vested right which the appellant had under section 34. The notice under section 33 (1) was merely a declaration to the tenant of the premises to terminate his tenancy and did not speak of any notice at all.

The petitioners were the sons of Khadim Ali who had never been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian under section 8 of the , as they had not been declared evacuees and their properties were evacuee property. Held, that the acts of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. The acts of Custodian in sofar as they deprived the petitioners ' property cannot he upheld. Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, (1910) L.R. 57 I.A. 222, followed. Ebbrahim Abubaker vs Khemchand Dolka, (1932) L R. 57 1. A. 222 and Ebazrahim Abaker vs Dolkwani, , referred to. The act of the evacuee in so doing was not a patty to the proceeding in which the order in dispute had been made. Strictly speaking no appeal lay against that order or was necessary. There was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting such knew Ali 's right in the house and the petitioners could not be held entitled to any relief under section 7 of the Act. Eabrahim Abobaker vs GHolwani (1911) L, R. 61 I. A., approved.

The assessee company was running at a constant loss as a result of which it had to raise a lorn of several lakhs of rupees from the Industrial Finance Corporation. Before expiry of this agreement, another agreement was entered into by the assessee Company with the agents on October 20, 1955 under which the agents were to get 6% interest on all the advances made by them, 1% commission on net sales and 50% commission at net sales. The selling agents M/s Saligram Premnath advanced a sum of Rs. 6,26,847/ and Rs. 871,873/ as 50% on net sale and 50 % commission on the net sales of the worsted plant in the course of two years, namely assessment years 195 to 57 ending on March 31, 1957 and 58 ending on April 31,1957. The assessee company accordingly filed its return for the year 1956 57 claiming the amount of Rs 37,157/ and RS. 73,787/ as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim but held that the deductions claimed were actually a division of profits after the profits had come into existence and had been ascertained, and therefore could not be claimed as a valid deduction under the provisions of the Act. On appeal by the Revenue, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner accepted the plea of the assessee company and held that it was a permissible deduction as it was incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The High Court in reversing the order of the Tribunal relied on certain materials which were not at all found by the Tribunal in its order nor were those materials mentioned in the statement of case. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The agreement between the parties was a sort of a partnership or a joint venture rather than a contract of agency. It is well settled that the Court in order to construe an agreement has to look to the substance or the essence of it rather than to its form. In these circumstances, if we construe the agreement as a sort or a Joint venture rather as a contract or a transaction like a partnership which has been given the form and appearance of a contract, or appearance of the contract of Agency, the law must have its course. [192 D E] (2) The High Courts were not right in holding that the transactions did not amount to a joint contract or an integrated venture with a view to division of profit. The test merely means that the court will place itself in the position of a businessman and find out whether the expenses incurred could be said to have been laid out for the purposes of business, profession or vocation. [195 A B] (3) In order to determine whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out, for the pur pose of the commercial expediency would have to be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not of the income Tax Department. It must be borne in mind that in order that a person contributes to some sort of joint venture which ultimately results in division of Profits, it could not he construed as a remuneration for services. [196 C D] (4) The fact that the agents agreed to finance the business of the company on the terms set out in the agreement and there was nothing to show that they could have made any better arrangements or would have been the intention of the parties as spelt out from the terms of the agreement or the surrounding circumstances, the nature or character of the trade or venture, the purpose for which the expenses are incurred and the object which is sought to be achieved for incurring those expenses.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income Tax Officer, after considering the accounts of the company as on March 31, 1958, determined a sum of Rs. 36,546.17 p. as dividend under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. In appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount was not liable to be taxed as "dividend" under section2(6 A)(e). The Tribunal also upheld the claim of the assessee that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not be construed as including current profits for the purpose of section 2. In the reference application filed by the Commissioner of Income Tax, the High Court held that Rs. 18,950 constituted accumulated profits for a purpose of Section 2( 6A)(a) and therefore computed a sum as dividend. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The amount was worked out on the basis that a sum in excess of Rs., 10,000 was paid as dividend by the company during the year in which the loans were advanced to the assessee. In fact, the Tribunal has overruled the objection, relying on Girdhardas & Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Gujarat II, Ahmedabad and Commissioner of Gift Tax, Bombay vs P. K. Badiani, , followed. (ii) The High Court was right in answering the first question in favour of the asses see. [950 A] (iii) In the instant case, the question whether the provision for payment of tax and dividend can be taken into account when computing the accumulated profits as on 31st March 1958 is not relate to the question of whether accumulated profits can take in current profits. The two questions involve the grant of separate and distinct reliefs and the decision on one question does not affect the decision of one question.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan. He held that as the defendants and their predecessors had been in possession of the lands for over 200 years, he was entitled to fair rent. The respondents filed suits against the appellant on the grounds inter alia (1) that the suit lands were not Mal lands comprised within Mouza Nala in Thouzi No. 1 which was comprised in the permanently settled estate of Burdwan and were Mal assessed to revenue; and (2) that as there had been a permanent Mokarrari grant made prior to the permanent settlement, neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them, and the entries in the record of rights published during 1931 showed that the lands were included as Malli lands within the zamindari of Burdwan. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the suits were within time under article 131 of the Limitation Act. The question whether a presumption of lost grant could be made in favour of the predecessors of the defendants must depend on the facts found and circumstances of each case. In the present case the suit properties formed part of the Malli land or assessed lands of the estate. The High Court had held that the plaintiffs were not tenants within the Malulah but had failed to prove that they were in possession without payment of rent for a considerable time. Held further, that on the evidence found no presumption of a lost grant can be made against the predecessors in title of the defendant. The suit properties constituted part of a village Nala within the Zamindari of Burdwan, and if a grant had been made in their favour by the predecessors, they must have been made by the Maharaja of Burdwan or by the Rajgunwar Asthal. The defendants had not established any hostile title.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of agricultural land. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that the land which was the subject matter of contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 (Tenancy Act ' for short) and as the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions Of the Tenancy Acts, the same could not be specifically enforced. The plaintiff sought to repel the contention by producing a certificate granted by the Mamlatdar certifying that the plaintiff is an agriculturist and in view of the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85A and 85A of the Transfer of Property Act prohibiting him from selling the land, and therefore, the civil court had jurisdiction to decide the issue. The Trial Court held that the certificate was not valid and that the defendant was an agriculturist. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court agreed with the finding of the trial Court with regard to the validity of the certificate. In appeal by certificate, the appellant contended: (i) that if the court does not take note of the exhibit 78, an issue arises in a properly constituted civil suit which the civil Court is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of Tenancy Act and therefore opposed to public policy; (ii) that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to decide whether a person is an agriculturists within the definition of the ' Tenancy Act, 1908, was ousted by section 63, of the , as it then stood, did not ipso facto oust the jurisdiction, of civil court to decide that issue if it arises before it in a civil suit; (iii) that even when a properly instituted suit is brought to the Civil court having jurisdiction to try it, it will have to frame the issue and refer it to the Mamlatdar and on the reference being answered back, to dispose of the suit in accordance with the decision recorded by the competent authority on the relevant issue. HELD: (1) The civil court would be competent to decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the authority under the Tenancy act. [592D] (2) The jurisdiction of Civil Court is ousted under section 85A. [593E] (3) The Civil Court has no jurisdiction to hear or deal in a matter which is not required to he decided or disposed of by the authorities mentioned therein and in this specific case the authority would be the Mamlatdar as provided in section 85 A. [594F G] (4) The High Court was wrong in clutching at a jurisdiction which did not vest in them and, consequently, on this ground alone it was competent to deal with the same. That question arose in the suit from which the present appeal arises.

The assessee, a heavy engineer ing concern manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. for the purpose of producing and articles for the four assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 claimed exemption under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 on the profits and gains derived from its steel plant and machinery. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the steel Foundry and the Jute Mill Division were an industrial undertaking to which section 15 C of the Act applied. The Tribunal accepted the claim for exemption under s.15C but rejected the claim. In appeal by certificate, the High Court held that though the two undertakings were not entitled to exemption under sec tion 15C(2) (i), only excluded three categories of industrial undertakings from the benefit of section 15D(2)(i). The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the two industrial undertakings, namely, the Steel Foundry & the Jute Mills Division were not formed by the reconstruction of the business already in existence. [776 B] 2. The word 'reconstruction ' is not defined in the Act but has received judicial interpretation. In order to deny the benefit under section15C, the new undertaking must be formed by recon struction of the old business. [771 C D] 3. The concept of reconstruction of business would not be attracted when a company which is already running one industrial unit sets up another industrial unit. The new undertaking should not be substantially the same existing business. The earlier undertakings are independently producing arti tions which may be of aid to the principal business but yet the undertakings are distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business of the assessee. Use by the assessee of the articles produced in its existing business would amount to starting of a new industrial undertaking on account of which exemption of tax under section 14C could be claimed. [764 D E] 4. The scheme of section15 C is an exemption section and not a conditional one. It is only when assets of the new industrial undertakings are separate and independent production units in the sense that new plants and machin ery are erected for producing either the same commodities or some distinct commodities. In the instant case, once the new Industrial Undertakings are separate, independent and independent produce units in that sense that the commodities produced or the results are commercially tangible products and the undertakings can be carried on separately without complete absorption and losing their identity in the old ties, they are not to be treated as being formed by reconstruction of old business.[776 E F] 5. The assessee claimed profit and there was no difficulty about ascertainment of the exempted profit as separate books of accounts were kept and the undertaking were at separate places. In view of the foregoing discussion, the assessee 's main business is of heavy engineering in the course of which it manufactures boilers, wagons, etc.

The inam lands were granted by the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926. The Inam grants were confirmed by the British Government and the inam lands resumed under section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowment Act, 1927. In 1939, the inam grant was made to the temple in which the inam was being enjoyed by the inamdars. The inam lands continued to be in possession of the inamdar till 1946 when the Inam was granted. On October 17, 1947, the Inam Commissioner passed an order under section 43 B(2)(d)(ii) asking for a decree declaring that the inam grants consisted of the melwaram only. The High Court dismissed the appeal and held that the inams were personal inams burdened with services and the order of resumption was therefore illegal and a nullity. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The inams were granted to the holders of hereditary offices as remuneration for services to be rendered by them in connection with the temple. There is a well recognised distinction between the grant of land burdened with a condition of service and the grant or of land as remuneration. [547 B C] (ii) The inam grants were not personal inams. They were granted on the footing that the Inamdars were entitled to the kudiwaram rights either against the inamdaridars or against Government. The lands were being enjoyed for services rendered by the Inamdar and were granted as inams. The inams originally granted, to the inam holders of the inams stood determined. [548 C D] (iii) The Inam grant was not a lease for a term exceeding 5 years howsoever long the lessee might have continued in possession. The words "has failed" in sub section (2)(a)(ii), and the words "had failed" are not qualified by the requisites of the Act. [549 E F] In the present case, the inams in the present ease were resumable under section 4 B(1)(a) (i). The inam grant did not comprise the kudwaram lands.

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by section 79(1) of the Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax at the rate of 7% of the gross annual letting value of the houses and the trustees duly paid such tax. After the formation of the State of Madhya Bharat, the legislature of that State passed the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1954 which came into force on January 26, 1954. The Indore Municipal Act was repealed by the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act,, 1954. Section 79(2) provided that in assessing the tax on buildings or lands, where the valuation determined under section (d) of sub section 1 is the annual letting price, a sum equal to 10% of such letting value shall be deducted therefrom in lieu of allowance for costs of repairs or any other account whatsoever. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of the levy on the ground that the excess amount was illegally recovered and the High Court dismissed it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The tax imposed on the basis of the ' gross annual rent value ' is obviously inconsistent with section 73(2). It follows that the appellant Corporation could do so because the rules made under the Indore Act are no doubt amongst other things saved and are deemed to have been made, framed or imposed under the new Act. [129 D] (ii) The appellant was entitled to adopt the assessment list prepared for the year 1952 53 for the two assessment years, 1953 54 and 1954 55. Under sections 75 and 76 of the Madhya. Municipalities Act the municipality has to prepare a fresh assessment list every year. It is not necessary that the Municipality should prepare a new assessment list once in every 4 years and can adopt an earlier assessment list only once in each 4 years. [131 E] (iii) The word 'if ' appearing in sub section (2) of section 79 means "as if" because the word "if" as used by itself makes no sense at all. 79 therefore has to be construed to mean that though a Municipality need not prepare a separate assessment list each year and need prepare such list once every 4 year and can adopting an earlier assess list every 4 months.

The assessee company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring rubber estates and for developing them. The Company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the sale of chemicals were also resulted in a substantial profit. Meanwhile, the assessment of the company for the year account ending April 31, 1944 bad been completed by the Deputy Commissioner of Income tax and the assessee company had been assessed on an income of Rs. 36,498 6. The Deputy Commissioner however reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,259. Before the Commissioner the Liquidator admitted that the profit from the sales of chemicals was Rs.1,15260 on the sale and that the stock of raw material was not sold in the course of ordinary trading but in a reali sation sale after the company had already been wound up. The High Court held that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business and that thus the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount obtained by way of realisation sale was properly brought to tax as a trading profits and not as a business profit, which was liable to assessment. HELD : (i) The High court was right in holding that there could be no doubt that the chemicals and raw materials were sold in ordinary course of business or that the assessee Company was carrying on a trading busi ness. The fact that the company was keeping the factory not on its own behalf but entirely on behalf Of the buyer would not by itself make any difference because the agreement clearly indicated that the Company was keeping its factory going, not on their own behalf and entirely on the behalf of buyer. [968 C D] (ii) The fact of a man cannot be considered as determining what it is that his acts amounted to a trading which would cause the profits that accrued to him from a trade or business. The case was therefore decided on the finding of the special Commissioners, for which there was enough material in evidence. [ 969 D E] (iii) The mere fact that a sale of the chemicals was not an act of trading does not make any distinction between a sale and a sale. It may well be accepted that they did so intend but yet the intention of a person cannot be judged as determining which it is to say, the price without the chemicals or raw materials and the price with them.
